 EASTON - The Talbot County Council will hold public hearings for three related pieces of legislation concerning the Lakeside at Trappe development on Tuesday, Oct. 24, at 6:30 p.m.The three resolutions all propose amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan as it relates to Lakeside.Resolution 338, introduced by council member Lynn Mielke in late February, would incorporate the provisions of the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant into the county's comprehensive plan.The resolution would mandate that any future expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.According to County Attorney Patrick Thomas, the resolution went before the county's public works advisory board in the spring, but did not yet go to the Planning Commission.Mielke had expressed interest in having a second public hearing for the resolution so the community could have both the public works advisory board and Planning Commission recommendations prior to speaking, Thomas said.Resolutions 347 and 348, introduced at the Sept. 12 meeting, address updated information on equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside development, along with clarifying Trappe's water and sewer service maps.The two resolutions were initially scheduled for public hearings at the council's first October meeting, but council members said Tuesday it made sense to schedule them to be heard all together.The Talbot County Planning Commission will consider and make a recommendation on all three resolutions at its Wednesday, Oct. 4 meeting. title: Oxford Uncovers Investment Policy - Policy Was Not Considered by Commission in Recent Votes on Investment Changes
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford uncovers investment policy - Policy was not considered by commission in recent votes on investment changes

 September 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - Unknown to current town officials and commissioners, Oxford has had a financial investment policy in place since the 1990s."In the 90s, the state of Maryland asked all municipalities in the state to create an investment policy and file it with them," Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said during a commissioners meeting Tuesday.Lewis said she had not been made aware of this policy when she was hired. She said she didn't believe the commissioners at the time she was hired, nor the person whose role she replaced, knew of the policy."The policy, I assume was written and filed away in the archives," she said. "That seems to be where it was at."Commissioner Katrina Greer said that when she emailed Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan last week to ask if an investment policy existed, Ryan said the policy had not been attached to the ordinance it was supposed to be attached to."I'm embarrassed for us and for Cheryl that we didn't know about it," Greer said during the meeting. "And so we are in the unfortunate position as commissioners and as a manager of not being in compliance with our own law. So this is serious, and I apologize and we will all apologize to you for that."In a text message Wednesday, Greer said it was "unacceptable" for town administration to say they did not know about the policy."Knowing the town laws and comporting with them is the primary function of an administrator," she said. "This is deeply concerning that a highly compensated long-term employee did not know about a town investment policy."During the town meeting, Lewis said that after learning about the policy, she created an updated version."So I've provided you with a resolution and then also [the original] investment policy," she said. "This is just being provided for this evening. This is not something that I expect anybody to act on."Lewis said she took the state's recommendations and spoke with Talbot County's finance manager to create the updated policy.Lewis listed three sections of the original policy that are "unique to Oxford," which commissioners could consider changing if they desired to.One section states that each commissioners and the clerk treasurer must disclose "any substantial personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County."Another section states that no more than half of the town's investment should be in a stable financial institution. Lewis said that other municipalities didn't necessarily state this the same way.The last section Lewis mentioned states that the length of maturity on an investment should not exceed one year."Obviously, which many people in the room are aware of, we did not follow these as they were written because it's pretty hard to follow a policy that you don't know exists," Lewis said.While the town has one certificate of deposit that is longer than 12 months, Lewis said it is in compliance with the section that states no more than half of investments should be in a financial institution.At the previous town meeting Sept. 12, the commissioners voted to temporarily move $2 million from an account with BayVanguard Bank to the investment bank, Maryland Local Government Investment Pool, until Lewis could come back with a report on alternative investment options.During the most recent meeting, Lewis reported on her review of three banks: BayVanguard Bank, Shore United Bank and Queenstown Bank. No decision has been made yet on where to keep that $2 million.After Lewis shared information on the investment policy and possible update, Greer said she wanted to wait before any action is taken."We are going to fix it," she said. "But we don't want to act hastily."Greer added that she feels a finance advisory committee is necessary so that the town can make "sound judgements" about its investments.In response to this, Commissioner Susan Delean-Bot-kin brought up the importance of having a paid adviser."They don't have the same responsibility if we are not paying them," she said. "They do not have the same fiduciary responsibility to the town. And that is very important for us to think about."Earlier in the meeting, Greer asked to discuss a draft resolution to create a financial advisory committee, which she drafted for the consideration of the commissioners."The idea is to advise the commission so that they may instruct the town administrator on the best options for investments," Greer said.Committee members would be required to have certain certifications, Greer said."This would be a very high-level, high-functioning committee and there are people here in town that have those certifications," she said.Delean-Botkin said she thinks the draft resolution should be discussed, but said it was not on the agenda for the meeting."You're trying to move through a resolution that none of us have seen," Delean-Bot-kin said. "I would like to stick to the agenda."Greer said she didn't expect the resolution to be voted on at the meeting and said she had sent a memo to the commissioners and Lewis to put it on the agenda.Commission President Tom Costigan said he would like time to reflect on the draft resolution."I would also like some time for our town attorney to review it and give us an opinion on it as well," he said. "And then we can revisit it at our next date."Later in the meeting, Ryan said that if the commissioners vote in favor of creating a committee, they might consider having the committee review the financial investment policy yearly."So that the policy is constantly being refreshed within the town government," she said.

title: Plan Starts in October to Protect Strand Beach - Focus - Talbot Towns
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Plan starts in October to protect Strand Beach - FOCUS - Talbot Towns

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News

 OXFORD - During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis gave an update on the Strand Beach project.The project, which was approved in April 2021, is intended to improve the beach shoreline.Lewis said she the project should begin Oct. 15, "give or take a day or two."The project will be completed in two phases, Lewis said. The first phase will take place in the water and on the beach. The second phase will be for the "above ground work.""The paving, the parking lot, that sort of thing," Lewis said.Lewis expects the first phase to be complete before the holidays and the second phase to be complete after the holidays, before spring. She said it will hopefully be completed in a six months."I just want to let everybody know because there will be some activity and you need to be aware of it," Lewis said. "Hopefully it won't be a huge deal because this is not the busiest time of year for that area of town."Along with the update, Lewis gave a breakdown of the project.For the beach, a berm will be created to run along the road between the road and the water. Hooks will be placed along the east and west areas of the Strand to help bring sand in, rather than erode out."The berm, the hooks, that will all be planted," Lewis said. "Typical living shoreline."Along with that, islands will be created in the water to reduce the waves that come onto the beach."Most of the time you won't even see [the islands]," Lewis said. "They'll be underwater, but they'll have grasses on them."To reduce erosion, living shorelines will also be constructed to the right of the ferry dock and behind the beach parking lot."The living shorelines are basically building up your beach," Lewis said. "Incorporating grasses that work well in the water and stabilizing the area."Lewis said the project will include reinforcing some of the areas between the parking lot and the Tred Avon Yacht Club building. These areas will be reinforced as living shorelines and incorporating a hook on the far west end of the Strand to reduce erosion.After that, Lewis said the above ground work will begin. The work will be between Norton Street and the last boatyard on the road. The road will be leveled out so that it doesn't dip down. A permeable layer will be added above the road before asphalt is laid on top of it."What that means is when we have the storm water or the flood water coming in, it will kind of sit under the road as opposed to on top, which is a problem we have now," Lewis said.The parking lot will be built with storm management areas underneath it so that storm water can enter it and be filtered before going back out."All we're really trying to do is to create a higher barrier along the north end of Oxford," Lewis said. "It will not stop flooding, per se. But it will add protection along that north end when it's hit by storms and prevent damage to our actual infrastructure."

author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commission shares top requests with Mid-Shore delegation

 October 4, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 23 | Section: News

 DENTON - The Caroline County Commission met Tuesday, Oct. 3, with five of the seven-member legislative team for state districts 36 and 37 to advance its annual "bill requests and discussion items" ahead of the 446th Maryland General Assembly Jan. 10 to April 8, 2024.The short list of priorities they asked legislators to support were:■ Providing supplemental funds for emergency medical transports.,■ Licensing for barbershops and beauty shops to allow one-site sales and consumption of alcoholic beverages under restricted circumstances.■ Allowing liquor-tasting and sampling in the county in addition to wine and beer tasting.■ Continuing local funding of legislative bond initiatives.■ Devising a better method of assessing electric vehicle use instead of imposing a mileage tax.The three-member commission met with the legislators for about an hour in the Health and Public Services Building in Denton.The meeting agenda was reversed, with commissioners' unanimously approving the consent agenda shortly after the 9 a.m. start time while they waited for Del. Jeff Ghrist, R-36-Caroline, to arrive. The annual presentation of the consolidated transportation program occurred at about 10:30 a.m.Besides Ghrist, attending the annual delegation meeting were state Sen. Johnny Mautz, R-37; Del. Jay Jacobs, R-36-Kent; Del. Steve Arentz, R-36-QA; and Del. Chris Adams, R-37B. Sen. Steve Hershey, R-Upper Shore, and Del. Tom Hutchinson, R-37B, were absent.Commission Vice President Larry Porter led the discussion by describing the county's critical need for help in funding emergency medical transportation.The Emergency Service Transporter Supplemental Payment Program addresses the difference between the cost per emergency transport versus the Medicaid reimbursement rate. Providers receive a supplemental payment to make up the difference, but it's not enough to cover the actual cost.Porter pointed out that "Caroline County is a long county. It's about a two-hour turnaround time for us to pick up a patient, transport them, get them into the emergency room in Easton or Dover or Seaford, and turn around and come back."Because the "program reimburses at a higher rate, we're able to keep our revenue coming in, so that we can buy the new ambulances, new equipment," Porter said.EMS Division Chief K.J. Marvel explained that Caroline County reimbursement for ambulance transportation per Medicaid patient is increasing from a $100 to $150. She said she was worried about the lack of clarity in the expiration date of the grant program, which was originally set to expire in 2025.ESPP is a federal program sponsored through the Maryland Department of Health, Marvel said. "It's actually been very beneficial for us because we have a lot of Medicaid transports with our population here," she said.Private insurance companies and Medicare pay the rate established by the Maryland health care system."It's very important to us," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "We do not have an emergency room in the county."Medicaid does not pay for transportation to urgent care or Choptank Community Health, nor for transportation back home from an emergency room, so county EMS ambulances and drivers must transport patients to hospitals and, often, back home.Marvel and Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox told the delegation the county is not looking for an increase in funding, but a continuation of the program.The financial benefit was $723,000 last year, Marvel said. Fox said losing those funds would be "devastating.""That's what? Two, three ambulances," Breeding said.He said the commission wanted to make sure "that our federal representation understands how important it is, and then also make sure that the state continues to have the regulatory and the grant writing structure in place to pass that funding through."The commissioners put forward requests to make three changes in the county liquor code, as recommended by the Caroline County Liquor Board. Assistant Director of Codes Crystal Dadds explained the requests.The board recommends allowing hair salons and barbershop to provide one 5-ounce glass of wine or 12-ounce beer per customer during a hair appointment, if the business were approved for an annual license fee of $100.Two other changes in the liquor code were proposed. Currently, beer and wine tastings and samplings are allowed in the county, but not the tasting and sampling of spirits. The number of two-ounce drinks per day for sampling would increase from six to nine to accommodate the typical number of three-sample flights.The commissioners requested support from the delegation for the Rural Maryland Council for fiscal year 2025. The state council, supported by the MidShore Regional Council, is requesting $9 million for rural development and projects. The funding request remains unchanged from fiscal year 2023.Though not included in the published bill requests, the commissioners voiced their concern about a proposed state mileage tax that would "disproportionately hurt rural residents because we travel more, and residents who travel in other states," Ghrist said.He said the state is "trying to figure out how to capture a use tax for EVs, but that's not the answer." Rather, "the better answer would be a titling tax when somebody purchases an electric vehicle.""Well, I think each day we find unintended consequences of this green energy agenda," Porter said. "Whether it's danger to our firefighters and first responders or the reduction in Highway User Funds, I think it went from $4 million to $400,000. This is just another unintended consequence of this ridiculous mess."A discussion about rural transportation needs, infrastructure needs and costs, and differences between urban and suburban versus rural mobility ensued."Something to keep in mind is, no matter what they do with EVs, as far as how we address that issue, they're still heavily subsidized," Arentz said. "The poor are the ones who are really going to get hammered by this. And we are not wealthy counties."Adams said the talk of a new tax prompted a blip on his wristwatch heart monitor. A politician who would even try to propose a new tax "with a recession coming on and inflation going through the roof" would have to put forth a convincing argument, he suggested."You can expect every person sitting at the table who represents Caroline County to push back and push back hard when it comes to raising taxes," Adams said."We need to be mindful of the economy on Main Street, not just on Wall Street," Mautz said.

title: Planning Commission Debates Resolutions on Lakeside Development
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Planning Commission debates resolutions on Lakeside development

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1198
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON-A multihour meeting of the Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday tackled a trio of comprehensive water and sewer plan amendments relating to the Lakeside at Trappe development, concluding with one finding of inconsistency and two postponements.The benches in the Bradley Meeting Room were packed as the five-member planning commission mulled numerous public comments on the three resolutions proposed by the Talbot County Council over the last several months.Because the legislation amends the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan, the council sought recommendations on Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 from the public works advisory board and the planning commission. The council's own public hearings on the resolutions are scheduled for its Oct. 24 meeting.Over a dozen letters commenting on the three resolutions were submitted to the planning commission prior to Wednesday's meeting, with more comments unfolding over the course of the morning.Concerns with the long-contested development centered on Lakeside's size, the capacity of its new wastewater treatment plant, negative environmental impacts, preservation of Talbot County's rural character and Trappe's sewer service maps. Planning commissioners raised their own contentions with the resolutions as well.RESOLUTION 338Introduced in late February by Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke, the resolution would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.The resolution would mandate that any future expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.The discharge permit, issued last October, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit (EDU), allowing only 400 residential units to be built.But according to the development's attorney Ryan Showalter, who testified at Thursday's meeting, the 250 gallon per day flow is a presumed flow for initial allocation of capacity and treatment. Once the plant is operational, the 100,000 gallon capacity is more likely to serve 500 to 600 houses, he said.A total of 2,501 residences are planned for the development.Showalter expressed opposition to the requirement for the developer to come back before the county for future expansion."The developer understands the requirement to go through a major permit modification; that process involves public hearings, public input, the County Council certainly can weigh in and comment on that, but the notion that every time the Lakeside wastewater treatment plant is required to expand, (and) should come back before the county for a water and sewer plan amendment-which is maybe another four-year process - is not acceptable to the developer," he said, adding: "We would not oppose 338 if that sentence was stricken."Alan Girard, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation's Eastern Shore director, said the nonprofit was supportive of the resolution's intent, but questions remained as to whether the intent could be achieved as it related to the timing of development criteria."The resolution rightly requires an amendment to the sewer plan when a major permit modification is sought, but it's mostly silent on other timing key elements, like the sewer service area maps, the 540,000 gallon per day discharge quantity and phasing, the automatic change to 'immediate priority service status' when the land is annexed," he said. "These timing elements are significant because they're linked to the major concerns the public has with this project."Girard urged the Planning Commission to work with the County Council to ensure the legislation's full intent was realized by updating the sewer service classifications in ways that best serve the community and environmental health.Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's town attorney, raised similar concerns to those voiced by Showalter."The town feels that this is overly cumbersome and would impede their ability to smartly manage growth and orderly provide adequate public facilities for development within the Town of Trappe," she said.RESOLUTION 347Resolution 347, introduced on Sept. 12, was spurred by MDE's request for the number of equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside development.The legislation provides the number of EDUs - 2,874 in total -for all six phases of the development, though the numbers for Phases 2 through 6 are estimated. The legislation includes the current water and sewer classifications.Points of concern voiced by members of the public centered on confusion with timing of the phases and water and sewer classifications for each phase.Ryan, again speaking for the Town of Trappe, said she thought there was a lot of misunderstanding about phases and planning of phases. The town never intended to require that each phase be developed before moving to a later phase; the phases were not intended to be sequential, she said.Ryan also confirmed that 81 residential units within Lakeside are being served and are connected to Trappe's existing wastewater treatment plant.On Monday, the county's public works advisory board voted 5-0 to recommend that the resolution not be adopted as written.RESOLUTION 348Resolution 348, introduced Sept. 12, was also drafted in response to MDE's request for clarification on Trappe's water and sewer service maps. The legislation addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside under a draft discharge permit.The parcels that were incorrectly shown on the exhibits are unrelated to Resolution 281. The parcels' classifications were not changed, making the resolution's purpose solely to clarify and confirm the water and sewer classifications.To Easton resident Lisa Ghezzi, a former county planning commission member, the resolution signified continued confusion on Trappe's water and sewer service maps. She pointed out that the lack of updates to the county's comprehensive plan is the source of the frustration."We're just spinning our wheels, and we cannot make any decisions until everyone, staff included, knows the facts behind this," she said. "I found confusion in staff's presentation at the outset of this discussion. (The) public works advisory board raised questions earlier this week. How can we operate like this?"Talbot County resident Mike McConnel urged the Planning Commission to consider a revised sewer service map for Trappe that only identifies one small section of Lakeside as an immediate priority and to revert all other sections of the development to unprogrammed."That will mean that as Lakeside progresses, they will have to come back to the Planning Commission and establish that the consequences of the development are consistent as it goes forward," he said.The county's public works advisory board reviewed the resolution on Monday, but tabled a decision until the board's next meeting on Oct. 19.DECISIONSAfter significant back and forth, the Planning Commission voted 3-2 to find Resolution 338 inconsistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan because it refers to a map that needs to be reviewed, but the commission endorsed the idea of a phased review, per the motion made.The commission voted unanimously to postpone its determination on Resolution 347 for further discussion.As for Resolution 348, the commission also voted unanimously to postpone consideration due to ongoing uncertainty that has not been addressed.

MDOT updates Caroline leaders on project plans - Officials outline six year draft budget, provide key project updates

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul J. Wiedefeld and other representatives of the Maryland Department of Transportation met Tuesday, Oct. 3, with Caroline County officials to discuss the department's six-year draft FY 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program.The spending plan "calls for a $21.2 billion, six-year investment to create a safer, cleaner, efficient and accessible transportation system connecting Marylanders to jobs, schools, recreation, health care and essential services," according to a MDOT press release."Delivering safe, reliable, equitable and sustainable transportation is critical to Maryland's economic health and the vibrancy of neighborhoods across the state. This draft CTP is inspired by that mission," Wiedefeld said."We know there are challenges ahead, and we are committed to fiscal responsibility and collaboration with local communities, stakeholders and elected officials as we deliver the transportation network Marylanders need and deserve," he said.In addition to Wiedefeld, officials attending included State Highway Deputy Administrator for Project Development Matt Baker; Motor Vehicle Administrator Chrissy Nizer; Maryland Transportation Authority Planning and Program Development Director Melissa Williams; Maryland Transit Administration Local Transit Support Director Travis Johnston; Maryland Aviation Administration Regional Aviation Director Ashish Solanki; and District 2 Engineer Ken Fender.At the meeting, transportation officials offered details and updates of several projects and programs affecting Caroline County.Baker said the agency is planning for potential improvements along three miles of state Route 404 from Harmony Road to Greenwood Road. A study looking at pedestrian and bicyclist safety improvements and traffic operations, as well as truck and agricultural traffic, is anticipated to be completed in spring 2024. An in-person open house meeting planned for this fall. In addition, a public survey to gather feedback on the study is available at mdot-sha-md404-harmony-rd-to-greenwood-rdco219b11-maryland.hub.arcgis.com/Baker said the State Highway Administration will advertise a $1 million contract for improvements at the state Routes 404 and 328 intersection, which will add turn lanes for safer traffic flow.Some interim improvements have been made to help reduce intersection conflicts and improve traffic flow during peak school bus times.Transportation officials noted other allocations for Caroline County in the draft CTP, including more than $1.1 million in operating and capital grants to support local transit operations provided by Delmarva Community Transit. In addition, Delmarva Community Service will receive a $123,000 Statewide Transit Innovation Grant to install a propane station for propane-powered vehicles, enabling Delmarva Community Transit to transition to a low-emission fleet.As "a charter member of the Ken Fender Fan Club," Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter thanked the District 2 engineer for his responsiveness, especially with improving traffic flow at the Goldsboro Volunteer Fire Company and traffic light timing at the intersection of River Road (State Route 328) and State Route 404, calling the latter a "tremendous benefit." Porter cited concerns with highway user funds being slashed to $400,00 from a high of $4 million, and a proposed mileage tax for electric vehicles.Wiedefeld said addressing changes in policy affecting EVs "is a challenge that's coming at us. We don't have any answers yet." Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding brought up the "four old timber bridges that were built in the '30s and '40s that are on our list that need to be replaced." Breeding said someone from MDOT "actually reached out to us to start the conversation about potentially pursuing some federal funding because these bridges are probably a million dollars or better a piece to replace, and that would just be too large of a hit on our (county)." Commissioner Frank Bartz thanked the State Highway Administration for repaving Route 578 between Harmony and Bethlehem but expressed concerns about future traffic detours when the Williston bridge is eventually replaced on state Route 16.Other concerns brought up by the commissioners were the long transport times for emergency services and the effectiveness of DCT's fixed routes versus a mobility-on-demand model.The draft CTP includes funding to maintain existing transportation facilities, expand transit opportunities, invest in Maryland's economic growth and support the state's long-term goals for mobility, safety, equity, environmental stewardship and economic growth.The program allocates funding for electric vehicle infrastructure, as well as investment in the transition to zero-emission transit buses and other carbon reduction and resiliency programs, "establishing Maryland as national leader in addressing climate goals," the press release stated.The program includes funding to promote Transit-Oriented Development to spur economic growth in transit corridors, and for projects to support Complete Streets - an initiative to make Maryland's roadways safer and more accessible for all users, and help reduce the number of roadway fatalities and injuries.The program outlines investments in each mode funded by the Transportation Trust Fund: Maryland Aviation Administration, Maryland Port Administration, Maryland Transit Administration, Motor Vehicle Administration, State Highway Administration and The Secretary's Office, as well as Maryland's investment in the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority.The plan includes an additional $2.7 billion investment planned by the Maryland Transportation Authority. Receiving no funds from the Transportation Trust Fund, the Maryland Transportation Authority's toll facilities are fully financed, constructed, operated, maintained, improved and protected with toll revenues paid by customers using those facilities.Motor Vehicle Administrator Nizer discussed the state's Vision Zero initiative - the goal of achieving zero fatalities on Maryland roadways. She noted that jurisdictions and organizations are encouraged to apply for safety grants through the Maryland Highway Safety Office to use for enforcement and education efforts.The Caroline County meeting was part of the Maryland Department of Transportation's tour of all 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City to discuss the funding plan and receive input from local officials and the public. The tour continues into November.Following the tour, the draft fiscal year 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program will be finalized and submitted in January for consideration during the 2024 General Assembly session.To view the full the program, visit ctp.maryland.gov.

title: Oxford Keeping Investment Policy
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford keeping investment policy

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - A decision to keep a decades-old financial investment policy, which the town didn't know about until recently, in place was met with applause at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday.Commission President Tom Costigan said that while the existing policy might not be perfect, it's what the town can work with for the time being."I think there's consensus from a lot of people in the room and a lot of people at this table that our existing policy is a good one. We should keep it and we should follow it," he said, which was followed with claps from residents in attendance.The policy features three sections that are unique to Oxford.One section states that each commissioner and the clerk treasurer must disclose "any substantial personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County." Another section states that no more than half of the town's investment should be in a stable financial institution.Lewis said that other municipalities didn't necessarily state this the same way.The last section states that the length of maturity on an investment should not exceed one year.At the previous town meeting Sept. 26, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said that Oxford has had a financial investment policy since the 1990s, which the current town officials and commissioners had not been made aware of.Lewis said that after learning about the policy, she created an updated version.She gave commissioners copies of the original policy as well a policy with her updates at the Sept. 26 meeting.After Costigan said the town should keep the existing financial policy at the Tuesday meeting, Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin asked if they would consider looking at the small updates that Talbot County had made to its financial policy."Would we consider looking at that and seeing (if) there (is) anything we need to address?" she asked.Costigan said the commissioners could look at "anything," but said that right now, the plan is to stick with what is already in place.Commissioner Katrina Greer said she was thrilled to keep the existing policy in place.During the meeting, commissioners briefly discussed whether to create a Budget and Finance Committee.During the last meeting, Greer had asked to discuss a resolution to create the committee, which she drafted.Commissioners agreed to discuss it at the meeting Tuesday.However, because Greer wanted to go through the language, Costigan suggested the commissioners hold a workshop next week to discuss the resolution.Greer said she would be happy with that, as long as the meeting was in the evening, rather than in the afternoon, so that more residents can attend.Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said she envisions that commissioners would discuss what they anticipate the committee would do at the workshop so that she can draft something to be put on the agenda for the next regular town meeting.Delean-Botkin said the first question the commissioners have to decide is whether the committee is necessary."Having gone through 40 phone calls of other entities on the Shore, Rockville, Frederick Annapolis, Anne Arundel County, Talbot County, Easton, Trappe, Salisbury, Cambridge, Denton, all the school boards - none of them have a citizens budget advisory committee," Delean-Botkin said. "When I asked the aldermen, councilmen, committee members and board members why not, it is because it is the duty of the sworn officials to manage the budget and finances is in every entity's charter." In response, Greer said Annapolis does have a Finance Committee.Costigan said the commissioners should first decide what the committee would be."Let's first define what it is and then we'll decide whether we need it or not," he said. "And we can vote on whether we want it or not." The commissioners workshop will be held Thursday, Oct. 19, at 5 p.m. in the Commissioners of Oxford meeting room.

 CAMBRIDGE - During a council meeting recently, the Dorchester County Council was given an update by Maryland Department of Transportation officials on different projects and programs affecting the county.The council heard from Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul Wiedefeld as well as representatives from the Maryland State Highway Administration, Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration, Maryland Transportation Authority, Maryland Transit Administration, Maryland Aviation Administration and Maryland Port Administration.Matt Baker, state highway deputy administrator for project development, talked about a traffic signal project affecting U.S. Route 50 and Maryland Route 750 that will enhance safety for pedestrians and bicyclists. The $208,000 project includes the implementation of countdown pedestrian signals.Baker also mentioned the new sidewalk on Bayly road, which runs between Maces Lane and Governors Avenue, that will make the road safer for pedestrians and bicyclists.Currently, the State Highway Association is doing an intersection study at Maryland Route 343 and Maces Lane to see what safety enhancements it might need to employ at that intersection, according to a press release from MDOT.Bob Munroe, Maryland Port Administration deputy executive director of administration and environment, talked about the Mid-Chesapeake Bay Ecosystem Restoration project. The project, in partnership with the U.S.Army Corps of Engineers and located in Dorchester County, will create shoreline protection for the county by using dredged material from shipping channels to rebuild James and Barren islands."On a macro-level, this project will give the state much needed Chesapeake Bay sediment replacement capacity for the next 30 years," Munroe said during the meeting. "Locally, we believe that the MidBay island restoration will help reduce storm-related shoreline erosion for up to 30% on the upper Hoopers Island area and the areas north of Fishing Creek." Munroe added that he believes the project will also increase overall property values in the county by more than $1 million.This is in part due to a reduced rate of energy and improved water quality.Barren Island construction has already begun and James Island construction is set to begin in 2025, Munroe said.These projects are a part of MDOT's six-year draft Consolidated Transportation Program, a $21.2 billion investment plan for the state's transportation system. According to the press release, the plan will be finalized and submitted in January for consideration of the General Assembly. MDOT is meeting with all of Maryland's counties and Baltimore City to discuss the plan.According to the press release from MDOT, allocations for Dorchester County in the draft Consolidated Transportation Program also include $919,000 to support local transit operations provided by Delmarva Community Transit, $123,000 to help Delmarva Community Services install a propane station for propanepowered vehicles and $337,000 to help fund HVAC improvements at the Cambridge-Dorchester Regional Airport terminal.During the meeting, the County Council presented a list of priorities it hopes MDOT can address, including traffic improvements, pedestrian and safety improvements around the county.These include:▪ Traffic and geometric improvements at the Maryland Route 392 and Route 14 intersection.▪ A pipe replacement on Maryland Route 336.▪ Pedestrian improvements on Maryland Route 392 through Hurlock.▪ Railroad crossing improvements at Indiantown Road and Maryland Route 331.▪ Turn lane improvements to Maryland Route 16 at Mount Holly Road.▪ Pavement marking updates in Cambridge.▪ Painting the jersey walls on Malkus Bridge.▪ A full-function intersection on westbound U.S.50 at Chateau Road.▪ Rumble strips on Mount Holly Road.▪ Visibility improvements on the drawbridge in Cambridge.The city of Cambridge and town of East New Market also submitted a list to the county to be presented to MDOT. Their lists include changes to the intersection at Maces Lane and Washington Street in Cambridge and assistance with speeding in East New Market, among other items.After hearing the presentations from MDOT officials, council members shared their comments with the officials.Council member Ricky Travers talked about the change in road width on Maryland Route 335.He said the road width changes by about 2 or 3 feet on either side."I really think the state needs to take a strong look at that," he said.Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer thanked the State Highway Administration District Engineer Mark Crampton."I wanted to thank you so much for answering emails and questions and concerns of the council in general and our citizens when they talk," Pfeffer said. "Mark has been phenomenal in customer service [and] getting back to us with answers, whether it's something we like to hear or something we don't." Detmer said the work Crampton and his team have done means a lot to him and to the residents of Dorchester County."From the little to the big, your local team here has been very exemplary in helping us," he said to the MDOT officials.

 OXFORD - Following direction from a Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Tuesday, a resident has moved forward with creating an informal committee to beautify the area surrounding the water treatment facility on Jl Thompson Drive.The committee will formulate a plan to be brought to the Commissioners of Oxford for consideration.Nick Papson, the resident tasked with creating the informal committee, submitted a petition, signed by more than 180 residents, to the town to "accelerate a beautification campaign along the fence surrounding the water treatment facility" on Jl Thompson Drive."For years, this has been an eyesore, which those of us who live nearby and pass daily have been asked to tolerate as higher priority facility and beautification projects have taken place," the petition said, which Commission President Tom Costigan read at the meeting.Since the meeting, Papson said he has assembled a committee of six residents.He said the committee will meet next week to begin the process of putting together a plan and getting quotes for potential projects. It has solicited the help of the owner and operator of Garden Design of Easton.Along with a beautification plan, signers of the submitted petition also requested an understanding of the costs associated with the project, an understanding of where on the list of town priorities it is and what could be done to accelerate the project, and the time table for the project.If the resources to create this plan and obtain quotes are unavailable, the petition requests a that a committee of "concerned citizens" be formed to create the plan and get quotes for it.In a letter submitted along with the petition, Papson said he had talked with Oxford's Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman to address some of Ozman's concerns.At the meeting, Ozman said his largest concern is the water main the comes off of the water tower and sends water to residences."That is smack dab in the center of that grass strip," Ozman said."And that's the reasoning behind not wanting deeply-rooted plants." Ozman said that trees, which have deep roots, could wrap around a waterline. He said anything with a shallow root system that could be replaced would be best.Costigan added that there could also be security issues depending on the height of the plants."We don't want to essentially block off view (from) inside," he said."Not that I'm suggesting we're a major terrorism target here, but you never know." Ornamental grasses and bayberries were discussed at the meeting as possibilities for the long strip in front of the fence.In an interview Thursday, Papson said that Oxford does a "wonderful job" of beautifying public spaces and this is another area that should be beautified.

title: Historic Armory Could Be Torn Down to Make Way for New Boutique Hotel
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Historic Armory could be torn down to make way for new boutique hotel

 October 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 668
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Despite a new detailed presentation from Washington College President Mike Sosulski, the Chestertown Historic District Commissioners say they need still more information before approving the college's plans for the town's historic Armory building."Though we have come to the commission before, this is essentially a new request that does comply with the original deed," said Sosulski. "The Maryland Department of the Military and the Department of Public Works heartily endorse our position." The College appeared before the HDC at their Oct. 4 meeting.The Armory, built in 1931, was used for seven decades for the Maryland National Guard, as well as community events, and was put on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980. When the state declared the Armory was "surplus," the building was offered to the Town of Chestertown who did not have the resources to develop the property.Washington College bought the property in hopes of renovating the building and using it as an environmental center, right along the river. After a walk through and mold testing, the college withdrew their plans to the commission a year ago to get more information, address public input, and seek investors.Washington College president Sosulski led the new presentation last week.Sosulski said, "The college agrees that the Armory has historical significance. But it's been a constant struggle to find a purpose for this building." The college investigated several plans similar to those done with other armories throughout the state, but the costs were found to be prohibitive.Sosulski said that proposals for just stabilizing the structure cost $4 million and no investment partners could be found.At the October meeting, Sosulski provided details to this new proposal for a boutique style hotel with numerous meeting spaces that can be used by the entire community. If possible, the hotel would keep the facade of the building and keep numerous military memorabilia in prominent displays, he noted. Hersha Hospitality has agreed to partner with the company using this plan.Business leaders have been supportive of the proposal.A hotel/conference center would bring jobs, increase tourism, and help the town and county continue to improve" said Bryan Matthews, Executive Director of Kent Forward. "Our community must seize the opportunity to turn a deteriorating building with major issues into a tremendous asset." Other residents are not so sure. Resident Steven Mitchell, a facilities and environmental manager, wants the commission to have their own independent mold remediation expert to get an unbiased opinion about the mold issue. "I believe the applicant should pay for it, or the town," said Mitchell. "Or if necessary I will pay for it." Jeremy Rottweil, another resident, believed the mold remediation done before the 2005 closing took care of the mold problems, and it returned due to the college not taking proper care of the property. "Two large sump pumps and the HVAC were turned off.This is a textbook example of demolition by neglect," said Rottweil.Commission member Samantha Hollomon said she would like a current condition structural report for the head house, the main hall, and then the additions."I would like to see the cost difference between using the facade and not using it," she said."I would like to have greater clarity on the development team," said Commission member Rebecca Murphy. "If possible, to get their tax credit applications." Commissioner Monica Sella proposed the college come back before the Commission with the infrastructure costs of the project, such as building roads, getting plumbing, and so forth.Another member voiced concerns about environmental impacts from the demolition.Despite all of the questions and concerns voiced, most people in the room were supportive of the idea.Richard Keaveney, chair of the Economic Vitality Committee of Mainstreet Chestertown, told the commission that at his recent meeting, "Every member of the committee was in favor of this latest proposal." Overall, Holomon said she was "really excited" about the amount of agreement in the room. "Stay patient. Let's treat one another with respect," she advised, "This will be a group effort."

 I am a lifelong resident of Easton, Maryland. I am expressing my opposition to the proposed rezoning and development of the property at the end of Camac Street in Hunters Mill on Matthewstown Road.There are many in my community who share my concern, and I am writing on behalf of them as well.The development would cause traffic and safety problems, create even more problems with schools that are already over-capacity, destroy local wildlife habitat and potentially lower the property values of the existing community. The addition of approximately 200 homes in the approved Gannon Estates and 120 apartments at the corner of Route 328 and Elliott Road will already increase the congestion and danger of the traffic patterns.Local neighborhood traffic will disproportionately surge during morning and evening rush hours, causing traffic issues during critical times for the existing area neighborhoods and commuters (including Hunters Mill, Matthewstown Run, Brentridge, Mulberry Station, Swann Haven and Caroline County commuters). The traffic surge during morning rush hours will also negatively impact the safety of children since students walk to the bus stop at the entrance of Hunters Mill.In general, the area traffic is continuing to increase, and heavy traffic is already common on Matthewstown Road.Schools in the area are already reported at over capacity, and the council should not approve multi-family dwellings that create or exacerbate this situation. Already approved housing developments in Talbot County will stretch public, private and parochial school admissions beyond capacity.Wildlife has been observed in the area and any development will destroy their habitat. Any planned development of the property should consider the continuing impact on local wildlife habitat.Within the project application, there are indications that the proposed planning area has several endangered species, which should be investigated by the appropriate agency before the approval of the project.Property values are likely to decrease in the area where multi-family apartments are built.Multi-family dwellings are inconsistent with the neighborhoods developed in this area.I am asking my community to attend meetings to speak out against the construction. There is a meeting set to be held on Oct. 24 at 6 p.m. on the second floor of 14 South Harrison Street. title: General Assembly Could Bring Big Voting Changes
author: David Reel
content:
General Assembly Could Bring Big Voting Changes

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: David Reel | Page: 7 | Section: Opinions 
 
 683
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When the Maryland General Assembly convenes for a 90-day session in January 2024, there may be at least three proposals that, if approved, could have a significant impact on politics and elections on the Eastern Shore.The first proposal would change the current process used to fill vacancies in the General Assembly that result from death, resignation, removal or other unexpected reason.Under current law, local Republican party central committees and local Democratic party central committees have a key role in the replacement process. The respective central committee is charged with screening and recommending potential successors who are affiliated with the same party of the departing or departed legislator. Once central committee members reach agreement on recommendations for a successor, they are sent to the governor who makes the final decision on an appointment to fill the vacancy until the next election.In previous General Assembly sessions, legislation has been introduced regularly to require special elections to fill general assembly vacancies that occur within the first two years of the four-year legislative term. None has been seriously considered.That may be changing sooner rather than later.Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson recently opined that he is uncomfortable with the power that local party central committees possess in filling general assembly vacancies. In response to a direct question asking if he was "fine" with the current system, Ferguson replied bluntly, "I do not think it is fine the way it is." Ferguson said the 2024 legislative session is a good time to consider change legislation, because any proposed revisions to the process to filling legislative vacancies could then be placed before voters in a statewide referendum.That said, obstacles to change remain. The most formidable is strong historical resistance from the State Board of Elections on using special elections to fill legislative vacancies. Their opposition is based on the Board's concern about the expense and an extra administrative burden on the state and local election boards in conducting such elections.The second proposal would change how vacancies are filled when a seat on the Talbot County Board of Education is vacated due to death, resignation, removal or other unexpected reason.Under current law these vacancies are filled by the governor.The Talbot County Council has been and is discussing requesting our local General Assembly delegation to introduce legislation authorizing the County Council and the Board of Education to name a replacement to fill a vacancy on the school board.Those discussions are ongoing.The third proposal that could have a significant impact on politics and elections on the Eastern Shore is adoption of ranked choice voting. This by far is the most far-reaching proposal in terms of change and complexity. It also is the least likely to get meaningful traction in the upcoming General Assembly session.A ranked-choice voting system is an electoral system in which voters rank candidates by preference on their ballots. If a candidate wins a majority of first-preference votes, he or she is declared the winner. If no candidate wins a majority of first-preference votes, the candidate with the fewest first-preference votes is eliminated.First-preference votes cast for the failed candidate are eliminated, lifting the second-preference choices indicated on those ballots. A new tally is conducted to determine whether any candidate has won a majority of the adjusted votes. The process is repeated until one a candidate wins an outright majority.Approval of this concept is not likely in the upcoming General Assembly session. On this change, Senate President Ferguson recently said, "I am almost entirely certain that ranked choice voting is the way to go, but do not believe the concept will be approved in the General Assembly anytime soon." He said his current prediction is due to the amount of suspicions some voters have about election integrity (his observation, not mine). Ferguson has further said "When there are so many questions about elections in general, I am reluctant now to move [ranked-choice voting] forward.I think more education is needed.But I do think it's something that will happen eventually." Again, his words, not mine. David Reel is a public affairs/public relations consultant who serves as a trusted adviser on strategy, advocacy and media matters. He lives in Easton.

title: Easton Town Council Vote on Cannabis Moratorium Delayed - Tabled Measure Leads to Heated Discussion Among Council Members
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council vote on cannabis moratorium delayed - Tabled measure leads to heated discussion among council members

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 710
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - A move by Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus to continue a hearing on a proposed cannabis moratorium drew strong reactions from other council members.A tense back-and-forth exchange between Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilman David Montgomery toward the end of Monday's council meeting stemmed from the council president's executive decision to delay a vote on the moratorium for an additional three weeks.The nine-month moratorium on cannabis businesses, introduced this summer, was originally slated for a public hearing and vote at the council's Sept.18 meeting. The matter had been tabled until Monday so all five council members could be present to vote.The moratorium, if passed, would place a pause on applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for a business that grows, processes or sells cannabis within the Easton town limits.The moratorium would also allow the town to consider and adopt a revised zoning ordinance.Easton's existing zoning ordinance already contains definitions and permitted zoning districts for medical cannabis dispensaries and growing and processing facilities, but does not include language on standards for recreational facilities.Montgomery strongly objected to Gunsallus' continuance, saying the council president did not have the authority to do so. Gunsallus affirmed that he did."Sir, you will contain yourself please," Gunsallus said, speaking over Montgomery, who started to make a comment.Gunsallus reaffirmed he had the power to continue discussion on the moratorium until the next meeting, explaining that he wanted to wait until the town's planning commission made an additional recommendation later in the week.However, in August, the commission unanimously gave a favorable recommendation to approve the ordinance.Montgomery called for a vote on the continuance, questioning Gunsallus' authority."The fact that four of us could reveal that we want to vote now means nothing to you, that you will override the wishes of the council because you are sitting there as the town council president," he said.Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh chimed in, saying the council can override the president's action. But in the past, the council has typically given members additional time to vote as a courtesy.Montgomery pointed out that the council had already given an additional month for consideration.Gunsallus reemphasized the upcoming planning commission meeting would provide more clarifying information."Excuse me, what information will that be?" Montgomery said."(The planning commission's) recommendations, as I've stated, so please contain yourself - you've already spoken more than permissible," Gunsallus said.Montgomery motioned to overrule Gunsallus and vote on the ordinance as presented.Ward 2 Councilman Don Abbatiello interjected, saying while he understood Montgomery and "definitely" disagreed with how the decision had been handled, he agreed that granting additional time to decide was in line with past council actions.Mayor Megan Cook, a former council president herself, interrupted the quarreling, calling for the councilmen to settle down."I agree that we are a group of five where you all are independent and you all have various opinions - absolutely.We must respect ourselves - the fighting, we need to" she said, trailing off and moving her arms to motion to calm down."Please." Ward 4 Councilman Rev.Elmer Davis Jr. initially seconded the motion, rescinding his vote just minutes later to agree with Abbatiello's stance on the council's precedent. He voiced worry with how the situation was handled."We have never had such a dialogue that we had tonight regarding issues and concerns," he said. "That dialogue - I'm quite concerned about things that have been said, I've never seen this on this council in all my days." The council will again table voting on the ordinance until its Monday, Nov. 6, meeting.Uncertainty still remains on the moratorium. During Monday's meeting, council members and town residents raised questions on the moratorium's duration, specifics on licensing for both recreational and medical facilities and zoning laws for both types of establishments.The Easton Planning Commission will discuss zoning requirements for adult-use cannabis dispensaries at its Thursday, Oct. 19, meeting.

title: Residents a No Show to Listening Session - Cambridge City Council to Vote on Ward Realignment
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Residents a no show to listening session - Cambridge City Council to vote on ward realignment

 October 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 721
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Only city staff and committee members showed up to a Cambridge Ward Realignment Listening Session on Thursday, Oct. 12.The city's residents, who the informal meeting was intended for, were not present at the City Council Chambers that evening.Neither the Ward Realignment Committee members nor city staff were surprised by this, though."The people who aren't affected looked at the map, said 'That ain't me. Ok,"'Ward Realignment Committee member Lou Hyman hypothesized.The ward changes, which the committee proposes Cambridge City Council vote to make, would affect less than 3% ofCambridge's population.According to a news release from the city, the committee is proposing:⯀Moving the area bounded by Locust Street, Oakley Street, Park Lane and Willis Street from Ward 1 to Ward 3.⯀Moving the area bounded by Robbins Street, Maces Lane, Bradley Avenue and High Street from Ward 2 to Ward 4.⯀Moving the area bounded byVirginia Avenue, Peachblossom Avenue, Washington Street, Front Street, Brohawn Avenue and Perimore Street from Ward 3 to Ward 5.■ Moving the area bounded by Washington Street, Peachblossom Avenue, Boundary Avenue and Front Street from Ward 4 to Ward 5.These changes would make it so that each ward has a population size within the lawful plus or minus 5% range of the city's mean population.Wards must be within this range for elections.According to city council documents, there are currently more residents in Ward 1 than the range allows and fewer residents in Ward 5 than the range allows.At the end of the listening session, the committee voted unanimously to move forward with its proposal as is."Well, we did not hear anything in the listening session that would make me think we should change (our proposal)," Committee Member Tal-ibah Chikwendu said, referencing the absence of residents and causing those at the meeting to laugh."So I can't see a reason to make any additional changes."Following the committee's vote to move forward, the city will draft a resolution to be put on the City Council's next meeting agenda for a first reading. In November, the City Council will hold a formal public hearing for the the resolution.Ifthe City Council passes the resolution, the city will communicate the changes to the Board of Elections, who will then notify the residents affected.The majority ofthe meeting, however, was spent talking about how to achieve more engagement from residents on different city issues.Chikwendu said residents who would be affected by the proposed changes might have showed up to the listening session ifthey had been notified of the potential impact via mail."We could have gotten people here ifwe had been specific in the targets," she said.Chikwendu also said having more diverse wards could facilitate increased community engagement with the city, overall."It would have impacted a whole lot more people, but we could have actually created more diverse wards and still maintained the balance that we needed to to not be in violation," she said.Because the committee didn't have more time, it opted for the "next best thing," Chikwendu said, adding that there is nothing wrong with its proposal."But ifwe're talking about trying to get more and more people invested to show up for things like that and to do things that we talk about need to be done, we need to, first of all, give people reasons to start to talk to people who aren't like them," she said.Having grown up in Cambridge, Chikwendu acknowledged that there are other obstacles to increasing community engagement."In general, people who live here don't like people who came here later to tell us what to do," she said. "If they're people who aren't (lifelong) Cambridge residents saying it, it's going to be hard to get people to listen."Committee Vice Chair Greg Meekins said education is fundamental in growing engagement."We're not building up another set ofleaders," he said about Cambridge. "That's critical."Meekins also said marketing is important."We've got a large segment of the population in poverty," he said. "And ifwe are going to be intentional about reaching them, we've got to create the material that's going to hit them square in the face in a very positive way."

title: Easton Mourns All Innocent Lives - Officials Express Support for Israel with Emotional Reading of Proclamation
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content: Easton - Town officials in Easton voiced public sympathy and support for Israel following the Oct. 7 attacks on the country by Hamas terrorists. Easton Mayor Megan Cook, joined at the podium by Temple B'nai Israel Rabbi Peter Hyman, read a proclamation from the town, her voice full of emotion, at the council's Monday meeting. "The Town of Easton unequivocally condemns Hamas for this deplorable and unprovoked attack on Israel and stands with Israel as it defends itself," she said. "The Town of Easton mourns all innocent lives, regardless of their religious beliefs, that have been and will be lost due to the atrocities," Cook continued, her voice breaking. Speaking tearfully, Cook said the town prays for those whose families have been killed, captured or injured, and calls for swift return of all hostages in hopes for a lasting resolution and peace. After hugging Cook, Hyman took a moment to share his thoughts, thanking the town for its support. "I'm rarely, as some of you know, rarely at a loss for words, but this is difficult," he said. "There are innocent people on both sides who are going to suffer as a result of the terrorism and the horror, and we deeply appreciate your friendship, your support and your acknowledgement." At the start of the meeting, Ward 1 Councilwoman Maureen Curry fervently prayed for refuge and safety for all those affected by the conflict, expressing hope for comfort and security. A moment of silence was observed by all in attendance. Temple B'nai Israel will hold an interfaith community vigil in support of Israel on Thursday, Oct. 19, at 7 p.m. at the temple's location in Easton.

content:
Bond projects 'rocking and rolling' - Town of Easton nears deadline for spending 2020 bond

 October 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; njones@chespub.com tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 441

 EASTON - The Town of Easton's 2020 bond projects are "rocking and rolling," according to Easton Mayor Megan Cook.As of Monday evening's council meeting, the town had spent $6,493,165 of the $7 million allocated for park and municipal building improvements within the town, Cook said.A majority of the funding - about $6.75 million - was allocated for parks, with the remaining $250,000 going toward town buildings.The town's engineering department is working with the finance department to process remaining invoices that are coming in, but Cook said she was confident the town would spend the last $500,000 by Friday, Oct. 20."We are going to hit the mark, we're going to land the plane and we're going to get over the bar," she said, drawing laughs from town officials.The funding, originally granted in 2020, needs to be spent by the end of the month.Projects include improvements to the Rails to Trails system, upgrades to existing parks, sidewalk additions and more.One popular project is North Easton Park's new skate park and pump track, where work is moving along well. The pump track is complete, Cook said.While workers were smoothing concrete earlier this week, two young scooter drivers were whipping around the curves that had already been finished."This park is really nice," said Ryder Cario, an Easton High School freshman who came to be one of the first participants at this park. "It is a lot better than what we had before." Fellow EHS freshman Emmett Rogan joined Cario at the park. The helmeted duo made their scooters move like surfboards on a wave. After each lap, they took a break, panting and smiling.The workers seemed happy that these kids were using their creation, adding to the complex's existing playgrounds and athletic fields, though workers said they were on tight deadlines and quick expectations to install everything.But for now, this windfall is a win for scooter and skateboard lovers alike.Work on other projects is also progressing steadily.Cook shared brief updates on the status of other projects, including the Brewer's Lane dog park and parking lot, the Hunter's Mill playground, field lights installation at North Easton Park and parks storage buildings.

title: Proposed Landfill Shocks Nearby Landowners
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Proposed Landfill Shocks Nearby Landowners

 October 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 844
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE - At last week's meeting of the Queen Anne's County Commissioners, residents from the Shrewsbury Farm neighborhood in Centreville wanted answers regarding the landfill being planned off of Harper Road."I had no idea about this when I bought my house," said Alex Queller whose home is one mile from the proposed Mid-Shore Three landfill site. "This has turned my world upside down."Residents close to the proposed location were notified three weeks ago of a public information meeting being held on Oct. 4 by the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE). The MDE has a process to review submissions and forward them on to the Maryland Department of the Environment for final approval.The landfill, titled the MidShore Level Three, is a result of an agreement between Queen Anne's, Caroline, and Talbot counties in the 1980's to alternate the operation of landfills for a period of 20 years, with Kent County joining the agreement in 1992.The Talbot Mid-Shore Level One and the Caroline MidShore Level Two have already been in operation. Queen Anne's County is set for Level Three beginning in 2031-2050. The county had identified the proposed landsite in 1993, behind the closed Centreville landfill.The Oct. 4 meeting was an information session only. Held by MDE and the landfill owner's engineering consultant GeoSyntec, attendees learned the county had confirmed the project had all necessary zoning and land use approval and that it conformed to the county's 10-year solid waste plan.The total site is 124 acres, with the landfill at 62 acres and the maximum elevation at 240 feet. The landfill will receive household refuse, solid waste from businesses, bulky waste, land clearing debris, and construction waste.The project is just in Phase I of five phases that would span seven years. There will more geological investigation of the site by an accepted engineer, and the findings will go to the MDE, State Department of Natural Resources, the Army Corps of Engineers, and the Maryland Health Department All documentation will be available on the MDE website and at the Centerville Library.County Commissioner Jack Wilson, who attended the Oct. 4 meeting, said he was open to a public meeting. "This is something the commissioners inherited from 1993, just like you," Wilson said. "I'm for being transparent." He told the attendees that Queen Anne's County has also been talking to the Caroline County government about keeping the present landfill for another 12-15 years. "We're going through the steps we have to at this time."County Administrator Todd Mohn said the landfill is included in the present county comprehensive plan and in the 10-year solid waste plan and as such "has been open to public comment each time."Mohn also noted the county knew 30 years ago "our landfills could not be another New York City.""As a region," said Mohn, "we knew that we would need to have something sustainable. We had to join forces. Talbot County went first, Caroline County then took their turn. They obviously have citizens who live near the present landfill that may not want to see it another 12 years."Shrewsbury Farm resident Anna Queller disputed the proposed landfill meets the county's solid waste plan requirement. Reading from the 2015 solid waste plan, she said when addressing the new landfill that "the county's offices of planning and zoning and waste management should conduct a preliminary review of the site."Attendees questioned whether the county had followed its 2020 Comprehensive Plan which dictated that site must be 1500 feet from a residence and 2500 feet from a portable well."There's no way," said Queller. Resident William Kyle was most concerned with the scope of the proposal. "When I went over the Bay Bridge, I measured the height elevation as being 212 feet. This proposal has the height of240 feet. You wouldn't be able to see anything else in the county."After hearing the concerns of residents' comments, MDE presenter Andrew Grenzer said, "Maybe the county needs to look at this again. But I'm not going to say here that their letter of confirmation is wrong."At the commissioners meeting on Oct. 10, Keith Palmer, a geologist who lives close to the location, told commissioners, "If you took a map of Queen Anne's County and chose a location for the landfill, the Centreville spot would be the last choice. It should be a 'do no harm' policy- not where you will impact people, not where you will impact drinking water, not where you will impact traffic. It's the head of the estuary Island Creek which feeds into the Chester River."Shrewsbury Farm resident Brad Dutton assured commissioners his home is well within the 2500 feet line. "As a parent, I try to instill a set of values in my kids. If they make a mistake, they stop, correct it, and make it right. I believe that moving forward at this point is a mistake.""We're not going away," Anna Queller told the commissioners. "The land that the county purchased for the landfill 30 years ago has changed."

 Words 

 Read News Document

 In advance of the upcoming Veterans Day holiday, the Town of Easton plans to illuminate town and county buildings green from Nov. 6 through 12 - part of Operation Green Light for Veterans.The nationwide initiative, led by the National Association of Counties, raises awareness around the unique challenges faced by many veterans and the resources available at the county, state and federal levels to assist veterans and their families.The Town of Easton will be working together with the Talbot County Government on this project, with plans to light up Town and County buildings along with encouraging local businesses and residents to join in support of veterans.Now in its second year, Operation Green Light is spearheaded by NACo and the National Association of County Veterans Service Officers, building upon successful efforts by the New York State Association of Counties and the NYS County Veteran Service Officers' Association in 2021.In 2022, over 300 towns and counties participated in Operation Green Light."It's a great way to remind our community of all that our veterans have done for our country over the years," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook."In addition to the green lights on our buildings, we also want to shine a light on the employees in our organization who have served, and in some cases continue to serve our country. We are so proud of and inspired by the veterans and service members on our team. This is just a great opportunity to honor them and let them know what they mean, n to us."In addition to lighting buildings and other meaningful landmarks, residents, businesses and other organizations are encouraged to participate by simply changing one light bulb in their home to a green bulb.This can be an exterior light that neighbors and passersby see or an interior light that sparks a conversation with friends."Operation Green Light is a gesture of support and appreciation for the public service of our veterans," said NACo Executive Director Matthew Chase. "With hundreds of towns and counties coming together to light everything from bridges to courthouses, we know veterans across the country will see and feel the gratitude we all feel for their service and sacrifices."Counties and residents across the country are sharing their participation on social media using the hashtag #OperationGreenLight.For more information on Operation Green Light, visit https://veterans.mary-land.go v/op e ration-g reen-light/.
