title: Oxford Financial Committee Decision Delayed Again - News
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford financial committee decision delayed again - News

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 811
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - No decisions have been made on two proposed committees by the Commissioners of Oxford.Following a workshop last Thursday, Commissioner Katrina Greer and Commission President Tom Costigan each shared their proposals for a Financial Advisory Committee and an Investment Advisory Committee, respectively, at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening.By the end of the meeting, it was decided that both proposals would be posted on the town website so that residents can compare them and voice their thoughts, either in writing or during the next Commissioners meeting on Nov. 14, before a decision is made."At the following meeting in December, more than likely, we will make a decision on this," Costigan said.The commissioners could decide to choose Greer's proposal, Costigan's proposal or they could chose to take no action at all, he said.At the meeting, Greer briefly read through her proposal first, which was shared in detail at the workshop last week.According to her proposal, the Financial Advisory Committee would be tasked with providing recommendations to the commissioners on issues related to town finances and other financial topics. Specifically, Greer said the committee would give advice on shortterm and long-term interest rates and types of investments."The committee recommends, the commissioners approve, the treasurer implements and manages and then the commissioners review" Greer said. "It is not auditing, it is not maintaining accounting systems, it is not collecting taxes or transferring money."After Greer spoke, Costigan shared his proposal for an Investment Advisory Committee that would be tasked with reviewing the towns investments quarterly, providing recommendations to the commissioners on investment opportunities, responding to other commissioner requests, and annually reviewing and providing recommendations on the town's investment policy.The committee would receive a packet of documents, which are listed in the proposed resolution, by the town manager. In Greer's proposal, committee members would be able to request information related to town finances that is accessible via the Maryland Public Information Act.Greer said she would vote in favor of Costigan's proposal pending three changes The first change would be to use the same language in the town's financial investment policy for the ethics requirement of committee members.The second change would be to include the word "demonstrable" to describe the experience that committee members must have.The third change would make it so that real property owners, along with those registered to vote in the Town of Oxford, can become committee members.Costigan's proposal makes it so that a committee member must be registered to vote in Oxford.This specific requirement ofwho can be a committee member was brought up multiple times during the meeting.When Greer shared her proposal, she said she wanted to include real property owners because no committee in Oxford is restricted to only voters and said it would be a shame to miss out on people with experience who are not registered to vote in Oxford.Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said that while there is no restriction within the charter, it has been the policy of the town that members on committees are fulltime residents that are registered to vote in Oxford.Greer gave an example of a chartered financial analyst who lives in another state but comes to Oxford regularly throughout the year to visit his mother."I think it's important to have stakeholders that are paying taxes, and therefore have a vested interest in the town, getting the most out of its investments safely," she said.At the workshop last Thursday, Costigan said Greer's committee proposal requirement that members must own real property in town was elitist and offensive to renters.During public comment, Russ Gray said a task force or ad hoc committee might be a better alternative to creating a formal committee."It requires a ton of work, it requires bureaucracy, which I think all of us are against," Gray said about forming a committee. "Based on what we're limited to investing in, are there going to be any hidden surprises in terms of dramatic changes over a period of time? Doubtful."Gail Rosenfeld spoke in favor of having a committee. She said it's always a good thing to have thoughtful people involved and added that having a committee is about transparency."We should know what's going on," she said.Rosenfeld added that she isn't a voter, but she is a resident."I adore this town," she said. "This matters to me greatly."After the meeting, former Commission President Jimmy Jaramillo said he supports Costigan's proposal because he thinks it's important that voters and full-time residents are the ones who can serve on the committee."They're invested, they're here all the time, they can make these meetings," he said. "Having someone that's not here full time, only three times a year, (and) lives in a different state - they're not invested."

title: Cambridge Council Not in Support of Harbor Project Plan
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge Council not in support of harbor project plan

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 690
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In a letter addressed to Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Executive Director Matt Leonard, the city of Cambridge expressed City Council's concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.The letter, signed by City Manager Tom Carroll, states that City Council does not support CWDI's current plans for Cambridge Harbor.In late August, CWDI, a private nonprofit, released a 2023 mid-year report to the community that detailed what the group has done so far and what it plans to do moving forward. The Cambridge Harbor project will include creating public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces.In an interview in September, Leonard said the goal is for the entire project to be complete in somewhere between five and 10 years from now. By 2025, CWDI expects it will no longer need public funds to operate Cambridge Harbor.The letter from the city gives four reasons for the council's lack of support for the project. First, the council thinks CWDI seems like it wants to be the site developer instead of hiring a "capable master developer." "The redevelopment of a site of this size and complexity requires a private sector development partner with a proven track record of success in similar projects," the letter says.The second reason cited is that the proposal for the project "does not generate enough economic value" for developing the project without "an unacceptably large public subsidy."The third reason is that the proposed tax increment finance district will take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades."The city and county need to be involved in shaping these public financing plans from the start," the letter says.The fourth reason for the lack of Council support is that the council does not approve of the governance of CWDI. The letter states that CWDI is not being transparent, accountable or responsive to the Council.In a September interview, Carroll said that communication between CWDI and the city has not been enough. He said that, having spent 27 years in local governments and having been a part of two major economic development projects, he has concerns about the financial feasibility of CWDI's plan.In an interview Wednesday, Leonard said he was shocked by the letter. He said CWDI met with the city back in S eptember to discuss the project and got "relatively positive feedback."Leonard recognized that not all Council members agreed with every aspect of the project, but he said they seemed generally OK with it.While Leonard said he and the CWDI board take the concerns of all stakeholders very seriously, he said they do not share concerns with the city for the direction of the Cambridge Harbor project."Our direction has come from community input over the last three decades," he said. "We have accounted for the community development aspects ofwhat the community says they want and the economic development aspects ofwhat we believe will be valuable to the city and the county, and the state and the community, of course, at large."Leonard said CWDI is concerned about its relationship with the city, however."That means a lot to us," he said. "And we've tried, and continue to try to make that relationship positive and productive."Moving forward, Leonard hopes to address the city's concerns during a meeting scheduled for Nov. 13. Leonard said CWDI has issued invitations to all of its stakeholders and development team members to discuss some of the more confidential development matters of the project."We hope that members of the City Council and leadership of the city staff will attend the meeting so we can address, in essence, a number of the issues that they raised in the rest of their letter," he said.In the letter, it says that the City Council thinks the Nov. 13 meeting is premature and the City Council will be reaching out to Dorchester County Council to talk about how to get the project "back on track."

title: Traffic Concerns Derail Proposed Apartment Complex - Board of Zoning Appeals Denies Aspire Apartments' Special Exception Request
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Traffic concerns derail proposed apartment complex - Board of Zoning Appeals denies Aspire Apartments' special exception request

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1093
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - After four and a half hours of testimony and deliberations, the Easton Board of Zoning Appeals denied Aspire Apartments' request for a special exception to use a property off of Mathewstown Road as a multifamily apartment complex.Almost every seat was full in the meeting chambers Tuesday evening as supporters and opponents waited for a chance to weigh in on the contentious proposed complex - and to hear the long-awaited decision on the project's requests.Brought forth by Aspire Outdoors LLC, a company owned by Easton resident Derick Daly, the project proposed a six-building, 162-unit apartment complex with 27 units in each building.The property is situated on the south end of Camac Street, southwest of the existing Hunters Mill neighborhood and adjacent to the Gannon Range, previously known as the Estates at Gannon Farm, planned unit development. It's also located within the R-10A zone, a residential district within the Town of Easton.A multifamily apartment complex within the district requires a special exception granted by the Board of Zoning Appeals, which prompted Daly's request.Daly also requested a variance to allow reduction of the rear setback dimension for the apartment buildings and parking area to be reduced from the town zoning code's required 75 feet to 50 feet due to the unusual size and configuration of the area.The project first came before the town planning commission last December, where Hunters Mill residents voiced concerns about traffic and accessibility.The proposal was initially slated to be heard by the Board of Zoning Appeals in April, but was delayed by 180 days to address ongoing concerns.Within the last few months, both town planning staff and the planning commission recommended approval of Daly's application with conditions, which included project phasing, addressing traffic mitigation and ensuring adequate wastewater capacity.The proposed phasing suggestion, which was incorporated into plans shown at Tuesday's meeting, indicated that access to the first phase of buildings would be via Camac Street.The second phase of construction would include access to the complex via Gannon Range and Camac Street. An additional entrance for the third phase of development was yet to be determined.To Daly, inspiration for the apartment complex was drawn from the opportunity to provide "much-needed housing" to Easton. About 25% of the profits are going to another one of Daly's ventures: Polaris Village Academy, a free private school located in the Port Street area.Daly said the complex was intended to be a higher-end property to serve employees of the new regional medical center, which has yet to begin construction.Board of Zoning Appeals member Gary Molchan questioned why Aspire Apartments couldn't have its own entrance like other complexes instead of running through residential neighborhoods. Daly said he was limited by wetlands, which would require a different set of approvals.Questions were also raised about the number of parking spaces for the entirety of the complex, the possibility of parking spilling over onto Camac Street and adequate public facilities.A significant portion of the meeting was spent discussing traffic - a primary concern of Hunters Mill residents.Betty Tustin, a senior project manager for The Traffic Group, said once fully developed, the apartment complex would generate 875 average daily trips. The number was one she deemed as sufficient for what was permitted under town standards.But to Troy Brestel, a professional engineer and project manager with Traffic Planning and Design, Inc. who testified on behalf of the project's opponents, said that he agreed with the number of average daily trips listed in the developer's traffic study, but disagreed with amount of average daily trips on Camac Street once the apartments were developed.John Franczak, the vice president of the Hunters Mill Homeowners' Association, led opposition to the apartment complex on behalf of the neighborhood."We feel that the town comprehensive plan should be followed, no variances or exceptions," he said. "The rules are there to protect people."The Town of Easton is also installing a long-promised park in the neighborhood, which means more young children and families out walking - a dangerous situation if there's heavy traffic flow from an apartment complex, Franczak said.Several members of the public took the opportunity to comment at the end of each side's presentation.The board's discussion on the variance request was brief, with members acknowledging its minimal impact - the property's use was more important. Approval of the variance request was unanimous.More detailed deliberations ensued on the special exception request.Molchan voiced concerns about the change in character of the surrounding area and traffic congestion."I would support that the Town of Easton needs apartments like this, but these apartments should not affect a community that already exists," he said. "What we're doing to the people on Camac we're turning a quiet residential neighborhood into a bustling thoroughfare for cars and delivery trucks and contractor vehicles, and that's after the apartments are built, that's not while they're being built. Who knows what that will be?"Board member Zakary Krebeck raised similar points, speaking about the "unrealistic" provision of parking spaces and the impact it would have on Hunters Mill.To board chairman Peter Cotter, traffic and congestion were the two main issues he was grappling with."I don't see how it's currently configured, how I can get to a yes using Camac Street," he said, "because I just think that regardless of how the plan is, that's going to be what is used."A motion to deny the special exception was promptly voted on, earning a unanimous consensus.In a phone interview Wednesday afternoon, Daly said he was "disheartened" by the special exception's denial, but understood why the board chose to do so. Looking forward, he plans to make adjustments to his proposal and come before the board again.Because the board denied the application, Daly must wait a full year before returning with the same proposal, per the town's zoning ordinance. A revised plan could be heard in less than a year if it's substantially different from the previous application. The denial can also be appealed in the county circuit court.In spite of the denial, Daly expressed gratitude to the board for hearing him out, along with thanks for positive recommendations from the planning commission, Easton Utilities and town staff.Franczak said while he didn't think the apartment proposal was bad, the project didn't go well with the adjacent single-family house neighborhood. The opposition wasn't personal; Franczak felt he was allowed to defend his house, neighborhood and the safety of both."Bottom line: no hard feelings," he said.

title: On the River - Heritage Trail on Chester River Aims to Improve Access, Promote History, Fishing, Boating
author: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
On the river - Heritage Trail on Chester River aims to improve access, promote history, fishing, boating

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com | Page: 28 | Section: News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - The Chestertown Heritage Trail is a project aimed at improving public access to the picturesque wetlands along the Chester River. It's rooted in the Chestertown Comprehensive Plan which, among other things, emphasizes the need to have more publicly-acces-sible land.Throughout history the river played a pivotal role for Native American communities, European settlers, and for both free and enslaved Africans - while also a critical asset to the region's agricultural economy.In the proposal letter sent by the Chestertown Council to the Kent County Commissioners, that sentiment is echoed. "Today the Chester River remains an integral part of the community, supporting recreational, educational, and economic activities like boating, fishing and crabbing," it stated.As of Oct. 11, the Council requested from the County, $350,000 to initiate Phase 1 of the Chestertown Heritage Trail plan. If approved, sections will be designed to cross wetland areas near the Washington College pavilion and the area south of the Armory site at 509 S Cross Street, Chestertown.The first phase involves detailed engineering, design and construction of the initial trail section. The 1,000 foot-long section consists of a bike and walking trail along with an observation platform for optimal river viewing.With the goal of creating an "environ-mentally-conscious and aesthetically pleasing trail," the project team will ensure all safety and accessibility measures are met.The initial drawings and designs can then be carried into future designs. Phase 2 seeks to expand public access along the wetlands, with a focus on recreational and educational opportunities.For example, the trail will be co-located with the site ofWashington College's Semans-Griswold Environmental Hall, which is a regional hub for research.Washington College's Chief of Staff and Vice President for Planning and Policy, Victor Sensenig said the trail also fits into their plans as well."We see it as fulfilling the long-term goals for the college's waterfront, and the public accessibility component of the project supports one of the goals of our new strategic plan, which calls for strengthened relationships with the town, county, and region."He added over the last decade, the college has made significant investment in a beautiful waterfront campus, and expressed enthusiasm about the prospect of welcoming more of the community to enjoy that space.In that space, during Phase 2, more trails can be added, beyond the Armory, to Radcliffe Creek. Ultimately, plans are to connect the Heritage Trail with the Rail to Trail network, known also as the Gilchrest Rail Trail.The council's proposal also notes opportunities for public art installations, scenic viewpoints, and educational elements integrated throughout.H erz said earlier in the year, the commissioners supported the project. He's hoping they'll do so again.In the request to the County, Herz included a letter dated March 2, to U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin, detailing the Kent County Commissioners' support of the trail project -$750,000 was requested at that time. In that letter, the County appreciated the importance of public waterfront access as well as any economic development it could bring.That original request was denied by Cardin, said Herz, but they were encouraged to re-apply.Now for a lesser amount, the Council is hopeful of the proposal being included in the 2024 state legislative agenda.Some potential funding sources include: Community Parks and Playground grants, Federal Land and Water Conservation Fund, Program Open Space, and the Rural Legacy Program.The next milestone date, Herz said, is Oct. 24 on which day Council will offer an in-person presentation of these materials to the county commissioners.H erz sees the importance of the project, "The Chestertown Heritage Trail represents a significant step toward enhancing local access to the Chester River, creating opportunities for connection to nature, appreciation of our heritage, and enjoyment of the scenic beauty the Chester offers."

title: 'A Testament to Our Shared Values' - Easton Mayor's Prayer Breakfast Marks 40th Anniversary Oct. 26
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
'A testament to our shared values' - Easton Mayor's Prayer Breakfast marks 40th anniversary Oct. 26

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 965
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - For 40 years, the prayer breakfast hosted by the mayor of Easton has brought local leaders together to break bread, support each other and invoke the help of God, with inspiring messages from those living out their faith in the community.Celebrating this milestone Thursday morning, Oct. 26, were about 150 Talbot County elected leaders, county and town administrators, law enforcement officers, clergy and citizens.They prayed, sang along to familiar songs and hymns, and connected over a buffet breakfast at the Tidewater Inn.After Easton Police officers presented the colors and led the Pledge of Allegiance, Katherine Tooley of Immanuel Lutheran Church in Easton led the singing of "God Bless America." Amy Steward served as mistress of ceremonies, and Mayor Megan Cook greeted the attendees."Gathering together each year is a testament to our shared values and our dedication to fostering a sense of community," Cook said."It allows us to celebrate our friendships, nurture new ones and reinforce our duty to support one another." Also attending the event were former Mayor Robert Willey and his wife Betsy, who, representing the First Baptist Church, read scripture from the New Testament.Both Cook and Willey were honored with official citations from the Maryland General Assembly, delivered by State Sen. Johnny Mautz, R-37, and Del. Chris Adams, R-37B."When you look at the news and walk down the street, you know now, more than ever, we need prayer amongst the business community and our political leaders," Adams said.Mautz said the morning was "very significant" and called for applause to mark the occasion.The guest speakers were two local servant-leaders who work primarily with youth and are active in their local churches. They shared very different testimonies of how they see God working in their lives and the lives of others.Claudia Reyes emigrated from Guatemala as a child and serves in Hispanic youth ministries with her husband Eliud, the pastor of First Hispanic Baptist Church in Easton. They have been married for 29 years and have four children.Her ministry in the Talbot County Detention Center, where she hears stories of addiction and exploitation, has convinced her that "evil is all around us." "We live in bad times, and if you saw the news last night or have seen the news for a couple weeks, you know exactly what I'm talking about. I can assure you that God sees the evil and through God, lives are being transformed," Reyes said. "As much as we have seen evil and destruction here in our community, we see more of God's grace and mercy." Referring to the rise of drug addiction and sex trafficking she is aware of, Reyes said, "Our youth here in our community are not for sale for evil. They are to be rescued.They are to be saved." Reyes encouraged attendees to pray because "prayer is very powerful," to become aware of the problems youth face and to "do something." Raised on a farm near Cordova and active in the 4-H program, Linda Saathoff Brown is a lifelong member of Immanuel Lutheran Church. She called herself a "farm girl, teacher, wife, mother and Nana." She has been married to Wesley Brown for 46 years and has taught in Talbot County Public Schools for 47 years.Sprinkling her talk with Bible verses and contemporary praise song lyrics, Brown shared "My Story, God's Glory," borrowing a title of one of her favorite songs by Matthew West.On the exact one-year anniversary of a surgery following a life-threatening fall that could have left her paralyzed, Brown shared ten miracles she said were evidence of God healing her through the prayers of friends from Cordova to Trinidad.Despite dire indications that she may never walk again because of five vertebrae that were either "crushed or cracked," Brown was able to return home without a walker and celebrate Thanksgiving with Amish friends from Lancaster, who brought a van load of food and the greeting, "Our fervent prayers are answered," she said."Thanksgiving took on a whole new meaning" and she "has been blessed beyond measure," Brown said.Local clergy reading scripture and leading prayers were the Rev. Demetrius Price of Union Baptist Church; the Rev. Elmer Davis, a district superintendent in the Peninsula-Delaware Conference of The United Methodist Church; Kennedy Siaw, youth minister of Oasis Church; and C.B. Nagel of Cru, formerly Campus Crusade for Christ International.Before leading a prayer for leadership, Siaw challenged attendees to reflect on their reason for attending the breakfast and reminded them that "true leadership is to become the servant of all," after the example of Jesus Christ.The Rev. Christian Jensen of Denton has been chaplain of the Maryland General Assembly for 23 years and attended the first Easton Mayor's Prayer Breakfast and "most of the intervening 40," he said.He is also the Maryland representative for the National Prayer Breakfast in Washington, D.C."It's a blessing to see an important tradition like this carry on through, regardless of what changes there are in political administration," Jensen said. "To see something like this continue on is a good reflection on everyone's ability to get along with one another and understand what's important."

title: Oxford Passes Charter Amendments, Policies
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Oxford passes charter amendments, policies

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 548
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - The Commissioners of Oxford voted on two charter amendments, one policy update and one new policy at a meeting on Tuesday.CHARTER AMENDMENTSThe commissioners voted to pass two resolutions to amend the town charter.These resolutions address a recently enacted charter amendment that changes the way commission vacancies are filled - from appointment to special election.The first resolution that was passed removes references to "general" elections in the charter to make it clear that it is referring to all elections, not just general elections.The second resolution passed clarifies that a person filling a vacancy would serve the balance of the term they are filling, rather than serving until the next election.While the commissioners were supposed to vote on a third resolution to amend the charter, which would address the deadline for filing a certificate of nomination, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said there was some confusion with what was posted online. The commissioners decided to postpone the public hearing for that resolution until their next meeting on Nov. 14.FINANCIAL INVESTMENT POLICYThe commissioners voted to repeal and replace the town's financial investment policy. The policy, which defines what the town can and cannot do regarding its financial investments, was originally passed in 1996.However, the town didn't know about its existence until recently.Commission President Tom Costigan said this update to the policy cleans up some references to outdated or no-longer-existing Maryland codes, gives the town an addition investment option of certificates of deposit account registry service, or CDARS, and allows the town to put money in the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool.The update also removes the word "substantial" from the section that states commissioners and the clerk treasurer must disclose "any substantial personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County." "So we must now disclose any personal investment or management role in any financial institution which conducts business in Talbot County," Costigan said.EMPLOYEE HIRING POLICYThe commissioners voted to put in place a Town of Oxford Hiring Policy and Procedure Guideline. Costigan said that last March, he proposed that an ad hoc committee of citizens be formed to develop this policy. He said the ad hoc committee met multiple times to look at best hiring practices in other jurisdictions and create a policy for Oxford."I feel that their work product is fair, balanced and will meet the town's needs going forward," Costigan said.Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin voiced her concern with a line in the policy that states applicants need to disclose any familial relationships with current town employees. She questioned whether that is legal to do.Ryan said that, because the town has an existing policy regarding conflicts of interest, she did not have any concerns with the line."I don't think the intent is that, when the applicant discloses (a familial relationship), they would be excluded from the application process," she said. "They're still involved in the application process." Ryan said the disclosure would allow those interviewing the candidate to understand that if there were a subordinate relationship, other revisions would need to be put in place."With that explanation, I think this is fine then," Delean-Botkin said before making the motion to approve the policy.

title: Beach Town Bans Smoking, Eating Cannabis - Pot Now Prohibited on Public Property and in Meeting Places in Chesapeake Beach
author: Marty Madden; mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Beach town bans smoking, eating cannabis - Pot now prohibited on public property and in meeting places in Chesapeake Beach

 October 31, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marty Madden; mmadden@somdnews.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With no comment from the public during a hearing or remarks from the town council during an Oct. 19 monthly meeting, the town ofChes-apeake Beach unanimously passed an ordinance addressing legal cannabis.The new law prohibits the smoking or ingesting of cannabis in several public areas, including town hall, Veterans Park, Bayfront Park, Kellam's Field, boardwalk and town pocket parks. Additionally, the ban includes public areas at local businesses.The ordinance was discussed during the mayor and council's September work session, with it then being introduced during that month's council meeting.Acting upon Maryland voters' approval by referendum of the legalization of recreational marijuana for adults 21 or older, the Maryland General Assembly passed the accompanying Cannabis Reform Act earlier this year."Because I'm a nerd, I probably read that 100-page bill 20 or 30 times," Chesapeake Beach Mayor Patrick "Irish" Mahoney declared during the September work session.After familiarizing himself with the new law, Mahoney told the council he has testified before a state Senate committee and worked with other mayors through the Maryland Municipal League to find ways to comply without ceding total control."Just common sense," Councilwoman Valerie Beaudin said of the ordinance draft. "It falls along the lines ofwhat's already in place" for smoking and vaping tobacco and drinking alcohol.Councilman Charlie Fink said he wanted assurances the ordinance wouldn't result in people "being stopped and frisked.""If you have it in your pocket, that's fine,"Todd Pounds, town attorney, stated.During that same work session the mayor and council discussed a second cannabis-related ordinance affecting the legal sale of the substance within the town limits.Mahoney noted that unlike many other states, Maryland lawmakers declined to consider a "local opt out" for state jurisdictions that don't wish to have cannabis sales within their confines."You're trying to create a wholesome environment," Mahoney said of a prohibition on cannabis sales.The mayor added that the way the state is planning to tax the newly legalized product and distribute receipts to jurisdictions would mean the town would receive "basically nothing."A public hearing on the latter ordinance proposal did not happen at the October meeting.When asked late last week why there was no hearing for the other proposed ordinance, Mahoney told Southern Maryland News that he learned at a Maryland Municipal League meeting recently that the state legislature is planning to revisit the law next session to clear up some of its ambiguous aspects.

title: Candidates Present Issues, Goals at Forum
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Candidates present issues, goals at forum

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1B | Section: News 
 
 1104
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO - Although he is running for mayor unopposed, Greensboro Town Council Member David Spencer showed up for a town council candidate meet and greet Thursday evening, Oct. 26, along with two incumbents, a former mayor, one first-time candidate and one making a follow-up bid.Current Town Council Members Robert Harrison and Pete Brelia defended their records and explained their goals. Joe Noon, who served as mayor from 2011 to 2019 before he was sidelined by a serious illness, wants to get back to work for the town.Greg North, who lost the Sept. 26 special election, was back to claim one of two seats on the council. Jessica Tamika Ortiz was new to the roster of candidates, as is Megan Lord, who did not attend the Oct. 26 forum.Moderating the forum held at the Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company Community Hall was Public Works Director Brandon Cunningham, with help from Community Outreach Coordinator and timekeeper Amanda Weaver and Town Manager Tammy Kelledes.Spencer's mayoral run created an extra vacancy on the council to fill the two remaining years of his term.The two candidates with the highest vote counts will serve a four-year term, while the candidate with the third highest count will serve the two-year term, Kelledes explained.The only Greensboro native, Spencer led the forum by summarizing his 44-year career in law enforcement and his history serving the town and in wider statewide associations.He was elected mayor 2007 and served as a council member for 12 years.Spencer said he would like to see more people attend council meetings and commended Greensboro Police Chief George Paugh and Lt.Lenox Trams for stabilizing and modernizing the police force.He said he wanted to see the town of 1,900 residents as a "clean and safe, family-oriented small community." Ortiz followed Spencer, describing how she moved from her native Philadelphia to Greensboro a few years ago and "fell in love with this little town." She said she wants "to keep the changes going" and help more people "understand what's going on." As an employee with Choptank Community Health System, Ortiz said, "I do speak Spanish, and I would like to be able to help the ones that cannot understand and know what's going on. I've been out in the communities, and I've been seeing that there's a lot of needs with (those with) Creole and Hispanic backgrounds." Both Ortiz and Brelia said they wanted to encourage small businesses to establish and continue in the town, but Brelia said he wanted to see careful control of growth so it doesn't happen too fast.North, a self-employed businessman who has been based in Greensboro since 2019, said, "I love the town of Greensboro." "I have seen a lot of improvements in town," he said. "I still think there's a lot more that we can do We have a lot of very wonderful events, but I just think there's ways we can make them bigger to attract more people to Greensboro." Calling himself "outspoken and strong-willed," North said he would apply the strategic thinking he employs as a business owner and "be a voice for every citizen." North promoted exploring solar panels to lower the cost of powering the wastewater treatment plant, and voiced an idea to investigate the possibility of purchasing electric vehicles for town employees.Town Council President pro tem Robert Harrison has lived in Greensboro for 32 years. He was succinct in his bid for reelection, piggybacking on improvements Spencer listed."I'd like to stay for another four years just to continue the things that we are working on with the town council and town employees," he said.Some of the priorities Harrison listed were resolving issues, overseeing the charter to "make sure that things are being run right," keeping employees happy, obtaining grants, and carefully creating an effective, well-researched budget.He said he feels good about phase one of the Kinnamon Meadows subdivision starting up, but is concerned about town water and sewer issues."We don't want to raise taxes," Harrison said. We have to budget things, but everything - just like everybody else knows - is increasing. We haven't raised water rates for over four years. Taxes have gone down.Doesn't sound like a lot when you're talking pennies on the 100 - it's still lowering the taxes." Harrison said issues look different from the perspective of a council member and dealing with "all these numbers and all the issues that we have gone through over the years." He urged residents to "come to the meetings.That's all I can tell you.come to the meetings and see what goes on." Pete Brelia, who began his career of service as a busboy at the Riverside Hotel on North Main Street, is a graduate of North Caroline High School.A former town police officer, he is a shift lieutenant with Caroline County Emergency Services. He was appointed to serve the council seat vacated by Brandon Cunningham.Calling the town is a "bedroom community" with many residents employed elsewhere, Brelia said he "would like to stay on the council for the next four years to complete the projects" it has begun."We don't have the industry that will support the economy that we need today, so I think we should enhance that environment," he said."We have a lot of water problems.We have a lot of sewer issues. There's a lot of infrastructure under the streets that has to be fixed." Noon, whose cancer diagnosis in 2019 forced his resignation as mayor, received the all-clear from his medical team to run for office.That news was greeted by applause from the nearly two dozen people who attended the forum.A graduate of Queen Anne's County High School, Noon has lived in Greensboro about 20 years. He praised the current council for doing a "great job," especially with regards to town office communication and road paving."I'm not putting my name in the hat because I feel that somebody did something wrong," Noon said."I'm doing it because I love Greensboro." He said he believes strongly in "happy employees, happy citizens.I've always believed that we have to get our employees to their fullest potential." To that end, Noon said, "It's time now to put somebody at the wastewater treatment plant" because of the town's current and future housing growth.He advocated sending "some people to school and get them to be a grant writer.Let's get this free money out there. Let's lower the spending out of taxpayers' pockets." For more complete biographical information on the candidates, visit the Greensboro, MD Facebook page or contact the town office.

title: New Park Seeks to Welcome Public to Easton's Waterfront
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
New park seeks to welcome public to Easton's waterfront

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 704
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Turning a former industrial site into a public park takes a lot of vision, according to officials from the Town of Easton.But as the Easton Point Park nears its completion, more than three years of planning are beginning to take shape."Before it was a dump and a highway you couldn't cross," said Kody Cario, project manager for the Town of Easton. "Now we are going to have a traffic light. We are going to have the trail. We are going to have the park, boat ramp. It is really incredible progress down here, and we are planting trees." The land used to take oil delivered by boat. Now, it is the home of Easton's only public waterfront park on the Tred Avon River, thanks to bond money secured by the town in 2020.The park spans 12 acres of waterfront at the end of Glenwood Avenue. Over 150 trees have been planted, and benches were installed to invite visitors to take in the surroundings. The new gate marks the main entrance at Flood Avenue.Easton Point Park is just one part of a series of projects costing the city $6.75 million in bond funding, which needed to be spent by the end of October, a goal the town was confident they would meet as the month drew to a close.The projects under the bond also included improvements to the Rails to Trails, the North Easton Sports Complex, access to John Ford Park, underground infrastructure for Port Street and several land acquisitions, among others."We were able to do a lot of different things. So there is everything from a new skate park to new field lights for the existing soccer, lacrosse and football. There is a new dog park down Brewers Lane behind the farmer's market. There is Rail to Trails work," said Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh.Though the Easton Point Park was been designed to make the town's waterfront more visitor-friendly, it has not completely lost touch with its roots.Much of the project involved taking old industrial buildings down as part of the bond, said Easton Mayor Megan Cook, but not all of the existing structures were demolished."There is the partnership with Phillips Wharf," Cook said. "So originally in the park design, that building was supposed to come down, but an opportunity to have them here and keep the building, it kind of fell in our laps a few years ago." "Phillips, for one, wanted to come closer towards Easton, where the schools are. They are a water-focused conservation nonprofit that has students." Along with the conservation organization, the new park is home to metal signs displaying environmental messages, courtesy of Jessica Hammond, a senior at Gunston School."We had a Girl Scout project.She just put up signs for a gold award. We worked with her. It is like an Eagle Scout," said Van Emburgh.Down the road, the park will feature a boat ramp that is based on the Town of Newcomb's dual boat access model. There will be more parking here than the boat ramp at Easton Point, officials said.The town is also going to stabilize the shore further with a living shoreline."A living shoreline uses natural marsh grasses to filter water quality - not only the existing water but water runoff. So it filters nutrients and pollutants in two ways then stabilizes the shoreline. It creates habitat," said Cario.Surveying the park's progress, the town officials couldn't help but comment on how much the site had changed in just a few years."So we are going from this to a park. Open space," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook, pointing to a before and after map of the project.She made a point of thanking all the engineers and skilled labor that helped to build it all."This is one of the things we are doing good for the environment and all of that is to the (Town) Council's credit for that as well," said Cario.

title: Planning Commission to Reconsider Lakeside Resolution
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Planning commission to reconsider Lakeside resolution

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 418
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday voted to reconsider an earlier finding of inconsistency on a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment relating to the Lakeside at Trappe development.Resolution 338, introduced in late February by Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke, would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, allowing only 400 residential units to be built.The resolution would mandate that any future expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.In a 3-2 vote in early October, the planning commission found the resolution to be inconsistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan because it referred to a map that needed to be reviewed.However, commissioners endorsed the idea of a phased review and determined its consistency with the comprehensive plan.The maps in need of review are water and sewer service maps for the Town of Trappe.Earlier this year, the Maryland Department of the Environment requested the county submit updated figures for water and sewer service in Trappe with correct classifications for all the town parcels, along with corrected exhibits to Resolution 281 - the original legislation approving water and sewer for Lakeside - to address certain parcels that were inadvertently shown on those maps.At Wednesday's meeting, planning commission member William Boicourt, who initially moved to find the resolution inconsistent with the comprehensive plan at the Oct. 4 meeting, said that while he recognized the issues with the maps, the commission still endorsed the resolution's basic principles.Given that the planning commission would be talking with the county council about other pending Lakeside legislation, Boicourt said he thought it was appropriate to reconsider the resolution's consistency in discussions with the council - a sentiment others agreed with.A joint work session with the county council and county planning commission on all of the Lakeside comprehensive water and sewer plan amendments is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 20 at 4 p.m.The planning commission will hold a special meeting with its attorneys and county staff on Wednesday, Nov. 8, at 9 a.m. to formulate and clarify its questions ahead of the Nov. 20 workshop.

title: Easton Town Council Passes Six-Month Cannabis Moratorium
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council passes six-month cannabis moratorium

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 334
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - After brief discussion Monday evening, the Easton Town Council passed a revised six-month moratorium for businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits.The support for implementing the moratorium comes three weeks after a heated discussion ensued on a decision to delay the vote to wait for further input from the town's planning commission.The moratorium, originally introduced this summer as a nine-month ban on cannabis businesses, will place a pause on applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for a business that grows, processes or sells cannabis within the Easton town limits.The legislation was originally slated for a vote in mid-September, but was postponed to mid-October so all five council members could be present to vote.It will also allow the town to consider and adopt a revised zoning ordinance.Easton's existing zoning ordinance already contains definitions and permitted zoning districts for medical cannabis dispensaries and growing and processing facilities, but does not include language on standards for recreational facilities.At its Oct. 19 meeting, the planning commission began discussing specific items to potentially be included in the zoning ordinance, said Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh.Following further discussions this month and in December, the planning commission expects to vote on a set of zoning amendments at its January meeting, according to a letter the commission's chair submitted to the council.The zoning amendments will then need to go through the town council's legislative process, which includes at least one public hearing.Van Emburgh estimated it would take about six months to fully pass the cannabis zoning legislation.That estimation prompted Council President Frank Gunsallus to propose an amendment to shorten the moratorium to six months, which was passed unanimously by the council. A unanimous vote on the amended moratorium followed.The planning commission will continue discussion on the zoning requirements for adult-use cannabis dispensaries at its Thursday, Nov. 16 meeting.

title: 'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In August, everything came to a head at Altair Apartments.Trash piled high outside the apartments on Greenwood Avenue for an entire week. Broken water heaters and air conditioners couldn't be fixed. Even the internet stopped working.Resident Rodaisia Brummell said she felt disgusted."It felt like we were abandoned," Brummell said. "Like they didn't really care about us." The reason for these conditions: its new California-based management company, FPI Management, hadn't been paying all of the bills since taking over the property in April.Property Manager Judkya Murray said that overtime, vendors stopped showing up, causing trash to build up and plumbing to remain broken.She said the problem was all caused by one person at FPI Management, who has since been let go. That one person wasn't paying the bills to keep everything at Altair running. FPI Management could not be reached for comment."I was literally sitting here pulling my hair out because we had no internet," Murray said. "We had no phones. I couldn't call anybody.I couldn't email anybody." At the time, Murray was the assistant property manager acting as the property manager. The previous property manager had left for another opportunity, Murray said.The week the garbage trucks didn't show, Murray remembers the garbage being so plentiful that the building's maintenance worker had to take garbage cans from inside the building to fill with the overflowing trash outside."We were trying to do everything we could possibly do to keep the trash contained somewhere," she said. "It was just too much trash." The building's staff was quitting left and right."Nobody really wanted to leave but it's like, the conditions - you have no choice but to leave," Murray said.Even Murray quit.However, in about three weeks, she was back."The senior director of FPI (Management), she actually reached out to me one day," Murray said. "She was like, 'Can you please come have lunch with me.'" At the lunch, Murray explained why she quit and said the senior director told her they were already working to let go of and replace the the person within the company that hadn't been paying the bills for months.With that conversation, Murray agreed to come back in early October, this time as the official property manager.Having a boss who pays the bills has made Murray's job easier since coming back, she said. But she still has a significant list of to-dos and goals, especially because so many people quit a few months ago.In mid-October, Murray said she has hired a new assistant and interviewed a potential new maintenance worker."And if we hire him, we'll just need one other maintenance guy and we'll be fully staffed," she said. "Once we're fully staffed, everything flows perfectly." Murray also has some big picture goals in the works to increase occupancy and create new community programming.She is working to increase the property's occupancy rate by filling the vacant apartments. Of Altair's 144 total units, Murray said 20 are vacant. She hopes to bring the occupancy rate from 86% to 94% by the end of the year.While the waitlist of applicants is "a mile long," Murray said maintenance has to get the apartments fixed up and ready before new residents can move in.PROBLEMS PROMPT RESIDENTS TO LOOK ELSEWHEREWhile Murray is taking applications to fill apartment vacancies, Millie Lewis and her husband Willie are filling out applications for other apartments in Cambridge. After more than 40 years of living in the Altair Apartments, the Lewises are tired of dealing with the problems.Recently, they dealt with the outcome of a recent water leak, which affected their kitchen, living room and bathroom. In all three rooms, water spilled out from the ceiling. In the kitchen and bathroom, water filled in the ceiling lights.The edges of the carpeting against one wall in the living room has turned from beige to rusted brown.For years, even before the leak, the carpeting in Lewis' bedroom has been coming undone from the floor.Lewis covers these spaces - where pockets of air separate the carpeting and the floor - with small area rugs. She said Altair won't fix this issue, even though she has complained about it.Although the ceilings were patched up by maintenance following the leak, it took weeks and a citation from the city for the mold, which grew from one of those patched up spots in the bathroom, to be removed.Lewis has COPD and asthma, which made her even more concerned about being in a home where there is mold in the bathroom that she and her husband use everyday."I pay my rent every month," she said. "Before I'm supposed to pay it.Why can't the head people do their job? Why can't they pay? Why can't they take care of what's got to be taken care of at these apartments hereft" Lewis isn't the only resident looking to live elsewhere.Tieonna Wisher, who has lived at Altair for three years, said she has already filled out an application for another apartment.She has concerns about how long it takes for management to respond to problems.Wisher has a hole in her wall that she said management hasn't done anything about for months."They keep saying they're going to come in here," she said.Wisher remembers one day when she unplugged a cord from a socket in her home and it sparked and caused half of the lights to go out in her apartment."They told me to call the emergency number," she said. "Call it and nobody answers. Go to the office.Like, nobody wants to do nothing." Brummell, who has lived at Altair for over a year, said she has also started submitting housing applications.In the time that she's lived here, Brummell has experienced a months-long leak in her bathroom and a leaking dishwasher. She said that when her dishwasher was leaking, all maintenance did was drop off a shop vac. She has yet to receive a working dishwasher.It took about three months before Brummell could get someone to fix the leak in her bathroom. She said that gnats are still flying around the apartment because of it.A mother of two young kids, Brummell has noticed her children keep getting sick. She fears it is from the building. The one time she saw mold in her home, a previous property manager told her to spray it with bleach."That's all she told me to do," Brummell said.THE CITY's INVOLVEMENTTo get problems solved, Brummell said she has started reaching out to the City of Cambridge. She said this has been effective because code enforcement can fine Altair for property violations."A couple weeks ago (workers hired by management) came in and painted and fixed my stuff that was supposed to be fixed," she said. "Only because I called the City of Cambridge.Because, if I didn't call them, it wouldn't have been that." Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said a goal of the city is to solve quality of life issues."That's not always going to be possible from the outside of homes," he said."We need to get people to the point where (residents) trust us and they are contacting us and they're aware of their tenants rights and they're ability to call us about issues they're having with their rental homes and their apartments." Hesson said they have been able to do this at Altair and are "still very present." Since August, Hesson said communication with upper management has been satisfactory. He said they shared an action plan with multiple items they plan to address. As of Nov. 3, Hesson said he was still waiting to see if they are following that plan.Hesson clarified that communication with Altair's on-site management "has always been pretty good." Murray said she is making sure that she stays in communication with the city."I know their biggest thing is nobody was communicating anything back to them," she said about the city. "They just need to know if somebody's on top of (a problem)." With all of the issues at Altair, Brummell said residents are paying rent and not getting the services they should be getting as tenants."Everything's being prolonged," she said. "But ya'll want things from us. You want rent money from us.You want us to go in the house at a certain time. But we're not getting the things that we properly need."

title: Elections Board Audit Finds Ineligible Voters, Security Issues
author: Tommy Tucker; Capital News Service
content:
Elections Board audit finds ineligible voters, security issues

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tommy Tucker; Capital News Service | Page: 11 | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - An audit released Friday found that the Maryland Board of Elections did not report for more than a year its findings that people voted or tried to vote more than once in the 2020 general election - well after the results were certified, according to The Office of Legislative Audits.The state elections board identified 134 voters who voted more than once and 1,371 voters who attempted to vote multiple times in the 2020 general election, but it did not report these individuals to the The Office of State Prosecutor until April 2022, the audit said. The audit is part of a routine physical compliance audit of the SBE conducted every three to four years."Definitely the (reports) for the 2020 general election were significantly late and I think they indicated that was due to staff turnover within their office," said Matthew Streett, an assistant director for the Compliance and Performance Audit Division of the OLA. "They reported them after the election results were certified." In the July 2022 primary election, the audit found, the elections board identified four individuals who successfully voted multiple times and 263 voters who attempted to vote multiple times, referring the information to the state prosecutors office in a "timely" manner.Election integrity has become a high-profile issue with former President Donald Trump and his supporters repeatedly challenging the outcome of the 2020 presidential election.The audit also noted that the elections board could enhance its procedures to fully identify deceased or duplicate voters. The audit identified 2,426 "potentially deceased individuals" whose voter registrations were active and 327 individuals with potential duplicate voter registrations."We're just pointing out areas where they can improve," said Streett. "The information they're getting from the Maryland Department of Health was not fully complete and accurate, so they were missing out on a certain pocket of deceased individuals." The Health Department could not be reached for comment on Friday.The audit also found deficiencies with the state elections board's security and control over its information systems, but did not go into detail for security reasons. The department's response to those concerns also was redacted from the report.The elections board did agree to implement the recommendations, but disagreed with several findings.The State Board of Elections could not be reached for comment on Friday.The current Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis took the helm in June 2023 after longtime administrator Linda Lamone retired.

title: MDOT Talks Investments in Talbot County
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
MDOT talks investments in Talbot County

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 784
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - State, county and local officials packed the meeting room at the Talbot County Free Library Tuesday afternoon to hear the latest updates on the Maryland Department of Transportation's investments in county projects.The visit to Talbot County capped off another leg of the department's statewide tour discussing its sixyear Draft FY 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program - a $21.2 billion investment into creating a safer, more accessible transportation system.The meeting, hosted by the Talbot County Council, featured Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul J. Wiedefeld and representatives from various state agencies.State Highway Administrator William Pines spoke about his agency's efforts to improve infrastructure and safety at several high-traffic locations within Talbot County.The agency initiated a $1.5 million study of Route 328 to assess safety and capacity improvements along a 1.6-mile stretch between U.S. Route 50 and Black Dog Alley. Delays are seen in this area from turning vehicles and queueing at signalized intersections, and there are limited pedestrian and bicycle facilities, Pines said.A public meeting on the Route 328 project is tentatively scheduled for this winter.Other transportation improvements within Easton include a $600,000 project for new lighting at the intersection of Route 50 and Route 322 (Easton Bypass) to improve visibility and safety, signal improvements and pedestrian upgrades - including a Rails to Trails link - at Route 322 and Glenwood Avenue, and a new signal at Route 50 and Chapel Road that will be activated by the end of November.In 2024, SHA will begin construction on two additional projects: reconstructing the signal at Route 50 and Route 309 and upgrading the flashing signal at Route 331 and Black Dog Alley to a full signal.Two local trail projects are also receiving federal and state grant funding, Pines said.$48,000 will go toward the final design of a 1.25-mile extension of the St. Michaels Nature and Bike Trail, and $30,000 will go toward the study and preliminary design of a rail trail connecting parks in Oxford.Turning to public transit, nearly $1.1 million in operating and capital grants are being allocated to support Delmarva Community Transit.$225,000 of this will fund preventative maintenance and two new small buses, said Travis Johnston, the Maryland Transit Administration's local transit support director.Delmarva Community Services will also receive $123,000 to install a propane filling station for future propane-powered vehicles, enabling DCS to transition to a low-emission fleet.Additionally, $24,000 in highway safety grants were awarded to the Talbot County Sheriff's Office and the Easton Police Department.Turning to the skies, the Easton Airport's runway improvement program is receiving $525,000 from the Maryland Aviation Administration to support the initial phase of construction.THINKING DOWN THE ROADLocal officials also weighed in on a number of priorities and problem areas they hope the transportation agency will address in the future.Discussions on traffic surrounding the proposed new regional medical center site off of Route 50 were top priorities for state legislators, the county and the Town of Easton. Rick Van Emburgh, Easton's town engineer, said he wanted to work with the county and the state on a regional traffic plan to handle the impact on local roads and infrastructure.Cheryl Lewis, Oxford's town manager, raised questions on the agency's response to flooding on the causeway and pedestrian safety in a town with few sidewalks.Queen Anne Mayor Philip Starkey asked if the agency would reevaluate fixing the bridge between the towns of Queen Anne and Hillsboro, which floods every time it rains, he said.Accessibility was raised as an issue in St. Michaels. According to Town Administrator Rob Straebel, all but one of the town's ADA ramps are not in compliance due to poor work from a contractor."I'm not sure what the way forward is, and I'm not here to point fingers or to blame anyone or to place culpability on anyone," he said. "But there really needs to be a sense of urgency to get this project rectified as soon as possible before our tourist season starts in the summer of 2024." Pines said the state was working to develop an "aggressive schedule" to get the project over the finish line.Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-37) further emphasized the need to fix the ramps, noting that Route 33, as the main road running through St. Michaels, doesn't just serve town residents, but residents of Claiborne, McDaniel, Sherwood and Tilghman.Several Royal Oak residents in attendance also raised concerns about the width and safety of Route 329 (Royal Oak Road), asking the transportation officials to lower the speed limit."I wish I could do everything that everyone asked immediately, but we will keep chipping away," Wiedefeld said, closing out the meeting.

title: St. Michaels Talks Tax Rates at Commissioners Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels talks tax rates at commissioners meeting

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 848
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - At a meeting Wednesday, the Commissioners of St. Michaels spoke about gathering stakeholders to discuss the town's tax rates.The discussion followed an issues brief sent to the commissioners from the St. Michaels Historic District Residents Association.The issues brief argues that St. Michaels, "a small tourist town with a tourism economy," is largely supported by its residents, rather than its businesses."The infrastructure needed to support Talbot County's and the town's tourism economy imposes a heavy tax load on St. Michaels homeowners, while those who benefit most are taxed the least, or not at all in the case of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum," the issues brief states.At the meeting, Commission President David Breimhurst said he was glad that the Historic District Residents Association is offering to be part of the solution. He suggested getting all stakeholders from every aspect of the community together to talk and see what they can come up with."I don't think it needs to be 'us against them' or adversarial in any way," he said. "Just to have a calm, adult discussion about where we stand." Dan Spiegel spoke on behalf of the St. Michaels Historic District Residents Association at the meeting Wednesday.He summarized some of the points made in the issues brief and named the four steps the group hopes the commissioners will take:▪ Begin a period of study and assessment of the tax options other towns use to raise revenue from business activities.▪ Engage with the Maritime Museum to urge they make a payment in lieu of taxes to the town.▪ Hold public hearings to discuss any plans that may develop.▪ Look at current residential property rates to determine whether they are "fair and appropriate," in the case that the town raises additional revenue from businesses.Spiegel said that most of the money the town uses to fund services and maintain its infrastructure comes from property taxes.He said that, based on data gathered from the state, there are 81 business structures that pay property taxes in town, compared to 796 homes and non-business structures."In other words, only 9% of the property taxes are paid by businesses," he said.Spiegel said that although Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is the "crown jewel" of the town's tourist economy, it is tax exempt and does not make any voluntary payments directly to the town. These types of payments are known as payments in lieu of taxes, or PILOTs."Many universities and colleges pay PILOTs to towns because of their use of the infrastructure and other things that impact the town," he said. "The museum makes no PILOT payments." Spiegel also said money generated by businesses does not stay in the town. He said that 97% of the town's commercial buildings are owned by non-residents and more than 90% of the business operators who rent the buildings are also non-residents."So non-resident landlords, business operators and employees spend their money elsewhere because there are very few normal types of businesses that they can spend money on that would attract their dollars," he said.After Spiegel spoke, Commissioner Tad DuPont said this conversation has already begun."You're stimulating a conversation, but it has started," he said.DuPont said that with the changing tourist economy, St.Michaels needs to change with it and be ahead of it.Commission Treasurer Al Mercier said he could envision multiple areas where the town could generate more revenue, including a tourism tax, an alcohol tax, an accommodations tax and parking meters."These are nine or 10 things that I think we need to put on the agenda going forward," he said.During public comment, Kristen Greenaway, president and CEO of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, talked about what the museum pays the town, including an annual event fees tax, and what services it offers residents.She said the museum offers free after school and summer programming for local and Talbot County youth, free museum membership for St. Michaels' youth and free entry for locals with passes that can be obtained at the library.Greenaway said the taxes on The Crab Claw restaurant property, which the museum is purchasing, will still be paid, as it will remain zoned as maritime commercial.Spiegel said the Historic District Residents Association is not anti-museum or anti-business."This is an informal group of residents that were organized, that live in the historic district, that are concerned about the future of St. Michaels," he said.John Marrah, a property owner in St. Michaels, said he enjoyed the Historic District Residents Association presentation."It's important that people think they're treated fairly from a taxation standpoint," he said.Marrah added that business and property owners are taxed "with no representation" in St.Michaels. He said that might be something the town should look into."I own properties in town, but since I don't live in town, I can't vote," he said. "I pay property taxes like everybody else."

title: Talbot County is green with gratitude
author: Staff Report
content:
Talbot County is green with gratitude

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Report | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Operation Green Light for Veterans, hosted nationwide by the National Association for Counties and the National Association of County Veterans Service Officers, invites counties and other government entities to show support for veterans by lighting buildings green each November.While the official time for green lights is Nov. 6 to 12, this year, residents and visitors alike may have noticed that local government buildings have been lit up green for the last few weeks.Talbot County and the Town of Easton chose to start their campaign early, according to officials."Talbot County is home to many veterans, and we appreciate everything that they have done to keep our country safe here and abroad," said Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan."Operation Green Light allows our community to show its support to veterans in many ways not just lighting up buildings in green, but also sharing resources for veterans, promoting the work of veterans in our community and sharing stories across the Mid-Shore." The county encouraged employee veterans to share their experiences from time in military service as part of the campaign."It's been a humbling experience to be able to read about (our veterans') greatest triumphs as well as challenging moments from their time in service," said Sarah Kilmon, communications manager for the county.The stories will be shared on the Talbot County Government's Facebook page."We are grateful for individuals who chose to serve then and continue to serve now as county employees," said County Manager Clay Stamp. "Veterans have unique skillsets and values, especially in leadership, that makes them important members of our team. They bring different perspectives, and that is invaluable to our efforts to serve our community." At their Oct. 24 Council Meeting, the County thanked Mid-Shore Behavioral Health and local veterans groups for their efforts to help our veterans and officially proclaimed Nov. 6 to 12 as Operation Green Light week. MSBH and Maryland's Commitment to Veterans also highlighted several local resources for Veterans and their families.MSBH connects individuals to mental health services and assists with referrals to behavioral health options for Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot County. They are ready to assist veterans with specific mental health needs and can be reached at 410-770-4801 or info@midshorebehavioralhealth.org.Maryland's Commitment to Veterans connects service members to needs and resources in their area. Veterans can reach out to their hotline to request assistance on services like housing, healthcare and employment at 1-877-770-4801.This week, the groups have been highlighting resources and promoting stories of veterans across the entire Mid-Shore region online, and they encourage businesses and individuals to share the information with the local community.Talbot County businesses, residents and organizations are encouraged by local officials to light their buildings green and share their own resources and stories for veterans on social media using the hashtag #OperationGreenLight.
