title: Naked truth about Lakeside: It's based on a lie
author: DAN WATSON
content:
Naked truth about Lakeside: It's based on a lie

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAN WATSON | Section: Columns 
 
 2168
 Words 

 Read News Document

 So here is the naked truth about Lakeside that everyone now knows: Talbot County's approval of that huge, billion-dollar subdivision was based on a bald lie, fictitious and as empty as the weavers' loom that wove the emperor's new clothes.Contrary to what was represented by the developer, before adoption of Resolution 281 in 2020, the entirety of Lakeside had never, ever been classified by Talbot County for any sort of development at all — meaning it had never been reviewed with regard to roads and schools and traffic and public safety or its impact on Talbot's rural character.
Like beanfields all over Talbot County, that land was simply designated "unprogrammeed" … not just "the southern 40%." All of it.
But approval of Lakeside was predicated on the falsehood that this unseemly project, no matter how incompatible with our Comprehensive Plan, had been considered and slated for development by Talbot County long, long ago. The developer's point was clear: OK'd earlier, it would be unnecessary and wrong — unfair, in fact — to subject it to another round of review. And so Lakeside got the green light.
THE RECOGNITIONFor over two years, key supporters inside the county continued to back the developer's false claim that the county had slated Lakeside for development in 2002, mocked the very idea that the land had been "unprogrammed," laid out numerous false proofs that the project had been reviewed long ago. After all, the real history was buried away in old documents no one would find, and so the county could get away with accepting as true whatever colorful story the developer wove, no matter how gossamer the thread.
But today both the Maryland Department of the Environment and all of Talbot County know the truth. By "all of Talbot County," I mean the county attorney, the county engineer, the public, members of the Public Works Advisory Board, planning commissioners and County Council members — whether all five acknowledge it publicly or not. The Lakeside land was never approved or even slated for development in years gone by, and in 2020 the developer essentially dodged the legally required review for consistency with our comprehensive plan.
We were conned.
MDE: Last Spring, MDE directed the County to adopt a new Trappe Area Sewer Service Map (the key development document) to correct mistakes made when Lakeside was approved in 2020. MDE confirmed the County's admission that "Map 23" showing Lakeside as UNPROGRAMMED was the proper map, and that reliance on another exhibit ("Map 24") had been a mistake all along. And MDE told the County to correct the mistakes that had been made "including the Lakeside development." In other words, face the truth.
TALBOT COUNTY: The County Engineer wrote MDE last Spring that Map 24 "has created a huge mess," and on numerous occasions since has confirmed that "Map 23," on which all of Lakeside is shown as UNPROGRAMMED, was always the correct Map to use. In responding to the MDE directive, the County Attorney, no doubt with support from elsewhere, seems to The Talbot Integrity Project ("TIP") to have done everything possible to dodge, obfuscate, and avoid the truth and its obvious implication, including drafting legislation that is about as opaque as possible. But finally, eight months after MDE's directive, Mr. Lesher introduced a proposal that compelled the County Attorney to put this simple truth in a recital to Amendment 1 to the Resolution (R348) that is now on the table:
WHEREAS PRIOR TO RESOLUTION 281's ADOPTION BY THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND FINAL APPROVAL BY MDE, FIGURE 23…DEPICTED THE LAKESIDE PARCELS AS "UNPROGRAMMED…"
There you have it. The Emperor stands naked before us. Even the County Attorney, perhaps the key defender of Lakeside, says it's so.
THE TRUTH SHALL SET YOU FREE! Well, maybe.
Given that Talbot County and MDE both acknowledge that the basis for the county's approval of Resolution 281 (and the reason it did not receive a proper review) was, let's say, a "misunderstanding." (in legal parlance, "fraud, surprise, mistake or inadvertence") One might think that mistake would be rectified as fully and directly as possible.
It's simple, really: change the Sewer Service Map to its status before adoption of Resolution 281 to the full extent possible (i.e., but for homes already completed). It's what MDE directed the county to do — fix the mistakes made when adopting the Sewer Service Map in 2020.
Resolution 281 never purported to change the southernmost 40% of Lakeside, and since all of Lakeside was unprogrammed before, that portion remains unprogrammed now. Don't pretend otherwise. And the sewer classification for the rest of Lakeside clearly was changed without proper review, because of "fraud, surprise, mistake or inadvertence" — so change it back, but for the homes already built.
This is the path that about 850 citizens have advocated since last May, having signed the petition still circulating online by the ad hoc Citizens' Committee to Fix Lakeside.
But instead of simplicity we have an opaque mess that pretty much assures that few will fully understand what happened and why until long in the fog has lifted, if ever. It appears at present that a 3-2 majority of the County Council is reluctant or downright unwilling to modify anything that will affect what the developer got out of Resolution 281, con job or not.
That is pretty remarkable.
Three resolutions (R338, R347 and R348) and four separate amendments are on the table so far. They are difficult to follow conceptually and textually. They interconnect and overlap. Depending on what happens to Resolution 348 (and its amendment), Resolution 347 could become moot or require wholesale modification. Map 24 is not eliminated, even though on May 9 MDE requested just that. Important details are buried in a way difficult to see. (e.g., elimination of the "approximately 84" house limit for houses discharging waste into the antiquated Trappe sewer plant).
Formatting is hard to follow. Some recitals are untrue. Resolution 348 purports to limit the Planning Commission's state-granted legal authority even to review the Lakeside property, for "fraud, surprise, mistake or inadvertence," but then Amendment 1 requires the commission to do just that. In a comment to a recent Spy article, a gentleman called it all "word salad". The Star Democrat's reporter Natalie Jones accurately described Mr. Lesher's introduction of the most recent amendment, but after reading the article can you understand how it all fits together?
Stand by for possible further amendments as the council ties itself in knots, trying desperately to pretend even now that the Emperor looks fine.
THE DECISION MAKERSOnly a majority of the County Council can adopt a resolution, but the Planning Commission is the real decision-maker here.
Talbot citizens should recognize that Planning Commissioners and the members of the Public Works Advisory Board (who provide advice on public infrastructure) are in a somewhat awkward spot. Council members are politicians, but members of the Publc Works board and the Planning Commission are not. They want to do what's right on the merits, of course, but no one likes a rocking boat — and no one is anxious for discord with county leadership. Still they have seen the evidence themselves, and now, with MDE's directive and the county's acknowledgement of Lakeside's unprogrammed status pre-Resolution 281, they all surely realize the truth: that in 2020, Resolution 281 was approved only because of the "misunderstandings." Yet it is also clear that some council members (and others they will continue to work with in coming years) are very adamant that Lakeside should not be curtailed in any way.
What to do?
The Planning Commission is the most important link in all this because the commission must first certify any resolution or amendment as "consistent with our Comprehensive Plan" in order for the County Council legally to adopt it. The Public Works Advisory Board advises the commission on infrastructure … and not just water and sewer, but on roads, schools and other public facilities — areas never evaluated in 2020.
The commission and Public Works board are having a joint public work session to review and discuss this whole set of issues at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, Feb. 7, in the Bradley Room at the Courthouse, and the discussion should be of considerable interest.
The Planning Commission does not itself draft or adopt legislation, but they can refuse to find consistent anything that they know is improper, and they can also clarify what a Resolution should include in order to be found consistent with the Comprehensive Plan.
TIP of course is self-aware that over a period of 33 months its advocacy has been not only direct, but sometimes edged towards the strident…which can be counterproductive. That is regretted, but it evolved in the struggle not just to find the truth, but to overcome incomprehensible resistance from some authorities to recognize how the process of approving this billion-dollar deal was corrupted. This is no NIMBY effort, but focuses on the integrity of Talbot County's land use approval process, the character of Talbot County in both senses.
TIP has gone to extraordinary lengths to assure that its claims are backed by actual evidence, hard facts, original documents (e.g., hyperlinks in this letter accessible on the paper's on-line version). Last September TIP delivered to the Planning Commission a letter detailing how Lakeside violates innumerable aspects of the Comprehensive Plan, with a 40-page appendix including transcript excerpts, photos and so forth. That important elucidation of how Lakeside is inconsistent with our Comp Plan has gone unrefuted—in fact, it has not even been discussed, forgotten in all the jockeying about whether the Planning Commission is even authorized to revisit Lakeside issues. TIP also authenticated on-line the whole sordid twenty-year history of Lakeside approvals, and even at this late date remains anxious to meet with any County official, Commissioner, or PWAB member to answer any question that remains.
THE RAMIFICATIONSHaving already acknowledged that prior to Resolution 281 all of Lakeside was actually unprogrammed — so had never before received proper review — the new Sewer Service Map of course should revert to its status before Resolution 281 was adopted (but for land underlying existing houses). The project can be resubmitted in its entirety or in phases, for proper assessment by the Planning Commission when the developer thinks he can demonstrate that it is consistent with our comprehensive plan.
At that point, Talbot County's integrity is restored, proper process in reinstituted, the comp plan honored. Talbot's 37,000 citizens are the beneficiaries. It's what should happen.
Yes, there are plenty of ramifications that fall on the developer. His plans are in disarray. He will have to circle back and actually demonstrate to the Planning Commission for the first time that his development scheme, revised or not, is consistent with the county comp plan. Timing. Schools. Roads and traffic. And yes, even sewerage.
Meanwhile, the developer did get MDE to approve a 100,000-gallon-per-day treatment plant that is under construction. It will serve the homes already built and whatever comes later at Lakeside. The developer's engineer, Rauch, already generated an engineering report on how that plant could treat wastewater in the existing town, which is so much in need of relief. Indeed, in November the town formally adopted that concept as its current policy, and perhaps this turn of events will make the plan even more feasible.
But whatever the repercussions, consider this when balancing the interests of 37,000 Talbot citizens with that of the poor developer: It was the developer's agents who wrongly claimed that Lakeside had been slated for development when in fact it was not. Who never mentioned that Talbot County's only prior review of Lakeside resulted in its rejection 5-0 by the County Council. It was the developer, again through the hard work of his engineer and lawyer, who in 2006 obtained sewer construction permits knowing full well the County had not classified the property "S-1" for immediate development as legally required…and then in 2020 held out those improper permits as evidence that Lakeside had been approved previously.
The emperor is naked. Because of a false premise Lakeside was never properly reviewed for consistency with the comprehensive plan. The right thing is to revert the map to the status quo ante, before adoption of Resolution 281, except for homes already built. When the project is resubmitted, as-is or modified, it can then be properly evaluated, including by the Planning Commission for consistency with the comprehensive plan in accordance with statutory standards.
Dan Watson is the acting chair of the Talbot Integrity Project. He lives in Easton.

title: CWDI and Dorchester County Council not in violation of Open Meetings Act
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI and Dorchester County Council not in violation of Open Meetings Act

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Maryland's Open Meetings Compliance Board has found Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. and the Dorchester County Council not in violation of the state's Open Meetings Act for a Nov. 13 closed meeting held by CWDI.In its opinions delivered Feb. 1, the OMCB stated that CWDI was not in violation of the act because it is not a public body. It did not find the County Council in violation of the act because the council did not go into a "meeting" at the Packing House Nov. 13.
At the meeting, which brought together city and county officials and development consultants, CWDI justified going into closed session using two exceptions listed in the Maryland Open Meetings Act: "to consider a matter that concerns the proposal for a business to locate, expand, or remain" and "to discuss a matter where public discussion would adversely impact the public body's proposal process."
CWDI, a nonprofit that was formed by the City of Cambridge, Dorchester County and the State of Maryland, has been tasked with planning and developing space along the Cambridge waterfront, known as Cambridge Harbor.
Plans include public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said that during the meeting, CWDI talked about business deals it is working on.
Before CWDI entered into closed session on Nov. 13, WHCP reporter Jim Brady and Star Democrat Executive Editor Jim Johnson objected to the meeting being closed to the public.
Following the meeting, the Star Democrat and WHCP sent a complaint to the OMCB, alleging nine potential violations of the Open Meetings Act, including that the agenda topics were not consistent with the exceptions CWDI used to justify the closed meeting. The complaints were directed toward CWDI and the Dorchester County Council.
Although City of Cambridge staff and elected officials were also present at the November meeting, the Star Democrat and WHCP did not allege violations regarding the city's involvement in the meeting.
City Council voted against going into closed session at the Nov. 13 meeting, and one commissioner left so the city would avoid an Open Meetings Act violation.
OMCB OPINIONSAccording to the Feb. 1 opinions document, the OMCB found that CWDI didn't violate the Open Meetings Act because the non-profit is not a public body, and the act only applies to public bodies.
To determine whether CWDI could be considered a public body, the OMCB looked at how the entity was created and how its members were appointed to the board.
"As we have said before, '(p)erhaps the Maryland General Assembly might decide at some point to broaden the definition, so as to encompass all entities that carry out public functions,'" the opinions document says.
Leonard said he was not surprised by the decision made by the Compliance Board. He said it affirmed what CWDI "has said since it's beginning" — that it is a private corporation set to a public mission.
The reason CWDI listed the Open Meetings Act exceptions before going into closed session, he said, was to make CWDI's public partners feel comfortable.
"We list those exceptions, although we're not required to," Leonard said. "It's something we've done as a courtesy out of respect for our public partners since the beginning."
Brady, who objected to the Nov. 13 closed meeting, said it would be good for the state legislature to review what is considered a public body.
"I just find it unfortunate and unfathomable that an organization that's spending that kind of public money and ruling over that kind of land is not open to the public," he said.
The OMCB found that the Dorchester County Council didn't violate the Open Meetings Act because the Nov. 13 "gathering" wasn't a County Council meeting.
According to the opinions document, although all members of the council attended the gathering, the question was whether the Council "convened to consider or transact public business."
The OMCB said it could not conclude the gathering was a meeting based on the record presented.
"As we understand it, then, the Councilmembers attended the gathering to receive information, but the discussion was not a step in the Council's decision-making process regarding an item that was certain to come before the Council," the document says.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he was glad to see the decision that was made.
"There was never an intention for the Dorchester County Council to be violating any confidence of trust," he said.
In its opinions, the OMCB noted that "the appearance" of business being secretly conducted doesn't "serve the purpose" of the Open Meetings Act to "increase the faith of the public in government."
"Our conclusion in no way condones the action of a quorum of the (Councilmembers) in creating what was, at the least, an appearance of impropriety," the board said.

title: Easton Town Council Approves Changes to Zoning Code
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Easton Town Council approves changes to zoning code

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 425
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council voted Monday to approve an ordinance making several changes to the town's zoning code.Although Town Planner Lynn Thomas characterized a majority of the amendments as "housekeeping" at a public hearing last November, one particularly notable change concerning middle housing types was ultimately removed from the approved version of the ordinance.
The final ordinance removed a previously proposed amendment, which would have changed some missing middle housing types from permitted via special exception to outright permitted uses in two residential districts, the R-7A and R-10A districts.
Middle housing units are multi-unit or clustered types of housing that bridge the gap between single-family homes and garden apartment building complexes, according to the existing code.
Duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and townhouses, among others, are defined as middle housing in the town.
The decision to remove that amendment came after a number of comments in November and a workshop with the town's planning commission in January.
Residents who commented in the fall expressed worries about increasing density and keeping the historic nature of the area intact.
At the Jan. 16 workshop, planning commission members requested the change to use classification for middle housing types be removed to allow for the development of a more comprehensive proposal for addressing a range of housing issues, including missing middle housing types.
Considerations that remain to be addressed include infrastructure needs and ways to work with developers to build more diverse housing, in terms of size and price points, according to Jennifer Dindinger, the chair of Easton's planning commission.
Though most middle housing types are only permitted by special exception in the two residential districts, cottage courts are already allowed by right in the R-7A district. Duplexes, either side by side or stacked, are allowed in both districts.
Contentions were also raised in November about the ordinance changing how quickly planned unit developments must begin construction after final approval, raising the time limit from two years to three years.
Extensions on PUD approval can be granted by the planning commission if requested at least 60 days prior to the PUD's expiration date.
Expired PUDs could also be considered for reinstatement by the planning commission with further documentation and analysis, and reinstated developments will expire two years after the approval of the reinstatement.
At Monday's meeting, council members asked for clarification on the reason to increase the time.
Further developing and receiving approval for engineering plans, along with lining up financing, can make the progress of a planned unit development take close to, if not more than, three years, Thomas said.
The final approved ordinance did raise the limit to three years.

title: Commissioners Introduce DAF Storage Legislation Package
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Commissioners introduce DAF storage legislation package

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 973
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — In an effort to address citizens' concerns about the storage of industrial waste products, the Caroline County commissioners introduced four resolutions establishing temporary moratoria.The moratoria, commissioners said, will give them time to study the issue and establish county regulations.
At their Feb. 6 meeting in Denton, the commissioners introduced the four pieces of legislation, each addressing a particular aspect of a problem that surfaced at the end of 2023 and culminated in a Jan. 23 public hearing that attracted hundreds of citizens and special interest groups.
The four resolutions have a common purpose of protecting "the public health, safety and welfare of Caroline County residents and visitors."
Legislative timelineCounty Attorney Stewart Barroll explained the lengthy timeline that includes two readings and a public hearing.
Each of the temporary moratoria have an effective date of 10 days after their adoption, or March 8, to be in effect until Nov. 1.
Public hearings on each moratorium will begin at 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, Feb. 27, at the Health and Public Service Building, Room 111, 403 S. 7th St., Denton.
The proposed moratoria also will be reviewed by the Planning Commission at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Feb. 14, at the same location.
"We have to go through a legislative process to make sure that this stands up should we be challenged in court," Commission President Travis Breeding said, admitting the process is "painstakingly slow."
While state legislation was introduced Feb. 5 in Annapolis to establish an industrial sludge utilization permit through the Maryland Department of the Environment, the language of House Bill 991, cross-filed with Senate Bill 1074, was not discussed during the commission meeting.
Four moratoriaAt the Jan. 23 public hearing on the first iteration of legislation to address the issue, most attendees were concerned with their health — breathing the "stench" emitted from stored DAF residuals, pathogens possibly leeching into well water and waterways, and the increase of flying insects and the possibility of their carrying diseases.
Resolution 2024-004, finalized on Feb. 5, focuses on a temporary moratorium on the "certain use of land or structures for storage of biosolids in Caroline County not permitted by MDE (Maryland Department of Environment)."
Biosolids is defined as "treated sewage sludge that meets the standards" for two classes of sewage sludge, according to the Maryland Code of Regulations.
Resolution 2024-005 addresses the "certain use of land or structures previously permitted for the discharge or storage of vegetable processing waste/wastewater and other specified substances."
The commissioners are authorized "to impose a moratorium on any activity governed by Zoning Chapter 175" or other chapters regarding the "issuance of permits or zoning certificates."
The commissioners also want to review the County's comprehensive plan and public laws "to consider the re-purposing of land or structures previously permitted for the discharge or storage of vegetable processing waste/wastewater for storage of any material or substance not generated on the lot for public health and safety concerns for the storage of this material."
Concerns had been raised by citizens about material being trucked in from outside the county and stored. This resolution addresses land and structures "previously permitted for discharge or storage of vegetable processing waste/wastewater, vegetable plant residuals/residue, non-contact cooling water and boiler blowdown for the storage of any material or substance not generated on the lot," defined in Chapter 175 of the Caroline County Code.
The focus of Resolution 2024-006 is the storage of "any material or substance other than livestock manure in a structure designed and/or permitted for the storage of livestock manure in Caroline County" and "the use of land or structures to store livestock manure which is generated at another location."
"This is not an argument with the poultry industry. This is not an argument with the many, many people who grow chickens on their farms," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "But in my opinion, delivering material that's generated at a poultry processing plant that is not even located in this county and bringing it here as a way to dump it and get rid of it is not what we're going to do."
Resolution 2024-007, revised Feb. 2, will supersede the original draft Resolution 2023-025. It tracks the same language in the original moratorium on the storage of food processing residual and DAF residual.
The commissioners again cited a Maryland Code of Regulations regulation to define food processing residual and DAF residuals, which is an "organic byproduct material created at an animal processing facility or rendering facility."
This moratorium "shall not prohibit storage at the processing location where legally created, nor a farmer or farming business from temporarily storing food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in a mobile, closed container for no longer than 45 consecutive days during the application process, provided that the stored material is applied to the same land on which it is stored."
State vs. county rolesPorter said it was "amazing" to him that "no government agency claims responsibility for storage of this material."
"You can't put a blow-up pool in the state without somebody telling you how many feet it has to be from somewhere, but this falls through the cracks," he said.
"Some residents are concerned as to why we are researching," Breeding said. "Well, some of the research is around what state agency regulates different aspects of this industry, and we have to make sure that we're not occupying a space that's already occupied by a state agency or we will be preempted."
Porter assured the public "Caroline County is an agricultural county. It always has been, always will be. I don't want anyone to leave here thinking that, with all these moratoriums … we're going to wave some kind of magic wand, and you're never going to smell anything again. When it's planting season, you are. We're going to address this important situation, but there are going to be noise and odors and traffic and combines. That's Caroline County."
To read the proposed House legislation establishing an industrial sludge utilization permit, visit mgaleg.maryland.gov/2024RS/bills/hb/hb0991F.pdf.

title: Denton Leaders Discuss Resilience, Upgrades
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Denton leaders discuss resilience, upgrades

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Among the agenda items discussed during the Denton Town Council meeting Thursday, Feb. 1, were flood resilience, expanding water and sewer to West Denton and providing town law enforcement officers with enhanced portable radios.Two ordinances were introduced and received unanimous consent to move forward.
Ordinance 751 would amend the code's subdivision code to allow shared access for minor subdivisions and improved right of way, which is not a component of the town, county state or federal road system.
In Ordinance 752, the town council amended the town code with two updated official zoning maps that align with the Comprehensive Plan adopted Dec. 11.
In December, the town council adopted the 2020 Comprehensive Plan, following a process that had been held up during the Covid pandemic.
The council green-lighted the first step in working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency in Philadelphia to receive free technical assistance through a memorandum of understanding.
Town Administrator Wayne Getchell said his "key takeaway ... will be that (FEMA) will come on site and do a needs assessment in our areas that we struggle with flooding in and around the Choptank, and develop an action plan that would be consistent with their grant program."
The second step would be to apply for FEMA money "to make whatever improvements are found to be made," but the 3-year MOU "was required by them to get started," Getchell said.
Crisfield is the only other town on the Eastern Shore who is working on a similar MOU with FEMA, he said.
The council approved the purchase of new portable radios for the Denton Police Department.
Bacorn asked the council to approve the purchase of 16 Motorola portable radios, 13 for officers, two for office staff and one to have on hand as a spare.
The radios will replace the 6-year-old BK Technologies radios "which have been failing regularly and without warning, which causes safety concerns," McNinch said.
Bacorn said the old radios were unreliable, and "as of late, they have been feeling, and they don't give any warning. We've had officers out on traffic stops who couldn't be contacted, on calls where they couldn't be contacted."
Bacorn said up to 75% of the $107,425 pricetag could be covered by grant money from the US Department of Agriculture. Even so, Getchell said ARPA (American Rescue Plan Act) funds were available, enabling the town to commit to ordering them. It will be Bacorn said the "backbone of Caroline County's radio system is a Motorola system. The compatibility is just better, the features are much better. So we're looking to upgrade and, more importantly, increase officers' safety."

title: 'Cambridge is Working:' City Staff Talks About Plans at Council Retreat
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'Cambridge is working:' city staff talks about plans at Council retreat

 February 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 682
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council and city staff looked both back into the past and forward into the future at a Council retreat Feb. 5.At the retreat, city officials reviewed the city's goals — which were determined a year ago — talking about the progress that has been made and what still needs to be done.
The first half of the meeting was dedicated to short presentations by city department heads, detailing the programs, initiatives and projects that they think contribute to the city's goals. The department heads talked about programs and projects that have already been started or completed, as well as those that are still in the works.
Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout called the written reports the department heads prepared, along with their presentations, "excellent."
"Turning Cambridge around is not something that is done on a dime or is done in a month, or six months, or a year or even many years," he said. "It is hard work that the staff has clearly put itself to — not only in preparing these documents, but in showing us what has been happening over this past year and what we look forward to in the coming months."
The city's goals, established last year, are to:
Be inclusive, consistent and fair retaining, assisting and attracting businesses with consistently applied rules and processes.Improve the City of Cambridge's organizational efficiencies and effectiveness.Create a more beautiful City with better and healthier housing, improved gateways, a vibrant downtown and a sense of pride within the City staff and the community as a whole.Engage Cambridge's youth and foster meaningful work for young adults.Develop improved infrastructure, long-term projects and capital plans, including the preservation and restoration of the old City Hall structure at 307 Gay Street by 2026.
The initiatives and projects brought up by department heads at the meeting ranged from upgrades to the city's camera systems and sidewalks to improving housing through the Homeownership Works pilot program and the creation of a land bank.
City Manager Tom Carroll said the city is in the process of implementing the government software, OpenGov. City staff hope this software will improve efficiency and accuracy when it comes to things like code enforcement, work orders and permitting.
City Engineer Carl "Bucky" Jackson talked about upcoming projects to resolve sewer issues in the city. These projects include the replacement of the West End sewer, located in the lowest lying area of the city at Water Street and Hambrooks Boulevard, and the replacement of the Trenton Street Pump Station.
Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd talked about its priorities with community-oriented policing and plans for focusing more attention on high-crime areas. Todd also talked about goals to implement more technology in policing. He mentioned wanting to start a drone program.
Rescue Fire Company Chief Adam Pritchett talked about recruitment being a focus this year. He said the fire company wants to start its cadet program back up and get back into schools to try to recruit the next generation of firefighters.
After the presentations, Rideout and commissioners discussed how to make these efforts known to residents.
"How do we get this information out to everyone else so they understand all the complexities, all the hard work that goes into this on some kind of a simplified basis?" Rideout asked. "Because I think its important for the community to become more engaged and to have a better understanding so that maybe they won't come and start picking on this one little thing when they know there's so much more that's being done."
Commission President Lajan Cephas said the phrase "Cambridge is working" comes to her mind when thinking about how to approach this.
"Because I know everything is working," she said. "We have a great city. We have great department heads, great employees, a great city manager. ... I guess to answer (Rideout's) question, is maybe if we have some sort of movement that says 'Cambridge is working.'"
Cephas said its important that the council recognizes city staff is short-handed and overworked.
"So I think this year should be more of a year of trying to complete what we've started in the previous couple of years," she said.

title: A Long Way to Go: No Decisions Made on Pending Lakeside Legislation
author: Natalie Jones
content:
A long way to go: No decisions made on pending Lakeside legislation

 February 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 1211
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although the Talbot County Planning Commission and Public Works Advisory Board have yet to make final decisions on the pending Lakeside resolutions, a joint work session Wednesday showed that uncertainty still remains.Both bodies stressed that the work session would not yield any final or binding decisions — it served only as an opportunity to work out lingering issues with Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 prior to separate recommendations from each board in future meetings.
But from the cross-table conversation in the Bradley Meeting Room, it was clear that more discussion remains before the boards can make a recommendation or finding on consistency with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
While the lack of action won't impede the Talbot County Council's planned public hearings on the legislation and its amendments at its Tuesday, Feb. 13, meeting, it will delay the council's consideration and vote.
The delay further extends the nearly yearlong process of answering the Maryland Department of the Environment's requests for clarification on some specifics of the Lakeside at Trappe development.
RESOLUTION 347Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units at Lakeside. Across all six phases of the development, 2,874 equivalent dwelling units are planned, with just over 1,200 designated for immediate water and sewer service.
In October, the Public Works Advisory Board voted against recommending the adoption of Resolution 347. The board declined to reconsider that decision in December.
But at a January meeting, the board was asked if they would be in support of the second amendment to Resolution 347.
The amendment would add language from the still-pending Resolution 338, which proposes amending the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit.
Expansion of the development's new wastewater treatment plant would require a change to the county's comprehensive plan.
Public Works Advisory Board Chairman Tom Lane referenced the board's previous recommendation that the council adopt Resolution 338, saying if the language from that resolution was incorporated into Resolution 347, it would give the county a chance to review the new wastewater treatment plant.
"It's a great chance to take a breath," he said. "...Knowing that going ahead, we can start working with what this is going to be, and really looking at the impacts and everything so we won't have a big problem five years from now … so it just seemed like a logical thing."
But to Brian Schmidt, the acting president of the Trappe Town Council, Resolution 338 and Resolution 347 should stand on their own, separately. And in his view, MDE's requests to the county were just addressing clerical errors, he said.
"Honestly, I don't understand how 347 has quite gotten to where it is," he said.
Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's town attorney, emphasized the town's position against both Resolution 338 and the amendment to Resolution 347, saying they treated Trappe differently than any other community.
"The Town of Easton has had 1,700 residential units developed since 2002 without a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment and could have another 2,500 without a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment," she said. "But you're telling Trappe to come back at every 400 to review those things that Easton would have the same impact on?"
Planning Commission member William Boicourt agreed that verbiage in regard to the county reviewing the development was in the wrong resolution, but still stressed its importance.
"I think that the ability to bring it to the county to review at the various phases of the MDE permit at 100,000 gallons is so important; if that's the only place we can get it, I'll take it," he said. "But I agree, there's an apples to oranges aspect."
Ryan said the lengthy process with approving the resolutions was a part of Trappe's concerns.
The town provided information on the number of equivalent dwelling units in the development, along with the maps attached to Resolution 281 — the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for the Lakeside development — to the county last July, and the legislation still isn't approved, she said.
Countering her, Planning Commission Vice Chair Chip Councell said confusion still remains with the southern portion of Lakeside's property, which has made the process longer. And the Commission needs to be sure of its decision, he said.
"Once the Planning Commission finds it consistent and the county council adopts it, there's no turning back," he said. "So, I think that's where we are."
To Ryan, the town not being required to come back at every 100,000-gallon expansion would be enough for the town to be on the same page as the county, considering MDE's review of the discharge permit and authority.
RESOLUTION 348The initially introduced version of Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281.
In early January, the Public Works Advisory Board voted against making a recommendation to the County Council to adopt Resolution 348, though it did say it would consider a revised version correctly explaining the differences in the property classifications from Resolution 281 to Resolution 348.
The Planning Commission has yet to make a finding on Resolution 348 or its amendment.
Most of the concerns with Resolution 348 stemmed from confusion with Resolution 281 regarding the classification of the southern portion of Lakeside's property.
To clarify that, the recently introduced amendment to Resolution 348 explicitly states that Resolution 281's "clear and unambiguous" purpose was to reclassify the northern parcels of Lakeside as immediate priority, while the southern portion would be S-2 and W-2 — priority for service in the next several years.
More specifically, the amendment clarified that prior to adoption of Resolution 281, the comprehensive plan depicted a portion of Lakeside's property as immediate priority for water service, with the remainder designated as unprogrammed.
However, Resolution 281 actually stated that some parcels within that portion were being redesignated from their "current" classification of W-2 to W-1, or immediate priority for water service.
And according to the amendment, prior to Resolution 281's approval, maps of sewer service areas in Trappe showed Lakeside's parcels as unprogrammed.
At Wednesday's work session, County Engineer Ray Clarke confirmed that prior to the resolution's adoption, Lakeside's parcels were unprogrammed for sewer.
Ryan did not dispute Trappe's existing land use map as showing the parcels as unprogrammed, but she said it was "clear" that Resolution 281's intent and purpose were to designate the northern part of the development as S-1, immediate priority for sewer service, and the lower portion as S-2.
Public Works Advisory Board member Cory Buxton maintained that ambiguity remained in Resolution 281's language.
"I think an argument can be made that it remains unprogrammed to this day," he said.
Boicourt said he had a tough time being comfortable with the amendment's assertion on the "clear and unambiguous" purpose of Resolution 281.
The text of the resolution overrode the maps, according to the county's legal team.
Planning Commission member Paul Spies said the commission had never been presented with the option to leave the southern portion of Lakeside as unprogrammed — a statement Ryan countered strongly.
"You could have decided (the map) wasn't consistent, you could have declined it, you could have changed the bottom portion," she said.
Public Works Advisory Board member Ed Sclichter noted the extensive amount of time both boards had spent hashing out the Lakeside resolutions.
"It gets more confusing all the time," he said. "The amount of time — it's extraordinary what we've done for this whole program."

title: Voters Should Decide Who Represents Them in Annapolis
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Voters should decide who represents them in Annapolis

 February 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 654
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the 2024 General Assembly session, discussion is again underway on changing the roles and responsibilities of local Republican central committees and local Democratic central committees.The primary focus of these committees has historically been on recruiting and supporting political candidates.
Under current law, local central committees also have a key role to play whenever a vacancy occurs in the General Assembly resulting from "death, disqualification, resignation, refusal to act, or expulsion of a state senator or delegate, or in the case of a senator's or delegate's removal from the city or county from which he or she was elected."
When that occurs, the local central committee or central committees in the legislative district with the same party affiliation as the departed member are charged with making a recommendation to the governor on a replacement. The recommended individual must have the same party affiliation as the departed member. The governor, in turn, "must, in accordance with specified procedures, appoint a person affiliated with the same political party to serve the remainder of the vacating senator's or delegate's unexpired term."
Such appointments are far more common than one might think.
Of the 188 members currently serving in the General Assembly, almost one fourth were not elected by the voters, but were appointed to fill a vacancy and complete an unexpired term.
Even more vacancy appointments may occur in 2024 if incumbent General Assembly members win bids for other offices and resign from their present office.
Reaching consensus in changes to the current vacancy process has been and is elusive. Presently, there are three proposals under active consideration, each with supporters and opponents.
One proposal would allow central committees to fill vacancies but would require public notice of vacancies and information on a central committee's application and interview process. It would require central committee interviews and votes to be open to the public and central committee members who apply to fill a vacancy to recuse themselves from the recommendation vote.
Another proposal would allow central committees to continue to fill vacancies but subject their recommendations to voter ratification under certain circumstances. Recommendations made in the first two years of an unexpired term would be subject to voter approval in the next presidential election. In the second two years of the unexpired term, the appointed individual would have the option of running in the next state election.
A third proposal would replace the current appointment process with special elections. If the vacancy occurs within the first three years of a term, voters in the district would fill that vacancy through special primary and general elections. If the vacancy occurs within the fourth year, central committees would name an initial replacement who would have to run for election in the next primary election. This proposal requires an amendment to the state constitution which needs a three-fifths vote of approval in the House and the Senate then voter approval in a statewide referendum.
Concerns have been raised about this third proposal based on estimated costs incurred by local and state boards of elections to administer multiple special elections.
The General Assembly is currently discussing a proposed $63.1 billion annual state budget. They also are discussing moving forward on an additional $3.8 billion in new state and local funding for public education over the next 10 years as mandated by the Blueprint for Maryland's Future (the Kirwan Report).
Emily Scarr at the Maryland Public Interest Research Group recently opined that special elections are "the cost of having a democracy. People have [a right] to vote for who represents them. It's a fundamental thing and if we're not spending money to ensure that right, what are we doing?"
I agree.
Now is the time to address the outsized role of political central committees and the governor in the process to fill vacancies in the General Assembly.
The way to do that is a new process that maximizes opportunities to let the voters decide.
David Reel is a public affairs and public relations consultant. He lives in Easton.

title: Citizens Need to Participate in Local Government
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
Citizens need to participate in local government

 February 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 619
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last month, I wrote about how it is important for citizens to be actively involved in government. That means going to city council meetings and reading the agenda and the documents beforehand to understand what will be decided at a meeting. It is also bringing issues of concern to the elected leaders and senior staff, such as the city manager, about your concerns. Sometimes we do not see everything that is happening in the city.The fact that someone raises an issue or a concern with us does not mean, however, that it will be acted on or given priority simply because you raised it. Local governments live with some restrictions. There are state and federal laws that provide guidance and direction as well as local ordinances that have been in place sometimes for years that need to be read, interpreted, and followed or changed.
Local governments also have to live within the budgets set each year and the funding that it receives from local homeowners, businesses, and state and federal grants.
The local government, through a retreat process of other direction from its city council or commissioners has established the priorities of what is to be done during the year. That does not mean that other things can't or shouldn't be done, but it does mean that what you want done immediately may not be done immediately or may have to wait for funding or staffing to happen first.
As part of how any government works, there are meetings beyond the city council meeting. In Cambridge there are several that address important issues about how some of the basics of government are done. They include the Historic Preservation Commission, Planning and Zoning Commission, Cambridge Utilities Commission, Traffic and Safety Committee, the Police Advisory Board, and the list goes on.
You can find a list of them at https://www.choosecambridge.com/201/Boards-Commissions.
These boards and commissions should be having public meetings with public notice of when and where they will be held. An example of their importance is the Police Advisory Board that received in January a report from the police chief on the final crime data for 2023 that showed some progress in crime reduction from prior years. Every other month we learn about all of the great work that our police department is doing to keep the city safe and address the crime that occurs here.
Another is the Cambridge Utilities Commission meeting in late January that helped me to have a more complete understanding of the current challenges that exist, especially with our sewer system, some of which has been in place for over 90 years.
It is from these types of meetings and the hard work that city staff does that come the staff recommendations and proposed department budgets that become the city budget that will give direction to the work done in FY 25 and beyond. Your attention to these meetings is as important as coming to city council meetings or emailing me or a commissioner about a complaint you have. The reason is that through these meetings and staff work the commissioners of Cambridge make the sometimes-difficult decisions about how much to spend to run the city and how much higher your taxes must go in order to pay for what needs to be done not what we all might want to be done.
I know that everyone cannot and will not come to all of these meetings. As I mentioned before, the Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods is a great group to join and support. They are at many of these meetings but would, I am sure, like to have volunteers to help with the other meetings that are addressing other important issues.
Can you be someone that will help?
Stephen Rideout is mayor in Cambridge.

title: Planning and Zoning Commission Approves Plans for Cambridge Harbor Promenade Extension
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Planning and Zoning Commission approves plans for Cambridge Harbor promenade extension

 February 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 491
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission approved the preliminary and concept plans for an extension of the wharf promenade at a Commission meeting Feb. 6.The application was submitted by Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.
The promenade extension is part of a larger project to develop space along the Cambridge waterfront, known as Cambridge Harbor. Plans include public spaces, a boutique hotel and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River.
This extension is the first construction phase of the Cambridge Harbor project. It will make it so that the existing promenade along the wharf, next to Yacht Maintenance, stretches around what is known as Lookout Point and to the Franklin Street boat ramp.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the promenade will be 20 feet wide with a 6-foot band of landscaping and bio-retention swales on the sides of the path.
In a memo about the design, City Planner Emeritus Pat Escher expressed concern with the width of the promenade and planters. She wrote that she believes the design should be wider.
"The promenade may be used for craft fairs, art and music events, etc.," Escher wrote. "The additional width will provide the vendors and performers with an adequate width to set up their venue."
Escher also said in the memo that the promenade could become part of a city-wide bicycle route, and if it does, a wider promenade would accommodate pedestrians and cyclists safely.
During the Commission meeting, Leonard said the width of the promenade cannot be changed because it has already been agreed to by the U.S. Economic Development Administration. The EDA has awarded CWDI for $2.4 million for the promenade extension.
"If we try to change it now, we can't get the funds and we can't do the project," Leonard said about the width of the promenade.
Leonard also said that CWDI's designers believe a 13-foot-wide path is wide enough for two-way traffic, both biking and walking. He said this makes the plan for a 20-foot-wide path "more than enough."
After Leonard and CWDI's civil and coastal engineer, Ken Usab of Morris & Ritchie Associates, spoke about the project, Commission Chair Mary Losty asked if the city engineer had reviewed the plans.
City Planner Holly Baldwin said the city engineer's comments had been addressed with CWDI during the creation of the plans. Usab said he and Leonard had met with the city engineer and will continue to meet with him.
"We're trying to be proactive and have very clear communication with the city engineer as we go along instead of submitting a plan and having a big issue," Usab said.
The Commission voted to approve the plans with a condition that the plans be subject to any additional comments from the city engineer.
Leonard said that per CWDI's contract with the EDA, CWDI will need to have the bids out for this project in April and have a contract for construction by July.
"So we've got a couple of months to get this (project) through the process of approval," he said.

MICHAELS — Thomas "Tad" duPont has resigned from his position as a St. Michaels town commissioner.According to a memo filed in the town's Tuesday, Feb. 14, meeting packet, duPont submitted a letter of resignation at approximately 4 p.m. Tuesday, Feb. 6. title: Talbot County Council Approves Purchase of Poplar Hill Farm
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot County Council approves purchase of Poplar Hill Farm

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An unsuspecting item on the Talbot County Council's Tuesday evening meeting agenda yielded a significant surprise — the council's unanimous approval for the county to purchase Poplar Hill Farm.Placed on the agenda as a nonspecific request from the county manager to approve a contract of sale to acquire property, the request asked the council to agree to purchase the 120-acre property for $6 million.
The newly approved purchase will take the long-proposed Poplar Hill housing development off the table.
The property is slated for future county use, including preservation of open space in the critical area, according to County Manager Clay Stamp.
The property is bounded to the north by Route 333 (Oxford Road) and to the southeast by Route 322 (Easton Bypass). It's near the Easton Club development, the small Papermill Crossing community and 197 acres owned by the Town of Easton for the Easton Woodland Park.
Council President Chuck Callahan said the council began the process of looking into the opportunity to purchase the property in mid- to late December.
The land was appraised in January, listing with a market value of $6,990,000, Stamp said. Funding for the acquisition will come from the county's fiscal year 2024 capital project enabling legislation, which authorized the county to spend up to $6.1 million on property for county purposes.
Stamp called the council's action to acquire the property "visionary," saying it opens up possibilities to address future needs, including facilities and open space. It also maintains critical areas.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said the previous County Council had eyed a piece of the property for future county facilities, of which there is a "huge need." The property's acreage and proximity to downtown Easton also made it a key purchase.
"I think that this is a really significant and unique opportunity, and I want to express my gratitude for the sellers for approaching us with this opportunity," he said. "This is a really, really significant deal."
One possibility for the site is future county schools, Lesher said after the meeting.
"This leaves the county in the driver's seat for that kind of decision," he said.
Original plans for the property, currently owned by 5001 SHR L.C., were a source of concern for Talbot County residents last year when a developer proposed turning the parcel into a mixed-use development with 456 residential units.
Most concerns stemmed from the developer's request for a critical area growth allocation to reclassify just over half of the property from a resource conservation area to an intensely developed area due to its location within the town's critical area.
The application for the 456-unit development was rescinded last August. A sketch plan for a smaller 119-unit subdivision in the same location was conditionally approved by the Easton Planning Commission in September.
Callahan said the opportunity to purchase the property was a decision the county would be proud of for years to come.
"It's phenomenal," he said. "It's something that we're all going to be proud of, and I'm glad this council chose to do that, that's for sure."
This story may be updated as information becomes available.

title: Governor Visits Cambridge to Discuss Poverty
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Governor visits Cambridge to discuss poverty

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 676
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A variety of Dorchester County leaders were brought to the table Monday afternoon to speak with Gov. Wes Moore following a press conference where Moore talked about the ENOUGH Act.The act, which Moore unveiled in late January, was created to address the root causes of poverty through place-based interventions. According to a press release from the governor's office, this program, run through the Governor's Office for Children, will enable communities that coordinate across sectors and address challenges holistically to apply for competitive grant funding for up to $10 million per year.
During a roundtable discussion at the Harry and Jeanette Weinberg Intergenerational Center at Chesapeake Grove in Cambridge, Moore said he was excited to listen.
"We need for Cambridge and Dorchester and all of the unique institutions here to be able to win if this state has any hope of winning, itself," he said. "And part of the thing we have to do is, we've got to just come and listen."
Moore said this is what the ENOUGH Act is all about.
"Working with each and every one of you, knowing how important you are to this long-term solution and our long-term hope that if we can do this right and we can actually collaborate, that we're going to win," he said.
The roundtable was made up of 16 people: a variety of municipal, county and state officials, nonprofit directors and other community leaders.
Although the roundtable was closed to press after introductions, MidShore Meals til Monday Executive Director Pam Allen said that during the roundtable, Moore opened the discussion to everyone.
"There was no agenda," she said. "We got to say what we wanted to say."
In Allen's eyes, this roundtable laid the groundwork for bringing different organizations and leaders in the community together.
"The key is keeping it going," she said, adding that figuring out what the next step is and how the people at the table can help each other is important.
This is something that Allen is hopeful will continue. She plans to be proactive with this.
"I'm going to make it my business," she said about connecting with other local stakeholders, "I'm going to reach out. ... Even if it's just once a month. Just to check in."
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said there were multiple things that piqued his curiosity at the roundtable, including some of the different programs offered in the county and a need for transportation for children's recreational programs.
"We have a lot of great resources and nonprofits in this county," he said. "I think we need to find a better way to link them all together so they have a common voice and to help direct people that need those services toward the correct service."
Pfeffer said he thinks the ENOUGH Act will give the county resources to link these organizations together.
At the press conference before the roundtable, Moore talked about the importance that the ENOUGH Act will have on the Eastern Shore.
"Together, we will help transform distressed communities into places with top schools, good jobs, safe neighborhoods, quality housing and economic momentum," he said during his speech. "And that includes communities like Cambridge."
Pfeffer said he was excited to hear the governor talk about bringing everyone to the table to join together in helping address these issues.
Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout said that it sounds like Cambridge will be a key place where the governor's office will focus its energy when it comes to reducing poverty. Before the roundtable discussion began, Rideout said bringing Cambridge to the table is "critically important."
"We have to come together as a community and start collaborating with one another effectively," he said.
Lucas Thorpe, executive director of ALL4LOVE, a Cambridge-based nonprofit that focuses on mentorship, athletics, academics and community engagement — mainly for high school-age boys — said bringing support to local organizations in Cambridge is important.
"We have 100 plus nonprofits in the Cambridge area," he said. "Every one of those nonprofits is needed and is important to the work we're doing. And so if we can share support and get support from the state level, then I think that'll be crucial."

title: Caroline Commissioners Pass Bills, Approve Roads Projects
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners pass bills, approve roads projects

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Road paving projects, legislative picks and pans, and zoning decisions formed the bulk of the Caroline County Commission meeting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Feb. 13, in Denton.After a lengthy discussion with Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox and Roads Superintendent Bryan North, the commissioners settled on beginning paving projects for two county roads.
Wolf Road near Henderson and a short dirt section of Jones Corner Road at Concord will be paved with tar and chip, and paid for with leftover American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 funding.
Two roads affected by flooding are awaiting better weather and materials. Fox said he will be getting a purchase order to the commissioners next week for $122,000 to buy the precast concrete needed to improve the River Road site. Unusually high tides have prevented work on Gilpin Point Road, although the replacement pipes are on hand.
Legislative actionsThe commissioners introduced legislation to change zoning requirements for solar energy systems in the R-Rural District, repealing subsections in Section 175 of the county code, and "reenacting the same with amendments." The legislation is Bill 2024-003.
Originally proposed in October 2023, public comment prompted the county Planning Commission to recommend changes. Screening requirements, including working with a licensed landscape architect and providing for a variety of buffers were not changed.
Also unchanged was the restriction on placing commercial solar on the portion of acreage that was used for transfer development rights. Road right-of-way setbacks were increased.
The second reading and public hearing for Bill 2024-003 is set for Feb. 20 at the County Commission meeting. The third reading is scheduled for March 12, with an anticipated effective date of April 26.
Two other pieces of legislation were read for the third time and enacted unanimously. Legislative Bill 2024-001, authorizes additional projects to be funded from the proceedings of the Consolidated Public Improvement and Refunding Bonds of 2019.
The projects are roof replacements for Federalsburg Elementary School, North Caroline High School and Preston Elementary School, as well as a new HVAC system for the Fretterd Center in Denton.
The bond proceeds were reallocated since the commissioners are not pursuing the renovations of the county detention center, anticipating the eventual construction of a regional detention center.
Legislative Bill 2024-002 revised stream buffer requirements for both perennial and intermittent streams, increasing them from 25 to 50 feet.
State legislation
Commission Vice President Larry Porter and Public Information Officer Jennifer Reibly have attended Maryland General Assembly legislative session updates with various groups.
The commissioners will send letters of opposition and directives to the lobbyists to oppose bills that "take away local autonomy" such as House Bill 1407, which would preempt a county's authority to decide if and where to place solar arrays, Porter said.
Porter recommended opposing a statewide school emergency response bill, consulting with the Recreation and Parks Department regarding legislation that would require counties to replace certain playground surface materials and opposing funding cuts to community colleges.
Because the county "has been a catalyst" for lithium battery safety, Porter recommended supporting House Bill 468/Senate Bill 530.
The commissioners discussed other pending legislation. To view the meeting of the commissioners, watch the video posted on the commissioners' website, usually within 48 hours of the meeting.
Agendas, videos and transcripts of commission meetings are posted at carolinemd.org.

title: Dorchester County Council Introduces Rental Registration Legislation, Zoning Code Amendment
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council introduces rental registration legislation, zoning code amendment

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council introduced two housing-related pieces of legislation at its meeting on Feb. 6.The first piece of legislation deals with rental properties. If passed, vacant buildings, short-term rentals and rental units would need to be registered with the county annually.
Short-term rentals are defined as properties that are rented for more than 15 days and less than 30 days.
County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the intent of creating these three different registrations is life safety and property maintenance. She said that with this registration, the county would be able to contact property managers in case of an emergency.
"Right now we don't have anything," she said. "If there's a vacant property out there, and there's a fire and the person lives out of state or out of the area, we have no way of contacting them."
Webb said the registration would also keep property owners accountable when it comes to property maintenance and following county codes and regulations.
"We don't get a lot of complaints about rental properties, but when we do, they're deplorable," she said.
Webb said although code enforcers aren't firemen and policemen, creating these registries and being proactive can help save lives.
Currently, the county doesn't know how many vacant and rental properties there are in the county, Webb said.
"We need to see how many we do have, and how much time and manpower we have to put into these properties," she said.
Because of this, Webb said the Council might have to revisit this legislation in the future to make it stronger.
The second piece of legislation would amend the zoning chapter of the county code to lessen restrictions on residential accessory structures.
Webb said 75% of the county's Board of Appeals cases in the past two years have been for accessory structures that are greater than what is allowed by county code. She said this has incurred more legal fees for the county and made meetings longer.
"We need to make a difference," she said. "I mean we've had some meetings that have gone later than 10 o'clock at night because the agenda's so big."
Webb said she thinks this amendment would provide relief to both property owners and county staff.
If passed, the amendment would make it so that, for lot size of up to 1.99 acres, a residential accessory structure could not exceed 200% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of two acres to 4.99 acres, a residential accessory structure could not exceed 300% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of five acres or more, a residential accessory structure could not exceed 500% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
According to current county code, for suburban residential, suburban residential-RCA, rural residential and rural residential-RCA zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property cannot exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,200 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
For agricultural conservation, agricultural conservation-RCA, resource conservation, resource conservation-RCA and rural residential-conservation zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property cannot exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,600 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
At the meeting, Council Vice President Mike Detmer verified the amendment would not give anyone permission to use the residential accessory structure for commercial use.
"Absolutely not," Webb said in response. "Every permit that comes into the office, I review and sign off on use to make sure that is compliant with zoning."
Council President Lenny Pfeffer said public hearings will be held for both of these pieces of legislation.

title: Candidates File for May Primary Election
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Candidates file for May primary election

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 597
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Voters across the state and on the Mid-Shore will have a full slate of candidates to vote for in this year's upcoming elections.Although 2024 will be marked nationally by a presidential election, Maryland residents will be casting their ballots for a U.S. senator and congressional representative. Locally, Mid-Shore residents will be voting for new county Board of Education members.
Maryland's primary election will be held on Tuesday, May 14, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Early primary voting will run from Thursday, May 2, to Thursday, May 9.
The general election is Tuesday, Nov. 5, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Early voting runs from Thursday, Oct. 24, to Thursday, Oct. 31.
U.S. Senate
The race for the next U.S. senator is a crowded one — 10 Democrats and eight Republicans have filed to run for the seat being vacated by current U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin. Three candidates not affiliated with either party have filed to run.
Several candidates are previous or current elected officials.
Congressional District 1Incumbent Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican, is seeking to maintain his position representing the 1st District. He's not without challengers, though — four others have filed in the hopes of winning the seat.
Blane Miller and Blessing T. Oluwadare, both Democrats from Harford County, filed to run against Harris. Fellow Harford County resident Chris Bruneau Sr. is running in the race as a Republican.
Caroline County resident Michael Scott Lemon, a Republican, is hoping to win the seat.
Talbot County Board of EducationSeven candidates have filed to run in this year's election for the three open seats in District 2, District 5 and District 6 on the Talbot County Board of Education.
In District 2, incumbent Board of Education member and current Vice president Candace Henry is running for reelection to her seat. Residents Connie Loveland and Ann C. O'Connor also filed to run for the seat.
In District 5, current Board of Education member Anna Howie is running for her first full term on the board. Howie was appointed to the District 5 seat last October after former Board President Susan Delean-Botkin vacated the district seat.
Trappe resident Karla Wieland-Cherry is Howie's sole challenger in the District 5 race.
The Board's District 6 seat will be the only one definitely seeing a new face after this year's election — incumbent board member Mary Wheeler did not file to run again.
Easton residents Kerry Gunshenan and Cynthia Marrah Jurrius will face off for the District 6 seat.
Dorchester County Board of EducationEight candidates filed for the three open seats on the Dorchester County Board of Education. Incumbents from each district are running to maintain their seats on the board.
In Councilmanic District 1, current board President Michael Diaz Sr. is running for reelection. Diaz is being challenged by Brandy Dawson Cumberland and Lucas Thorpe.
In Councilmanic District 3, current board Vice President Susan V. Morgan is vying for reelection. Cambridge resident Christine LaMonica is seeking the seat as well.
Chris Wheedleton, the incumbent Councilmanic District 5 board member who was appointed to his seat last year, is running for a full term on the board in this year's election. Candidates Jerome J. Harris and Michael Hartford also are running for the open seat.
Caroline County Board of EducationAlthough the terms of three members of the five-member Caroline County Board of Education are ending this year, only two are up for election by the public: the District 1 and District 2 seats.
A third seat opening up this year will be filled by gubernatorial appointment.
No candidates have filed to run for the District 1 seat.
In District 2, Stefanie D. Johnson is the sole candidate seeking the open seat.
