title: Dorchester County Charter Review Committee Makes Recommendations
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Charter Review Committee makes recommendations

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Following a presentation by the Dorchester County Charter Review Committee on recommended changes to the county charter, the Dorchester County Council wants to hear from the public.At a County Council meeting March 5, the council agreed to hold an open comment period at its upcoming March 19 meeting so that residents can comment on these recommended changes.
The County Council aims to gather thoughts and opinions from residents before deciding which, if any, of these recommendations to include as referendums on the November ballot. This would give Dorchester County residents the ability to decide if any changes to the charter.
During the presentation, committee Chair William Layton said the committee recommends making eight changes.
"The county charter has not been changed since it was written," he said. "So there are a number of things that could be changed in there. We picked out eight things that we thought were most important."
Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer said it's important that the council hear the public's thoughts on these recommendations.
"I feel that we owe the people that elected us, our citizens of our districts, to hear from them what they feel about all this," Pfeffer said.
County Attorney Chip MacLeod said that once the council has decided if they want to move any of these recommendations to the ballot for referendum, the questions will need to be drafted and delivered to the state by the third Thursday in August.
RECOMMENDATIONSThe committee's first recommendation is to add language that solidifies the differences between the county manager's responsibilities and the council's responsibilities. This includes language that says:
The county manager is the only one who can hire, fire and direct employees.The county manager cannot take direction from an individual council member without majority council approval.The county manager must be available full time.The search for a new county manager must begin immediately once the position becomes vacant.If the vacant position is not filled in a timely manner, alternative search measures must be taken.
The committee suggested removing the residency requirement for the county manager and director of finance positions.
Layton said the committee thought it was important for the most qualified candidates to be hired to these positions. He said the committee thinks this gives more flexibility.
Another recommendation the committee made was to require an administrative review to take place the first fiscal year of each new council. Although an administrative review is already required every four years per the charter, Layton said that if the review is done in the third or fourth year of a term, it is useless because a new council will be coming in soon.
The fifth and sixth recommendations the committee made were to change the due dates for the proposed county budget and the adoption of the budget.
If this recommendation is taken, the proposed county budget would need to be submitted by May 15 each year, rather than May 1, and the budget would need to be adopted by June 15, rather than June 1.
Layton said the May 1 deadline for the proposed budget didn't give everyone enough time for comparisons and vetting with budget items, "especially compared to other counties."
To ensure transparency, the committee recommended adding language to guarantee "the most effective means are used to disseminate meeting information."
Layton said the committee wanted to ensure that council meetings continue to be streamed online.
The last recommendation the committee made was to limit County Council members to three consecutive four-year terms. Currently, there are no term limits for County Council members.
"Even within our group, this was not unanimous," Layton said. "But the majority of our group thought that this was something that should be done."
COUNCIL DISCUSSION
After the presentation, council members discussed some of these recommendations.
Council member William Nichols said he is against having term limits.
"You're taking the will of the people away," he said.
Detmer called implementing term limits a double-edged sword.
"You're getting new perspective and losing old knowledge," he said.
Regarding the transparency recommendation, Pfeffer asked about a request made by the committee to provide public access to council meeting documents. Pfeffer said parts of these documents would need to be redacted before the public could see them.
The council also talked about the ballot and how the questions would need to be phrased.
MacLeod said these would need to be "yes or no" questions.
"That's why there's a little bit of wordsmithing that goes into how you phrase these questions," he said.

title: Shelter Seeing Success
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Shelter seeing success

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein | Section: News 
 
 705

 Read News Document

 Centreville — Queen Anne's County animals continue to be in "good paws" as officials presented updates to ensure the safety and wellbeing of those in their care to the Queen Anne's Board of County Commissioners Feb 27.The Queen Anne's County Animal Control Commission (ACC) introduced updates to the Animal Control Comprehensive plan, Chapter 9.
While there have certainly been changes over the years, the Animal Control ordinance has never seen a line by line holistic review of documents such as this before, said Jennifer Nowak, commission chair.
"It needed a major upgrade," she said.
Revisions were especially needed to make the ordinance more applicable for animal control cases, Nowak noted. The extensive revision includes housekeeping items and definition changes to make the documentation flow better.
Updates to the animal control ordinance include three full document reviews, hundreds of hours of work and strong collaboration from officials including Animal Control, emergency services and animal services, according to Nowak.
A public hearing regarding the ordinance is expected at the commissioner's March 26 meeting.
In other business, Queen Anne's County Animal Services (QACAS) presented 2023 overviews and 2024 projections to the county commissioners.
Animal Services Chief of Services Kelly Hamilton presented a year in review and projections for the shelter moving forward.
The shelter continues to lead the way in providing care care for forlorn animals of the Eastern Shore with an impact stronger than ever, she said, it was a very successful year of diligent volunteers, engaging events, and successful community support and 2024 only looks to continue.
The organization considers itself a quintessential No-Kill Shelter of the state of Maryland and the Eastern Shore, Hamilton said, with the Live Release Rate determined by the number of animals leaving the shelter via adoption, returned to the owner or transferred to another shelter.
The national standard to be considered a No Kill Shelter is 90% and with a 94.6% rate, QACAS is proud to be one of 12 such shelters in Maryland, she said.
A total of 1,324 animals entered the county's shelter in 2023, whether as strays, seized or transferred in, a 29% increase from 2022, according to Hamilton.
Through QACAS, 679 animals found their "furr-ever" families in 2023, she announced.
Nearly 900 surgeries were performed onsite ranging from routine neuters, to life saving procedures.
The shelter has ramped up its social media presence including facial recognition software to instrumentally connect owners and pets and help 166 animals find their way back home in 2023.
"It's amazing, the technology is there," Hamilton said.
Hamilton credited volunteers and foster families as the "true heroes" for their tireless dedication to the animals.
"It really takes our team to invest all this time and energy in these animals to get them ready for that adoption floor," she said.

title: Talbot Planning Commission Plans to Draft Memorandum for New Farms
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Planning Commission plans to draft memorandum for new farms

 March 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 519
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Wednesday morning, the Talbot County Planning Commission met to approve local requests and discuss the potential of refining the language for farm-based recreational use properties.The Planning Commission voted to approve the major site plan for Brad and Lisa Bebbe's farm-based recreation use. The Bebbes plan to rent out their farm as a venue for weddings and other events. This was the second time Bebbe representatives met with the Planning Commission.
The first time, they were told to "do more," which Zack Smith, a representative for the Bebbes, described as vague.
"We felt at that time and still feel today we demonstrated compliance with technical requirements of the code for that use," Smith said. "... If you feel like what's in the code today isn't consistent with what that intent was, then maybe, like you discussed last month, (this may be) reason to revisit it and perhaps make some modifications."
The commissioners expressed uneasiness with having a farm's primary function be solely an event venue. The commission wanted the owners to view the farm less as a venue and lean more into agriculture.
Smith shared the Bebbes' plan to add bee colonies to the property.
Smith said that Lisa Ghezzi, a master beekeeper from the Maryland State Beekeepers Association, would establish two bee colonies on the property and invite members of the public to learn about beekeeping and raise awareness of bees' role in pollination agriculture. Smith added that there would be potential to market honey, beeswax and other beekeeping products from the colonies.
The commission voted to approve the application; they saw the beekeeping and education component as positively supplementing the farm-based recreation application.
The commission concluded that this application brought up an essential topic regarding language and intent to the commission. Commissioner Paul Spies expressed concern about setting a precedent by allowing recreational-use farms under the current language of the ongoing code and not focusing on agriculture farms.
The other commissioners agreed that the code should prioritize agriculture as the primary use and profit driver rather than supplemental activities like weddings.
The Planning Commission plans to draft a memorandum summarizing the discussion at the Wednesday morning meeting about refining the language for farm-based recreational uses in the zoning code. The commissioners will forward the memorandum to the County Council for consideration, with recommendations to strengthen language ensuring supplemental uses are genuinely ancillary to the primary agricultural use.
The commissioners said they want to help support working farms and young farmers in the agricultural industry, which can be financially challenging. Spies felt concerned that setting a precedent where the supplemental uses could become the main primary income rather than agricultural could lead to more properties being used primarily for non-agricultural events rather than actual farming over time.
Spies said allowing supplemental income was meant to help farming families, not replace farming as the leading enterprise for these businesses.
"It's hard to be a young farmer, it's hard to start out in the industry, it's hard to maintain organic, but if we gave them (farmers) an opportunity to supplement that income with something, then I could see more opportunities in the industry that I love and support," Spies said.

title: Budget and County Leadership Worries Shared with Eastern Shore Delegation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Budget and county leadership worries shared with Eastern Shore delegation

 March 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With the state facing a budget shortfall in coming years, Maryland counties may see an increase in unfunded mandates.That was the message Maryland Association of Counties Executive Director Michael Sanderson delivered to the Eastern Shore Delegation Friday morning.
He began the presentation by saying that as the counties face many different issues, a state agency is "just never going to have the on-the-ground view" that local governments have connecting with the community and getting input from the people who live there.
Among the causes of concern for straining county budgets, Sanderson said, is the Blueprint education plan, an education bill passed in 2021 that increases annual education funding by over $3.8 billion over the next ten years.
Del. Christopher Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), delegation chair, later commented that the budgets could be similar to what happened in the 2007-2008 financial crisis when teacher pension costs were shifted to counties.
Sanderson warned that the projected state budget shortfalls over the next few years could squeeze county budgets, especially as the costs of fully implementing the Blueprint education plan begin taking effect a couple of years from now.
He said that local governments "don't have a bunch of money" like the state does to push this problem out and call it a "future problem." He said it is urgent for county budgets, mainly because of an existing transportation funding crisis.
Adams expressed his own concerns, saying that the budget that's coming up over the next two to three years will not only be stressful for local officials but may also put them in a position to handle an unfunded mandate.
"The state may or may not have any other choice but to take these education shortfalls, and that's what this budget shortfall is going to be in two to three years. It's all about education," Adams said.
Sanderson warned that the coming economic difficulties will be the first exposure for many local leaders to a situation where their county budget is in trouble.
"About 40-something percent of our local elected leaders only have experienced in the last three or four years with this kind of paper over the economy, healthy state budgets and surpluses and so forth," Sanderson said. "And this will be the first exposure for a lot of them, for suddenly their county budget is in crisis."

title: No End to This Game?
author: Staff Writer
content:
No end to this game?

 March 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox

 Words

 With the introduction of the latest resolution by the Lesher/Melkie team, we again find ourselves at a new beginning in the ongoing attempt to control the growth in the Town of Trappe. Unfortunately, this "new" resolution is nothing more than a repackaging of the same resolutions we have watched the county wrestle with for more than a year with no outcome in sight.Changing a few numbers and giving it a new title does not in any way change the obvious intent of all this legislation, which is to keep the Lakeside development under the control of a minority group with their own agenda. What that agenda is has been unclear but obviously their intent is to drag out the process in any way they can to buy time for more interference.
A recent letter to the Star Democrat went so far as to imply that the Town of Trappe needs to be ready to build schools for the new students from Lakeside. Since when did small towns begin building and paying for their own schools? Isn't that a county function? I thought that's what we pay county taxes for?
The implication was that citizens in Talbot County shouldn't have to educate Trappe children. Does that mean Trappe taxpayers shouldn't pay for schools in other parts of the county? That is not how government works. What next? Does Trappe need to build it's own hospital?
I have paid county taxes for the 25 years since retiring here. I would like to know what my taxes go for. I see many expenditures approved at County Council meetings using funds that include my taxes. Why should I feel guilty when I expect to be treated like any other county citizen?
The Lakeside development is simply Trappe's attempt to make up for years of lackluster or nonexistent growth so that our town can enjoy a tax base that can provide the funding needed to function as a modern, financially stable municipality. The county also will benefit in the long run with additional residential and commercial taxes, more housing for county residents, not to mention jobs to reduce unemployment in the area.
Why doesn't anyone want to look at the positives of a planned development instead of focusing on the negatives? This whole situation has dragged out long enough and doesn't need new legislative smoke and mirrors in an attempt to drag it further. All of this waste of time and resources is an unnecessary cost we should not be forced to bear.
And on a final note, I really want to express my disbelief that Mr. Lesher and Ms. Melkie would insult the intelligence of their constituents by their attempt to blatantly force their old legislation through as something new, just by making such a minute change, which will only add one to three years more to an already time-consuming process.

Trappe

title: State Cities Have Range of Governing Structures
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
State cities have range of governing structures

 March 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 603
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When Gov. Wes Moore came to Cambridge on Feb. 12 to bring awareness to his proposed ENOUGH Act, we heard his vision for how some state funding for youth in poverty and otherwise challenged would come to communities.It is a new and improved way for the state to support the good work being done by communities all over Maryland. It is placing an opportunity and challenge before local governments and the communities they serve that include the faith community, local nonprofits, state and regional agencies, and the business community. That challenge is how do we work better together and identify and collaborate on those human service challenges that we all face but fail, at times, to address as effectively as we can.
At the end of February, I was in Annapolis for a two-day conference of the Maryland Mayors Association. There were meetings, training sessions, visits to the House and Senate, and time to learn from one another about how we can help improve our communities. We heard from Senate President Bill Ferguson the details on several issues of which juvenile justice and housing were probably the most important to our cities.
Some people may look at these conferences differently than I do. I see them as a time to learn about how other communities are doing things differently and maybe better than we are. Having the opportunity to talk with other mayors gave me the chance to give them ideas about challenges that their communities are facing and also learn from them.
One of the most interesting things that we learned about is the many different types of local governments there are in Maryland. We have what are called "strong" mayors and "weak" mayors. We have council-city manager/administrator cities. We have city councils with "presidents" who act as mayors. We have mayors who have a vote on issues; mayors who can vote only if there is a tie vote; and mayors who can veto legislation and those who cannot.
Each Maryland city has developed its own type of governance over many years and at least two are now considering changes. Any change has to come in the way of changing their city charter, which is like their constitution. It is the basic document that says how the city is to be run. In Cambridge, for instance, a group of citizens joined together in 2012 and worked for 2½ years to gather information and convince the City Council to change our government from a weak mayor form to a council-city manager form.
Looking back, it was the right thing to do for the future of Cambridge.
A charter change, for cities, can come from one of two ways — action by the city council or by public referendum. Counties are different in that any charter change must be put up for a vote by residents either after enough signatures have been collected for a referendum or after the county council has placed on the ballot some questions regarding possible charter changes that the public then gets to vote to accept or reject.
With cities, if the city council or commissioners approve changes to the charter, the residents have the right to collected signatures from registered voters within a certain time frame to require a referendum vote by all of the registered voters on how the city council proposed to change the charter.
The above is a short story on this issue but points out, once again, that an engaged public is important to how well your city or town is run, no matter how big or small it is. Get involved. Be involved. Stay involved.
Stephen Rideout is mayor of Cambridge.

title: Trappe Town Council/March 6
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
TRAPPE TOWN COUNCIL/March 6

 March 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On March 6, the Trappe Town Council met and approved construction bids, an easement agreement and a smoke test for Trappe.BUDGET
The council voted to accept Schumer Inc.'s bid for the pumping station construction project, contingent on the U.S. Department of Agriculture's approval.
The pumping station project is comprised of three out of the seven pumping stations around Trappe. The three that are a part of this phase of the project are located on Rumsey Drive, Main Street and Harrison Circle.
The budget for the pump station construction has increased due to engineering and construction contingencies, according to Lyndsey Ryan, town attorney. The USDA has recommended applying for additional funding to cover the cost of the project.
Due to upcoming grant deadlines, Ryan suggested a resolution allowing Town Administrator Erin Braband to sign loan and grant applications with the USDA.
The resolution limits the signature to this specific project for the additional amount beyond Phase 1 that needs to be funded. It would allow her to execute any application and any necessary documents without having to come back to the council.
The administrator would not be authorized to accept the funding on behalf of the council. Ryan said Braband only would be permitted to submit the application for the funding.
The council approved the motion with all commissioners approving except for Commissioner Rosalee Potter. Potter said she was "unsure" of the information provided.
EASEMENT
The council unanimously approved the easement agreement for a new sewer line serving the Dollar General store. This agreement is contingent on either the agreement being revised to include an easement for the existing line or confirming the town already had an easement for that line.
The agreement would allow the town access under both the new and existing sewer lines located on the Dollar General property in the future if maintenance were required. The sewer main will run along Route 50.
Ryan said they would review whether the town already had an easement for the existing line or revise the agreement as needed before final approval.
SMOKE TEST
The Town of Trappe will schedule a smoke test for the sewer system on April 23. This test will help identify infiltration issues and, by allowing smoke to escape, show where there are holes in pipes and clean-outs.
This smoke test is expected to help determine which sections of town should be prioritized for camera scoping of sewer lines. The public works staff would document the locations of any issues found during the smoke test. The overall cost for the town-wide smoke test was estimated to be between $200 and $300.

title: Dorchester County Council Tables Solar Bill
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council tables solar bill

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 513
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council voted to table a bill that would amend a part of the Dorchester County Code that deals with utility-scale solar energy systems at a council meeting March 5.Specifically, the legislation would put a cap on how many aggregate acres in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems. This would mean that up to 1,800 acres of land in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county could be used for utility-scale solar energy systems.
The legislation would also make it so that a 75-foot-wide alive and maintained vegetated buffer must surround the solar energy systems.
This legislation was introduced at a council meeting Feb. 6.
At the meeting March 5, County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the county recently learned the state could be adopting new solar legislation.
"That should be approved or disapproved sometime in April," she said. "Not sure if that would affect anything that we have in this document."
Following a public hearing for the bill at the meeting March 5, Council Member Ricky Travers motioned to table the bill until the council sees what happens in the state legislature.
"I'd really like to defer this bill until we see exactly what Annapolis passes in this session," he said. "I like some of the things that are in it, but I can't see us passing it right now."
Before the county voted to table the bill, three people spoke in opposition of it.
Cambridge resident Charles "Chad" Edmondson said the bill would restrict or hinder the implementation of some solar energy sites "drastically." He said the the aggregate acreage cap didn't seem equitable for the county and for the property owners and tax payers interested in investing in renewable energy.
Leah Meredith, Mid-Atlantic senior manager of the Solar Energy Industries Association, listed multiple factors that a solar developer has to consider when determining where to place a grid-scale solar project. This includes access to a proper power connection, the availability of a utility connection and flood vulnerability.
"Solar development is thus naturally limited by these technical and practical considerations," she said. "And the additional red tape created by (this bill) will make it difficult to economically develop grid-scale solar projects in the county."
James McCullough, a utility scale development manager at RWE Clean Energy — which is currently developing a utility-scale solar project in the county — said the bill would make it difficult to construct projects like theirs.
"(It) would also discourage other companies from investing in the county," he said.
Before the vote at the meeting, Council Vice President Mike Detmer addressed the commenters, saying that he appreciated what they had to say. He said the reason he has been pushing for this legislation is not to prevent solar, but to prevent bad solar.
Detmer said government decisions at the state level could take away the county's ability to consider solar projects on a case-by-case basis.
"That's what we're concerned about," he said. "Is that we're not going to be able to have that case-by-case consideration. That's what we're afraid of. We're afraid of the bad actors."

title: Lane Closures Anticipated During Bay Bridge Redecking
author: Eric Sylvia Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Lane closures anticipated during Bay Bridge redecking

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ERIC SYLVIA Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Phase 1 of the deck replacement on the eastbound Bay Bridge is underway with an anticipated completion date in spring 2025.The first section, on the Eastern Shore side of the eastbound span, is almost one mile of the overall 4.35-mile-long bridge. During construction, the project will utilize off-peak lane closures during the day to get work areas ready to ensure successful night work.
The eastbound span will close at night, weather permitting, with two-way traffic in effect on the westbound span. Crews will remove at least one section of the deck and replace it with a new precast section during the same overnight shift.
During construction, the project will utilize existing off-peak lane closures during the day to get work areas ready to ensure successful night work.
Weather permitting, when the eastbound span closes at night, two-way traffic will be on the westbound span. Temporary joint-connection grates will be utilized for this crucial work, allowing for travel lanes to reopen each morning and for a smoother driving transition across work areas.
While the work is significant, the MDTA has designed the project to limit traffic impacts while maximizing safety for contractors and customers during this crucial work.
Cranes are in place and visible while crossing the bridge. Transportation Authority officials urge drivers to be alert and not distracted by construction.
Work is underway to relocate existing electrical power, communication and fiber-optic lines from the roadway barriers to a dedicated utility corridor.
Relocation of the utilities will not only eliminate the need for temporary relocation during construction of the new roadway deck and barriers; the under deck location will be accessed for maintenance activities without working in a temporary roadway closure.
Installation of the new conduits will be staged from the water, with barges and cranes used to lift material and equipment to temporary under-deck platforms located adjacent to the access catwalk. Almost 10 miles of new conduit will be installed as part of this project.
A top priority of the Transportation Authority is protecting the environment. For the eastbound deck replacement project, the MDTA is using environmentally sensitive technologies and construction practices to reduce environmental impacts on plants and wildlife in the vicinity of the Bay Bridge and beyond. As part of the Maryland Artificial Reef Program, the MDTA will recycle deck panels removed during this project.
These deck panels will be deposited at the existing Love Point artificial reef located in an approximately 20-25 feet deep, 50-acre area in the Chesapeake Bay northeast of the Bay Bridge. It is estimated that approximately 145,000 square feet of deck will be deposited.
A Stormwater Management Plan includes a 1.04 acre pocket pond that is proposed to address the stormwater management needs of the deck replacement project. The pocket pond will be constructed in a grassy area bounded by U.S. Route 50 westbound lanes, Revell Highway, and the ramp from Oceanic Drive to westbound Route 50 on the western shore.
The pocket pond will provide treatment of runoff from existing, untreated pavement owned by the MDTA along westbound Route 50 and improve the hydrology in this area.
As part of the landscape management plan, turf grass will be planted and native grass species will be established around the pond including tussock sedge, pickerelweed, arrow arum, lizard's tail and soft stem bulrush. On the Eastern Shore, an approximately 1.1 acre site will be treated for invasive species and replanted with native species.
Additional information is available at mdta.maryland.gov.

title: 250th Anniversary Proclaimed in Caroline County

content:
250th anniversary proclaimed in Caroline County

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 353
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Historian Chad Dean came to the Caroline Commissioners' meeting March 12 to read a 250th anniversary proclamation for Caroline County.The county was formed in 1773.
"This is very enjoyable to put together as have all the 250th anniversary events so far," he said. "We are hoping to plan and execute many more in the future."
He delved into the history of the early people who created the county.
"Where as a pragmatic acknowledgement of a desire of late colonial dwellers and planters near and along the banks of the Choptank River, Tuckahoe Creek and Marshy Hope Creek to duly enjoy more convenient access to the services of the county seat," they created Caroline County, Dean said.
He went on to read that Caroline was formed on November 5, 1773, from portions of Dorchester and Queen Anne's County. He listed all kinds of vocations that have emerged from Caroline, like artists, doctors and military personnel.
"Now it is hereby resolved that we, commissioners of Caroline County, proclaim March 15, 2024, to be the official commencement of the celebration of the 250th anniversary of this venerated place and encourage all loyal friends of the green garden county to reflect on, participate in and support the many planning events and activities of our Jubilee Year," Dean said.
There will be a VIP celebration of the green garden county on from 5 to 8 p.m., Friday, March 15, at the Museum of Rural Life, located at 16 N. Second St., Denton.
Guest speaker Julie Markin, director of Washington College archaeology, will talk on the topic of "Melville's Warehouse and Barwick's Inn." Beer, wine and hors d'oeuvres will be served.
Tickets cost $50 per person and can be found at donorbox.org/250th-anniversary-vip-event-tickets. For more information, go to carolinehistory.org.
The next day, there will be a St. Patrick's Day event from 2 to 4 p.m. on Market Street from Second to Fifth streets. This family-friendly event will include tricycle races, bowling, corn hole contests, face painting and arts and crafts with the Caroline County Arts Council.
There will be jazz bands from both North Caroline and Colonel Richardson high schools. Market Street will be closed to traffic.

title: Commissioners of Oxford introduce FY2024 amended budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford introduce FY2024 amended budget

 March 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The time to approve budgets is right around the bend for the Commissioners of Oxford.At a town meeting Tuesday, the commissioners introduced an amended fiscal year 2024 general budget and heard from Town Manager Cheryl Lewis on a preliminary draft budget for fiscal year 2025.
At the previous town meeting on Feb. 27, Lewis said she always starts this time of year with going over amendments to the current budget.
"It's almost like a training session for the real budget for the public and commissioners," she said.
According to an amended budget document posted on the town website, the town's revised income for fiscal year 2024 is $5.57 million The original budget listed $6.33 million for income.
The town's revised expenses for fiscal year 2024 was $5.76 million. The original budget listed $6.59 million for expenses.
The revised net income is negative $183,560. On the original budget, the town's net income was listed as negative $252,465.
For fiscal year 2023, the town's revenues were $2.61 million and its expenses were $2.79 million.
At the meeting Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer noted that the town had $120,000 more in investment income this year.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin said she was concerned that legal fees were $30,000 higher in the amended budget than the original budget for fiscal year 2024.
Lewis said legal fees are always estimated in the budget.
"When you have more legal needs than any other year, it's going to happen," she said. "In the last nine months, we've had more legal needs."
After introducing the amended budget, the commissioners scheduled a public hearing for April 23.
PRELIMINARY DRAFT
The Commissioners of Oxford also heard from Lewis about a preliminary draft budget for fiscal year 2025. Lewis went through different capital expenditures that the commissioners will need to consider as they begin the budget approval process.
"Those are the things you really need to pick through and decide what items you think you want to do," she said.
One budget item Lewis pointed out was $20,000 for improvements to the Community Services Building, where the Oxford Town Office, commissioners meeting room and Oxford Police Department are located. Lewis said these funds would go toward replacing the deck on the back of the building and painting parts of the building.
For the police department, Lewis pointed out $68,000 that would go toward replacing or purchasing a new truck for the department and toward furnishings needed for the office.
Lewis said she put $10,000 in the preliminary draft budget to purchase two AED units — one to be placed outside the Community Services Building and one to be placed at the ferry dock.
Lewis said the Public Works Department would like to trade in and upgrade one of its tractors. She said the cost would be between $70,000 and $80,000. Along with the tractor, she said public works has asked to get the shop painted.
Lewis said she added another $10,000 to the budget for public works that could be used to purchase a trailer or to purchase a few smaller items.
For the Roads Department, $150,000 is currently earmarked for a paving project that would include the post office and bank parking lots. Although this project was originally a part of the fiscal year 2024 budget, Lewis said the town would not be able to go out to bid, get a contractor and pay for the project before fiscal year 2025 begins.
Lewis said the Oxford Community Center — which is owned by the town — also asked to be included in this paving project so its back parking lot, which is currently gravel, could be paved.
Lewis mentioned a $100,000 optional budget item to replace water lines under the street. She said the town could earmark money for this in the event that it identifies a real problem.
For wastewater, Lewis highlighted a $200,000 budget item for a backup pump. Lewis also suggested incorporating $100,000 into the budget every year to pay for water lines and sewer lines on an alternating basis. She said this had been set up before the COVID-19 pandemic, but hadn't been continued.
Lewis said she will come back to the commissioners with a date for a budget workshop so that the budget can be adopted by May 31.
In a text, Lewis said the goal is to adopt the budget 30 days before the start of the new fiscal year, July 1.
"It is always possible to have the process carry past that date," she said. "I try to set it up so the commissioners understand their target dates far enough in advance to keep things on schedule."

 VIENNA — The Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration will begin maintenance on the U.S. Route 50 bridge over the Nanticoke River in Vienna this week.Crews will spend the week installing barrier walls on the east and westbound shoulders of the bridge. Further maintenance, which includes bridge rehabilitation and scupper repair, will continue next Monday.
Crews will work weekdays, 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., on first the eastbound lanes and then the westbound lanes.
Motorists can expect shoulder closures and single lane closures while the work is taking place. Weather permitting, the project will be complete by early summer.
In an ongoing effort to improve work zone safety, SHA will deploy the Maryland SafeZones Automated Speed Enforcement system in the work zone on Route 50. Starting next Monday, the Maryland State Police will authorize citations for those driving above the posted speed limit of 55 miles per hour in the work zone.
Drivers are asked to stay alert, stay focused, look for reduced speed limits as well as driving pattern changes and slow down in work zones. Motorists in need may dial #77 on their mobile devices for roadside assistance.
For a list of all major SHA projects, visit Project Portal or the homepage at roads.maryland.gov. For a look at real-time traffic conditions, go to md511.maryland.gov.

Centreville Town Council moves forward with land acquistion

 CENTREVILLE — At their March 7 meeting, the Centreville Town Council approved an ordinance to move forward in acquiring a parcel of land from the Maryland Highway Administration for stormwater management and green space habitat.Located at the bottom of the hill on South Commerce Street, across from the Citgo gas station and next to Hillside, the property is currently owned by the State Highway Administration, who purchased it as part of its mitigation for the Route 301 overpass, according to Town Manager Carolyn Brinkley.
The town has been looking at this property for a while to assist with stormwater management, green space and wetland mitigation, Brinkley said.
Now the state is clearing house, and the town worked with the State Highway through about four different appraisals to acquire the property, Brinkley said.
The State is selling the parcel for about $345,000, which the town will be able to fund almost completely through Program Open Space funding thanks to assistance from Queen Anne's County, she noted.
During the March 7 meeting of the council, no public comment was made, but testimonies in support of the purchase were submitted in writing prior to the meeting.
Next, a letter of intent along with the ordinance will go out to the State Highway Administration, Brinkley said.
The town manager will keep the council informed of the ordinance progress as it moves along to the Maryland Department of the Environment and the Board of Public Works meetings in May.

title: Dorchester County Council Passes Property Registration, Accessory Structure Bills
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council passes property registration, accessory structure bills

 March 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council passed two housing-related bills at its meeting on March 5.The first bill establishes property registrations for vacant buildings, short-term rentals and rental units. These properties and units would need to be registered with the county annually.
Short-term rentals are defined as properties that are rented for more than 15 days and less than 30 days.
At a council meeting Feb. 6, County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the intent of creating these three different registrations is life safety and property maintenance.
She said with these registrations, the county would be able to contact property managers and owners in case of an emergency. Webb also said that the registrations would keep property owners accountable when it comes to property maintenance and following county codes and regulations.
The second bill the County Council passed on March 5 amends the zoning chapter of the county code to lessen restrictions on residential accessory structures.
The amendment makes it so that, for lot size of up to 1.99 acres, a residential accessory structure can't exceed 200% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of two acres to 4.99 acres, a residential accessory structure can't exceed 300% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
For a lot size of five acres or more, a residential accessory structure can't exceed 500% of the building footprint of the principal residential structure.
Before this bill was passed, for suburban residential, suburban residential-RCA, rural residential and rural residential-RCA zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property couldn't exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,200 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
For agricultural conservation, agricultural conservation-RCA, resource conservation, resource conservation-RCA and rural residential-conservation zoning districts, the sum total of residential accessory structures on a property couldn't exceed the building footprint of the principal residential structure or 1,600 square feet, whichever is greater, without a special exception by the Board of Appeals.
At the Feb. 6 council meeting, Webb said the amendment would provide relief to both property owners and county staff. She said 75% of the county's Board of Appeals cases in the past two years have been for accessory structures that are greater than what is allowed by county code, which has incurred more legal fees for the county and made meetings longer.

title: Oxford Holds Workshop on Hiring Practices
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford holds workshop on hiring practices

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 550
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With Town Manager Cheryl Lewis set to retire at the end of June, Oxford residents packed the commissioners meeting room Tuesday evening to hear about hiring practices.The Commissioners of Oxford workshop was moderated by Carol Kachadoorian, an Oxford resident and executive director of dblTilde CORE, a nonprofit whose mission is to advance knowledge about and planning for sustainable mobility and wellness in communities.
Don Borut, former executive director of the National League of Cities, and David Deutsch, a former city manager, were invited to speak about the process of hiring a new town manager.
Borut said a search firm will work with a commission to identify the skill sets that it feels would be most beneficial to its community. He said there are things a search firm does that a town might not get from advertising and hiring for a job position on its own.
These benefits include having knowledge of candidates that would be interested as well as finding candidates that didn't apply but could be a good fit.
"Ultimately, this is about helping you," Borut said. "It's not about someone coming in and telling you what you should do. It's rather providing counsel, expertise and experience that you can draw on to the extent you want."
Deutsch — who is currently a senior associate at Mercer Group Associates, a company that does executive recruiting for local government — explained how this process works. He said this process is generally the same across search firms and said he was not at the workshop to promote his group.
In explaining the process, Deutsch said search firms will first hear from a commission on the qualities and traits they would like to see in a new town manager. From there, that search firm will create a brochure that describes the town government, community and position. Deutsch said this brochure is then used as the main advertising piece.
The value in using a search firm, he said, is that a firm will go beyond local advertising.
"I've had some luck, for example, advertising in the Virginia Municipal League and the Pennsylvania Municipal League for Maryland positions because of our geographic proximity," he said.
Along with this, Deutsch said, search firms have databases of potential candidates.
After Borut and Deutsch spoke, Commissioner Katrina Greer asked how a search firm might engage the public.
Deutsch said he would take guidance from the commission. He gave an example of one experience in another municipality where they held a community meeting.
Commission President Tom Costigan asked about the cost of these services.
Deutsch said most public sector recruitment firms have a fixed price contract that they negotiate at the start of the process. He estimated that most firms would charge somewhere in the mid-$20,000s.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin asked Deutsch if he had an idea of the number of applicants they would provide the town with.
Deutsch said that for a national search, he would like to see 25 to 35 applicants.
Delean-Botkin also asked if they use any instruments, like the Hogan Values assessment, to evaluate candidates. Deutsch said there are methods of evaluating, and if the commission requested that, it would be an additional fee.
During the regular meeting that followed the workshop, Greer asked to discuss at the next meeting the possibility of using a recruiter to recruit the next town manager. Costigan said they can discuss that.

title: $425 Million Added to Purple Line
author: Sapna Bansil Capital News Service
content:
$425 million added to Purple Line

 March 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 570
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore and the state's chief financial officers approved nearly half a billion dollars in extra funds for the Purple Line on Wednesday, even as they condemned the embattled project's mounting delays and escalating costs.Nearly seven years after construction began, transit authorities returned to the Board of Public Works yet again this month, this time seeking an additional $425 million for the light-rail project. It was the fourth such request since 2016 to supplement the Purple Line's original $5.6 billion budget.
Following the three-member board's unanimous but reluctant approval, the total cost of the Purple Rail is now approaching $10 billion.
"Not anyone in our administration is happy that we find ourselves, once again, in a position to have to increase the cost of this project," Moore said.
"Competence is a basic ask of the people of this state," he added, "and we are still cleaning up this mess from years of mismanagement on this project."
The 16-mile east-west line, designed to run between New Carrollton and Bethesda, is being built through a public-private agreement with the Purple Line Transit Partners. The group is responsible for constructing, operating and maintaining the system until 2057.
The administration of Moore's predecessor, former Republican governor Larry Hogan, brought in private companies to work with the state on the project. The public-private partnership, known as a P3, was part of an effort to mitigate the cost burden on taxpayers. But the project has endured a number of issues, including significant construction delays and disputes with contractors.
A spokesperson for Hogan offered a different critique after Wednesday's meeting.
"The Purple Line doesn't need to be 'fixed,' it needs to be finished — and for the good of the region, that should be the sole focus of everyone involved in the project," said Mike Ricci, a spokesperson for Hogan, currently a candidate in the Republican primary for U.S. Senate.
"We recognize Maryland Democrats are in full panic mode about Governor Hogan's campaign, but turning a procurement meeting into a political war room reeks of desperation," Ricci said in an email to Capital News Service.
During Wednesday's discussion about whether to increase funding, board member Brooke Lierman, the state's comptroller, took aim at public-private partnerships, saying that the Purple Line demonstrates "the folly of relying on P3 models for complex, long-term transportation projects."
"Everyone in the state of Maryland is bearing the burden of the errors made by the past administration today," Lierman said. "I don't enjoy voting yes on this, but we have to be committed to ensuring that we meet our obligations to the riders in the state of Maryland."
At Wednesday's meeting, Holly Arnold, administrator of the Maryland Transit Administration, said the Purple Line is more than 65% complete, with construction underway at 13 of 21 planned stations and 17,000 linear feet of rail installed. The expected completion of the much-delayed project has been pushed back to winter 2027.
Arnold added that the $425 million would be paid out to Purple Line Transit Partners over several years and is contingent upon achieving certain milestones, an accountability measure aimed at encouraging progress with the project.
Still, board member Dereck Davis, the state's treasurer, lamented the project's problems. "I just want to raise hell," he said. He added that he'd been considering casting a "no" vote on additional funds but ultimately decided the project is too far along to abandon.
"We're literally approaching 100% [cost increase,]" Davis said, "with no real guarantee that that's the end."

title: Voters Need Voice on Dorchester Charter Changes
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
Voters need voice on Dorchester charter changes

 March 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 850
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OK, Dorchester voters including those in Cambridge, Hurlock, and all of the other towns in Dorchester County, you now have the opportunity, and I think the obligation, to speak out on a very important topic. You need to let your voices be heard now and in November with regard to the Dorchester County Charter Commission's recommendations for changes to the current County Charter.You can do this now by coming to the County Council meeting on March 19 at 6 p.m. in the County Office Building or you can email, call or speak in person to your County Council representative.
What the Charter Commission was able to do is complete and improve on the efforts of the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government that sought to collect enough signatures from registered voters throughout the county to have a vote on possible changes to the county charter as part of the last election cycle. We fell short.
The Dorchester Charter Commission has done what we were not able to do and added other proposals.
They developed a list of eight recommendations with explanations that were part of a presentation to the County Council earlier this month, and the council is asking the public to provide their thoughts on which of the proposed changes should go on the ballot in November 2024. Hearing from the citizens is always important, so you need to speak out in support of what your fellow citizens have suggested after months of work.
In November, whatever issues are placed on the ballot, 50% plus one of the voters has to approve the proposed changes that the County Council will have approved for consideration and vote. While we do not know how much public input from the voters is required for the County Council to act, the more people that tell them to place all of the proposals on the ballot, the more likely those proposals will be on the ballot.
That will allow for a formal up or down vote on each proposal in November after you, the voters, have had the chance to learn more about all of them and the pros and cons for each. I am confident that as part of the upcoming elections there will be people who are for or against a proposal.
I know that the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government will be urging passage of whatever is on the ballot, as these proposal make for good sense and help create better government. During our efforts to obtain signatures, we obtained over 1,300 signatures in support of two of the proposals having to do with the county manager and transparency.
I would suspect that most of you who reside in Dorchester County, including its towns and cities, may not know what the proposals are. That is understandable. It is also understandable that all of them should be on the ballot so that you can give your voice to which ones you want and which ones you do not want.
The county charter has not been changed, I am told, since it was originally passed many years ago. Much in our world has changed since then, and one of the most important changes is that most larger cities, like Cambridge, and counties have gone to a form of government called council-manager where there is a paid experienced and full-time manager for the day-to-day running of the government that includes the hiring and firing of staff, while a county or city council creates the vision, policy, and direction for the county or city for the manager to run.
The Charter Commission provided both an explanation for each proposed change along with a suggestion of the appropriate language. While those explanations and the proposed language are too long for this report, the proposed changes are these:
Add language that would solidify the difference between the responsibilities of the County Council and the county manager. We would like to emphasize:
County manager is the only one allowed to direct employees.When position is vacant, search must start immediately.If position is not filled timely, alternative search measures must be employed. o County Manager must be available full time.County Manager can not take direction from individual council members.Only the County Manager can hire and fire county employees.
Change the requirements of the county manager to remove the residency requirement.
Change the Administrative Review to require it be done in the first fiscal year of each new Council.
Change the requirements of the county Director of Finance to remove the residency requirement.
Change the due date for the proposed county budget.
Change the adoption date for the county budget.
Add language to Section 606 to increase transparency and to insure that the most effective means are used to disseminate meeting information.
Add language to the County Charter to limit a County Council member to three four-year terms (for a total of 12 years).
I hope to be able to provide more information regarding the above proposed changes, but the important thing for you to do now is to contact your County Council member (not city council) and let him know that you want to have a vote on all of these proposals in November.
Stephen Rideout is mayor of Cambridge.

title: Candidates Vie for Trappe Town Council Seat
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Candidates vie for Trappe Town Council seat

 March 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On March 19, the Town of Trappe will hold a special election to fill a position for town commissioner. This candidate will hold office for a one-year term expiring May 2025. The election will be held at the Trappe Town Council meeting room on Tuesday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.The elected candidate will fill the remainder of former Trappe Town Council President Nicholas Newnam's term. Newnam resigned from his position earlier this year.
Jeremy Newnam is the only candidate listed on the ballot. Stephanie Chester and Marcell Pritchett are running as write-in candidates.
The Star Democrat reached out to the three candidates competing for the seat to ask questions about their campaigns.
STEPHANIE CHESTERWhy are you running?
"I believe that council representatives should be committed servants. I would be the bridge that assists citizens in bringing their issues to the council and simultaneously be part of seeking solutions."
What are your hopes for the town?
"That it continues to be a safe small town, maintaining its historic character; that its businesses thrive and keep up with today's economy. That its sense of community is enhanced."
Tell me about your thoughts on Lakeside.
"Lakeside is here now. It is imperative that it behaves like a good and contributing citizen to the welfare of Trappe. It serves no purpose to rehash the issues concerning whether or not Lakeside was a good investment for the Town of Trappe. That decision having been made, the better question is what issues does its presence present that impact its immediate neighbors and the town in general.
There are concerns about tanks … impacting neighboring property. The council needs to address this immediately."
What skills will you bring to the commission?
"Thirty years of teaching in the public school system has taught me to be a good listener, problem solver, motivator, leader and team player. These skills I believe would prove invaluable to making the Town Council and the community work closer together."
What would you like to say to the community of Trappe?
"I would like to be your partner in keeping Trappe historic, safe and enjoyable. I would like to be your voice to convey concerns and your assistant in providing solutions."
JEREMY NEWNAMWhy are you running?
"I'm a firm believer in doing your part within your community. I've served in the Fire Department for the better part of a decade and believe there is still more for me to do to serve my community that I call home."
What are your thoughts on Lakeside?
"I believe Lakeside provides adequate housing opportunities to bring in new residents to the community but also continues the growth of the town in the commercial atmosphere. I hope with the increased population commercial entities will be interested in filling a void within the community causing residents to travel to nearby towns for their necessities."
How do you plan to attract business to the town?
"By exploring adding additional amenities to the Town of Trappe for the existing residents first, I hope to then draw other nearby residents with the appeal of the town."
What skills will you bring to the commission?
"I believe in the service for others, not the service for yourself. I have held numerous administrative roles throughout my life. Most importantly I have lived in Trappe for the majority of my life and been a town resident for over five years, my decision within my community directly affect the place I have called home for so long."
What would you like to say to the community of Trappe?
"Regardless of who the residents vote for, I encourage everyone to come out and vote if possible. Their vote impacts the day to day operations of the area they call home, the area I've called home for the majority of my life."
MARCELL PRITCHETTWhy are you running?
"I would like to continue to be able to help the folks of Trappe, Maryland, and to be involved with the local government. I attended several other training events and just looking out for the people in Trappe just so they have a voice."
What are your hopes for the town?
"The hope for the town is to continue to grow. And for everyone to be able to really work together."
What are your thoughts on Lakeside?
"I think Lakeside is a wonderful idea. And it seems to be going well. And it's bringing more to the town and just bringing some more insight."
What skills will you bring to the commission?
"I am a 26-year resident of Trappe, Maryland. I have management skills, and I'm very much diverse with people and helping them. I want to do what's best for them."
What would you like to say to the community of Trappe?
"Get out here and vote so that we can make a difference in Trappe and work together."

title: Caroline County Organizations Make Their Cases for FY2025 Funds
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County organizations make their cases for FY2025 funds

 March 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 761
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On March 12, several locals stood before the Commissioners of Caroline County to make their cases for funding from the county's fiscal year 2025 budget.At the hearing, which was designed for commissioners to hear testimonies on operating and capital requests, documents were distributed, giving a picture of the county's revenues and expenditures going into the annual budgeting process.
The requested expenditures for fiscal year 2025 come to $72,095,934, and the revenue estimates for 2025 are $71,459,230. That leaves a projected shortfall of $636,704.
The commissioners will have to pass a balanced budget before the new fiscal year begins on July 1. This will require addressing the more than $600,000 deficit.
Commissioners Larry Porter and Frank Bartz presided over the March 12 hearing. Commission President Travis Breeding was not present.
There were four groups who pleaded their cases to either retain current funding from the county or get an increase.
Phil Starkey, president of the Queen Anne-Hillsboro Fire Department, spoke on behalf of all the firefighting companies in Caroline County.
"The initial request was a 10% increase on the operating side," he said. "Fire companies struggle with fundraising efforts. Materials to do fundraisers have gone up along with everything else that we do. Equipment has gone up. Trucks are up to a million dollars, equipment. You guys know, 10% (increase) is a fair ask in my opinion, considering most of our stuff is going on 20% (more than) last year."
Starkey asked that the commissioner prioritize retaining programs that aid local fire departments with volunteer retention.
"The other thing is the $2,500 real estate property tax reduction program. It is a good retention tool," he said. "You guys supply us with the LOSAP program (Length of Service Awards Program). You get someone who comes in at 20, they have to wait until they are 62 before they get any benefits. This tax program is a good program to retain people that have to meet their 50 (annual) points. To retain the $33,000 to meet the needs of the (fire reporting) program is a needed thing. It is a big cost on the fire departments clear across the board."
He also highlighted the 508 money that comes from the state of Maryland and pays $330,000 a year across all of the fire companies in Caroline County. Mostly it helps to buy equipment and trucks, Starkey said.
Porter expressed support for Starkey's requests, saying local fire departments "have to fundraise just to be volunteers."
Three other residents advocated for the county's support at the hearing. These were Debby Bennett, executive director of the Caroline County Library; Sue Simmons, interim manager for the Caroline County Council of the Arts; and Susan Reynolds of the Human Service Council.
"What the commissioner's budget allows us to do is have two additional staff," Reynolds said. "Without that budget, we either have to cut a full time person, of which there is only two of us, or I would have to cut programs. I request $25,000. We got about $57,000 less from the state. We have had to cut Men for Change, the YMCA program and the mentoring program."
Bennett was next in front of the commissioners.
"We are asking for an increase in the operating budget," she said. "It is always about the staffing and trying to recruit and retain good staff. On the capital side, I want to thank you for your funding. The local match for the last part of the renovation at the central library, which was the pitched roof in the back of the library and the elevator, that is 85% done. We are requesting $30,000 capital funding for the central library parking lot."
Porter responded to her statements.
"Bottom line, we have got to have places that we can keep warm, and keep cool and keep the doors open," he said.
Towards the end of the meeting, Simmons said, "I want to bring to your attention to not only the Arts Council's request, which is $6,500. It is a relatively small fraction of the budget. The majority comes from a non competitive grant through the Department of Commerce through the Maryland State Arts Council. I want to say thank you and please write that same level of check."
The next public meeting concerning the county's budget is scheduled for May 7 at 6 p.m. at the Caroline County Courthouse. At it, the commissioners are expected to continue receiving testimony on operating and capital budget requests. They will also hear testimony on the constant yield tax rate and municipal property tax differential rate, which are expected to be set in a proposed budget by the commissioners on April 9.

title: Cambridge City Manager Resigns Over Concerns With CWDI
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge city manager resigns over concerns with CWDI

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 909
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Tom Carroll, Cambridge's city manager of two years, submitted his resignation on Monday.In a letter addressed to the mayor and commissioners, Carroll said his last day as city manager will be no later than May 17.
Carroll shared the news of his resignation with City Council Monday night in a closed session following the council meeting.
"This was a hard decision for me to reach, but I do know it is the right decision to make," he wrote in an email to the Star Democrat Tuesday morning.
In an interview Tuesday afternoon, Carroll said he has accepted a city manager position for the City of Lexington, Virginia. He said that in December, he came to the decision to pursue employment outside of Cambridge in the new year.
The reason for this decision, he said, was his concerns with Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront. Specifically, Carroll pointed to three events that led to his decision.
The first was a Dec. 15 email from CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard. The email, sent to CWDI stakeholders, said the city's words and actions were jeopardizing CWDI's deal with a company to build a hotel, Carroll said.
When Carroll, at the request of City Council President Lajan Cephas, reached out to two of the city's representatives on the CWDI board, he said he didn't hear back from them on the topic for months.
Along with this, Carroll said CWDI's "fussiness" regarding a now indefinitely tabled ordinance that would give the city the authority to appoint an individual to represent the city on a non-city governed board — and also remove that individual, and subsequently impose a fine or jail time if the individual continued to act as a representative of the city on said board — made it clear that CWDI was unwilling to change any part of its plan in response to criticism from the city.
Carroll said the third event that led to his decision was when he learned of a "significant ethical issue" involving CWDI's attorney. CWDI is represented by the law firm Miles and Stockbridge.
This is not the first time Carroll has spoken about his concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.
In late October, a letter addressed to Leonard and signed by Carroll stated that Cambridge City Council was not in support of the plans for the project. The letter stated concerns with the CWDI's governance, the proposed tax increment financing and the lack of a private sector development partner for a project of this size.
Carroll himself said in a September interview that having spent 27 years in local governments and having been a part of two major economic development projects, he had concerns with the financial feasibility of CWDI's plan.
In his email to the Star Democrat, Carroll said he hopes that he is wrong and that Cambridge Harbor will "become a story book success."
"But I fear that I will be correct in its lasting and long-term negative impacts for Cambridge unless it is fundamentally changed," he wrote. "I can no longer standby while this project moves forward in its current form and with the current governance structure."
Leonard said Carroll's reasons for leaving are his reasons.
"I don't know what all the reasons are," Leonard said. "If that's the one he has chosen promote, I'm sorry to see that. It doesn't make a lot of sense to me, but his reasons are his reasons."
Leonard said one of the reasons CWDI was formed was to have an organization in place that can "transcend political turmoil or disruptions in leadership."
"We've done everything we can to make sure that we can continue the progress on the project despite political changes," he said.
In his Monday letter to the mayor and commissioners, Carroll mentioned some of the city's accomplishments since he began serving as city manager, including the Cambridge Police Department's commitment to community policing and the city's undertaking of significant capital projects.
He said he was "particularly proud" of the city's wages and classifications system that has helped the city's workforce become more reflective of the community.
In a press release, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he and the commissioners are saddened by Carroll's decision to leave, and his expertise will be missed.
In an interview, Rideout called Carroll leaving a significant loss for the city. He said the city has been making progress like he hasn't seen since it established its current form of government in 2015.
City Council President Lajan Cephas called Carroll a gift to Cambridge, adding that he has made a lasting impact on the city.
"Although he's leaving, he's still going to be with us, with the changes that he's made," she said.
Both Rideout and Cephas said they still have concerns about Cambridge Harbor. Cephas said her concerns lie with the direction CWDI's leadership is going in.
Rideout said this search for the next city manager will begin soon. The mayor and commissioners are responsible for hiring for the position. Carroll said he has offered to assist with the first steps in recruiting the next city manager.
In the interview Tuesday, Carroll said he expected to serve the rest of his career in Cambridge.
"I love Cambridge and think it has so much potential," he said. "I think this community will benefit by getting very serious about structural racism that we have in this community. And CWDI, the Cambridge Harbor project is something that makes me feel like their approach to this project demonstrates that Cambridge isn't serious about that important conversation."

title: Easton Council Approves 7 Vehicles for Easton Police
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Easton council approves 7 vehicles for Easton police

 March 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Monday evening, the Easton Town Council voted to provide additional financial assistance to the Easton Police Department.On the agenda, the council modified Ordinance 810, a budget modification ordinance to allocate over $1.69 million from the American Rescue Plan Act.
The council had initially allocated funds to the Doverbrook affordable housing project, the North Harrison Street stormwater project, the North Hazel Street stormwater project and finally, the purchase of four police vehicles.
The remaining funds from the American Rescue Plan Act were about $240,885.
Before voting to approve Ordinance 810, Councilmember David Montgomery said he would like to modify the funds for the police department. Montgomery suggested that the remaining funds should be allocated to assist the Easton Police Department with purchasing the rest of the department's police vehicles.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey originally requested financial assistance for eight vehicles, but the council approved the purchase of four police vehicles.
Montgomery offered an amendment to increase the allocation of police vehicles from four to seven, using the remainder of the funds from the American Rescue Plan Act.
"I would like to see us fully fund the police vehicles that are needed, according to Chief Laurie, rather than leaving money on the table at this point," Montgomery said. "I think that's a clear need. It's a public service safety, which should be our highest priority."
Councilmember Maureen Curry supported the modification of additional financial support. The council estimated that each police vehicle would cost approximately $80,000. The council agreed to increase the funds from the original $320,000 to $560,000, an increase of $240,000.
The council unanimously approved both the amendment and the modified Ordinance 810.
Other News
The council unanimously approved Resolution 623, authorizing a lease agreement between the town of Easton and the state of Maryland for a district court facility.
The council approved Resolution 618, authorizing a lease agreement between the town of Easton and the state of Maryland for a Maryland Veterans Affairs Office. The council unanimously approved the resolution.
The public hearing for Ordinance 809 regulating cannabis uses was continued to the next meeting to allow for updates from the state legislature.

title: Trappe Planning Commission Approves Phase 1D Lakeside Plans
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe Planning Commission approves Phase 1D Lakeside plans

 March 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Planning Commission met and approved a minor amendment and Phase 1D subdivision revision plat for the Lakeside development. By approving this, they have cleared the way for the Trappe Town Council to vote on this phase of the Lakeside development.The commissioners approved Phase 1D of the subdivision revision, with the notation that the areas identified as public open space on the plat would be clearly labeled as such.
Trappe Attorney Lyndsey Ryan stated that open space is defined as active and passive open space for public use and enjoyment.
Robert Rauch, president of Rauch Inc., the engineering, architecture, and environmental firm constructing the Lakeside development, told the commission that there may be some confusion about the distinction between public open space and private space.
Rauch wanted to ensure that the areas labeled as public open spaces were properly understood to be used by the public.
The open space would not be within stormwater management. Rauch explained that the areas in the exhibit will be green open areas for "throwing frisbees." The exhibit has two parks: Lakeside Public Park and Wooden Public Park. There is public access to the sidewalks between the two areas by trails.
Open space areas would be under the homeowner's association's mandate and management, regardless of whether they are designated as public or private. Rauch clarified that for any areas designated as public open space, the HOA would have the obligation to provide a permanent and perpetual public easement for access and use.
The development agreement states that the public shall have a permanent and perpetual easement to use and enjoy the open space, which may not be limited by the petitioner or any HOA.
The commission voted to approve the revisions of the subdivision to make sure that all designed public spaces were clearly labeled.
Cannabis
Ordinance 1-2024, an ordinance for the town of Trappe to establish reasonable zoning regulations for cannabis businesses, was also approved by the Planning Commission and will be recommended to the Town Council for approval.
Margaret English, a resident of Trappe, was a vocal advocate against approving the zoning regulations for cannabis businesses.
"I don't think you should recommend it," English said. "I don't want drugs in my town, and I ain't moving."
Commissioner Edgar Harrison noted regardless of whether or not he agreed with her; he didn't think the state would permit the town to outlaw the introduction of cannabis businesses into town. After the meeting, he sat down with English and listened to her concerns regarding cannabis.
