title: Returning Bay Ferry Service Faces Choppy Waters
author: David Reel
content:
Returning Bay ferry servicey faces choppy waters

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 500
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On June 30, 1952, a ribbon-cutting in Anne Arundel County marked the beginning and the end of transportation options between Maryland's Eastern Shore and western shore. On that day, the first Chesapeake Bay Bridge opened for vehicular traffic. That same day, a ferry service that had carried 2 million passengers and 1 million vehicles on the Bay since being launched in 1930 ended.Conventional wisdom then was ferry service would never return to the Bay. Now an effort is underway to return ferry service that is very different from that which ended abruptly 72 years ago.
Currently nine Maryland counties — Queen Anne's, Anne Arundel, Calvert, Somerset, St. Mary's, Wicomico, Talbot, Kent, and Dorchester plus the city of Annapolis — are working with a consultant to study the feasibility of a new passenger only ferry service on the Bay. Their final report will include recommendations on next steps if the consultant's feasibility study concludes such a service is viable and sustainable. It is a work in progress. Routes may be added deleted or modified.
With all due respect to the supporters of this concept, I suggest there are two critical issues they need to consider if they have not done so already.
One issue is the ferry vessel under serious consideration for the proposed new service. It is the Candela P-12 all-electric ferry. It sells for approximately $2 million, does not carry vehicles, seats a maximum of 30 passengers, and has limited storage space for carry-ons such as bicycles, strollers and wheelchairs.
This vessel will not be a practical alternative for the huge number of tourists who use Route 50 when going to Ocean City ("downy shore").
Accordingly, this proposed new ferry service is not likely to generate significant support from Eastern Shore residents and public officials hoping for a solution to regular summer traffic jams on Route 50.
The second issue is the increasingly limited potential for state funding for this concept.
During the past several weeks in the General Assembly, there has been intense (and yet to be resolved) differences of opinion on how to address structural deficits in the state transportation trust fund and projected structural deficits in the state budget. Those deficits are almost certain to become worse based on the devastating impact on the state economy and state revenues from the tragic collapse of the Key Bridge in Baltimore.
Securing state funding for the launch and operation of a new ferry service on the Bay is not going to be a high priority in Annapolis in the foreseeable future.
I am not suggesting these are insurmountable obstacles or the only obstacles. I am suggesting they are very serious obstacles that cannot be ignored by the proponents of returning ferry service on the Bay.
One path forward may be securing private investment for this concept from investors with the resources to launch and operate it.
Otherwise, returning ferry service to the Chesapeake Bay may be an interesting idea whose time has not yet come.
David Reel is a public relations and public affairs consultant who lives in Easton.

 I write to provide corrections to the recent Star Democrat article titled "Town Council discusses moving employees to exempt status." Our discussion centered on a small number of managerial employees, such as department heads, needing to be classified as exempt.Councilwoman Curry pointed out that receiving paid overtime was not standard practice during her prior tenure as an exempt employee. Davis emphasized, there should be no reductions in overtime for anyone in the Police Department.
Second, the statement that "all employees would get a 3% pay increase" with the switch to exempt status is inaccurate. This is a proposed COLA (cost of living adjustment) for all employees, unrelated to the proposed change in overtime for exempt employees. Mayor Cook has proposed salary increases for exempt employees that would equal their average overtime payments over the past five years. The council is still considering that proposal.
Councilman Rev. Davis rightly emphasized that exempt employees should receive fair market value salaries without overtime.

This workshop marks the beginning of a series as part of the budget process, with additional meetings scheduled for April 9, 10 and 17.

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council is sending a letter of support for a United States Senate bill that would exempt seafood processors from the numerical limit on H-2B nonimmigrant visas.At a regular meeting April 2, the County Council voted unanimously to send the letter of support.
According to the U.S. Department of Labor, the H-2B program allows employers in the United States to temporarily hire nonimmigrants for nonagricultural labor or services.
Currently, there is a cap on how many H-2B visas can be issued every year. According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Citizenship and Immigration Services, the cap is currently 66,000 H-2B visas per fiscal year.
If Senate Bill 3013 is passed, seafood processors would be exempt from this cap.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said at the meeting that it is important to emphasize in the letter the "huge impact" that the limit on H-2B visas issued has on crab picking houses in the county every year.
"Especially in the southern part of our county where everybody is working on the water or adjacent to them," he said.
Detmer said the letter should include the number of workers needed in the county to open all the local picking houses, "and maintain our heritage and our economic development." He said this number is a small one "compared to a larger pool."
Council President Lenny Pfeffer agreed and said that county staff could contact the Dorchester Seafood Heritage Association for those numbers.
"We can have good factual information put in our letter," he said.

title: Caroline Commissioners Vote to Keep Proposed Tax Rates the Same
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commissioners vote to keep proposed tax rates the same

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners unanimously voted to leave the county's proposed property tax rate unchanged for fiscal year 2025 at a meeting on Tuesday.The current tax rate, which would remain the same for the next fiscal year, is 98 cents per $100 of assessed valuation.
In an interview, County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said that rate hasn't changed since 2015.
The vote included the tax differential rates for towns in the county. Tax differentials are lower county property tax rates for properties within municipalities. At the meeting, Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked about Ridgely's tax differential.
"I would say that the logical question would be Ridgely," he said.
On March 13, the Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely Police Department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, according to a press release from the town.
At a County Commission meeting March 19, the commission said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Maryland State Police would divide responsibilities for providing law enforcement to the town.
At the meeting Tuesday, Fox said his current understanding is that Ridgely is discussing the possibility of continuing its contracted service with the the Caroline County Sheriff's Office at 140 hours per week.
"So if that holds true, I think they, by formula, would be entitled to the same differential," he said.
Fox said the hard part of this is that the town still has the opportunity to back out until a contract is signed and endorsed. He said Ridgely's differential is about a $60,000 reduction in property taxes.
"So that would be the number if the board chose not to do a differential," Fox said. "We would receive an additional property tax revenue."
Before making a motion to keep the tax rates the same, Commission President Travis Breeding said he was ok with keeping the rate the same.
"I'm ok with keeping it the same for the year and seeing where they end up," he said about Ridgely.
Caroline County will be holding a public budget hearing on May 7 at 6 p.m.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this article.

Board President Angie Hengst said people will be able to submit questions and get clarification on some of the topics "that have been circulating as of late." She said CWDI has been "the topic of conversation" over the past few weeks.
On March 18, Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said in a letter that his last day as city manager would be no later than May 17.
Carroll said he resigned over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project, a project that will create public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Cambridge waterfront.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard told the Star Democrat in March that Carroll's reasons for leaving are his reasons.
"I don't know what all the reasons are," Leonard said. "If that's the one he has chosen to promote, I'm sorry to see that. It doesn't make a lot of sense to me, but his reasons are his reasons."
In her April letter, Hengst said some of the recent conversations about Cambridge Harbor and CWDI have been inaccurate or a "mis-representation of the facts."
"I know many community members feel they are getting conflicting information from various sources and feel confused or unsure about what is really happening," she said.
The letter said CWDI will hold a public session on April 18. The session will be held at 6 p.m. at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center in Cambridge. It will also be live-streamed.
Hengst said that the public can always reach out to her at Angie.hengst@cwdimd.org, Leonard at matt.leonard@cwdimd.org or the other board members with questions or concerns.

title: Caroline Commissioners Hear Options for Landfill After 2030
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Caroline commissioners hear options for landfill after 2030

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County could remain the host of the regional landfill for 12 years longer than originally planned.At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday morning, Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn, CPA and Queen Anne's County Consultant Joe Zimmerman and Queen Anne's County Commissioner James Moran came to speak about the possibility of using the Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill in Ridgely through 2042 rather than building a new landfill in Queen Anne's County for 2031.
During their presentation, Mohn said Maryland Environmental Service has been working with county administrators to evaluate the future of Mid-Shore II, and it has concluded that the landfill could "easily provide service" to the citizens of the region through approximately 2042.
The Mid-Shore II landfill, which was opened in 2011, provides services to Talbot, Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties.
Mohn explained that in the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, if the partnering counties agreed, they could instead extend the lifetime of Caroline County's landfill.
During the presentation, Mohn listed reasons why Queen Anne's County feels this option makes sense. For Caroline County, he said that this option would provide economic stability for Ridgely businesses and that the county would get a host fee for the extension of service.
He said the option would also maximize the value of public infrastructure, defer liability for debt to construct a new landfill, maintain shorter haul routes for Talbot County and avoid the cost of a transfer operation.
Moran said landfills are at a premium.
"We want to maximize that," he said about the space in each landfill. "And if this (provides) us with an extra 30 years of life that we didn't have coming into this 80-year deal, then that's a good thing for the environment, it's a good thing for the Eastern Shore."
If this proposal moves forward, all of the partnering counties would need to come to an agreement on a modified arrangement, including the host fee for Caroline County.
At the meeting, Zimmerman presented three options for host fees and annual tipping fee increases for the Mid-Shore II landfill:
A host fee of $2 per ton of waste growing to $4 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.15% in tipping fees.A host fee of $3 per ton of waste growing to $5 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.35% in tipping fees.A host fee of $4 per ton of waste growing to $6 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.5% in tipping fees.
"We think these are achievable options," Zimmerman said about the three options. "It's really the question of how much risk the counties want to take on in terms of their competitive posture."
He said that historically, tipping fees have, on average, annually increased by 1.42%.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said he has made it clear to MES that he agrees with keeping the landfill operating in Caroline County for environmental and economic reasons, but he would like to make sure the county retains "any of the savings associated with the extension of the landfill."
He said the county's residents are the ones burdened with the affects of the landfill operations, including truck traffic and bad smells from time to time.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter spoke about the impact of MES operations on the county.
He said that although this proposal is an opportunity to generate more revenue without raising property taxes, having the landfill in the county has affected the condition of the roads where trash is being driven, including trash left on those roads. He said the extension of the landfill's services would be a hard sell to the public.
"For me, anything that we do is going to have to involve MES stepping up to the plate and fulfilling what I think the obligations and responsibilities are," he said, adding that roads would be part of that obligation, in his mind.
Porter asked the presenters if it appears that the other partnering counties are on board with keeping the landfill in Caroline County and paying a host fee. Mohn said everyone seems to be in agreement.
"The question is, what is that host fee going to be?" Mohn said.
Porter said the county will have a public hearing on this in the future. He did not give a date.

title: Housing Commission, Developers Break Ground on Doverbrook Apartments
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Housing Commission, developers break ground on Doverbrook Apartments

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 475
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although some foundations have already been laid for the new Doverbrook Apartments in Easton, the Housing Commission of Talbot and project developer Pennrose hosted a ceremonial groundbreaking at the site off Dover Street Thursday morning."Try to ignore the fact that we've got building foundations in place," Pennrose Regional Vice President Patrick Stewart said, "because this is a groundbreaking."
Those in attendance for the event included Stephanie Staats, a field office director for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development; Gregory Hare, assistant secretary for the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development; Easton Mayor Megan Cook and members of the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council.
The $25 million redevelopment project is to replace the apartment complex's seven buildings — which had been around since the 1970s — with five new buildings. Project partners estimate apartment doors will open to new and returning residents in spring 2025.
Although there will be two fewer buildings when complete, the new complex will have 14 additional units, bringing the total to 64 units. There will be a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom energy-efficient apartments, all of which will be a part of a housing choice voucher program known as Section 8 housing.
In December, Housing Commission of Talbot Executive Director Don Bibb said the project includes the creation of a playground in the center of the community and a facelift and addition to the Easton Housing Authority building located on the property.
At the groundbreaking, Bibb spoke about the importance of realizing the effects of this project, and not just talking about "the bricks and sticks."
"It's about the people," he said. "We can build buildings all the time. But giving the quality of life and living in an environment that's conducive to what people should have is what this is all about today."
Staats said the groundbreaking memorializes the beginning of a project that will create 14 new affordable units.
"Those 14 units symbolize 14 families who will now have safe, stable, desirable housing," she said, later adding that at the core, "that's what it's really all about."
According to a press release from Pennrose, the project is being funded through state and local proceeds, Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and a loan from M&T Bank. This funding includes a $350,000 grant from the Town of Easton and a $350,000 grant from Talbot County.
In mid-December, the apartment complex officially closed its doors to residents so the redevelopment project could begin. In a December interview, Bibb said residents of the previous apartments were relocated or given vouchers for other properties.
At the groundbreaking, Hare talked about the addition of units to the redevelopment project.
"But we're not just making more housing," he said. "We're making it better. ... When it's complete next year, Doverbrook will become a fantastic accomplishment and a great example of how public and private partnerships work to benefit the community."

title: Talbot Council Approves Resolution 338 and Its Amendment
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Council approves Resolution 338 and its amendment

 April 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 1051
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Tuesday evening, the Talbot County Council approved a resolution amending the Talbot County Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan and requiring any future expansion of the new Lakeside wastewater treatment plant shall require an amendment to the comprehensive plan.Resolution 338's passage has been long awaited. The process of developing and approving it began over a year ago.
Patrick Thomas, Talbot County attorney, said prior to voting that if this resolution is approved, it will go to the Maryland Department of the Environment, and the MDE will have the ability to either approve it, modify it or revise it.
The MDE could deny the resolution. Thomas said that if that were to happen, there would be an opportunity to request a hearing before the MDE secretary.
The council had an opportunity to pass Resolution 353, a resolution already approved by the county planning commission, but chose to table the resolution for another time.
BackgroundLakeside is a residential development project that has been 20 years in the making. It has been a hot topic of discussion for residents of Trappe and throughout the county. Lakeside is a planned 2,501-unit development spanning more than 850 acres off of U.S. Route 50 in Trappe.
According to Erin Braband, Trappe's town clerk, 114 building permits have been issued, and 109 connections have been made to the town's existing wastewater treatment plant.
Trappe's existing plant accommodates wastewater from the development's first 120 homes. The flow will eventually be diverted to a new wastewater treatment plant serving the development. The plant is expected to be operational by the beginning of June, according to Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Lakeside's developers who spoke to commissioners at an April 2 meeting.
Before the introduction of Resolution 338, attempts were made to amend Talbot County's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of the development's property for immediate priority for water and sewer service. The resolution created was called Resolution 281.
The MDE approved the resolution in November 2020. But a month later, the agency sent a letter stating that Resolution 281 did not provide the number of equivalent dwelling units for the different phases of Lakeside's construction — information needed for further development.
Council member Lynn Mielke, who introduced Resolution 338 in February 2023, called 338 a "standalone resolution on a specific issue that the Maryland Department of the Environment has brought forth. The other issues have to deal with subsequent comments by MDE that they wanted answers to."
The legislation proposes amending the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit. Any expansion to the new plant would require a change to the plan and a certification of consistency from the Planning Commission.
The amendment, approved alongside the resolution, states as a requirement that any amendment to the comprehensive water and sewer plan must include a certification by the Planning Commission that the amendment is consistent with the county's comprehensive plan.
The language to be incorporated from Resolution 338 proposes amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.
The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, allowing only 400 residential units to be built.
Amended Resolution 338 was found consistent with the county's comprehensive plan in December, with Planning Commission Chairman Chip Councell saying it would be the county's only chance for a review of potential expansion.
The council approved the resolution and its amendment with a 4-1 vote on April 9. Talbot County Council President Chuck Challahan voted against it.
The council voted to table discussion of Resolution 353, a resolution approved by the Planning Commission last week, until its May 14 meeting, along with two other resolutions relating to Lakeside, 347 and 348.
Resolution 353 "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas.
On April 2, the Talbot County Commission found Resolution 353 to be consistent with the Talbot comprehensive plan and moved it toward approval by the County Council.
During their discussion of Resolution 353 April 9, County Council members raised questions relating to two changes in wording made to the resolution by the Planning Commission on April 2.
The Planning Commission decided to revise aspects of Resolution 353 before finding it consistent with the comprehensive plan, fixing wording to make it compatible throughout the resolution. The revision also includes the removal of language pertaining to the initial flow for the units.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits — maps displaying updates to Trappe's proposed water and sewer service areas — to Resolution 281.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from the still-pending 338.
Alone, Resolutions 347 and 348 were deemed by members of the Planning Commission to be confusing, and 348 and 347 were voted to be inconsistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan at the April 2 meeting.
Public CommentDuring a public hearing before the vote, Brian Schmidt, Trappe Town Council president, opposed the proposed Lakeside resolutions and their amendments.
Schmidt said the county has been treating Trappe differently than other towns, hurting the growth of the municipality.
"We did not ask this council to intervene," Schmidt said. "MDE is the controlling authority in matters of wastewater discharge, not the county. Disguising growth legislation as wastewater discharge is not proper procedure is only impeding the town's authority to control its own growth. Passing any of these resolutions, not only will you then be making decisions for the county, but you will also be making them for Trappe as well."
In a press release by the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Alan Girard, Maryland advocacy director, said in a statement that citizens, businesses and CBF members have long sought greater oversight for Lakeside and appreciate the county's decision.
"Lakeside is no longer being left up to chance," Girard said. "Talbot County Council's decision to conduct limited oversight of the project is a positive step to protect residents and the environment. The authority to periodically review Lakeside will give county officials an essential opportunity to evaluate the project's impacts on the environment and public investments like schools, roads and emergency services."

title: Walk This Way: County Presents Draft Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Walk this way: County presents draft Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein | Section: News 
 
 494
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On the path to more connectivity for all, Queen Anne's County presented the first look at the Pedestrian & Bicycle Master Plan during a public meeting with the community April 4.Katelyn Widness of Kimley-Horn, project consultant, presented a draft of the master plan to provide pedestrian and biking networks throughout Queen Anne's County April 4.
Embracing health, safety and accessibility for the entire community, the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan stands as the county's first basis to connect gaps between existing facilities and to further prioritize transportation networks projects.
In the works for about a year, "the master plan is really trying to achieve a connective, accessible and safe network," said Wideness presenting an overview of the plan, public feedback, the visions to achieve, and project prioritization.
The master plan sets the stage for subsequent study and design phases that will need to occur before implementation and successful use is achieved, she said.
Both committees led development efforts and the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan came about through collaboration with various stakeholders, county departments and public feedback, she said.
The intent of the study has been to identify safe routes with a focus on connectivity and public input was instrumental in voicing concerns and identifying any barriers that may deter users from utilizing the paths, Widness said.
Studies gauged community interest with hundreds of responses and feedback through surveys and an interactive map, according to Widness.
Notable takeaways highlighted the need for safety and connections needed between towns, businesses and rural areas.
"Key things we heard was the importance of connectivity between the South Island and the Cross Island Trails as well as the crossing of Route 50 and providing walkability within the towns," she said.
From an economic development perspective, there is a strong focus on trails as a tourism attraction incentive.
"Currently the trails that are within Queen Anne's bring people into the county and the more they are connected and the more that they expand, recreational tourism is going to increase," Widness said.
As developing new networks can be costly, key areas of focus for the plan have been identifying how to utilize existing resources and infrastructure as much as possible and build upon the county's existing 26 miles of trails, three miles of bikeways and 111 miles of sidewalks.
The master plan is currently gearing up and developing route recommendations. While there is no specific timeline for the completion of each component, projects have been prioritized as what will have the most impact on the community as resources become available.
Goals of the plan going forward look to explore how to encourage walkers and bikers of all ages to utilize the paths for a stroll or a spin and highlight the safety, sociability and transportation benefits, according to Widness.
The draft Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan is expected to be presented for adoption at the Queen Anne's County Commissioner's meeting April 23.
Community feedback and involvement is continually encouraged as the plan moves along and reviews of the draft plan are available at https://www.qac.org.

title: Upgrades Needed to Handle Wastewater in Centreville
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Upgrades needed to handle wastewater in Centreville

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 529
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Doubling plant size and finding alternate means of discharging waste are some of the topics as proposed Centreville wastewater treatment plant upgrades come closer to fruition.Along with Whitman, Requardt and Associates, the engineering consultant to the town, Jenial Turner, Maryland Department of Public Works program manager presented information on the upgrades needed to the town's Wastewater Treatment Plant to the Centreville Town Council April 4.
The project to expand the liquid and solids treatment capacity of the plant has been in the pipeline for at least three years, Turner said.
The Centreville wastewater treatment plant was last upgraded and expanded in 2003, and the facility is in significant need of an upgrade, according to Turner.
At this time, approximately 80 percent of the plant's current capacity of .542 MGD (million gallons per day), is being utilized, she said.
A new wastewater treatment plant project proposes an increase of .458 MGD for a total capacity of one MGD.
Currently, the wastewater treatment plant discharges to a local water reuse farm through spray irrigation and Corsica River groundwater disposal, Turner said.
For a capacity increase in that size, the town will have to seek options for discharge and disposal of excess waste as the plant's current groundwater disposal methods would not be sufficient enough to support one million gallons, Turner said.
The public works department and engineers are currently in the process of developing the preliminary engineering report and concept design for the new treatment plant and are currently reviewing comments and feedback received from MDE in December 2023.
Public works continually meets with MDE to discuss year-round stream discharge and is leading interest groups regarding effluent disposal and various options going forward, she said.
Noting the concern citizens can have when told the plant is discharging into the river, "We want to make sure that we are armed with information so that we can provide that to the community," Turner said.
The preliminary engineering report is expected to be finalized by June with the design phase to immediately follow for a year of planning. The construction and permitting bidding phase is proposed to start for the end of the year and be concluded by 2026. Final construction for the wastewater treatment plant is expected to be completed by 2029.
"All while still working on trying to figure out where we're going to dispose of the effluent," she said.
Public works is also continually thinking ahead of continual growth of the town and further adjustments and scalability of the plant's design decades down the line.
Wastewater treatment plant upgrades and expansions have been adopted into the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
The total project is estimated at $38 million with grant options currently being explored.
Thus far revenue sources include Bay Restoration Funds in the amount of $14.9 million, congressionally directed spending $2.1 million, and $2 million worth of American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding.
Council President Ashley Kaiser, who has a background in nonprofits and raising state government funding, encouraged fellow council members to continually advocate on the town's behalf for large projects funding.
"It's an exceptionally challenging budget year in a lot of places, here included," she said.
More information about the wastewater treatment plant is expected to be presented to the council around July.

title: Easton Works Toward Approval of Fiscal Year 2025 Budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton works toward approval of fiscal year 2025 budget

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Mayor Megan Cook said there isn't a lot of fluff in the $28 million proposed overall budget for fiscal year 2025."We continue to fund salaries and all training and safety," Cook said in an interview. "That's our No. 1 priority."
Cook said some tough decisions needed to be made to get that number down to $28 million.
"The original asks for the proposed budget might have been $34 million," she said. "We've had to cut back. And each department has been really good about helping to identify areas where we could cut to save some money."
According to town documents, the combined general fund and capital fund budget for fiscal year 2024 was $36.2 million.
Council President Frank Gunsallus said one of the biggest changes to the budget this year is the change in overtime.
"That's a very big step, and it's long overdue," he said.
At an Easton Town Council workshop on exempt and non-exempt employment status April 1, the council discussed the possibility of switching some employee statuses from non-exempt to exempt. Cook said in an interview April 3 that around 13 department heads would be affected.
"Adjusting the classification of specific employees from non-exempt to exempt status is not a routine practice," Gunsallus said. "Therefore, we will carefully consider this allocation of related funds."
Budget workshops have begun. Two were held this week — one on Tuesday and one on Wednesday. Another budget workshop is scheduled for next Wednesday, April 17.
Cook said the town has presented a balanced budget to the council.
"So anything that we're adding back in, we're going to have to take something back out," she said about the process ahead.
The council plans to approve a budget June 3 so that there is enough time for the budget ordinance to go into effect on July 1, the first day of fiscal year 2025.
Cook said she plans to have a first reading of a budget ordinance and presentation for the council on May 20.
"That'll give them that meeting to discuss any changes," she said.
Cook said the budget workshops have gone well so far.
"The department has done a great job presenting and answering questions from the council," she said.
Because there are three new members on the council, there have been a lot of questions, Cook said.
"There are a lot of questions about where the numbers come from and things like that because it's the first time they've been through the process," she said. "But department heads have done a great job presenting their priorities."
Gunsallus called the proposed budget a rough draft, saying that it's now a matter of deliberating on certain allocations, scrutinizing potential purchases and discussing what should take priority.
"Once you get out of the core essentials of what each department needs to operate, that's when you really get into the splitting of the remaining funds," he said.
Cook said she will sit down with the finance department and Town Manager Don Richardson, as well as department heads, after the next budget workshop to make any changes to the proposed budget based on comments from the council.
Gunsallus said Easton is in a good position, where it is able to fulfill all departments' needs.
"But then you get into the requests beyond basic needs," he said. "And then that's where the hard work and the group collaboration comes in."

title: Oxford Clerk-Treasurer Takes Oath of Office
author: Maggie Trovato

Oxford clerk-treasurer takes oath of office

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has a new employee in its office.Vickie Sharp was sworn into the role of clerk-treasurer at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday. Commission President Tom Costigan administered the oath of office.
After Sharp was sworn in, Costigan introduced Sharp. He said that she previously worked for the Town of St. Michaels. According to the Town of St. Michaels website, Sharp was the town's finance clerk and Water Department and billing clerk.
"We're thrilled to have her with us, and we expect great things," Costigan said to Sharp.
The clerk-treasurer is a new position for the Town of Oxford.
According to the job posting on the town's website, Sharp will be tasked with directing and managing the town's finances under the town manager's direction and implementing policy set by the Commissioners of Oxford. The clerk-treasurer will act as the chief financial officer of the town.
The creation of this position was talked about at a Jan. 11 commissioners meeting, when Commissioner Katrina Greer said she wanted to discuss the possibility of hiring someone to take on the town's financial duties.
At the Jan. 11 meeting, Greer said this could address a material weakness detailed in the town's audit for the town's lack of internal controls. This has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
"This would take some burden off the manager and enable us to comply with the audit recommendation of having multiple people performing financial roles," she said at the meeting.
Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said she had shared this idea with the commissioners originally because hiring more employees is the way to solve the internal controls issue.
"Admittedly most towns our size can't afford more staff," Lewis said at the Jan. 11 meeting. "Oxford is not in that situation, per se."

title: Market Brings Sense of Community to Pine Street
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Market brings sense of community to Pine Street

 April 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 623
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The clouds opened up over Pine Street Community Market just in time to let the sun shine down Friday afternoon for a ribbon-cutting event.The ribbon-cutting, hosted by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, brought together community members and local and state officials to celebrate the opening of the market, a convenience store with a restaurant that serves breakfast, lunch and dinner — from eggs and home fries to hamburgers and subs.
For Pine Street Community Market owner Eddie Beasley, the opening of the market has been a long time coming. He's been working on getting it opened since 2015.
"I just feel like I've done something," he said. "I was in the 10th grade when Pine Street had the fire and burned down all the businesses. And from then until now, there was always this talk about building it back. So this is a great start."
In 1967, a fire burned much of Pine Street, a historically Black neighborhood in Cambridge. The fire broke out after civil rights activist H. Rap Brown gave a speech in town
Because the Cambridge Rescue Fire Company took hours to arrive on the scene, the fire to spread to much of the street, burning homes, businesses, schools and other structures to the ground.
For many Cambridge residents, this is about more than a convenience store. It's about a thriving community.
Cambridge resident Mercy Pinder said the store will provide a sense of community as well as more jobs for residents.
"It's amazing because, for those who don't have transportation, they could walk here," she said. "And that's how it used to be here in Cambridge. You really didn't have to go on (Route) 50 for anything. Everything was walking distance."
Revitalizing the historic Pine Street neighborhood has been a city goal. In late March, the Cambridge City Council voted to establish a land bank authority. At a January meeting with city officials and state legislators, City Manager Tom Carroll said a land bank authority would allow the city to take an "interventionist approach" to its housing market in the Pine Street neighborhood and throughout the city.
Beasley is hopeful that Pine Street will successfully be revitalized. He said that Habitat for Humanity Choptank, which he is on the board of, is building new houses behind the store.
"As that goes on, and if we can encourage and bring somebody along to put something else up here, we'll be on our way," he said about revitalizing the neighborhood.
Beasley said Pine Street Community Market "is doing the old-fashioned thing," with plans to add more to the menu.
"The food is old-fashioned," he said. "We're making our hamburgers up from scratch."
People can expect great food, great service and a nice and neat space when they come into the store, Beasley said.
The store has already been a benefit to Bonita Perry, who lives in the neighborhood. She said the market is easy to walk to, and she likes the food they serve. She said getting a meal there is easier and cheaper than going to the grocery store. Perry's go-to order is the cheesesteak.
At the ribbon-cutting, Mary Handley from the Maryland Office of the Comptroller presented a citation to Beasley and the market. Robyne Chaconas from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, which helped fund the project, said it's all about the impact of these projects.
"We're extremely proud to be partners on this project with you," she said. "This is going to be a great asset for the community."
Pinder, who grew up nearby, called the addition of the store a 360 from when she was a kid.
"When I was younger, this was actually a store where you could come in and get your groceries and things of that nature," she said. "So this is a 360 for me."

title: City Manager's Departure Will Bring Change
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
City manager's departure will bring change

 April 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 732
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I have often heard that "change" is the only constant in our lives. I once saw a Dilbert sweatshirt that had written on the front "Change Is Good! You Go First."By the time you read this, the commissioners of Cambridge will have appointed Brandon Hesson, our assistant city manager, to take the management lead for Cambridge while we search for our next city manager. We will have looked at ways to support Brandon to help ensure that the progress that we have made with Tom Carroll's hard work will continue. City staff leadership will be focusing on implementing multiple projects to improve the city including housing, and our challenges with sea level rise, storm water runoff and our infrastructure.
With Tom's announcement that he was leaving his position as the Cambridge city manager, I decided to take some time before trying to provide some context and meaning to his departure. While it is a significant loss and one that I wish did not happen, it has. Tom has been an excellent city manager and one who has helped the city and the city council move forward to make changes that are beneficial to our entire community. He has strengthened our city staff structure and staff leadership.
Now, "change" in Dorchester County and Cambridge has to be taken in some context. It is not something that normally occurs quickly. For example, 2024 is the 340th anniversary of the founding of Cambridge. From the date of its founding, it took over 100 years for it to become an incorporated city. 2023 was the 230th anniversary of that event. It then took us over 220 years to change the form of the Cambridge City government to a "city council — city manager" government in 2015. That came about because a group of dedicated citizens worked to research other governments and convince our city commissioners that change was the wise thing to do.
During my time as mayor since September 2022, I learned a great deal from Tom. While I have experience in other fields and had been a city commissioner, I learned what Cambridge could achieve when it made good decisions based on sound reasoning. I also learned from my prior experience on city council what harm government can bring to a community when decisions are made on hope but with inadequate foundation.
In the early 2000s, the City Council committed to expanding the city marina and building the police department and firehouse on Washington Street. The cost of these projects was significant for a city that had and still has a high poverty rate, but the promise for paying for the bonds needed to fund the proposed change was that developers were going to come and build homes that would bring in the tax revenue to pay the bond payments.
So the bonds were issued; the police-fire building and marina were built; and then, change came that we could not control. It was called a recession that lasted a few years but had a much greater and longer impact on Cambridge because of decisions that had been made. Very few, if any, of the promised houses were built to pay for what the city had borrowed. From the time of the recession until federal and state money came in 2022 from the ARPA funding, the City of Cambridge struggled to pay its bills, lost police officers to other jurisdictions, raised city real estate taxes, but was unable to give raises for staff.
We are at a very different place now because of the ARPA funding that will run out soon but also because of the experience, hard work and vision that Tom Carroll brought here. His time with us, as well as that of our other two prior city managers, requires us to look at what has been achieved since the change in 2015 that has improved the lives of our citizens and the stability of our community.
Have all of the problems been solved? No.
Are we better off because of the work of Tom Carroll and our prior city managers? Yes.
What have we learned from him and our past experiences? I hope it is that our local government must make decisions now and in the future that are grounded in both our past experiences and known data and not promises. If so, we will make better decisions to protect the city that we love.
Stephen Rideout is mayor of Cambridge.

title: Zoning Amendment Fails in Cambridge Council
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Zoning amendment fails in Cambridge council

 April 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 468
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — An ordinance that would have amended zoning to make four contiguous parcels at the corner of Washington and High streets the same zoning district was struck down by the Cambridge City Council before it could be voted on.The ordinance, brought to commissioners at a council meeting April 8, would have amended zoning for three parcels.
Jesse Hammock, an attorney representing the owner of the four parcels, said the parcels had once been owned by Cambridge resident Millie Lake and her family and were used as a bus lot.
Currently the four parcels are zoned three different ways. One is zoned Downtown/Waterfront Development District, one is zoned Neighborhood Conservation District and two are zoned General Commercial District.
The owner of the parcels, Quality Housing of Cambridge, asked that all of the parcels be zoned the same.
"Having disparate zoning classifications for those four lots makes it near well impossible to come up with a comprehensive development plan for the four lots that meets the requirements of the zoning code, comprehensive plan," Hammock said.
If it had been passed, the drafted ordinance would have made zoned the four parcels Downtown/Waterfront Development District.
At the April 8 meeting, City Attorney Patrick Thomas said the council had to make certain findings of fact before the council could vote on the ordinance.
"In order to grant the rezoning, you would have to find that all criteria had been satisfied," he said. "But even if you find that all criteria had been satisfied, you don't necessarily have to approve the amendment."
The findings Thomas listed included that the population of the area won't be substantially impacted by the amendment, that the amendment is unlikely to substantially affect traffic patterns and that two parcels were mistakenly remitted from a rezoning where one of the parcels was rezoned Downtown/Waterfront Development District.
Commissioners Brian Roche and Jameson Harrington voted in favor of all of the findings being considered fact. Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioners Sputty Cephas and Laurel Atkiss voted against it.
Lajan Cephas said she took issue with the statement that the parcels were mistakenly zoned.
"I believe it's possible that properties could be intentionally deadlocked so families can be stuck, and they don't have the ability of selling or developing," she said.
After the vote, Cephas said that her concern was whether the council could say it was a mistake.
"If it's intentional, is it really a mistake?" she said. "How do we determine what a mistake is?"
In response, Hammock said the only evidence available is a statement from a previous planning director saying that the two general commercial parcels not getting rezoned Downtown/Waterfront Development District was a mistake.
"Respectfully, there is no evidence that it was intentional," he said.
Without enough votes to consider the findings of fact, the ordinance could not be voted on.
The property owner could file an appeal regarding the council's decision.

title: Time Off Would Be Beneficial
author: Staff Writer
content:
Time off would be beneficial

 April 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 223
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Time off wouldbe beneficial
I agree with most of the editorial on overtime for town executives and managers; this is standard practice nearly everywhere. I also agree that 1-for-1 comp time is too much.
Where I part with the editorial, however, is the notion that there should be no compensation for extra hours and overly long days.
I have no dog in this fight — I know only one town employee — but it doesn't take much to imagine a scenario where, say, a Public Works manager works practically around the clock during a heavy snowstorm or a flood. Do you really think that person shouldn't get a day off or at least be able to come in late one day?
Same kind of thing for the execs at Easton Utilities. If they have to work endless days to manage power outages, shouldn't they get some time off, especially since they're not getting overtime?
I am certain there are enough extraordinary exigent circumstances, no matter the department, that require extra-long days from these managers, who would benefit from some immediate relief in the form of time off. It would be good for the person, and good for the town.
In addition, having some form of comp time policy would show these employees that they, and their work are valued by all of us who pay their salaries.
JEFF BARRON
Easton

title: Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nearly two months since opening a public hearing on the topic, the Easton Town Council has passed an ordinance revising the Town Code to regulate zoning for cannabis-related uses.At its meeting Monday, the council voted to pass Ordinance 809 with amendments.
The amended ordinance permits the use of dispensaries through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district and the general commercial district. It also permits, through special exception, cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments are prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the ordinance.
The passing of the ordinance comes about nine months after the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses took effect. In November, the council passed a six-month moratorium on businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits, which expires May 9.
"If we don't vote today, we must at the next meeting in order to be handled before our moratorium expires," Council President Frank Gunsallus said at the meeting Monday.
The council waited to vote on the topic while the General Assembly discussed the topic in Annapolis. At the council meeting April 1, Easton Town Planner Lynn Thomas said the Maryland Senate had passed a bill that is different from the House of Delegates. He said said that, considering the General Assembly would be adjourning, the town should have the information it needs to vote at April 15's Town Council meeting.
At the meeting Monday, Easton Director of Planning and Zoning Miguel Salinas said that House Bill 805, which deals with cannabis restrictions, had gone through the Senate and House of Delegates and is now awaiting Gov. Wes Moore's signature.
Salinas listed the amendments to Easton's ordinance, including a separation requirement of a half mile between dispensaries. Salinas said that is in House Bill 805.
Salinas said other amendments to the ordinance include the addition of parking standards for dispensaries and the addition of a requirement that a professional engineer or equivalent qualified professional certify that that the proposed odor measures established effectively eliminate outdoor odors.
Before voting on the ordinance, Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello asked that they change the ordinance to permit cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district through special exception, rather than just permitting it.
"There's one industrial area in particular that is off of Dover Road that backs right up to an entire neighborhood," Abbatiello said. "I'm sure that those individuals would at least like the opportunity to share their concerns or joy that a growing facility is going in that area."
Abbatiello said this change would not prohibit growing and processing facilities from the industrial zoning district, it would just give residents "an extra opportunity" to voice their thoughts.
Gunsallus made a motion at the meeting to approve the ordinance with the amendments from the town and the amendment requested by Abbatiello, which passed.
At the end of the meeting, Abbatiello thanked Thomas, Salinas and Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh for their work on the ordinance.
"This has been a long process," he said. "It's been a difficult process. And I really do appreciate all their effort to give us the best information so that we can make a decision."

title: Cambridge Mayor Proposes Amendments to CWDI Articles of Incorporation
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge mayor proposes amendments to CWDI Articles of Incorporation

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 762
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to get the relationship between Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. and the City of Cambridge "back on track," Mayor Stephen Rideout is proposing amendments to the organization's Articles of Incorporation.According to CWDI's Articles of Incorporation, the mayor of Cambridge is its sole member. This means that Rideout has the authority to make amendments to the Articles of Incorporation.
Tuesday morning, Rideout conducted a meeting to share and review his proposed amendments to the Articles of Incorporation. He said he thinks these changes will benefit CWDI's Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront that would include a promenade, parks and a boutique hotel with a restaurant and bar.
"These amendments to the articles make it more likely for the project to be successful," Rideout said.
Cambridge Harbor has been a hot topic of conversation in recent months. On March 18, Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said he was resigning over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.
In late October, a letter addressed to CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard and signed by Carroll stated that Cambridge City Council was not in support of the plans for the project.
At the meeting Tuesday, Rideout discussed four main areas of the six-page CWDI Articles of Incorporation document that he wishes to amend. He said he will convene another meeting in the next 10 days to make his final decision regarding the amendments, and he welcomes comments and advice from the CWDI Board of Directors and the public.
PROPOSED AMENDMENTSThe first change Rideout proposed has to do with CWDI's membership. The amendment would make it so that Cambridge's commission president would become CWDI's sole member in the event that the city is without a mayor.
Currently, according to a red-lined document of the Articles of Incorporation that Rideout handed out at the end of the meeting, CWDI's Board of Directors would become the members of CWDI if the city did not have a mayor.
"Given the differences of opinion that have developed between the city and CWDI, having the CWDI board become the sole member in the future is not acceptable," Rideout said.
Rideout's second proposed change would give CWDI's sole member the exclusive right to amend the Articles of Incorporation and the ability to inspect all CWDI records and attend all open and closed CWDI board meetings.
Rideout called it "critical" for CWDI to be transparent and accountable to its sole member.
The third main change would make it so that the Articles of Incorporation "prevail" over CWDI's bylaws in the case that there is an inconsistency between the two. It would also require the Board of Directors to provide any proposed bylaw amendments to the sole member of CWDI at least 15 days before adoption of that proposed amendment.
The fourth change to the document would explicitly give the city, county and state the authority to remove and replace their appointees to the board at any time.
Rideout said he believes that — at least for the city — this authority already exists. But he said the amendment would ensure that authority.
This is not the first time the city has considered clarifying that authority. In the beginning of the year, the council considered an ordinance that would have given the city the authority to appoint an individual to represent the city on a non-city governed board; and also remove that individual, and subsequently impose a fine or jail time if the individual continued to act as a representative of the city on said board. At a Feb. 12 City Council meeting, the ordinance was tabled indefinitely.
The proposed ordinance had garnered attention from CWDI.
In November, Attorney J.W. Thompson Webb of Miles and Stockbridge, representing CWDI, wrote the council that the city was overreaching its authority with the ordinance. In a Jan. 2 letter from Leonard to Rideout, Leonard asked the city to abandon the ordinance altogether.
CWDI city-appointed board member Shay Lewis-Sisco also asked for this at a Jan. 8 City Council meeting.
Toward the end of the meeting Tuesday, Rideout said that CWDI can "regain the complete confidence of" the city through embracing these proposed amendments.
"I hope my friends on the CWDI Board of Directors embrace this opportunity," he said.
After the meeting, Leonard, who was in attendance, said he didn't have a lot he could say about the meeting because he hadn't yet had a chance to review the amendments Rideout is proposing.
"I believe anybody who wants to make CWDI better comes in good faith," Leonard said. "We're always happy to listen to their suggestions. And so I'm going to look at it that way."

title: Housing Secretary Visits His Hope Ministries
author: Tom McCall
content:
Housing secretary visits His Hope Ministries

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 668
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day, came to His Hope Ministries in Denton Tuesday to learn about the nonprofit's vision for the future.The organization, which provides services and shelter to those experiencing homelessness, wants to develop a new building and move to Market Street.
They toured bunk rooms at 409 Aldersgate Drive, where neat piles of clothes, toothbrushes, laundry detergent and ear buds lie. The shelter welcomes guests from September through the end of April, with accommodations for families, single men and women, and youths.
"They are seeking to grow because the demand is high," Day said. "Part of that is that there just are not enough housing units, particularly affordable housing units in the Mid-Shore. We have underbuilt for the last 15 years. The consequence is that people are unhoused."
Executive Director Stefanie Johnson showed Day some architectural plans for a new facility she would like to build to expand His Hope's services.
"I did show him our design so far. We have an idea in mind for land, but so far, it is not available from the town yet. We have our Senior Haven, which is a three bedroom one bath home. It has three seniors in it. Seniors or disabled — it is transitional so they can stay there for up to three years," said Johnson.
There is a vacant lot next to this senior home where His Hope hopes to build their expanded facility.
One of the barriers to completing the project is its cost. Some of the visit was talking about money.
Day said he believes the best fiscal options for His Hope to complete the project is through the Community Development Block Grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The state has $7.5 million to fund CDBG annually, he said.
"Probably for the Eastern Shore it is CDBG money. It gets to the end user when it is ready to be executed and spent for construction and design. This federal money has to serve the low income population," Day said.
The other option Day mentioned is Sowing Empowerment and Economic Development Inc., a nonprofit organization providing food, education, and training while promoting self-sufficiency and empowerment directly to low-to-moderate-income families.
"I believe both predevelopment and development costs are eligible. SEED is the institutional version of this. For the town, all it has to be is a community development goal that they're interested in. Helping unsheltered homeless be sheltered has positive health outcomes. A hospital and a shelter would go hand and glove," Day said.
Andrew Breeding, treasurer for His Hope Ministries, called their hoped-for property the Market Street Property. The land is owned by the Town of Denton and used to be a Southern States facility.
"The challenge is putting a homeless shelter literally anywhere," said Breeding.
Johnson said some local politicians are hesitant about the idea of building a shelter in town. Day said that representatives from his office, including him, could come and testify to the town council on behalf of His Hope's story.
Day asked some pressing questions about how His Hope Ministries and the community interact.
"What's that look like between you and other organizations in the community?" he asked.
Johnson responded, "It is impeccable. When we closed (for the warmer months), we called and said, 'Hey, do you have room for our families? Talbot Interfaith in Easton, and in Cambridge the Salvation Army, we are all on speed dial. Even the Christian Shelter in Salisbury. This community is so giving."
Day also toured the office and youth drop-in center of His Hope Ministries on 105 Gay Street, housed in a spacious Victorian house with a broad porch. The inside is inviting and colorful. There is room for classes on financial literacy, and there are many positive affirmations on the walls.
Amidst a big black board filled with affirmations, Day was invited to grab some chalk and add his. He wrote, "A mistake will not define you. Get back up and keep going."
This report has been updated from earlier versions to correct the name of His Hope's treasurer.

title: Community Wishes Library Director a Fond Farewell
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Community wishes library director a fond farewell

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — It was a heartfelt goodbye for Executive Director of the Kent County Library Arnessa Dowell on Friday.She's leaving for Guam, where a new job awaits her as supervisor librarian at Andersen Air Force Base.
In the new position, Dowell said she'll take with her the values she has learned in Kent County since she started early in 2021, such as the importance of building partnerships in a close-knit community.
As executive director during the Covid-19 lockdowns, she was celebrated for her dedication under trying circumstances in a rural library system.
Natalie Hagan, director of technical services commended Dowell.
"She nearly doubled our staff since the time she was here," she said.
Hagan also pointed out that Dowell exercised creativity under a system with limited resources.
Dowell dealt with the logistics of those issues while having to relocate both the Galena and Rock Hall libraries during her tenure.
In a brief farewell speech, Dowell expressed how important libraries are to her.
At one point in her life, during financial turmoil, her job at a library was a refuge, offering her hope for future endeavors.
Dowell reflected on the time she had in the Kent County community. She was thrilled with the development of the KCPL Cares program, a quarterly free giveaway initiative that lets the library connect with and support the community in a variety of ways.
It was birthed out of the pandemic. Dowell and staff kept seeing a need in people's lives. They gave away Kindles, COVID kits, cold weather clothing and other necessities.
With a ready smile, Dowell said, "Thank you to everyone for your support, mentorship, advice, hugs and laughs. I just really appreciate it. I'm immensely proud of my staff. It was challenging and I've grown so much as a leader because of it."
The community showed appreciation back to her as well.
While they enjoyed tacos and a sumptuous red velvet cake courtesy of Happy Chicken, Cynthia Saunders president of the Friends of the Kent County Public Library, presented Dowell a portrait of the Chestertown waterfront.
Hagan, on the search committee for the new executive director said the library already has a few applicants for the position and expects to have many more in the nationwide hunt to fill Dowell's shoes.

title: Local legislators reflect on General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Local legislators reflect on General Assembly

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Wednesday morning, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted a Legislative Wrap-up Breakfast with Maryland senators and delegates from the Eastern Shore.The meeting provided a summary and discussion of the recent Maryland state legislative session, the General Assembly. Topics discussed included DAF residual legislation and solar energy.
Sens. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) and Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), along with Dels. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), were in attendance.
Jacobs spoke on his work on the Environmental and Transportation Committee and the work both delegates and local leadership in Caroline County had on regulating dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals.
"I really do appreciate the fact that all three county commissioners and Caroline County were there because it had a huge impact on the committee in Annapolis," Jacobs said. "With an issue that meant that much to the county, all three county commissioners showed up and gave very compelling testimony as to the real problem."
DAF is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
House Bill 991 and its pair, Senate Bill 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County, who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery); Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation; and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation.
The bill is awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
SOLAR DEVELOPMENT
Delegates expressed concerns over legislation they said took away a vital part of the comprehensive solar development planning process, giving local communities less determination over solar expansion.
Jacobs spoke on Senate Bill 783, or the Brighter Tomorrow Act, which would lower the cost of developing Maryland solar projects and increase the value of solar energy for consumers across the state.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who was in attendance, argued that if counties are forced to have more solar, they should be able to negotiate and charge what they want from solar facilities. SB 783 attempted to limit taxes charged to commercial solar facilities.
"I made a comment in the committee: If solar was as good as we are told it's good … Why doesn't everybody in this room have it?" Arentz said. "We're pushing so hard for something we can do. And I think the General Assembly has to, at some point, wake up."
The state's Renewable Portfolio Standard had already established a nation-leading mandate to deploy solar that equals 14.5% of Maryland's electric demand by 2030. Maryland has fallen behind the pace to meet that goal, only meeting 55% of the policy's intermediate 2022 target.
After the delegates had reflected on this year's legislative session, Arentz expressed his appreciation to his fellow delegates for the work that was accomplished during the legislative session.
"I appreciate the time. You guys are wonderful. And as these guys said, this is kind of a love fest. We do it here. We do it up in Cecil County. And we're very, very lucky because we have a lot of like-minded people to communicate, we talk, and we work well together," he said.

title: Moore Celebrates Bipartisan Wins in Second Session
author: Kiersten Hacker Capital News Service
content:
Moore celebrates bipartisan wins in second session

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 1078
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore bragged the other day about "going 26 for 26" in passing his bills through the General Assembly, a display of bipartisan achievement he called "Maryland's win."With his second legislative session now in the rearview mirror, Moore has been touting bipartisan support for his agenda the past two sessions since he took office in 2023.
Even though he and the General Assembly again failed to resolve the state's projected long-term fiscal imbalance, Moore is still laying claim to a measure of victory. He managed to reach his legislative goals while also navigating a crisis in the Port of Baltimore and the back-and-forth budget negotiations that had put the General Assembly at risk of an extended session.
"At a moment when people seem to care more where'd the idea come from than is it a good idea, we in Maryland, we've just chosen to move differently," Moore said. "And it's the reason we're able to work together, that we're able to get big things done."
Moore celebrates his achievements as rooted in common ground, working all session to emphasize partnership and restore both bipartisanship in the legislature and cooperation with the executive — even as a rising star in a national Democratic Party facing increasing divisiveness.
In January, Moore headed into the second year of his term with an extensive agenda of 16 bills and the goal of passing a state budget without raising taxes. However, in March, his plans were uprooted with just about two weeks left in the session when the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore collapsed, launching Moore and his leadership into the national spotlight.
Out of the first-year honeymoon period, Moore planned to address key issues such as public safety, affordable housing and education while facing a projected budget deficit expected to balloon to billions of dollars in the coming years. He proposed a $63.1 million spending plan that closed an expected $1.1 billion cash shortfall without a hike in taxes.
But budget negotiations shaped up to be no easy task in the General Assembly. The House had hoped to pass a $1.2 billion revenue package to address education and transportation funding needs. The Senate didn't think the time was right to impose new taxes on Marylanders.
While negotiations were underway, the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore suddenly collapsed after a container ship collided with the structure. Moore's attention immediately turned to Baltimore where he held daily press conferences, removing him from the public and daily wrangling of budget discussions in Annapolis.
"That's the thing about being governor, is you don't get to set the whole agenda," Sen. Jim Rosapepe (D-Prince George's and Anne Arundel) said. "Real events set the agenda. And so it was his first crisis and I thought he rose to the occasion."
Even Republicans agreed with Moore's priorities in responding to the Key Bridge.
"He's rightly spending his time where the citizens of Maryland need him to be," said Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's).
Lawmakers have repeatedly thanked Moore for his response to the crisis and his administration's actions to get emergency legislation passed providing relief to port workers and businesses. Despite being absent as budget negotiations got down to the wire, many lawmakers, including key Republicans, have said publicly that Moore was exactly where he needed to be.
Sen. Johnny Ray Salling (R-Baltimore County) said Moore has been "above and beyond," approachable and communicative about the next steps as a leader.
"I've always said we work together and we work across the aisle because it's the only thing we can do to get things done," Salling said. "But again, we might not agree with everything. But it doesn't mean that we can move forward in other areas."
Moore also put his weight behind the PORT Act, which will provide relief for port workers and businesses as well as establish a scholarship fund for families of transportation workers who died on the job. Sponsored by Senate President Bill Ferguson and Del. Luke Clippinger, both South Baltimore Democrats, the measure passed in the late hours of the final day of session.
Ferguson said he's known the governor personally for a while and he excels as a leader of people as he did in combat. The law was the first of many to receive Moore's signature.
"The legislation will empower our administration to stay nimble in our response in the collapse," Moore. "Even though session is now over, it does not mean Maryland's response will cease."
Moore also racked up a win when the General Assembly responded to his pressure to reach a compromise on the budget. The spending plan they approved will increase taxes and fees on things like tobacco products and vehicle registration fees but does not include broader sales or income tax hikes. Revenues generated from these taxes and fees will be used to fund trauma resources, transportation projects and the Blueprint for Maryland's Future education reform plan.
However, the state faces a darker fiscal picture down the road and will need to come up with new solutions for funding programs and projects. Moore has repeatedly said he has a "high bar" for raising taxes, and he has told reporters in recent days that will continue throughout his term.
This session was a year for smaller steps toward resolving more long-term budget issues, said Rosapepe, vice chair of the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee.
The House wanted to pass an aggressive increase in revenues to fund priorities like transportation, education and the environment, which Rosapepe said are needed. But the Senate and the governor wanted to take it "one step at a time," Rosapepe said, and they were able to work well with the House to reach a compromise.
"We made progress, we didn't solve all the problems in the world, we rarely do in one session, we never do in one session," Rosapepe said.
The budget ensures that "we're not going backwards" on transportation while funding the Blueprint for the next few years and making a down payment on climate change goals, Rosapepe said, but more steps will need to come in the future.
The rest of Moore's bills on his agenda passed by midnight on the final day of session, including his package of housing bills.
Moore emphasized working in partnership with the General Assembly as a main theme of this session, and many lawmakers saw that come to fruition on both sides of the aisle.
"Governor Moore totally has a partnership mindset," Rosapepe said. "And I hear my Republican colleagues speaking very highly of him too, in that regard."
