title: Bradshaw Runs for Cambridge Mayor Against Lajan Cephas
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Bradshaw runs for Cambridge mayor against Lajan Cephas

 August 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw has thrown his hat in the ring for the city's mayoral election in October.Bradshaw, who served as mayor through 2021, resigned in January 2022 after being charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. In April 2022, Bradshaw pleaded guilty to five counts of distributing revenge porn.
Current Mayor Stephen Rideout, who is not seeking reelection, was elected to fill the remainder of Bradshaw's term.
Bradshaw will run against Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas, who served as the city's interim mayor after Bradshaw resigned and before Rideout took office.
Cephas also has faced legal issues. In 2022, she was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
As of Monday, Bradshaw and Cephas were the only two listed as approved candidates for the Oct. 19 mayoral election on the city's website. The deadline to file is Tuesday.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Bradshaw said he is running primarily due to an "outpouring of support" that he has received.
"And that was, I think, largely based on the background that I had when I was in office previously and our ability to move forward various parts of a broad-sweeping agenda that was aimed at improving Cambridge throughout the city," he said. "Not just in one neighborhood or in one aspect of the city's needs, but across all the various areas of need and geography in Cambridge."
Bradshaw wants to keep the focus of his campaign on where Cambridge is now and where it is going, rather than on his past legal issues. He said he thinks voters feel the same way.
"While I understand that there will be some thoughts and some attention given to those things, I think that where we stand now and where we can go in the future is really where I want to keep the focus," he said.
A news release from the Bradshaw for Cambridge Committee said during Bradshaw's time in office, the city started giving residential property tax credits for public safety officer recruitment, increased salaries for police officers, replaced and upgraded Cambridge Police Department and Public Services Department vehicles, expanded ethics reporting requirements for city representatives and began the planning and implementation of the Homeownership Works program, a state pilot program created to increase affordable homeownership opportunities.
Bradshaw said he thinks that as mayor, he served as a catalyst for the city council to move issues forward and work toward solving them.
"And I think the same will be true this time," he said. "That though there will be commissioners that have excellent ideas, that I'll be able to serve as a catalyst to get those ideas from the point of discussion to the point of decision."
Cephas, who has served on the city council since 2021, said in a text that being qualified for the position of mayor doesn't make you the best candidate. She said that after Bradshaw's resignation, she proved that she is capable and committed in the position of mayor.
"During (those) nine months with powers of mayor, we established the Gun Violence Task Force, resulting in 65% decrease in murder and decrease in violent crime in the city," she said.
Cephas said it's important for voters to believe in the legal system and "allow it to work."
She spoke about the importance of moving forward with a vision of a one Cambridge.
"We've notice Cambridge is divided on many platforms from policing, CWDI, businesses, race relations, community development and housing to name a few," she said. "We are divided in many ways in Cambridge, and (the) mayor should be the unifying agent bringing the city's business forward, not back."
Cephas said that if elected mayor, she will be committed to moving the city's business forward "with the spirit of ONE Cambridge."
Cambridge's city election will be held Oct. 19. All five Cambridge city council seats will be up for grabs, along with the mayor's seat.

title: Easton, Town Manager Agree to 'Part Ways'
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton, town manager agree to 'part ways'

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Easton and Town Manager Donald "Don" Richardson have come to a "mutual agreement to part ways" effective Monday, according to a Tuesday press release from Mayor Megan Cook.Terms regarding the separation are still being considered by both parties.
"This difficult decision was made with the best interest and long-term health for the Town of Easton in mind, and the continued success and well-being of our employees and community as our top priority," Cook said in a statement. "Personally, I appreciate the work and support Don provided when I served on the council and again during my transition to the role of mayor."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Cook said she couldn't say why the decision was made and probably would not give any detail in the future, but she reiterated it was a mutual decision. Cook was in charge of the decision, she said, as the mayor has the power to hire and fire the town manager.
Richardson began his career with the Town of Easton in 2007, serving as a code official. He was instrumental in helping the Town of Easton Building Department become Maryland's first International Accreditation Service accredited building department. Richardson was then appointed to town manager by Mayor Bob Willey in September 2016 and was instrumental in overseeing the administration, operations and budget of multiple department.
During his tenure, Richardson was involved as a leader on numerous major projects, including Mistletoe Hall Commerce and Business Park, Housing on the Hill, Rails to Trails, Easton Point Park and stream restorations.
Richardson was not present at the Easton Town Council meeting on Monday.
Cook said the process to hire a new town manager has not yet begun but will as soon as possible. She said the town will advertise the position through the Maryland Municipal League, the Maryland Association of Counties and "all other avenues" they have used in the past for hiring other positions. A committee will be tasked with going through resumes, she said.
Once interviews have been held and the list of candidates has been narrowed down, Cook will make a recommendation to the Easton Town Council. The council will then either approve or deny the request.
Cook anticipates it will take about three to five months to hire a new town manager.
In the meantime, Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey will serve interim town manager. Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council voted unanimously to approve Lowrey as the interim town manager.
Lowrey said although he hasn't been a town manager before, and there's a lot for him to "come up to speed on," the Town of Easton already has a good team in place, which will make it easier to lead.
He said that while he is maintaining both roles of police chief and interim town manager, Deputy Chief Greg Wright is "well-capable" of keeping operations running at the police department.
Cook said she thinks Lowrey will be a good fit for the interim position.
"I really like his way of thinking," she said. "He has a very analytical mind and a good perspective."
Cook said that with Lowrey and Wright, the Easton Police Department has "two good leaders." She said she felt that "would offer an opportunity" for Lowrey to spend part of his time in the main office.
"I want to thank him for taking on this additional responsibility," Cook said in the news release. "Our focus is to ensure a smooth transition and maintain the excellent services we provide to our community."

content:
For the Record

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

title: Emergency Residual Storage Bill Gets Caroline Commissioners' OK
author: Tom McCall
content:
Emergency residual storage bill gets Caroline commissioners' OK

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — After an Aug. 6 public hearing on a controversial bill concerning the permitting of food processing residuals, the Caroline County Commissioners unanimously voted to approve the bill.Storing residuals in Caroline County will now require a permit, and the bill allows for inspection and civil or criminal penalties if a storage site is found to be in violation.
"This is not banning storage of food processing residuals," Commissioner Larry Porter said. "If someone feels strongly about using it as a soil amendment and wants to store it, they can come in and apply once these regulations are set."
The bill requires the use of closed-top storage tanks for food processing residuals, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly. House Bill 991, which took effect July 1, created a state permitting process under the Maryland Department of Agriculture for the use, storing and hauling of the residuals.
Caroline County's bill is the latest development in what has been months of packed public hearings and extended moratoriums on residual storage tanks. For county commissioners, the main hurdle has been cracking down on a few "bad actors" that store the residuals irresponsibly.
The bill garnered mixed reviews from Caroline County residents, environmental experts and representatives of the poultry industry at prior public hearings. Several took to the podium Aug. 6 to voice their opposition or support of the legislation.
Mike Woodward, the owner of a Ridgely farm right next to an open-top residual storage facility, voiced support for the bill.
"I am 400 yards from the tank itself... We have a lot of issues with flies. The odor is atrocious at times," Woodward said. "We had a vet come out. We were having trouble with our horses. Their eyes were watering and runny and nasty. We couldn't figure out what was going on with them. The vet checked them out and the flies were laying larvae inside their eyes."
Brad Sears, a Ridgely commissioner, said, "I come before you on behalf of the Town of Ridgely in support of the emergency legislative bill. I offer this testimony to advocate for the men, women and children, who live, work and attend school and play within the town limits. We have concern because of improper storage of FPR (food processing residuals) poses well documented threats to human life, health and wellbeing."
He said open-top containers do nothing to limit "odors, the exposure to vectors, the airborne bacteria and viruses."
Holly Porter, executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, has been a vocal opponent of the county's bill in prior public hearings. She spoke again in opposition of the legislation on Tuesday.
"I really and truly would like the commissioners to consider some way of grandfathering in the farmers who are utilizing and storing food processing residuals for years without the complaints we have had in the past," she said. "If we do not do that, we are impacting other farmers who are becoming collateral damage because of one unfortunately bad actor."
Responding to Holly Porter's comments, Larry Porter said, "Grandfathering in, unfortunately would have to include grandfathering in what Miss. Porter referred to as the 'bad actor.' ... you can't enforce laws on some people and not all people."

title: As Cambridge Draws Closer to October Election, Candidate List Finalized
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
As Cambridge draws closer to October election, candidate list finalized

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 893
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — It's off to the races for the candidates in Cambridge's Oct. 19 election.Following the Aug. 6 filing deadline, the city has released a list of the approved qualified candidates for the mayoral race and each ward's commissioner race. According to the list, every race except for the Ward 5 commissioner race has at least two people running.
MAYORAL RACEThere are three candidates vying for the open mayor seat: Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas, former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw and former Cambridge Commissioner La-Shon Foster.
Current Mayor Stephen Rideout said in June that he would not be running for reelection. He told the Star Democrat when he ran in 2022, he only intended to fill the remainder of the term of Bradshaw, who resigned in January 2022 after being charged for distributing revenge porn on Reddit.
Bradshaw told the Star Democrat Aug. 5 that he is running primarily due to an "outpouring of support" he has received. He said when he was previously in office, the council moved forward multiple pieces of "a broad-sweeping agenda" aimed at improving the entire city. He said he thinks he served as a catalyst for city council to move issues forward and work toward solving them.
"And I think the same will be true this time," he said. "That though there will be commissioners that have excellent ideas, that I'll be able to serve as a catalyst to get those ideas from the point of discussion to the point of decision."
Bradshaw wants to keep the focus of his campaign on where Cambridge is now and where it is going, rather than on his past legal issues, and he thinks voters feel the same. In April 2022, Bradshaw pleaded guilty to five counts of distributing revenge porn. He had been charged with 50 counts.
"While I understand that there will be some thoughts and some attention given to those things, I think that where we stand now and where we can go in the future is really where I want to keep the focus," he said.
Cephas has faced legal issues as well. In 2022, she was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
Cephas, who has served on the City Council since 2021 and served as interim mayor when Bradshaw resigned, said in a text that after Bradshaw's resignation, she proved that she is capable and committed in the position of mayor. She spoke about the importance of moving forward with a vision of one Cambridge.
"We've notice Cambridge is divided on many platforms from policing, CWDI, businesses, race relations, community development and housing to name a few," she said. "We are divided in many ways in Cambridge, and (the) mayor should be the unifying agent bringing the city's business forward, not back."
Foster, who ran in Cambridge's last mayoral election, said she is running again because she thinks she has expertise that will benefit the city. She talked about her more than 30 years of experience as a social worker and community organizer, which she said puts her in the right position to help move Cambridge forward.
Foster said the city needs to invest in its children. She said there needs to be activities that meet the needs of the majority of Cambridge's children. She said lot of the activities available now are not affordable for all families.
"I feel that with the right leadership, with the right dedication and the right motivation, the citizens of Cambridge can win and we can all win and we can all arrive at a good place at the same time, together," she said. "And I feel that I am that candidate that will bring Cambridge together holistically."
COMMISSIONER RACESIncumbent Commissioner Laurel Atkiss is running against Brett Summers for the Ward 1 seat. Atkiss was elected in June 2023 in a special election to finish the unexpired term of then Ward 1 Commissioner Brian Roche.
Jenna LeCompte, Nancy Jackson, Jermaine Anderson and Shay Lewis-Sisco are running for the open Ward 2 seat, which is currently held by Lajan Cephas.
Frank Stout and Gary Gordy will vie for the Ward 3 commissioner seat, which is currently held by Commissioner Jameson Harrington. In June, Harrington told the Star Democrat that he would not be seeking reelection. He said he likes to volunteer and help, but politics is "just not my forte."
Incumbent Commissioner Sputty Cephas and former Commissioner Dave Cannon are seeking the Ward 4 commission seat. Sputty Cephas has served as commissioner since 2021.
Incumbent Commissioner Brian Roche will be the only candidate on the ballot in the Ward 5 race. Roche was elected as commissioner of the ward in June 2023 in a special election to finish the unexpired term of former Commissioner Chad Malkus. Before that, Roche served as commissioner of Ward 1, which he was sworn into in 2021.
Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said that in the races with more than two candidates, there will need to be a run-off election unless a candidate secures more than 50% of the vote on Oct. 19. If necessary, a run-off election will be held Dec. 3.
The election is being run by the city. Hesson said the city is using a third-party company to handle the ballots. The deadline for voter registration is 4 p.m. on Sept. 27. Residents can register to vote at the Dorchester County Board of Elections.

title: Dorchester Republican Central Committee Establishes Headquarters on Gay Street
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester Republican Central Committee establishes headquarters on Gay Street

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 330
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Republican Central Committee has set up shop on Gay Street in downtown Cambridge.Committee Chairman Michael Dodd said the organization has been occupying the space at 322 Gay Street since late July.
This is something the committee does every two years, though not always in the same location. Dodd said each election cycle, they open a brick-and-mortar headquarters "for the run-up to election day."
The headquarters acts as a central location where residents can get Republican candidate campaign materials or receive assistance in registering to vote or switching their party affiliation.
Dodd said the committee knows there are "JFK Democrats" in the community that no longer align with the Democratic Party. He said the committee also wants to register young voters who identify with Republican policies.
Having a headquarters in the heart of Cambridge, where many people will see it, is something that is important to the committee.
"The headquarters opened just (one week) after the attempted assassination of President Trump, and we saw the timely establishment of our headquarters as a message that we remain undeterred by political violence."
Dodd said that since setting up on Gay Street, the headquarters has received a positive response from the public. He said there has been a "massive demand" for campaign materials from the committee.
Although store hours have yet to be announced, the committee will be hosting a grand opening for its new digs on Friday, Aug. 9 at 6 p.m. Dodd said the committee plans to have light fare and merchandise giveaways at the event, which is open to the public. He said they will also have some "special guests" at the event.
Attendees will be able to purchase merchandise for the committee's Choptank River Boats for Trump Parade, which will be held Aug. 11 at 1 p.m. The parade will start at Long Wharf in Cambridge and end at Suicide Bridge Restaurant in Hurlock.
Dodd said the committee can be reached via Facebook or email at docomdgop@gmail.com. He said it always welcomes volunteers.

title: Approval for 2025 Delmarva Pride Festival Permit Tabled at Town Council
author: Konner Metz
content:
Approval for 2025 Delmarva Pride Festival permit tabled at Town Council

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 335

 EASTON — Despite appearing on the agenda for Monday's Town Council meeting, a vote on a public assembly permit for next year's Delmarva Pride Festival was not held.The assembly request, which was prepared by the police department and posted with the meeting agenda on the town's website, shows that the Delmarva Pride Center applied for the 4th annual festival to be held on June 14, 2025, with an estimated attendance of 4,000. It would close South Harrison Street from Dover Street to South Street.
Easton Police Department Chief Alan Lowrey asked during Monday's meeting that the item be withdrawn from the agenda and delayed to a later date.
"I'd like to withdraw that from the council's consideration," Lowrey said. "I've talked with the organizer, Kyle O'Donnell. Given that it's not until June, we would like to do some further work on it and seek approval as we get closer within six months of the actual event, so we have a better idea of what the security situation and things are closer to the event, as opposed to 10, 11 months out."
O'Donnell, chair of the Delmarva Pride Center, said in a statement to The Star Democrat that the organization hopes for the permit vote to be held soon.
"While same-day changes to the Easton Town Council agenda are frustrating," O'Donnell wrote, "Delmarva Pride Center looks forward to our public assembly permit being heard at a future meeting and hope that's sooner rather than later.
"It takes time to plan large events," he continued. "Applying for a public assembly one year in advance is reasonable."
The request posted online shows recommended approval from the police department and an approximate cost of $600 for officer overtime. The document noted "blocking vehicles/barriers" for four road closure points as the only current concern for the police department.
The vote for the 2024 Pride Festival was held in January. The Easton Town Council approved the permit in a 3-2 vote, with council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery voting against the permit.

 EASTON — A public hearing for a proposed 33-unit housing development at the site of the former Safeway closed during Monday's Town Council meeting. Despite mixed public reactions at past town meetings, no members of the public spoke Monday evening.The proposal comes from Lane Engineering on behalf of NAI Saturn Eastern and Safeway, along with Miller Development Corporation, the potential developers of the project. It includes 24 partially-connected townhomes and nine standalone units. The property, which has been vacant since 2017, sits at 139 N Washington St.
Council members mentioned discussions with developers about a per-unit contribution to the town's affordable housing efforts. Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry said it's her "understanding that the developer has agreed" to those contributions.
"We discussed the possibility of a $10,000 per-unit support of the affordable housing fund," Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said, "with $5,000 coming at the building permit stage and $5,000 at the moment of getting the permit of occupancy."
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said she will work with Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Miller Development Corporation, in the lead up to the next town meeting Aug. 19 so that a potential vote on the proposal comes to the council.
FIRE DEPARTMENTSonny Jones, chief of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, presented a report to the Town Council on Monday detailing the station's activity through the month of July.
As of July 31, the department has responded to 540 fire or rescue incidents this year, 255 of which came in the months of May, June and July, Jones said.
"I really want to point out that this is an all-volunteer organization, and as of July 31, our members have spent 8,515.07 hours in service to the community," Jones told the council. "And I'm very, very proud of all the men and women who do that."
Jones pointed out that Mondays around 3 p.m. tend to be the department's busiest time. He also said there's been a decrease in the number of false alarms.
"(Ward 2 Council Member Don) Abbatiello has assisted us with that in taking great strides to try to reduce the amount of false alarms," Jones said. "We have done some outreach to businesses which were problematic, and encouraged them to have a system to maintain."

"This is an exciting project for us," Jones said. "It's the first of its kind in the area … And we're going to see some significant start in September for the building of that."

title: Leonard, CWDI 'Mutually Agree' to Terminate Leonard's Contract
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Leonard, CWDI 'mutually agree' to terminate Leonard's contract

 August 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 725
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Matt Leonard is no longer Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s executive director.According to a Thursday news release from CWDI, the organization and Leonard have "mutually agreed" to terminate his contract, effective immediately.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said that all board members and Leonard made this decision and signed an agreement on Thursday.
"It was just a mutual agreement, just deciding that moving forward it was best for both parties," she said.
Hengst said she could not elaborate on why it was best for both parties.
Leonard was hired as CWDI's executive director in January 2022. In the last year, Leonard and CWDI have been in the spotlight. The Cambridge Harbor project — a project to develop land along the Choptank River — has become a frequent topic of conversation in Cambridge.
In May, tensions between CWDI and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit against CWDI alleging the organization had violated a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. Later that month, the city and CWDI entered into mediation before a retired judge.
Hengst said the ongoing mediation had no part in the decision to terminate Leonard's contract.
"The board thanks Matt for his tireless efforts and commitment to the organization and its mission," Hengst said in the news release. "He has played a significant role in the success of the project to date. We enjoyed our time working together, and we wish him well in his future endeavors."
Some of the progress CWDI made during Leonard's time as executive director includes securing grant funding; creating Waterman Way, a new street on the Cambridge Harbor property that has yet to be paved; and moving the project to extend the promenade along the waterfront forward.
The news release says Leonard chose to retire to Cambridge five years ago after he fell in love with the city.
"I answered the call to help my chosen forever home by joining the CWDI team," Leonard said in the release. "All of the CWDI board members I worked with are talented professionals dedicated to CWDI's community-first mission. I'm proud of what we accomplished together. I wish them all the best going forward and look forward to enjoying the fruits of their efforts for a long time to come."
According to the news release, in the interim, CWDI's Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr will serve as CWDI's "day-to-day contact," and the organization will "continue with its active projects" and continue working with its partners to advance the Cambridge Harbor project.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Narr said he has been involved with the project for almost 31 years. He said he is passionate about what can and should be done at Cambridge Harbor and wants to do it right.
Hengst told the Star Democrat the CWDI Board of Directors hasn't started looking for a new executive director to fill Leonard's position and, at the moment, won't be.
"Unfortunately, based on our financials, which we presented at our board meeting, we do not have the funds to take a new executive director," she said.
At the most recent CWDI Board meeting on July 31, Narr brought up the need for CWDI to sell property so that it can use that money to pay for other things. Since the lawsuit was filed in May, CWDI has not sold a piece of property it has been planning to sell to Yacht Maintenance Company. That property is part of the land that the city transferred to CWDI in the 2021 transfer agreement.
Narr also told the board that CWDI is $200,000 over budget when it comes to legal expenses, which is due to litigation with the city.
Hengst said Narr will serve in the day-to-day role and the board will work through things as best it can without an executive director "for the time being." She said the board's financial situation will determine when it can begin the search for a new executive director.
Hengst said the organization's financial situation did not play a part in the decision to part ways with Leonard.
"We just really thank Matt for his time and efforts that he put into CWDI and the Cambridge Harbor project," she said. "He put in a lot of work, a lot of hours, and we couldn't have gotten to where we are today without him."
This story may be updated.

title: 'It's Iconic': Tunis Mills Residents Push Back Against County Design for Bridge Replacement
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
'It's iconic': Tunis Mills residents push back against county design for bridge replacement

 August 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 692
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TUNIS MILLS — More than 50 people gathered at St Stephens AME Church Wednesday evening to engage with county leaders regarding proposed construction to replace the Leeds Creek Bridge in Tunis Mills.County employees and project engineers presented plans to replace the 345-foot wooden bridge. Designs propose a structure with a "laminated timber deck" and "asphalt wearing surface."
Residents living in and around Tunis Mills expressed a bevy of concerns about county designs Wednesday evening. Many testified to the bridge's uniqueness and fit in the community, while others are worried an asphalt surface would jeopardize the safety for residents, particularly children and teenagers.
"People love this bridge, it's iconic," Doug Marvin, who lives near the bridge, said. "I didn't grow up here, and I heard about it years before I bought the house where I did. It's like tradition for every kid that goes to school in this county to jump off the bridge … It's used in photographs, for tourism, to get people to come to this county."
Prompted by a question from the audience, nearly every single attendee raised a hand when posed with the choice of a timber surface versus an asphalt one.
At the end of the meeting, County Manager Clay Stamp said that the county and its public works department "will go back to the drawing board to a degree" to explore the wooden surface option.
"At this point I think it's fair to assure you that moving in the direction of a wooden deck bridge is the direction we are seeking," Stamp said.
PROJECT DESIGNSThe meeting began with a presentation of the proposed designs, which the county has said is around 90 to 95% complete.
Proposed changes to the bridge include adding an additional two feet of clearance, replacing timber piles with steel piles, adding a wooden laminated deck that can be paved over, widening the bridge slightly for walkers and improving a ramp and unloading platform. Several other bridges in the county have undergone similar laminated deck replacements.
The Talbot County Council first discussed replacing the bridge in 2007, allocating $1.8 million to the replacement project. Now, the project's estimated cost is around $6 million, with around $4.5 million federally funded.
Mark Ledebur, an engineering consultant, noted drawbacks to a full timber structure at Wednesday's meeting.
He said county experiences show an asphalt surface is less labor-intensive, easier to plow, smoother and easier to replace. Ledebur also presented quotes obtained by the county for timber boards in the case of replacement.
One resident asked if the county could compare costs for timber boards and asphalt, along with how often each material may have to be replaced. County Engineer Ray Clarke said his department could work on those comparisons.
A project schedule shown to attendees on Wednesday projected a final decision for the bridge replacement this September, though Clarke emphasized the county is not ready to submit and is keeping the option of a wooden surface open.
RESIDENT INPUTSusan McDermott leads a citizen group vowing for the bridge on Tunis Mills Road to remain as a full wooden structure.
The group, which has met with the county in the past, asserts that a timber structure is more durable than other materials and has environmental benefits. During the meeting, McDermott emphasized that the Leeds Creek Bridge is unique compared to busier bridges in Talbot County.
"Don't put an asphalt smear in the middle of our community," McDermott said. "We don't want it, and we don't need it."
Many residents that spoke Wednesday said an asphalt surface would only encourage speeding across the bridge. Both the current posted speed limit and the proposed one are 15 mph.
Some were worried for the safety of children and teenagers who jump off the bridge into the creek as an unofficial tradition in the area. Resident Claudia Donegan said kids "interact with this bridge intimately."
Peter Stifel lives right across from the bridge and has driven over it for almost 60 years. On Wednesday, Stifel said his support for a wooden replacement is a "vote for tradition."
"It is the heart and soul of a village," Stifel said of the bridge. "And I'd hate to see it succumb to the plastic, push-button world that we are all being forced into."

title: Leonard Provided Vision; Let's Make It Happen
author: Staff Writer
content: The City of Cambridge owes Matt Leonard a huge thank you. Some people might find that statement unusual. This newspaper has been critical of Leonard and his leadership of the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. His actions as the executive director have rung up more than $200,000 in unbudgeted legal expenses and driven an excellent city manager from Cambridge. This week, corporation board President Angie Hengst announced that Leonard was leaving as CWDI executive director effective immediately. No reason was given, other than to say the decision was mutual. According to Hengst, the board decision was unanimous and the board members and Leonard signed an agreement on Thursday. Hengst said "moving forward it was best for both parties." Hengst would not elaborate on why it was best for both parties. Leonard was hired as CWDI's executive director in January 2022. In the last year, Leonard and CWDI have been in the spotlight. The Cambridge Harbor project — a project to develop land along the Choptank River — has become a frequent topic of conversation in Cambridge. In May, tensions between CWDI and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit against CWDI alleging the organization had violated a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. Later that month, the city and CWDI entered into mediation before a retired judge. Also in May, Cambridge lost its city manager, Tom Carroll. In his resignation letter to the mayor and City Council, Carroll cited ongoing concerns with the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s Cambridge Harbor project, in particular the financial feasibility of the project. In an email to the Star Democrat in May, Carroll said he hoped that he was wrong and that Cambridge Harbor will "become a storybook success." "But I fear that I will be correct in its lasting and long-term negative impacts for Cambridge unless it is fundamentally changed," he wrote. "I can no longer stand by while this project moves forward in its current form and with the current governance structure." The agreement for Leonard to leave could be that fundamental change Carroll talked about. Leonard leaves CWDI in poor financial shape, and the board will have to its work cut out to fix that problem. Hengst said neither the ongoing legal disputes nor the development corporation's dire financial situation led to Leonard's departure, but she noted that CWDI does not have the money to hire a new executive director at this point. "Unfortunately, based on our financials, ... we do not have the funds to take a new executive director," she said. So why should Cambridge residents thank Matt Leonard? For all of his faults — and there were many — Leonard offered a grand vision for Cambridge and a prime piece of real estate along the Choptank River. Leonard dreamed big. The projects he proposed were spectacular and would have transformed Cambridge Harbor. The CWDI board needs to repair its ties with the City of Cambridge and its residents. The vision Leonard proposed is worth pursuing. It just needs to be done in a financially prudent manner and needs to involve the community from start to finish. We heard a developer recently talk about Cambridge residents, describing many of them as disillusioned and defeated. A successful Cambridge Harbor project could change that. We think that Angie Hengst has the leadership skills to rebuild trust in CWDI and begin a new partnership with city officials to move the Cambridge Harbor project forward. Removing Matt Leonard was a good first step. Now she will need to put those leadership skills to work and make this project a reality. We wish her luck.

title: Route 662 Closure Is Not an Emergency Situation
author: Lynn Leonhardt Mielke
content:
Route 662 closure is not an emergency situation

 August 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LYNN LEONHARDT MIELKE | Section: Columns 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last Wednesday evening I attended a community meeting to discuss the Leeds Creek replacement bridge. County staff, the County Council and the project engineer were present to present the plan to the public and hear comments. Immediately I reflected: Why wasn't there a community meeting to discuss Shore Health System's new request for the closure of a portion of Longwood's Road (state Route 662) near the planned new hospital?Eleven years ago, Shore Health Systems had presented to the County Council development plans for the new hospital. The plan required a realignment of Route 662, with construction of a new, relocated section of Route 662 first, in order to maintain continuous traffic flow on Route 662 during the hospital construction phase.
It was unanimously approved by the 2013 County Council. Bill 1231 enacted March 26, 2013.
Fast forward to early this year — Shore Health Systems, without involving the County Council, approached county staff (not the elected officials) to push for a temporary closure of a segment of state Route 662. This closure was to occur before the completion of the new, relocated section of Route 662. The urgency of this request was tied to Shore Health System's desire to start hospital construction, claiming that the building design had "changed slightly," necessitating the relocation of a small corner of the hospital over Route 662. This change, according to Shore Health Systems, made it "urgent" to close the road to begin foundation work.
County staff, including Public Works, Roads and the Sheriff's Department, recognized the significant impact this closure would have. The proposed detours would redirect traffic to nearby county roads: Hiner's Lane, Hailem School Road, Goldsborough Neck Road and Airport Road from October 2024 to May 2025 (assuming the construction stayed on schedule). These roads would require upgrades to handle the increased traffic, and there were also serious concerns about safety and the negative impact on the farming community.
Despite the diligence of county staff in communicating these concerns to Shore Health Systems, the hospital would barely budge. Even though there was a perfect opportunity in May to address the issue while amending another existing agreement, the County Council was only substantively brought into the process late in the game, with a "work session" with Shore Health Systems not held until July 23. However, this work session felt like a charade. It was clear that its plan was a fait accompli, essentially a done deal.
Now, based on discussions led by the county manager — conversations that did not substantively involve the County Council, as a body, they were left out of the process — the council is now being asked to rubber-stamp this "emergency" change of plans.
Bill 1577 will come before the council for a public hearing on Aug. 27 as an "emergency" bill. But let's be clear: an emergency, as defined by Webster's, is "a sudden, generally unexpected occurrence or set of circumstances demanding immediate action."
Shore Health Systems has not demonstrated that an emergency exists to justify the closure of Route 662 before the new route is completed. This is not a sudden or unforeseen occurrence. As the hospital's legal counsel admitted, the hospital design was only "changed slightly."
If Shore Health Systems recognized back in February that the design change required the closure of Route 662 in October, they had ample time to either revise the construction plan and avoid closing the road or begin the construction process for the new road earlier this year.
We all want the new hospital, and I fully support and want to facilitate the timely construction of the new hospital. However, for the sake of the public there must be a transparent process.
I cannot support their request that compromises the health, safety and welfare of our citizens. The hospital should not have requested the closure of Route 662 before constructing the new section and should have adhered to the original plan as outlined in Bill 1231. Any changes Shore Health Systems needs to make should be at its own expense to comply with the approved plan. This approach is not only best for the county residents but also respectful of their welfare and safety.
Lynn Leonhardt Mielke is on the Talbot County Council.

Cambridge mayor further delays sharing full statement on CWDI

 CAMBRIDGE — Although a written public statement regarding Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. was expected from Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout at a Cambridge City Council meeting on Aug. 12, Rideout shared two updates following the closed session of the meeting without naming CWDI in either update.Following the closed session portion of the council meeting, Rideout said the council voted unanimously to sign an agreement and the council nominated two candidates for a board. He did not provide specifics on either action.
At the end of a July 22 closed-session council meeting — where the council reportedly discussed personnel and legal issues regarding CWDI, the group spearheading the Cambridge Harbor project — Rideout said he would not report anything about the closed session portion of the meeting that day due to the complexity of what could and couldn't be shared with the public. He said he would share a written public statement at the next meeting, Aug. 12.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Rideout said he could not elaborate on either of the two decisions he shared on Aug. 12, including what the agreement is and which board the nominations were made to.
He said transparency is important to him and the City Council, and he wants to share more information regarding these updates with the public as soon as possible, once things have been finalized. Rideout said he will share a statement that "summarizes the general terms" of what was done in closed session at the next meeting.
The CWDI Board of Directors is one board that the City Council can make appointments to. The city can appoint three members to the seven-member board. Currently, the CWDI board has one vacant city-appointed seat due to Rich Zeidman's resignation in May.
Board Vice President Shay Lewis-Sisco, who is running for the Cambridge Ward 2 commissioner seat, and board member Dion Banks are serving as city-appointed members on the board.
Before the council entered into closed session on Aug. 12, Commission President Lajan Cephas said there is transition happening at CWDI. She mentioned the recent departure of Executive Director Matt Leonard, who "mutually agreed" with CWDI to terminate his contract, according to a news release.
"I hope we as a council see this as an opportunity, hopefully a path forward, so we can try to get this development moving forward and try to rebuild relationships," Cephas said.

title: Tangier Post Office Serves Island Community
author: MILES LAYTON APG Media
content:
Tangier Post Office serves island community

 August 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MILES LAYTON APG Media | Section: News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TANGIER, Va. — A small town post office is a community gathering spot and a lifeline to the mainland for a small island in the Chesapeake Bay.Tangier is about 12 miles from the mainland at Crisfield, Maryland, with the mail boat, the Courtney Thomas, running six days a week, weather pending, across the Tangier Sound between Maryland and Virginia.
Postmaster Dolores Daley is a familiar face to many with her glasses and warm smile — she talks to everyone as they check their mail. Daley explained what she likes best about working at the post office, a centerpiece for the town.
"I like that I can stay right in my hometown, and I like that everybody comes to me," she said. "I know everybody on a first-name basis."
There's no mail delivery to home or business addresses on the island, so Tangier's 400 residents receive their mail in tiny post office boxes that have served the community for decades.
"Because of our location and how close everybody is, we don't have any mail carriers," Daley said.
Daley said folks can pick up their mail anytime, but afternoons are when the latest mail arrives so that is "when people tend to visit the post office the most to talk and share news about their friends, family or neighbors."
Remember the term "golden ticket" from the movie "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory"? When someone sees a golden ticket — a yellow post office letter announcing the arrival of a package — then folks get excited because they know they've received something good from the mainland. Whether it's rubber boots for wet weather or a laptop for a soon-to-be college student, many packages from Amazon arrive each day.
"The golden ticket is the card — the yellow card — that says come and get your package," Daley said with a smile. "And when the package is too big, which most of them are, to go into the post office box, we put that card in and you bring it in to get your package. Most people like the yellow slips, and they call them golden tickets."
A lifelong resident of Tangier, Daley, 67, has worked for the post office for 38 years.
"Yes. Absolutely — we get everything," she said. "We get grass cutters through here occasionally. We get a lot of things through here. We just got chicks the other day. We've received caterpillars for the island's school to turn into butterflies when they do science projects."
Important announcements from Town Hall or residents are taped to the windows by the front door leading into the post office, whether it's the time and date for the island's annual homecoming or news of a funeral service.
"We've always been a big part of the community," Daley said. "We have a bulletin board of the things that are happening in the town because everyone is going to stop by the post office."
Married to a longtime waterman, Mickey Daley, now retired, Dolores said she loves island life.
"I love living here, being here," she said. "People here — we can go off and tend to anything we need on the mainland and come back when we've had enough. Living here in Tangier is my most favorite thing."

title: Cambridge Hires New City Planner
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge hires new city planner

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 CAMBRIDGE — After more than six months without a planning and zoning director, the City of Cambridge has filled the position.Brian Herrmann is set to take the role on Aug. 26.
Acting Cambridge City Manager David Deutsch made the announcement at a City Council meeting on Aug. 12. Deutsch said Herrmann and W. Glenn Steckman, who was recently hired as Cambridge's city manager, will both begin their roles soon.
Steckman, who served as city manager in Nome, Alaska for about five years, will begin in his position on Sept. 4, Deutsch said at the meeting.
Herrmann comes to Cambridge from Crystal River, Florida, where he served as the city's director of planning and development services. In an interview with the Star Democrat, Deutsch said Herrmann's "solid background in urban planning" makes him a good fit for the position.
"He's grappled with a number of issues that will be helpful here in Cambridge in terms of working on development and working on various code updates, working on comprehensive plan updates, all of which he will be working on here," Deutsch said.
In mid-January, Cambridge's previous planning and zoning director, John Steven Kaii-Ziegler, resigned from the position. Four days before his resignation, Kaii-Ziegler was indicted in Anne Arundel County in connection to a fatal hit-and-run in January 2023.
The nine charges in the indictment include negligent manslaughter, criminally negligent manslaughter, leaving the scene of an accident involving a death, driving under the influence of alcohol, driving while impaired, reckless driving and negligent driving. Kaii-Ziegler has a plea hearing scheduled for Aug. 14.
Deutsch told the Star Democrat that Herrmann, who hails from Montgomery County, had indicated in the interview process that he and his wife wanted to move back to Maryland to be closer to family.
Deutsch said that with Herrmann's experience, he doesn't think Herrmann will be intimidated in his role in Cambridge.
"It will take a little bit of time to get up to speed, but he's reading as many things as he can that will help in that regard," Deutsch said. "We're looking forward to a great tenure from him here."

title: Hurlock Opens Walking Trail, First of Three-Phases
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Hurlock opens walking trail, first of three-phases

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 570
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Hurlock residents have a new place where they can soak up the final weeks of summer: a paved walking trail.Using funds from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the town has completed the first phase of a three-phase, 1.5-mile trail project. This first part of the project, a 2,080-foot trail, stretches from Jackson Street to Delaware Avenue.
Hurlock Town Manager John Avery said the trail is a "relatively flat," six-foot-wide, paved asphalt trail with eight solar streetlights, three steel benches and trashcans placed along it.
Since its opening, the path gotten a lot of use. Avery said residents have reacted positively to the new public space.
"Everybody said that it's great they can have a place they can walk that's safe, that's lit at night," he said.
Hurlock Town Council Member Russell Murphy said in an email that the trail has been used "much more than expected."
"Every time I have been on it or ridden by it, there are people using it," he said. "We are so looking forward to completing phase two and phase three."
Murphy said he first introduced the idea for the trail as a way to light up Railroad Avenue and make it safer.
"Once seeing some of the rails-to-trails projects going on, it was brought up again as a way to provide a path from one end of town to another with safety and health also being in the forefront," he said.
Once all three phases of the project are complete, the trail will stretch 1.5 miles from one end of the town to the other, ending at North Main Street Park. To complete the last two phases of the project, Murphy said the county will need to take ownership of the railroad and then the town can ask for the county's permission to proceed with applying for grant funding.
Murphy said the Town Council hopes the trail will draw in visitors.
"We are hoping that anyone passing through will want to walk the trail and see what Hurlock has to offer," he said.
On Aug. 3, the town held a grand opening for the trail. Avery said the event went well, with Hurlock Mayor Rev. Charles T. Cephas and four of the Town Council's five council members in attendance.
Murphy called the grand opening "a monumental event." He said although the turnout was light, he hopes that word will get out and the trail will bring in prospective residents and businesses.
It took about two years for the trail to get built. Avery said the majority of that time was spent securing grant funding from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, which funded $82,000 of the approximately $105,000 project through the Community Parks and Playgrounds Program.
"The property is owned by Delmarva Power, so there was a joint-use agreement that had to go in place between Delmarva Power, the Department of Natural Resources and the town," Avery said. "And it took quite a while to get that worked out."
Avery said that after the agreement was worked out, the town was able to secure the grant funding for the project.
Murphy said the project could not have come to fruition if not for Avery and Cephas. He said the trail can bring residents closer together.
"When an activity, such as a park or trail, gets people outside, it will bring the community closer together," he said. "Its great to see neighbors and friends out and about so we can communicate and stay in touch with each other."

title: Motion Fails for Trappe Softball Field Grant Application
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Motion fails for Trappe softball field grant application

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 437
 Words

 TRAPPE — A motion to approve grant funding application requests to add a softball field to HomeRun Baker Park failed at the Trappe Town Council's most recent meeting. Now, the council has scheduled a special session to again go over the requests before the application deadline passes.During the meeting on Aug. 7, community member Cheryl Lewis went before the council and requested approval for two items.
The first was permission to submit an application request on Aug. 21 to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources Community Parks and Playgrounds Program to obtain funds for a girls softball field.
The second was to make a motion to approve, contingent on the state, a change in the joint agreement between Talbot County and Trappe required for the grant fund application. The change would name the county as the local government responsible for the park maintenance.
According to Lewis, Maryland has pre-prepared a joint agreement for seeking park funds stating the local town government is responsible for maintaining the park's "attractive appearance."
Lewis requested the town council pass a motion changing the joint agreement to clarify that Talbot County will be responsible for the park, not Trappe.
Commissioner Walter Chase, a member of the county park advisory board, said Lewis should attend a park advisory board meeting for further approval.
"I'm on the park board, so I'm gonna have to get a field from the park board before I sign anything right here because I don't get myself in trouble," Chase said.
Lewis said she had met with the county's parks advisory board during their last meeting and they had approved the concept of the softball field.
"(The park advisory board) did approve the concept of the softball field," Lewis said. "The joint agreement part they don't have authority to do. That's between (Trappe) and the Talbot County Council, and I'm talking to the... County Council at their meeting next week."
Lewis urged the council to pass the two motions, stating that applications are only accepted within the month of August and once the month passes they will not be able to apply until next year.
During the vote, Commissioner Rosalee Potter and Chase did not approve the motion to approve the application, and it failed to pass.
Chase said he would like to bring it back up with the parks board for approval. Potter said, "this is not anything personal. I am just accustomed to doing things more in order."
In order to stay within the August deadline, the Trappe Council will hold a special meeting the morning of Aug. 19 with the purpose of reviewing the grant funding application requests to be submitted. The public is welcomed to appear.

title: Dorchester County Purchases Race Street Property for Health Department
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County purchases Race Street property for health department

 August 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 452
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Health Department is moving.At a Dorchester County Council meeting on Aug. 6, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced the county has purchased the former Department of Social Services building, located at 627 Race St., for the health department.
In his announcement, Pfeffer said this has long been a wish of the department's health officer, Roger Harrell. Pfeffer said the current building, located at 3 Cedar St., has had mold and mildew issues, and the department has dealt with windows falling out.
"I know you've done interviews in mop closets over there," Pfeffer said to Harrell, who was at the meeting. "So hopefully now we can get you into a facility that's great for the citizens and their employees."
Harrell said in an interview with the Star Democrat that the department needed more space. He said the building on Race Street has about three times more square feet than the department's current building. He said the new building also has up-to-date heating, air conditioning and ventilation.
The Race Street property was purchased for $6.1 million from Leeward Holdings LLC. Pfeffer said they went to settlement the week before the County Council meeting.
Harrell said he was "very appreciative" of county officials for making this happen. "It's going to be nice to have more room to provide the services we provide for our community," he said. "It's exciting times."
When the department moved to Cedar Street in 2000, the plan was to stay for a couple of years, Harrell said. He said for various reasons, the department stayed longer than planned.
According to an Aug. 9 news release from the county, next steps for the move include "minor renovations" to meet the needs of the department as well as the transfer of technology and infrastructure from Cedar Street to Race Street. The release said the start date of when the department will begin offering services out of the Race Street building is "fluid and largely dependent on when the aforementioned next steps are completed."
Harrell said the minor renovations include putting in exam rooms and fiber internet.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Pfeffer said that once the health department has moved out of the Cedar Street property, that property will be surplussed.
At the end of the Aug. 6 meeting, Council Member Ricky Travers said he was glad and said this move is long overdue.
"I'm sorry your agency's had to work in this situation it's been (in)," he said. "And I'm glad to see it move forward in the right direction."
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said moving the facility to Race Street puts it "in the heart" of the community. "And I think it's going to be a great thing," he said. "It's well-deserved by your team."

title: Oxford Adopts Administrative Guide, Clarifies Agenda Setting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford adopts administrative guide, clarifies agenda setting

 August 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 344

 OXFORD — On Tuesday, the Commissioners of Oxford approved a resolution to adopt an administrative guide for town employees and commissioners and to clarify the authority to set agendas for commissioners meetings.The resolution also makes it so that commission meeting agendas will now have a consent agenda, which groups agenda items to be voted on together. Department head reports will be placed on the consent agenda. Commissioner Katrina Greer said this will allow for more legislative time at meetings.
The resolution, effective immediately, permits the commissioners to develop and adopt administrative policies that "promote good governance and transparency."
Greer made the motion to pass the resolution at the commission meeting on Tuesday. The resolution was passed unanimously.
"We've been talking about how to best deal with each other and the staff and setting up some norms," Greer said before the vote.
When it comes to agenda setting, the resolution sets deadlines for when items can be submitted and states that the commissioners must approve the agenda.
The administrative guide will break down what commissioners must approve and be notified of and what decisions and tasks are under the authority of the town manager or clerk treasurer. The guide will also details that in the event there is not a town manager, those duties will be taken on by the clerk treasurer with guidance from the commissioners.
The town has been without a manager since the retirement of former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis at the end of June.
The commissioners' next open session meeting will be next Tuesday, Aug. 20 at 6 p.m.
Greer said the commissioners will also be holding a special closed meeting on Friday to discuss search firm contracts. The town is seeking a search firm to help in its search for the next town manager.
Commission President Norm Bell said the commissioners started with a list of seven search firms and have since narrowed it down to five. He said some due diligence is still needed before the commission can come to a decision, but if all goes well, the commissioners will vote on a search firm next Tuesday.

author: Maggie Trovato

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Concerns over tree trimming — from tree safety, to property safety, to aesthetics — took up much of the first half of a Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Tuesday.At the meeting, two representatives from Delmarva Power and Light spoke about the tree trimming they have done in Oxford and other towns on the Shore every four years.
Renee Sheehy, senior public affairs manager at Delmarva Power and Light, acknowledged that residents had questions and concerns regarding the trimmings this year. She said Delmarva Power and Light recently met with the town about it.
Jeff Middleton, senior program manager for vegetation management at Delmarva Power and Light, said that across the nation, between 40 and 50% of all electrical outages are caused by trees, making the maintenance of vegetation near power lines important. He said the company follows industry standards when it comes to trimming trees, including using directional pruning to "encourage vegetation to grow away from the power lines."
During the meeting, residents expressed concerns that the trees had been trimmed back too far. Art Murr said his neighbor's tree was trimmed all the way back to the bird's nest.
"The tree, honestly, was butchered," he said.
Resident Barbara Paca said the tree Murr is referring to will probably die of sunscald due to the way it was trimmed by the contractors hired by Delmarva Power and Light.
In response to residents' concerns, Middleton said he understood the change can be "stark" and "jarring."
"But please know the trees that we're looking at, they were trimmed four years ago," he said. "The trees that were lush, they are going to be lush again. I wouldn't have a job if I killed every tree along the power lines and if they didn't grow back."
Murr said he understood what Middleton was saying, but wanted to point out the "stark" difference in how his neighbor's tree was trimmed this year compared to four years ago.
Other concerns brought up by residents include the look of the trimmed trees, Delmarva Power and Light's notification standards and safety to personal property.
Resident Leslie Howells said when the tree outside her home was trimmed, no one knocked on her door to notify her to move her car, which was parked beneath the tree in the driveway. She said her car was within four feet of the tree that they were pruning "big tree limbs" from.
Middleton said that if there is any concern about damaging private property, the workers will not proceed.
"Apparently the people that were there, they felt comfortable that they could perform the work safely, and they proceeded," he said.
Howells said that was unacceptable and residents should be properly notified of when the tree trimmings will take place.
Oxford commissioners also voiced some concern at the meeting. Commissioner Katrina Greer said when she and Oxford Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman approached one of the sites where trees were trimmed, there was no supervisor.
Both Greer and Commission President Norm Bell, acknowledging they aren't arborists, said some trees looked over-cut.
Sheehy said this reaction from residents is common when the trees are trimmed. She said utility directional pruning is different from how an arborist might prune because some limbs need to be trimmed in a way that could seem over-cut.
"But it has to be done there because of the nature of directional pruning," she said.
Middleton said he suggested to the commissioners that the community put together a tree council.

 EASTON — On Tuesday, Talbot County Council members approved two requests from the public works department for design services in preparation for road improvements in Easton.The council approved a recommendation to award about $347,000 in design services for road improvements on Black Dog Alley. The engineering firm, Wallace-Montgomery, will complete the design for road widening and drainage improvements.
Wallace-Montgomery is designing those improvements for Black Dog Alley's stretch between Matthewstown Road and Dover Road. The portion of the design approved Tuesday is just under a mile and is meant to mitigate increased traffic.
"I think working with the Sheriff's Office, the southern portion of Black Dog Alley is the most needed section of roadway that needs to be upgraded," County Engineer Ray Clarke said to the council.
Council President Chuck Callahan asked how long the road might be closed when construction occurs.
Clarke said "we could potentially do the construction where maybe we do the widening component and then ultimately we still have two-way traffic on it." But he added traffic may be "one-way at some point."
Council members also approved a request from public works to award design services for a new culvert under Chapel Road near its intersection with Klondike Road. Clarke said the tunnel is a common place for flooding during storms.
"Ultimately, the county in the past has had issues with this culvert flooding," Clarke said, "so this is basically looking at putting in a new culvert … (and) raising the road a little bit so we don't have that flooding."
Design services, awarded to engineering firm Davis, Bowen, & Friedel, will cost approximately $117,000, County Manager Clay Stamp noted. Clarke said it's a "problem area" for flooding, and that the county will perform a drainage analysis to help reduce flooding.
"Once we have that (analysis), we'll work to apply for the permits with MDE and then hopefully utilize the permit as our bid package and then put that out for bid," Clarke said.

title: Rising Sun Draws a Line in the Sand Over Its Future
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Rising Sun draws a line in the sand over its future

 August 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RISING SUN — Town officials have said publicly for the first time what has been troubling them for awhile: the resistance they get from Cecil County to allow those outside of town limits to connect to its water supply."Don't be fooled by what the county is doing," Commissioner Augie Pierson said in a two-page statement he read aloud at the Tuesday night town meeting. "They are trying to dictate the size of water lines to prevent the town of Rising Sun from being a partner in the economic benefits of county investments in the area."
Pierson pointed out that town residents pay the county $2.5 million in property taxes and get little in return.
"The truth is the county has invested millions in the MD 5 Star and Calvert Regional Park and I believe the towns should have a seat at the table," he said. Pierson also said that Rising Sun could easily run its water lines to those projects and others in the vicinity, if the county would allow.
Ordinance 2024-08 — which was approved at the meeting — adds to the town's existing Code of Ordinances "to incorporate recognized engineering standards for the construction of water and sewer lines within the town..." the legislation reads.
Pierson — a retired Baltimore City firefighter — said in his statement that the county is ignoring those engineering standards that guide the size of water and sewer lines and are putting the public and firefighters at risk.
"We refuse to support any measures that would handicap their ability to protect our community by imposing undersized water lines with inadequate fire flow or insufficient hydrants," he said. He said the county's Master Water and Sewer Plan runs counter to those standards that require a larger main to aid in fire suppression — both sprinkler and hydrant — and protect life and property values.
Town officials claim their comprehensive plan follows standards for the size of pipes dependent on such things as flow and force of the water. Pierson says the county is ignoring that standard.
"We are introducing this ordinance that establishes strict standards to ensure adequate water flow for fire protection, fire hydrants and properly sized water lines," he said. "We want to be clear: the town will not compromise on public safety. We will not permit undersized water lines that fall short of recognized engineering standards, nor will we allow connections to systems that use our water that fail to meet these essential standards."
Rising Sun has a daily capacity of one million gallons from Chester Water Authority. However, only about 275,000 gallons are used by the current customers. Officials say selling the excess capacity will save money for all customers of the system, especially town residents.
"The town of Rising Sun stands firm in our sovereignty as an incorporated municipality under the Maryland Constitution," Pierson said. "We will not be dictated to or bullied by Cecil County officials who continually attempt to undermine our autonomy."
Pierson added that county claims to preserve the rural character of the county — focused on Northern and Southern Agriculture Region zoning — are misleading.
"This narrative conveniently ignores the reality of their zoning code, which permits the very construction and development they claim to oppose," he said, adding, "The truth is the county is delaying the expansion of town water systems not to preserve the rural character, but to give Artesian Water time to fill in those areas they have targeted for development of the profit and benefit of Artesian Water. Cecil County sold its rights to Artesian years ago and they are doing everything they can to take over the water rights of all the towns and for the benefit of Artesian."
Joseph DiNunzio, Executive Vice President and Corporate Secretary for Artesian, said the company has no expansion plans for these county projects and was unaware of the claims made by Rising Sun.
"Artesian has not been involved in any way in the matter," DiNunzio said Thursday.

title: Proposed St. Michaels Tourism Board Met with Pushback
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Proposed St. Michaels tourism board met with pushback

 August 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 738
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, St. Michaels commissioners were faced with outcry from residents regarding the town's proposed Tourism Advisory Board.Residents raised an array of concerns, including potential conflicts of interests and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
An exact timeline for further creating the tourism board has not been established, according to Commissioner Jay Hudson. But commissioners voiced a desire to act quickly on the matter during Wednesday's meeting.
"There was a pushback on what we proposed towards the board, which was a little surprising, which means that we have to go back a little bit and get some modifications and see if we can't come to a resolution," Commissioner David Wojciechowski said. "In the end, we are running out of time."
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during a commissioners candidate forum hosted by the St. Michaels Business Association last April, when representatives of the Business Associations stated a need for marketing assistance due to a decrease in revenues within the last year.
During that forum, David Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were all later elected as commissioners, said they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The Tourism Advisory Board was again raised during a July 10 meeting while the town was hearing marketing bids. At the direction of the commissioners, an ordinance was pulled together to establish the board.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
The board would comprise seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership would include residents not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
DATADuring the public hearing Wednesday, resident Daniel Spiegel said the establishment of the tourism board is based on anecdotal information provided by St. Michaels business owners and not on actual data.
"The major rationale for this board, according to the language of the ordinance, is to promote business and retain business in this town," Spiegel said. "And I'd like to know whether the commission has been presented (with data) other than anecdotal information?"
Wojciechowski said part of the purpose of the Tourism Advisory Board would be to obtain data. He said he felt the board would provide an incentive for businesses to volunteer their revenue data so the town can have a better understanding of the needs they may have.
David Breimhurst, a resident and former St. Michaels commissioner, said he appreciated Wojciechowski's words on data gathering, but he proposed other means of obtaining it.
"I would suggest an in-depth economic study by a first tier economic study group would be the first step, so that we understand the true nature of our economy," Breimhurst said. "… So the data is most important, and I don't see any data supporting the rationale for creating this board in the first place."
CONFLICT OF INTERESTThe secondary concern brought by residents was the "conflict of interest" this board would pose to the town.
"You are making these business people and using representatives part of the structure of this town," Spiegel said. "And you will defer to them in terms of their ideas and recommendations, and their ideas and recommendations are going to have a budgetary impact that are going to impact their own financial well being, and that is a conflict of interest that should be avoided."
Commissioner Alexis Roiter gave a brief comment emphasizing the tourism board would focus on advising. It would not be a governmental board, she said.
"You can call it anything you want," Spiegel said "This is a board you are appointing. This board, they are governed by the laws and the rules and the ordinances of this town. You aren't creating a business advisory committee that you meet with from time to time. You are creating a mechanism that has all of the attributes of the Planning Commission."
After a bit of back and forth, Roiter suggested the town may need a tourism task force rather than a tourism board — an idea residents seem to agree on.
Toward the end of discussion, commissioners agreed to bring the subject of the tourism board up for discussion again at the next meeting in September.
