title: Town Short on Funding for Port Street Infrastructure Project
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Town short on funding for Port Street infrastructure project

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 777
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council learned at Tuesday's meeting that the town is well short of necessary funds to complete an infrastructure project on Port Street, leading to a lengthy back-and-forth between councilmembers and town employees.Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh and Mayor Megan Cook presented Ordinance 828 to the council, which would reallocate four separate amounts of fiscal year 2025 carry forward capital funds.
Two of the proposed reallocations involve removing $1.1 million in funding from the second phase of the Port Street project. The project, which leads down to the Tred Avon River, involves digging trenches and putting conduit pipes underground, running them on the side of the road. It's part of the town's efforts to revitalize the Port Street waterfront area and the nearby Easton Point Park.
It has an estimated cost of around $3.1 million.
"The money that we have that was carried forward equals $1.1 million," Van Emburgh said, "so we're $2 million short of having the money needed to complete that project."
The ordinance proposes $862,000 to be reallocated to Easton Woodland Park improvements, $50,000 for accessibility upgrades at the Easton Visitor Center and $225,000 for rails-to-trails work.
That $225,000 comes from American Rescue Plan Act funding, which must be obligated by the end of 2024 and used by the end of 2026.
Tuesday's discussion honed in on the funds proposed to go towards Woodland Park, a 200-acre property off Oxford Road near Cooke's Hope. Proposed amenities at the park include a 35-space parking lot, walking trails, a restroom facility and reforestation on 10 acres.
"We have 60% drawings completed to do improvements to the road and the small parking lot for that park," Van Emburgh said. " … These funds could be used for that project to bring that project to completion. That's not saying that we wouldn't ever do the Port Street project, we just don't have the funds. We're just kind of stuck in the middle, where we have some funds but not nearly enough funds to do that project."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry asked if the town is abandoning the Port Street project. Cook said it isn't, adding that the town can start on the Easton Woodlands project while searching for funding for Port Street.
"By reallocating the just over $800,000, we can actually start getting people to this park and utilize the 200 acres of parkland," Cook said. The town acquired the woodlands property last year using a $5 million state grant.
COUNCIL CRITICISMCouncil President Frank Gunsallus, along with other councilmembers, questioned why the reallocation proposal wasn't brought up sooner. "When was it determined that there wasn't enough for the underground project?" he asked.
"As the project grew, we knew that we just couldn't afford it," Cook responded.
"I just ask because we spent several months going through the budget process, and it seems like the perfect kind of thing that should have been discussed," Gunsallus said. The town passed its FY25 budget in June.
"It was probably overlooked at the time," Cook said.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis also asked why the council was not made aware of the insufficient funding for the Port Street project until Tuesday. Van Emburgh said carry forward funding is a "piece of the budget (that) needs to get more attention." He added, "I know we got to do better on the next round."
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery took issue with the fact that the Woodland Park project was placed above "high priority items" that the town wasn't able to fund last year.
Cook said moving the money to Woodland Park is "keeping in the spirit of pedestrian access and parkland," since the original "theory behind the funds was to extend pedestrian access to Easton Point Park."
"And that's more important to you than continuing to fix our stormwater management system where it's failing or acquisitions that we know we're going to have to make for failing equipment?" Montgomery asked the mayor.
"Not necessarily, but this is the start of the conversation," Cook answered. "That's why it's in the ordinance."
Montgomery pushed for a "budgetary argument" of why the money was proposed to fund Woodland Park improvements compared to other projects. "No rationale for that?" he asked.
"No rationale then," Cook said.
Councilmembers pushed for a workshop on the carry forward fund ordinance, which Cook agreed to. They asked for the workshop to include a list of potential projects in addition to the Easton Woodland Park that could use funding, along with a breakdown of American Rescue Plan Act funds that must be obligated by the end of December.
"Please bring your budgetary argument or strategy," Davis said during the end of the discussion. A workshop is scheduled for Sept. 16 before the Town Council's next meeting.

title: Washington College Court Win Confirms Partial Demolition of Armory Will Proceed
author: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Washington College court win confirms partial demolition of armory will proceed

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Chestertown Historic District Commission's May 1 decision to grant an application to Washington College to partially demolish the John H. Newnam Armory will most likely stand following a judge's ruling Wednesday.Over the summer, the college hit a speed bump in its plan to build a boutique hotel and conference center on the property that once headquartered the National Guard.
After the Historic District Commission's decision, there was a citizen's appeal made to the circuit court by residents Barbara Jorgenson, Tom Kocubinski and Steve Mitchell. They were opposed to the college's plan, favoring restoration over partial demolition.
But on Wednesday, with local Judge Harris Murphy recusing himself, visiting Judge Sidney Campen sided with the college.
Campen's decision came on the grounds that the petitioners didn't have legal standing to make their appeal.
In his opening argument, Collin Wojciechowski, an attorney representing the college, brought up a case he said was similar to this one.
Ray v. Mayor and Maryland City Council of Baltimore, he said, had "striking parallels in this matter."
In that case, citizens lived within 1,000 feet of the property, but the city still moved to dismiss the case, a move with which the Maryland Supreme Court agreed.
Unlike in that case, the petitioners, Wojciechowski claimed, can't argue by proximity since none of them live within 1,000 feet of the applicant property.
He said other than proximity, the burden of proof for the petitioners is to prove their "personal or property rights are adversely affected in a way different than the rest of the public."
"... Petitioners can't show that here. None of the history of the individuals is unique from their neighbors. That uniqueness is needed and Maryland courts have never found it to exist," Wojciechowski said.
Nelson rebutted, saying this case was indeed unique.
"There's no appellate authority that addresses the question of standing in the historic district," Nelson said.
Furthermore, he said he had actually worked the case referenced by the defense, arguing it in every stage of litigation.
That issue, he said, was a zoning decision over a 200,000-square-foot Walmart, not an historic district decision of a building constructed in 1931 in a small town.
He firmly disagreed with Wojciechowski. Residents within the Chestertown historical district are the exception, he said, because demolishing and rebuilding will affect the petitioners' taxes, property values and insurance.
Then pointing to the Historic District Commission guidelines, he read, "If an owner within the historic district allows a building to fall in disrepair, that adversely affects the character of the district."
And again in the guidelines, "The loss of any contributing historic building diminishes the district and can never be replaced."
Nelson said in this situation, the college allowed the building to go into disrepair. Additionally the Historic District Commission then violated guidelines by not issuing a written statement summarizing their decision on May 1, he said.
Combined with the written testimonies from the petitioners, it proves they should have standing, he said.
Wojciechowski countered, stating this is straightforward case, and the arguments about the Historic District Commission were merit questions, not about standing.
He said if the judge allowed this, it would set a precedent encouraging the appeal of Historic District Commission decisions.
After both sides presented their arguments, the judge agreed with Wojciechowski, dismissing the petitioner's claim.
He said Nelson did not present enough evidence or case law to show the petitioners would be adversely affected differently than any other resident in the district.
Mike Sosulski, president of the college, said he was satisfied with the judge's decision. "I think's it's the right result," he said. "While we appreciate our neighbor's position, we're pleased that the project's going forward."

title: Dorchester County Thanks Chief of Staff for Almost 19 Years of Service

Dorchester County thanks chief of staff for almost 19 years of service

 Cambridge — Dorchester County Chief of Staff Donna Lane was thanked at her final County Council meeting as a county employee.During the meeting, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced that Lane has taken a job with the state. In her 18 years and nine months as a county employee, Lane served a variety of positions, from administrative assistant to acting county manager.
Pfeffer, who called the news "bittersweet," thanked Lane for being a valuable resource in the county, as well as a friend.
"Even before I was elected, when I would sit in the audience and I'd have questions about how the county works, I'd come to you, and you would give me answers, and I greatly appreciate that," he said to her.
Council Member William Nichols teared up as he recounted Lane's first day as a county employee.

During public comment, Derek Griffin, who is on the county's Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee, said Lane has "provided exceptionally outstanding support" to the boards he is on.
Pfeffer thanked Griffin for his comments and said the reason they asked Lane to provide support to those boards is because of her attention to detail.
"She knows how the programs work," Pfeffer said. "She knows how the legal system works with us. Donna, I can't say enough about all that you do here, so thank you again."
Before the meeting ended, County Attorney Chip MacLeod said that over the years, he's always copied Lane on emails.
"Knowing that whatever happens, if Donna knows I've sent this email, there's going to be a record and we'll figure something out," he said.
MacLeod joked that with Lane leaving, he is going to have more to do.
"I think I'm going to have to pay attention a little more (to) what's happening at these meetings," he said, laughing. "Thank you."
At the end of the meeting, Lane said that it has been a pleasure working with county staff, the County Council, and previous councils.
"I'm honored to be able to do that and also focus on the best that we could do for our citizens of the county," she said. "And I know that'll be continued with this council and staff."

title: Easton Council Supportive of Potential Spike in Hotel Tax Rate
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton council supportive of potential spike in hotel tax rate

 September 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A plan to increase the accommodation tax rate in Talbot County was presented to the Easton Town Council at Tuesday night's meeting.Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of economic development and tourism, recommended the increase to the council. It would raise the accommodation tax, or hotel tax, from 4% to 6% in the county.
"Anybody who's renting a room to someone for less than four months who's considered a 'transient' would be required to collect accommodations tax," Vanhooser said.
Vanhooser pointed out that Talbot County's rate is the lowest in the state. Around $2 million was collected throughout the county in accommodation taxes in fiscal year 2024. If the rate had been 6%, that total would have increased to just above the $3 million mark.
She noted the success of the county in the tourism industry. Despite the rate remaining stagnant since 2004, Talbot County has more than doubled its accommodation tax revenue.
"We consider this as an indicator of our success as a tourism destination," Vanhooser said. "We know people are coming here. We know we're commanding a premium price, and people are willing to pay that."
In order to raise the rate, the county needs to ask state delegates this October to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year. The county is looking for support from three towns, including Easton, in order to move forward.
The towns of Easton, St. Michaels and Oxford collect revenues from the 4% tax on all hotels and short-term rentals within respective town limits or within a mile of those limits. The county collects the tax from lodgings that don't fall in or within a mile of town limits.
"The county would like to hear a vote from you on whether you would support this or not, because obviously, we don't want to go to the state legislature and ask for something that you do not support," Vanhooser said.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello asked if the county reached out to hotels in the area for feedback on the spike. Vanhooser said the county's tourism board has hotel representation, adding that the county is aiming to reach out to all hotels as a courtesy.
After a short discussion, the council voiced support for the proposed increase, unanimously voting in favor. No formal resolution was required for the agenda item.
"Talbot County obviously is not unique," Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said. "But we have attractions that are not matched by our neighbors, and for that reason, I fully support raising this to 6%."

title: EDITORIAL: 10-Cent Paper Bag Fee Should Be Optional
author: Staff Writer
content:
EDITORIAL: 10-cent paper bag fee should be optional

 September 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 923
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Earlier this week, the Easton Town Council debated a proposal to remove a 10-cent fee on paper bags used to bag groceries and other purchased merchandise.We think that fee should be optional — if retailers need to charge the fee to cover the cost of the bags, they should be able to do so. But it is also important that store owners be able to provide the bags at no charge as part of the service they offer customers.
The April 2023 Easton ordinance banning the use of plastic bags required retailers to charge customers a fee of at least 10 cents for each paper bag used, encouraging shoppers to bring reusable bags. It came as the Town Council banned the use of plastic bags for packaging purchases in stores such as groceries and retail shops. Restaurants and food establishments are exempt from the ban.
This is a hot topic in Eastern Shore communities.
Late last month, the Commissioners of Oxford debated a similar ban for Oxford before tabling the proposed ordinance.
Like it does in Easton, Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the Oxford ban would apply to retail establishments including grocery stores, convenience stores, shops, department stores and service stations. The ordinance would not apply to restaurants and food service establishments.
During the Oxford public hearing, some business owners and employees expressed concerns with the proposed ordinance. Graham Norbury, the general manager at Safe Harbor Oxford, said that while this may be a national issue, he doesn't observe plastic bags being littered often in Oxford.
"Why is restricting a retailer's right to choose the best delivery mechanism for their products, why is that something that the commissioners feel necessary?" he asked.
Oxford Vintage and Trade owner Barbara Ranson said in her six years of being in business in Oxford, she has always used paper bags. She said she doesn't understand why the commissioners are looking at this legislation when "it may or may not target three very small businesses."
We think Oxford should follow in Easton's footsteps and ban plastic bags and even expand the ban to include restaurants and food service establishments.
Plastic bags have severe and dire affects on the environment.
Non-biodegradable: Plastic bags can take hundreds of years to break down in the environment. Instead of decomposing, they break into smaller pieces called microplastics, which can persist in the ecosystem for even longer.
Pollution: Plastic bags often end up in waterways and oceans, where they can cause severe pollution. Marine animals can ingest or become entangled in plastic bags, leading to injury or death.
Harmful chemicals: As plastic bags break down, they can release harmful chemicals into the soil and water, which can contaminate ecosystems and pose risks to wildlife and human health.
Energy and resources: The production of plastic bags involves the use of fossil fuels and energy, contributing to greenhouse gas emissions and resource depletion.
Waste management: Plastic bags can be challenging to recycle due to their lightweight and flimsy nature. They can clog machinery at recycling facilities, leading to higher costs and lower recycling rates.
Just this week a Star Democrat editor watched a plastic grocery bag go airborne from the bed of a pickup truck crossing the Bay Bridge. The bag floated into the air where a breeze caught it and sent it flying over the Bay, eventually landing in the water. That bag became a death trap for a fish or a bird. This is not an isolated incident, we are sure readers can recount similar experiences seeing wayward plastic bags.
So we stand firmly behind banning plastic bags and think more towns should follow the lead of Easton and Oxford.
Our complaint comes with the imposition of a 10-cent fee that Easton requires retailers to charge a fee if a customer requests or needs a plastic bag.
There is a good reason for that fee: It provides an incentive for customers to begin using reusable bags, which are far better than even the paper bags.
"The reason for the proposal to remove this fee comes directly from the voices of many Easton residents who are feeling its impact," said council President Frank Gunsallus in explaining the proposal to make the fee optional, "especially those in lower-income brackets who are already stretching every dollar to make ends meet."
Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery both said they've talked to residents who do not support the current 10-cent fee. The rest of the council, though, stated otherwise.
"I have heard from many people the exact opposite, that the ban is working and that the 10 cents is not onerous in any way, shape or form," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello and Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis stated the fee has incentivized people to bring their own reusable bags. Abbatiello said, "the reason for that (fee) is because paper bags pollute just as much as plastic bags do."
All valid arguments on both sides of the issue. Our thought is that this is an issue that should be left to individual retailers to decide what is best for their businesses.
Nearly everybody from the audience who spoke at Tuesday's council meeting supported leaving the mandatory fee in place.
Easton resident Shari Wilcoxon held a different stance, questioning why the businesses are forced to charge the 10-cent fee.
"I don't know why people are afraid of freedom of choice," Wilcoxon said. "Why don't you let the merchants decide if they want to charge or not, what's wrong with that?"
We agree with Wilcoxon and hope town council members look to making the fee optional when the issue is discussed again on Sept. 16.

title: Ridgely Not Planning to Reinstate Police Department
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely not planning to reinstate police department

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 735
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Despite a state criminal investigation against Ridgely's police chief coming up empty, Ridgely commissioners announced on Monday that they have no plans to reinstate the town's police force, which has been suspended since March.A report from the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor stated an investigation was opened into Ridgely Police Department Chief Jeff Eckrich due to "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office. The investigation found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution," the July 25 report said.
The commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department on March 12, providing minimal explanation to residents. Since, the town has entered into an agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide police coverage in place of the suspended officers. With the start of the new fiscal year July 1, the Ridgely officers were laid off.
Chip MacLeod, an attorney representing the town, read aloud a statement at the beginning of Monday's town meeting.
"The commissioners recognize the pain this unfortunate situation has caused their friends and neighbors in the town," MacLeod stated. "At the same time, the commissioners are pleased that most of the former Ridgely Police Department employees have secured employment elsewhere. Thus, the commissioners realize that those employees would be unlikely to return to their former positions even if those positions were available."
"The commissioners recognize that reestablishing the Ridgely Police Department would be a complex and expensive undertaking," MacLeod later said. "Such an effort would require a high level of citizen support, not just political support, for operating the Ridgely Police Department, and a commitment to funding and seeing the process through. Accordingly, the commissioners believe that it is in the best interest of the town to continue the present arrangement with the sheriff and the county through at least fiscal year 2025 and to reevaluate the sheriff's engagement when preparing the fiscal 2026 budget."
MacLeod said commissioners and town staff will provide no additional comment regarding the police department.
Many residents reacted negatively after the statement was read. Some asked why there wasn't an apology provided to the officers, and others pointed out the town didn't acknowledge the police chief was cleared of wrongdoing.
One resident asked the Caroline County Sheriff's Office sergeant in attendance which three officers are currently assigned to the town for coverage.
"We're not answering no questions. I'm in charge," Commissioner John Buckle said.
Resident Jennifer Nesselroad spoke during public comment, asking the commissioners for an itemized list of police and town vehicles. She also expressed frustration with the commissioners' statement.
"You never apologized for disbanding our police department, not even issuing an apology for everybody being exonerated," Nesselroad said. "That was very, very rude and inconsiderate to us and those police officers that gave every day around this town, even for you all, everybody sitting up here. That was very cowardly."
Heather Amador asked commissioners why the town did not follow its charter, which states the commissioners must hold a vote to remove an officer or town employee.
"A criminal investigation's going to trump anything in the town charter," MacLeod said.
"Absolutely, against one, against the chief," Amador said. "The others were never under investigation."
"You heard the statement I read," MacLeod said. Amador responded, "I did, but it doesn't answer my question."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Ridgely resident Robin Martin expressed concern over the fact that the commissioners have not clearly stated who directed them to suspend the police department back in March.
Monday's statement from the commissioners noted that on March 12, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office executed a search and seizure warrant issued by the county's circuit court. It stated that "commissioners were directed to order all RPD officers to surrender" firearms, vehicles and other equipment to the town, but did not clarify who provided that direction.
The decision to suspend the department came "without guidance" from the state prosecutor, according to the state prosecutor's report.
"I think we have a distrust for the commissioners of the town," Martin said. "We've been way more involved in things that are happening in the town, because we don't trust that they have our best interests at heart anymore."
During public comment, Martin asked commissioners for "less closed-door activity and more community involvement" in town decisions. After the meeting, Martin said her heart breaks for the officers.
"They participate in everything around town, and I think that's kind of what Ridgely should be about, community policing," Martin said. "This has been something so shameful for the town."

title: St. Michaels Proposed Dog Park Must Find New Location
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels proposed dog park must find new location

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The long-desired dog park for St. Michaels has faced yet another barrier in its journey to becoming reality. Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, a volunteer group advocating for the park, have decided to move away from the proposed Bradley Parks location due to concerns from residents.During the Aug. 14 Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting, members of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park spoke up and suggested Bradley Park as the location for the future park. According to Mitch Ettinger, the founder of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, the one-acre park was "underutilized" with few residential homes located nearby and had the added bonus of already being maintained by the town.
But last week, St. Michaels residents were sent a message from Ettinger stating the group had requested the commissioners remove the planned dog park discussion from the Sept. 11 meeting.
Ettinger said the decision came after hearing concerns from those living adjacent to Bradley Park. These concerns included noise from barking and the effect the park would have on the property value of their home, Ettinger said.
"Quite frankly, I just couldn't see myself standing up and saying, 'disregard these neighbors.' That's not the way that I think. That's not the way that my committee thinks," Ettinger said. "And so we withdrew the proposal for Bradley Park and asked the commissioners to take it off the agenda for this week."
The effort to have a dog park built in St. Michaels has been ongoing for more than three years. Ettinger said the dog park has been volunteer-led since its origins and is widely supported by residents of the town, according to a survey conducted when an architect was coming up with a master plan for seven acres at San Domingo Park. The site did not work for a dog park due to grant requirements that would prohibit fencing.
Moving forward, Ettinger said he would like to see commissioners of St. Michaels to take initiative and assist with the finding of a new property.
"It's time for the commissioners to step up, and they've been supportive of this concept, but they have yet to propose a location," Ettinger said.
Ettinger said his group would continue to work behind the scenes to assist commissioners in picking a location, and currently there are a couple of options that are under consideration.
Dan Conway, a member of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, said he and the committee are still committed to the dog park project. For him, it is more than just a place for dogs to run around. It is a community building area and would benefit owners and dogs alike in St. Michaels.
"Dog parks aren't really for dogs ... They're for people, and they help make a municipality, a community," Conway said. "In my experience, it's where townspeople can get together and renew acquaintances and make friends and share experiences. And so that, to me, is the beauty of a dog park."

title: Tides of Grace Welcomes New Transit Van
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Tides of Grace welcomes new transit van

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News

 Read News Document

 Centreville — Supporting the Eastern Shore through kindness and compassion, local non-profit Tides of Grace welcomed the addition of a transit van to more effectively service the community with a ribbon cutting ceremony at the Liberty Building Sept. 10.Thanks to a $12,500 grant received from the Queen Anne's County Commissioners covering the van, wrapping and insurance, the new vehicle for Tides of Grace will enhance the non-profit's ability to more efficiently serve the community through collections and deliveries, according to founder Leann Rhodes-Ickes.
Before the van, Tides of Grace volunteers utilized their own personal vehicles to distribute and collect goods for drives, she said.
"The support and love of the community is what keeps us going," Rhodes-Ickes said.
The mission of Tides of Grace is to support the community through kindness and compassion by providing a helping hand to those in need of resources and services.
What started as a holiday toy drive in 2022 has blossomed into needing its own designated set of wheels to serve the community, according to Rhodes-Ickes.
Tides of Grace provides free monthly services and drives for the community including collecting and distributing prom dresses, food bank goods, and hosting family photos, and family fun days.
More than just monthly events, Tides of Grace also staunchly keeps an ear out to who is in need and what is needed most in the community.
"Connecting the dots with the community has allowed us to make a full circle," Rhodes-Ickes said, as she credited Linette and Tim Miller with being instrumental in connecting Tides of Grace with the van within their price range.
"Keep doing what you're doing. It's about the community," Linette said.
Thanking Rhodes-Ickes and the Tides of Grace team for their initiative in servicing the community, County Commissioner Phil Dumenil noted it can be easy for the commissioners to fund worthwhile outside agencies, but "it takes a single person to get to that point," he said.
Serving about 300 people a month, the Stevensville based nonprofit would like to eventually expand to a larger space, Rhodes-Ickes said.
Tides of Grace is continually growing and is always looking for more involvement from the community and volunteers.
More information about Tides of Grace can be found at tidesofgraceinc.org.

title: County Introduces Zoning Change Resolution for Potential Housing Project
author: Konner Metz
content:
County introduces zoning change resolution for potential housing project

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 405
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Council introduced a resolution Tuesday proposing a zoning change waiver for around 17 acres of land off of U.S. Route 50 for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project in Easton.The development on the east side of Ocean Gateway is planned by developers Corrigan & Trippe Ventures. Easton Town Council approved the annexation of the land back in July.
The resolution states that the proposed rezoning from the county's town conservation zoning to the town's residential zoning "will result in substantially different uses or substantially higher density" than would be allowed for proposed development under the county's zoning.
Thus, the town is requesting the zoning change along with a waiver on a five-year hold. That hold would restrict the ability to develop annexed land for five years after annexation for such uses that are either substantially different or of a substantially higher density.
The county's town conservation zoning, which the land is currently under, allows for one dwelling unit per acre, Talbot County Planning and Zoning Director Brennan Tarleton said. The town's residential zoning would allow for 3.5 dwelling units per acre, he added.
County Council President Chuck Callahan asked about the total number of units that could be proposed in that area if the zoning change is made. Tarleton said around 50 to 60.
"That's not an exact number because there are included environmental constraints," Tarleton said. "These properties are relatively heavily forested, so I'm sure there will be some environmental buffers included in that."
He noted that the property is expected to be proposed as a planned unit development to the town in the future, meaning "it could be proposed at a larger density permissible on these properties" than the town's residential zoning. Developers initially told the town a maximum density could be around 240, though town council feedback was mixed on whether that mark was excessive.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher brought up accessibility to the property, asking if there will be publicly accessible entrances other than U.S. Route 50.
"No, unfortunately it doesn't appear that there's any connectivity to any existing subdivisions within the town or within the county based on where these properties exist today," Tarleton responded. " … It's likely that the access for any future development on this property would come directly from Route 50."
"That's a nut for the town to crack," Lesher said.
The resolution was introduced Tuesday, and a public hearing will be held at the council's Oct. 8 meeting.

title: CWDI Board accepts member resignation, fills two open seats
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CWDI Board accepts member resignation, fills two open seats

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During the closed session of a Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors meeting on Wednesday, the board accepted the resignation of board member Dion Banks and accepted appointments from the City of Cambridge for two vacancies.In an interview with the Star Democrat, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said Gaver Nichols and Natalie Chabot will fill the seats of Banks and former board member Rich Zeidman.
Cambridge City Council President Lajan Cephas said the new board members were the "best candidates" for the open seats.
"(They are) people who know this community, and they understand it," Cephas said. "And I know they have the best interest at heart."
Hengst said both new members have the experience the board was looking for and fill in knowledge gaps on the board. She said Nichols has development and architecture experience and Chabot has a long history with the community.
Nichols, who is an architect, is currently a member of the Cambridge Board of Zoning Appeals. Hengst said Nichols will be resigning from that board.
Cephas said Nichols' experience with the Board of Zoning Appeals will give CWDI the advantage of understanding what's expected when it comes to zoning.
"That should build an even stronger relationship between the city and CWDI so that they're prepared before they go to the table knowing what will pass and what likely is not going to pass," Cephas said.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Nichols said he is proud to be on the board. He said he hopes to see the waterfront become "an outstanding place to go" as a local and as someone visiting Cambridge.
Hengst said Chabot is "invested in the community." In her career, Chabot has served as Cambridge's economic development director and Dorchester County's tourism director. She also served on the Sailwinds Park Board for more than a decade.
Cephas said throughout Chabot's career, she has "always protected the historical fabric of our community." Cephas said Chabot is "well-versed" when it comes to grant money that is available for development projects.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Chabot said she views the appointment as a great opportunity for herself and for the board. She said she thinks she can bring a lot to the table with her experience and passion.
Chabot said she is looking forward to being a proactive member on the board and seeing significant action on the waterfront.
Zeidman, who was appointed to the board by the city in 2018 and reappointed in 2021, resigned in May. In a May 23 news release from CWDI, Zeidman mentioned the progress that CWDI has made on Cambridge Harbor and his desire to spend his retirement years in actual retirement as reasons for his resignation.
That month, amid a lawsuit with the city, CWDI alleged in a court motion that Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout had sent a letter to Zeidman in October requesting his resignation from the CWDI board.
Banks joined the board as a city appointee in 2022. Hengst said in a text message that Banks resigned due to "increased travel demands in his current position at work," which made him unable "to devote the necessary time to the board."
Cephas said she is sure this decision is something Banks thought long and hard about and felt was best, not just for himself, but for CWDI.
"That's just the type of person that Dion is," she said.
Banks did not immediately respond for comment.

title: Partial Closure of Route 662 Will Begin in October

Partial closure of Route 662 will begin in October

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 Words

 EASTON — A portion of Route 662 is expected to temporarily close beginning in October, according to the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health.Shore Regional Health's project on Longwoods Road in Easton is bringing a new medical center to the region. Due to a portion of hospital designs that sit on top of the current Longwoods Road, or Route 662, the roadway is expected to be closed for seven to eight months.
That projected timeframe gives Shore Regional Health time to construct a modified portion of Route 662 slightly eastwards. The closure will ensure there is no delay or interference with construction work on the new hospital.
"While we regret possible inconvenience this may cause to motorists, we want to assure the community that detailed contingency and emergency management plans are in place," Shore Regional Health CEO and President Ken Kozel said in a press release on Friday.
"We have been working collaboratively with the State Highway Administration as well as Talbot County and Easton roads and emergency management officials to plan for safe and efficient management of a wide range of emergency scenarios."
The state's official detour will be Route 50. However, many residents and farmers have raised concerns that the temporary closure will impact traffic on nearby county roads, such as Hiners Lane, Airport Road and Goldsborough Neck Road.
"Our priority is to minimize disruptions while ensuring that essential services remain accessible throughout the construction period," Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said in a press release. "The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is working closely with all partners to maintain safe and reliable transportation routes during this time."
On Wednesday, the Maryland Board of Public Works approved the State Highway Administration to transfer about a half-mile of Route 662 to Talbot County.
That step will allow Talbot County to transfer the road to Shore Regional Health prior to Oct. 1 so relocation work can begin. Last month, the Talbot County Council approved a bill that permits the road can now be transferred to Shore Regional before the new route is completed.
The closure will extend from Airport Road north to Hiners Lane, which is around a mile stretch of the road. On Friday, Shore Regional Health said the closure will begin "on or around" Oct. 1.
Shore Regional Health's medical center is scheduled to complete in the summer of 2028. It is replacing the current medical center on South Washington Street.
To follow construction progress on the hospital, visit umshoreregional.org/rmc.

title: Easton Looking into Using AI, Safeguarding Against Dangers
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton looking into using AI, safeguarding against dangers

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As artificial intelligence extends its reach, the town of Easton is having preliminary discussions on how AI can be a tool in its daily operations.Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus believes there are practical uses in which AI can help governments operate more efficiently, such as sifting through data sets so employees can dedicate more time elsewhere.
"It's as big as the internet or the printing press when you look at humanity, really, the history of it and innovative technologies that come about," Gunsallus said. "In my opinion, this is one of those that has a way to systemically change the way the world functions and commerce transacts."
While Gunsallus said its benefits are exciting, he noted that it's not "something to rush into." At a town workshop on Sept. 3, councilmembers hosted a discussion regarding AI and how the town can move forward in using it responsibly.
One of the major action items was to look into developing an acceptable use policy so employees understand proper usages of artificial intelligence in a town setting. One of the distinctions brought up during the workshop was free programs, such as ChatGPT, versus paid programs and whether information is more at risk when free programs are used.
Scott Messick, the town's IT director, worked with AI in creating the town's parking application that reads license plates and detects activity in parking lots. He emphasized one's purpose when using the technology is of the utmost importance when it comes to security.
"It's not so much the tool you use, but what you're doing with it," Messick said on Sept. 3. He said if an employee is putting personal information into an artificial intelligence tool, "then that is not appropriate."
Easton Utilities, a not-for-profit utility and telecommunications company, provides electric, natural gas, water, internet and more to residents. The company has begun to embrace AI.
Easton Utilities uses a paid program to maintain cybersecurity. Chief Information Officer Fred Christie said it has worked AI into its acceptable use policy.
"The knowledge base or the data store that it's using is where all of the risk is," Christie said in an interview. " … It's very important to make sure that you have an acceptable use policy that tells your employees how they should use it and how they should not use it, and that's where the town of Easton is right now."
Christie noted the cybersecurity defense is an example of predictive AI, in which a program detects "anomalies" and learns on its own what is normal and what isn't. Easton Utilities also uses generative AI, whether it's for internal communication or marketing.
Though not used at Easton Utilities, some companies use predictive AI programs for vegetation management to protect infrastructure or prepare in the case of a hurricane.
"AI is not rocket science, it really isn't," Christie said. "It is essentially a very sophisticated, math-based, statistical-based search base."
Christie said training and educating employees is key to managing the technology effectively and responsibly. While it increases efficiency, AI is not replacing any positions at the company. "It's just going to make us do our job better," he said.
Gunsallus, whose day-to-day job is at an IT service provider in Easton, was happy the town held a workshop so the public knows the town is exploring both the potential benefits and risks of AI programs.
"The good it could do is make things more efficient," Gunsallus said. "It (helps with) savings of time and money. When you're handling other people's money, in my opinion, it is paramount that you are doing just exactly that — being efficient and prudent stewards of the town's finances."

title: Oxford Commissioners Mull Meeting Procedures After 'Disruptive Behavior' at August Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners mull meeting procedures after 'disruptive behavior' at August meeting

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford will be considering a resolution to establish meeting procedures at its next meeting on Sept. 24.At a regular meeting on Tuesday evening, the commissioners agreed to table the proposed resolution, which would establish general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings.
Commission President Norm Bell, who read the proposed resolution and rules aloud, said the purpose of the policy "is to create an atmosphere where the elected officials, staff and members of the public can attend to business efficiently, fairly and with full participation."
Before reading the resolution, Bell said the proposed rules and procedures were developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at the previous town meeting on Aug. 27.
During the public comment portion of that meeting, yelling broke out between residents after resident Scott Rensberger asked to sit down with Bell at a later date to discuss a public letter Bell wrote in April. The letter mentioned videos made by Rensberger about government transparency in Oxford.
The incident caused resident Tom Campbell to say that he has a hard time recognizing Oxford anymore.
"This can't be every town meeting," Campbell said Aug. 27. "We're getting nowhere. And it's making it hard for me to cheer on my community anymore."
If the resolution is passed, unless there is a public hearing, public comment would not be permitted until the end of the meeting. Public comments would need to be related to public business, and commenters would not be allowed to ask questions.
"This part of the meeting is not a question-and-answer period," Bell read from the policy. "If a question is asked, it will not be answered."
The policy would limit public comment to three minutes and would allow the commissioners to limit the total time of the public comment period.
The policy would prohibit cheering, booing, interrupting and any other forms of heckling. Defamatory comments, profanity and obscenities will also not be tolerated.
The proposed policy states anyone who wants to record the meeting must do so from a "designated area" in the meeting room and cannot walk around to move equipment during the meeting.
On Tuesday, Bell said it's important that the commissioners conduct business in an environment "where everyone feels safe (and) no one feels threatened, bullied or harassed."
After Bell read the proposed policy, commissioners Katrina Greer and Tom Costigan shared their thoughts on it.
Greer said that she thinks there should be a meeting policy in place, but she didn't want to vote on it on Tuesday and asked that they postpone the vote until the Sept. 24 meeting.
"Anything that we vote on that's as important as public comment should be posted for the public to see five or six days in advance so they get a chance to comment on it," she said.
Greer said she did not like that public comment would only come at the end of the meeting. She said there should be an opportunity for the public to speak before the commissioners take a vote on something. Greer also asked that the policy be amended to take out the part about public comment not being a question and answer period.
"If people ask a question, we should, if we can, answer that question," she said.
Costigan said he agreed with everything in the resolution. But he said he didn't have a problem waiting to vote on it until the next meeting.
"I think that we should put either a thumbs up or a thumbs down on this at our meeting on the 24th," he said.

title: Easton, Can You Spare a Dime for a Paper Bag?
author: Marion O Arnold
content:
Easton, can you spare a dime for a paper bag?

 September 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARION O ARNOLD | Section: Columns 
 
 714
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus has introduced an ordinance aimed at the town's Plastic Bag Law by doing away with the paper bag fee.The law prohibits stores from providing plastic bags and requires retailers to charge a 10-cent fee for paper bags. The fee helps retailers with the higher cost of paper bags. According to Maryland Retailers Association's Sarah Price, who testified at the last Town Council meeting, the 10-cent fee helps level the playing field between retailers allowing them to recover the cost of paper bags for shoppers who take them, reducing overhead and keeping prices lower for all shoppers. It's a fee, not a tax. Retailers keep the fee.
Paper bags come at an environmental cost, so the 10-cent fee also helps the law from inadvertently substituting one environmental problem with another. Paper bags require trees and a polluting process to make them. Paper bags can be recycled or composted, but most will end up in landfills where they become a source of planet-warming methane gas.
For shoppers, the fee makes things more equitable. Those shoppers who take paper bags pay for them. Not having a fee will raise prices on other goods since retailers will have to recoup the increased costs of giving out "free" paper bags. Those of us who bring our own bags will end up paying higher prices, even though we won't be using disposable paper bags.
Most importantly, the 10-cent fee incentivizes shoppers to bring their own bags. It's your choice. You don't have to spend a dime if you bring your reusable bags.
I think of major environmental laws like the Clean Air and the Clean Water acts. Businesses had to make big investments to meet the demands of the laws or meet up with stiff penalties and fines. Here, with our plastic bag law, we're just asking businesses to charge a small fee for paper bags and to keep every dime they collect.
Without the 10-cent fee the law loses a part of its environmental impact. No one is saying let's bring back plastic bags, but if free, paper bags will fly out retailers' doors — and smaller retailers will bear the cost. Laurel, Maryland, passed a bag law in 2022 without a fee. Two years later, they changed their law to add a 10-cent paper bag fee because more than two-thirds of shoppers there just took the free paper bags. Since January, shoppers in Laurel taking paper bags has dropped to 32%.
Easton's plastic bag law was the result of months of work by a team of town leaders, Easton residents, and community representatives, with encouragement and backing from Talbot watermen, local businesses and environmental organizations. Since then, plastic bags no longer hang from our trees, pile up in hedgerows and ditches, and end up in our waterways. The economic and environmental benefits for Easton are many.
Jeff Harrison, president of the Talbot Watermen Association, was an early supporter of the plastic bag law. He has said, "We have to understand, whatever we do on the land eventually ends up in the water." At the last town council meeting, he testified to the law's success, saying he "doesn't see bags in the water anymore."
The law works, and we can readily see the results.
Mr. Gunsallus argued that repealing the 10-cent fee was for those "who are struggling." I have no doubt that people struggle, but no one shopping in Easton is required to pay that 10-cent fee either. There's no fee if you bring your own bag. Bing Crosby's big hit from 1932, "Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?" came to mind. Back then you could go to a five and dime store and do some damage with that dime in your pocket. You could get two pairs of socks or two cups of coffee. Today, about all you can get for a dime is a brown paper bag.
Mr. Gunsallus does not take into account the greater cost of pollution from paper bags. It affects us, the creatures we share this space with, and causes economic and environmental damage. The 10-cent paper bag fee helps the plastic bag law work. Thanks to our enlightened town leaders, the law is a great success and a benefit to us all. As the old saying goes, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it."

title: Whole System Falls Apart
author: Staff Writer
content:
Whole system falls apart

 September 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 390
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We were disappointed by the Star-Democrat's recent editorial regarding the bag fee that was included in last year's town ordinance banning the use of plastic bags.The editorial laid out all the reasons why this fee and the bag ban are needed, including the negative effects that plastic bags have on the environment, both via their production and disposal.
As the op-ed states, the fee is a way to encourage shoppers to bring their own reusable bags. This helps lessen the need for paper bags, which are provided to customers when they don't have their own bag. Paper bags also use resources to produce and recycle.
The only reason that the editorial provides for the removal of the mandatory bag fee is the opinion of one community member who melodramatically tried to make her point during the recent town council meeting.
She and two council members claimed to have heard from numerous citizens that the bag fee is a burden. No one else who attended made the same claim.
What stood out to us during the meeting were the salient facts laid out by a representative from the Maryland Retailers Association. She provided actual numbers — the upfront costs of the paper bags to retailers and statistics about how businesses must defray the costs of the bags if they aren't able to charge a fee.
The actions businesses may take include raising prices and possibly reducing staff numbers, in order to afford the bags. We highly recommend residents watch the recording of the meeting and listen to her comments.
Many businesses will stop charging the bag fee to stay competitive. Then shoppers will have less incentive to bring their own bags. The whole system falls apart.
We are sorry the editors of the Star-Democrat fell for the theatrics of one Easton resident and two council members. This issue has been raised not to protect consumers but to rile the public and get names in the paper.
Easton is a very giving community, and we are sure there are resources to provide reusable bags for those who don't have them and cannot afford to pay the bag fee. There are other ways to solve this problem, if it exists, besides dismantling a system that is clearly working. We know it is working due to the lack of plastic bag debris in our rivers, roads and trees.
MISSY CORLEY
CAROLYN COON
VICKI CARUTHERS
Easton

title: Rep. Harris, Local Republicans Speak at Denton Rally Supporting Trump
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Rep. Harris, local Republicans speak at Denton rally supporting Trump

 September 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 587
 Words

 DENTON – Republican leaders and supporters gathered for a Caroline County rally Saturday in support of presidential candidate Donald Trump and Maryland Republicans running for office this November.The event, which took place at Caroline County 4-H Park, was organized by Caroline County Republican Women. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md., 1st) was the featured speaker Saturday afternoon.
As he runs for his eighth consecutive term in the House of Representatives, he asked voters to support him as well as the entire Republican ticket. He emphasized a tight race in Congressional District 6, where Republican candidate Neil Parrott is vying to potentially join Harris as conservative representation in the House.
"We got a job to do. Because if President Trump is going to succeed, we need to have a House majority, so I'm going to ask for your vote," Harris said.
"Those of you who know people who live out in western Maryland, call them up and tell them to vote for Neil Parrott, because I'm tired of being the only Republican in the House delegation from Maryland, and we got a shot," he said.
Caroline County Republican Women member Joanne Smith helped organize Saturday's event. She said the group held a gathering back in 2020 as well. In her eyes, Trump is a fit for Caroline County voters.
"I think Trump represents our values," Smith said. "We're a very red area. Everybody in Caroline County that's elected is Republican."
"We desperately want to see a change in our government and Trump's our man," she added.
Much of Saturday's discussion centered on ensuring Republicans secure a Senate majority. Harris encouraged attendees to vote for former Gov. Larry Hogan as he runs for Maryland's seat in the Senate against Democratic opponent Angela Alsobrooks.
Harris emphasized that without a Republican majority in the Senate and a Trump victory, conservative judges cannot be placed on the Supreme Court bench.
Adorned in a 'Make America Great Again' baseball cap, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) also asked voters to toe the party line.
"Vote straight down the ticket, Donald Trump, Larry Hogan, Andy Harris," Mautz said. "Whatever it is, whatever the qualm is, it doesn't matter. We need to get out and we need to vote."
"This is war," he continued. "We're at a national crossroads right now and we need to put all of our cards on the table."
Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Jeff Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) attended Saturday's rally, as well as Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker.
Speaking to eventgoers, Hutchinson predicted that November's general election will play out similar to the 2016 vote, with Trump claiming swing states and the presidency. "We can't wait to see it happen again," he said.
The state delegate said in an interview with the Star Democrat that the economy is the number one reason for residents on the Shore to support Trump.
"We see with our rising food prices, gas prices, housing prices, it's affecting everybody here on the Shore," Hutchinson said. " … I see it within my district, how it's really affecting the middle-income and low-income families."
Smith and Harris both noted an increase in enthusiasm among local Republicans to win back the White House. "We want to get back to the Trump years," Harris said in an interview.
Denton resident Thomas Conneely Jr. attended Saturday's gathering and echoed that sentiment.
"I see that there's more energy," Conneely Jr. said. "But I also see an urgency that it's an emergency. That's what I see. I see people looking at it as, 'We have to.' If we don't, we're in deep trouble."

title: Residual Bill Passed by Caroline County Commissioners
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Residual bill passed by Caroline County Commissioners

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday morning, the Caroline County Commissioners voted to approve the long-discussed bill that would establish county regulations for storing food processing residuals, animal waste from the food processing process.These residuals, particularly dissolved air floatation, or DAF, residuals have been the topic of several heated discussions in the county since residents began raising health complaints and environmental concerns over how the material was being stored by some in the county late last year.
The county came up with a permitting system. There will be a universal permit requirement in order to store food processing residuals. It creates limitations on how residuals can be stored and permits the county to fine violators.
It would require that those storing the material use closed-top containers, going a step further than recently passed state legislation.
Attorney Stewart Barroll said commissioners and Caroline County staff had heard "voluminous" public comments that have been taken into account.
Prior to voting, two amendments were approved by commissioners involving distances from the storage containers.
Commissioner Franklin Bartz said he would prefer the storage distance and an occupied dwelling be increased to 2,000 feet measured horizontally rather than the 1,250-foot distance that was in the bill.
After discussion, the commissioners unanimously voted to approve the change.
Commissioner J. Travis Breeding requested a second amendment that would require the storage not to be within 500 feet of a well. This way, it would allow property owners to move wells somewhere else on their property to be 500 feet away from stored residuals to not contaminate water sources.
Commissioner Larry Porter brought up the discussion of postponing voting on the act until the Maryland Department of Agriculture shares their regulations. The vote had been postponed at the prior two meetings so the commissioners could review the proposed amendments to the legislation.
Breeding said there would not be a need to postpone for regulation changes because commissioners are acting well within the parameters of Maryland statue.
"There's only so much that the Department of Agriculture can do," Breeding said. "Everything that we have done inside of this legislature is not in conflict with the statue that the state has."
The bill was unanimously approved by the commissioners and has been enacted into the county law.

title: Easton Retains 10-Cent Paper Bag Fee Following Public Hearing
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton retains 10-cent paper bag fee following public hearing

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 738
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After a lengthy public hearing during Monday's meeting, a divided Easton Town Council voted against an ordinance that would have removed a 10-cent fee on paper bags used by retailers after the council last year banned plastic bags.Council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery were in the minority, voting in favor of removing the fee. Public opinion was varied, though most residents spoke in support of keeping the fee in place.
In September 2022, the council passed an ordinance prohibiting retailers from giving customers single-use plastic bags. The law, which went into effect in April of 2023, required retailers to charge customers a fee of at least 10 cents for each paper bag used, encouraging shoppers to bring reusable bags.
On Monday, many residents pointed to the environmental benefits of the 10-cent fee, saying it trains shoppers to bring reusable bags. Some highlighted the effectiveness of a paper bag fee in other towns.
"The law works. The fee is proven effective nationwide," said Marion Arnold, a member of Plastic-Free Easton. "Our law is not a one-off experiment. Millions of plastic bags were never circulated as a result."
Speaking on behalf of the Maryland Retailers Alliance, Sarah Price said grocery stores would make paper bags free to stay competitive with other businesses if the 10-cent fee requirement is waived. One clothing department in another store Price talked to saw an increase in bag costs from $7,000 to $30,000 when the required fee was not present.
Alan Girard, advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, encouraged council to reject the ordinance.
"Compared to plastic bags, paper bags produce two times the solid waste, three times the greenhouse gasses and four times the water consumption of plastic bags," Girard said.
Supporters of the ordinance, including Gunsallus, argued that the 10-cent fee is a burden on low-income residents.
Resident Shari Wilcoxon spoke for more than nine minutes during the public hearing in opposition to the fee. She said she helped collect more than 850 petition signatures from those who want to see the fee requirement removed.
"We are not for bringing back plastic bags," Wilcoxon said. "We are for allowing the merchants the freedom to decide for themselves to charge or not for their customers' bags."
Nearly seven minutes into Wilcoxon's comment, Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said, "I think time has expired," referring to the time allowed for individuals to comment.
"It has not," Gunsallus replied, stating the extended comment is "permissible" per the town charter.
Public comment has typically been limited to three minutes for individuals and five minutes for organizations. At previous meetings, Gunsallus has asked those who went over the three-minute mark to cede the podium and return after others have spoken.
"We do not have the right to cap speech," Gunsallus said Monday, adding that speakers to follow would receive the additional time afforded to Wilcoxon. " … Anything in this meeting that goes over that, now has to be afforded to every single other speaker. That is the rules that we have. If you want to come back up and speak, you are more than welcome to."
Once the public hearing ended, Gunsallus emphasized that the goal of the ordinance was to remove just the 10-cent paper bag fee and not the plastic bag ban entirely.
Prior to the vote, Montgomery expressed his reasoning for wanting the fee requirement eliminated. He disagreed with claims that the 10-cent fee is manageable for residents.
"It's not trivial to the business community, so we cannot claim that it is trivial to the people who have to pay that fee," Montgomery said.
Davis looked for the council to move past the topic.
"I think we've used an enormous amount of time to discuss this matter, when I have far more things in Ward 4 that I should be dealing with," Davis said. "(I) can't deal with those because we are dealing with this issue."
Davis called for the vote. He joined Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry and Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello in voting no on the ordinance.
Abbatiello said if the fee requirement proves ineffective moving forward, he's willing to take a second look at removing it "down the road."
"If people are not doing the right thing and recycling and reusing their bags, then this will not work," Abbatiello said. "I'm putting my faith in the folks in Easton and the folks in Talbot County and the folks that come here to shop, that they're going to do the right thing."

title: Why did a local library suddenly close? Town offers some clarity on temporary shutdown
author: Staff report

Why did a local library suddenly close? Town offers some clarity on temporary shutdown

 Author/Byline: Staff report | Section: Local News

 There is a little clarity to why a local library unexpectedly closed last month.It somewhat brings the old expression "the check is in the mail" to life.
According to to a statement from the Sudlersville Town Commissioners some confusion over grant money allocation resulted in the sudden weeklong closure of the Sudlersvllie Library from from Aug. 8 to Aug. 14.
As owners of the independent municipal public library, the town of Sudlersville is sent a check of grant money every year from Queen Anne's County to pay for library operations.such as repairs, payroll, maintenance, the letter stated.
Upon receiving this year's check on Aug. 8, it was deposited into the library's account at People's Bank rather than the town's account as it usually is, according to the statement.
"Due to this event, the town's commissioners were compelled to close the library until the check could be placed into the correct account so that the funds would be available to take care of the library and its staff. The library was instructed to cease normal operations and only open for any events they had already planned," the statement read.
"Please know that this was not a lightly made decision for the commission," according to the statement.
The library staff has been back paid for any time that was missed during the library's closing, the commissioners said.
The library has since returned to normal hours of operation.

title: Planning Commission Tables Approval of Silo Square Housing Development
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning commission tables approval of Silo Square housing development

 September 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 766
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The proposal for a 28-unit townhouse development at the site of a former Perdue AgriBusiness grain operation is drawing hesitation from community members as well as Easton's Planning Commission.At the commission's Thursday meeting, developers from Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, presented sketch plans for a mixed-income housing project at 410 Needwood Avenue.
As part of the Silo Square proposal, the 2.36-acre lot near downtown Easton would be converted into 16 three-story townhomes and 12 two-story townhomes.
The 10 grain bins currently on the lot, often referred to by community members as silos, would be demolished.
Zach Smith, an attorney representing the developers, said the proposal adheres to the town's comprehensive plan and fits what is sought for Easton's planned redevelopment overlay district.
"This is truly infill development in every sense of the word," Smith told the commission. "Not just within the town's boundaries, but within sort of our historic, central core. It's truly a walkable site. It's along the rail trail. But it's also connected to town."
Smith emphasized the project will "provide a greater variation of housing types" and partly create affordable housing. "Not all of the units will be rent control, some of them will be market rate," Smith said.
Ross Benincasa, vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said seven units would be set aside for workforce housing.
"What we're expecting to see here, frankly, is going to be an EPD officer and an instructional assistant at the high school," Benincasa said. "It's going to be a single mom that has three kids, potentially."
Commission members applauded that the design wasn't driven by cost, but they raised extensive concerns about the lack of a traffic study.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said that during the staff review period, there was no requirement for a traffic study, though the commission could request one. The 28-unit mark fell under what would've triggered a traffic study per town policy for planned redevelopment.
Many of Thursday's public comments came from residents who live in the surrounding "silo district," some of them concerned about increased traffic on narrow streets.
"The project will increase traffic on Maryland and Needwood Avenues as well as the very narrow Higgins and Davis Avenue," resident Maury Schlesinger said. "And (there are) no mitigations proposed."
Resident Matthew Carberry asked the commission to request a traffic mitigation study. He disputed the town staff's analysis of the sketch plan and proposal, which concluded there'd be no adverse effects on health or safety. "Of course it's going to be more hazardous," Carberry said.
Commission members brought up the option of having developers return at an October meeting for a final vote of approval so a traffic study could be included. Both Benincasa and Smith asked that the commission make a motion of approval contingent on the study's completion instead of delaying.
"Is there some reason why that isn't a good way to go?" commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint asked.
"There's a lot of things you make conditions on, and they're easy for the staff to confirm and verify, but a traffic study's a lot bigger deal and could have greater implications," Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said.
"It relates to a finding you have to make," she continued. "And if you can't make that finding today, because you don't have a traffic study, then I don't think you can approve it with a condition."
The three commission members present at the meeting voted unanimously to table potential approval of the application until October's meeting, upon the completion of a traffic study, as well as the removal of a section of fencing in the design.
OPINIONS ON DESIGNThe design of the townhomes yielded mixed feedback on Thursday. Developers stated the design intended to "pay homage" to the Perdue site.
In the middle of the lot, there is a gazebo in the shape of a silo, meant to call back to Perdue's grain bins. Renderings show metal roofing on the townhomes, similar to the material of the silos.
"Is there anything we can do to dress them up a little bit with peaks, bricks or shutters or something?" Commission Member Thomas Klein asked. "It just seems really flat and plain to me."
On the other hand, commission Vice Chairperson Michael Ports said he appreciated the simple design.
Schlesinger, who met with neighbors in the silo district to discuss the site, presented worries about the lack of open space other than the gazebo. He added that he doesn't think the callbacks to the industrial history of the site will ring obvious.
"If the design attempt was to recall the former silos on the site, perhaps only a few will see that connection," Schlesinger said.

title: Planning Commission OKs Apartment Project on North Washington Street
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Planning Commission OKs apartment project on North Washington Street

 September 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 625
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Last week, the Easton Planning Commission approved a proposed 16-unit, two-story residential apartment complex at the intersection of North Washington Street and Aurora Street.The application, which came from Lane Engineering and 350 N Washington Street Investments, was presented at Thursday's commission meeting. Developers sought approval for a plan that outlines a 27,000-square-foot complex consisting of four two-bedroom units and 12 one-bedroom units.
While still needing approval from the Easton Town Council, Thursday's thumbs up was a step forward for transforming the lot into multifamily housing. The lot is wedged in between commercial buildings on Aurora Street and homes on Washington Street.
Attorney Brendan Mullaney spoke on behalf of developers at Thursday's meeting.
"We believe that this is a use that is appropriate at the scale that it's proposed for this property, that doesn't create any undue impacts to traffic, congestion, or the health and safety of residents on the property, or property owners in the area," Mullaney said to the commission.
Mullaney said early estimates on rent rates for the apartments would be as follows: between $1,400 and $1,600 for the one-bedroom units, and between $1,800 and $2,000 for the two-bedroom units.
"(That's) pretty consistent with what's been called attainable or workforce housing for other projects in the town," Mullaney said.
Since the proposal comes in the town's commercial business zoning district, developers went to the Board of Zoning Appeals prior to the Planning Commission's meeting. That board unanimously gave special exception approval to the project after a lengthy review.
Designs have 27 total parking spaces, with 16 off-street and in the apartment lot and 11 on-street. One parking space was removed from initial site plans in order to avoid limiting sight lines on Washington Street. A 12-by-45-foot loading area was also added to the site plan.
Commission Member Thomas Klein appreciated developers for slightly changing those designs after hearing community feedback.
"I applaud the development team for listening to the public," Klein said. "You guys have made several adjustments to your original plan based on the letters and the comments that you received."
All three commission members present approved the application with the condition that developers work with town staff to adjust the originally proposed roofline elevations.
SAFETY CONCERNSMike Lenhart, president of Lenhart Traffic Consulting, told commission members that a traffic study revealed negligent impacts to the surrounding area if the complex is built. The study showed almost no increases in traffic delay at the intersection during the peak morning and evening hours, he said..
However, many nearby residents expressed reservations about the development due to the safety of the Aurora and Washington intersection.
Kevan Full, a member of Talbot Thrive, asked the commission to consider the area's difficult sight lines and lack of accessible sidewalk crossings, among other concerns.
"Before any construction gets started, let's get the intersection, roadways, sidewalks, crossings and bike lanes addressed," Full said. "Don't work backwards by installing an apartment complex first, as that leads to workaround solutions."
Sheila Lawson, who lives on Washington Street, said she's not against the apartment complex, but provided her worries about the intersection's safety.
"I won't even drive that intersection, I've almost been t-boned twice there," Lawson said. "I've seen five accidents in the three and a half years that I've been here. I'm just asking you guys to really think about that. It is a chance to improve it, and improve it in conjunction with what''s going on with the development there."
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said the town is in the process of a "complete street study," along with taking a closer look at sidewalks and potential bike lanes to improve safety on North Washington Street.
As the town embarks on a traffic signal improvement project, the intersection will be one of the spots for a traffic consultant to analyze in the future, he added.
