title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Dirt Road Paving
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss dirt road paving

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners convened on Sept. 24 to discuss several issues, including funding to pave dirt roads.Daniel Fox, deputy administrator; Robin Eaton, director of public works; Megan Gallagher, GIS specialist; and Leslie Grunden, assistant director of planning at Department of Planning and Codes, all came before the commissioners.
Fox said they are collecting the data to look for funding to upgrade and pave some of the roads in the county. There are county priorities and there are federal Protect Grant priorities. Where those two intersect is where funding can happen, he said.
"What we are trying to do is take a whole new look at dirt roads as a whole. Try to put as much information together and start to figure out where we can look for funding to start upgrading and possibly paving certain areas throughout the county," Fox said. "With the spreadsheet that we have outlined, we can really start to score and put metrics together with areas that bode well with different grant applications."
The group showed the commissioners maps of dirt roads in the county and data-rich spreadsheets about the dirt roads. The measured many things like how many homes per mile and the road's condition. They also plugged all that data into a GIS map so the commissioners could see exactly which roads needed help.
Trunk Line, Bates and Gregg Roads were identified as the most expensive dirt roads to maintain. Fox noted Gilpin Point, Blades Road and Noble Road have been identified by Public Works as needing work.
A few citizens who live on Trunk L ine Road came to speak about how dusty the road is. School bus driver Robert Smith said he had to wash his tail lights clean every time he drove on the dirt road.
American Rescue Plan Act funds could be used to pay for dirt road paving, Fox said.
The Department of Transportation also offers a PROTECT (Protect Resilient Operations for Transformative, Efficient and Cost Saving Transportation) grant. It could be a two-year process to get the funding said Fox.
"Last year the notice for funding opportunity came out in September. This year is it will probably come out in November. There is usually a month to a month and a half from the funding opportunity to the deadline for the grant. We are big believer in well begun in half done," Grunden said.
She wanted to know what the county priorities were before they proceeded to ask for the grant.
Grunden said the minimum these planning grant can offer is $100,000 and the minimum for a resilience grant that could include some construction is $500,000. She said there was no ceiling of what the county could ask for.

title: Proposed Dorchester Property Transfer Could Result in Pickleball Courts
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Proposed Dorchester property transfer could result in pickleball courts

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 302
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — Brand new pickleball courts could be coming to Cambridge.During a Dorchester County Board of Education meeting on Thursday, Dorchester County Recreation and Parks Director Duc Trieu, on behalf of the County Council, proposed a property transfer that would allow the county to build pickleball courts on a parcel of land behind the Judy Center on Glasgow Street in Cambridge.
In August, the Board of Education voted to approve a project by the James G. Busick Tennis Foundation to resurface the Glasgow Tennis Courts. The decision left many local pickleball players disappointed and frustrated because it meant that they would no longer be able to play on those courts.
With the resurfacing project, the courts are losing the lines drawn for pickleball. This is because a grant from the United States Tennis Association, which the Busick Tennis Foundation received, does not allow anything other than tennis lines to be drawn on the courts in the first five years after they are resurfaced.
At the Board of Education meeting on Thursday, Trieu said the resurfacing of the Glasgow Tennis Courts upset many people in Cambridge's pickleball community.
"So that kind of put the county in a pickle, no pun intended," Trieu said.
Trieu asked that the Board of Education consider transferring the Glasgow Tennis Courts and the adjacent parcel, which is located behind the Judy Center, to the county. He said the county would be able to create pickleball courts behind the Judy Center and offer youth and adult tennis and pickleball programming on both courts.
Trieu also gave an update on the resurfacing of the Glasgow Tennis Courts during the meeting. He said the project is ongoing and expects it to be over within the next week.
"So you're going to start seeing a lot of tennis players out there on the newly resurfaced courts," he said.

title: Elk Neck State Park Re-Opens Access to Turkey Point Lighthouse
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Elk Neck State Park re-opens access to Turkey Point Lighthouse

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 377
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NORTH EAST — The new trail system to Turkey Point Lighthouse is now open to the public since construction is complete, according to Mary Ironside, manager of Elk Neck State Park.The trail was closed in March to allow Kibler Construction to build a new trail and a new parking lot for the popular spot overlooking the Elk River and the Chesapeake Bay, at a cost of $3.8 million. It was finished five months ahead of schedule.
"We now have more parking," Ironside said. "The new trail gives easier access to the lighthouse."
To get that new trail, Park Ranger Shannon Whalen said the original parking lot is now a turnaround for vehicle traffic and another field was used to create the larger lot with 52 parking spots instead of 26. Ironside said residents of the neighboring Chesapeake Isles community will no longer fight with traffic.
"Our goal was to alleviate the heavy traffic at Turkey Point Lighthouse," she added, noting there is a new route connecting the larger parking lot to the historic lighthouse.
Whalen said there is now dedicated handicapped parking closer to the lighthouse.
"They can drive right up to the lighthouse," Whalen said. Handicapped visitors need only call the park ranger at 443-252-4258 and ask for access, which will unlock the gates.
Repositioning the location of the trail also mitigates erosion issues on the high shore line.
"We abandoned the old trail, which will be replanted to stabilize the soil and eliminate erosion," Ironside said. "We will turn that back with native vegetation."
Meanwhile, progress continues on the renovation of the campgrounds at Elk Neck State Park.
"We have limited camping for the campground," Ironside said. "A lot of loops are being shut down."
It reduces the available spaces from 300 to 76. Only two loops will remain open plus the youth group camp.
"The beach and Rogues Harbor will remain open throughout," she added. So will Turkey Point Lighthouse.
Whalen said the work to address parking made slight changes to the trail.
"It's the same loop but now it's .8 miles instead of 1.2," Whalen said. "And we have port-a-johns in the parking lot."
Turkey Point Lighthouse will be open every weekend in October from 10 a.m. until 2 p.m. for tours. The park itself is open seven days per week from 7 a.m. until sunset.

title: Talbot County Discusses Draft Legislation for Cannabis Operations
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County discusses draft legislation for cannabis operations

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council and Planning Commission held a lengthy work session Monday to discuss draft legislation regarding cannabis zoning.On June 1, state legislation took effect providing local governments additional flexibility to change requirements for cannabis businesses.
Planning Commission members discussed potential zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that generally fall under three categories: dispensaries, growers and processors. They honed in on concerns about the odors that emanate from cannabis processing facilities and strategies for regulation.
Gary Nusinov, a former vice president at a cannabis cultivation business, spoke during the work session as a subject matter expert. Nusinov was awarded a lottery license for cultivation by the state this cycle.
"We know that many of the counties on the Eastern Shore have not really addressed the zoning," Nusinov said. " … Because the conditional licenses for most of these lottery winners happened in July, … we have a six-month period to prove our capitalization and that we are able to locate in a properly-zoned area."
State law regulates that dispensaries may not locate within 500 feet of schools, places of worship, playgrounds, libraries and public parks. Counties, though, may reduce that requirement. Counties are also permitted to increase the required 1,000 feet between dispensaries up to a half-mile, or decrease that 1,000-feet rule.
Under the new state law, local jurisdictions may not restrict licensed dispensaries more than alcoholic beverage retailers.
Nusinov explained that for dispensaries, most odor concern stems from a dispensary that has its own packaging operation. He suggested the county require treatment to ventilation so odors are decreased.
"When you are making formulated products such as a gummy or chocolate, the odor of that confection mixed with the smell of cannabis will emanate from the air," Nusinov said.
"The stigma of the past still exists for some, but for most, it's really not there," Nusinov added. "You don't want to have a noxious odor or constant smells. It can give some people an allergy or a headache."
PROCESSING FACILITIESPlanning Commission Vice Chairman Chip Councell emphasized the commission's main concern was with processing facilities and odors from those operations.
Tim Crosby, principal of Crosby & Associates, has experience with local and international cannabis projects. He suggested the processing facilities be limited to just light industrial zones or agriculture zones in order to avoid high-density, retail areas.
"It can be dealt with, but to say that there isn't an odor coming out of those, even the best of systems, I think that would be disingenuous," Crosby said.
He said a reasonable setback from residences for processing facilities would be at least 200 feet. Crosby also encouraged the council and commission to consider its restrictions on agricultural practices as a whole.
"Remember you're opening up a Pandora's box here," Crosby said. " … Processing cannabis is an agricultural practice, and I think the (cannabis) owners would come back to you and say, 'What are you doing about chicken houses?'"
Following the discussion, Councell and other commission members agreed that cannabis-processing facilities are best fit for agricultural areas. Brennan Tarleton, planning and zoning director, said the county could either put odor mitigation rules in the county code or require all processing facilities to go through a special exception use through the Board of Appeals.
The commission and council members came to two drafted requirements for processing facilities that may show up in future legislation: at least a 1,000-foot setback requirement from residences and a maximum building size of 10,000 square feet.
Before the County Council can introduce any cannabis zoning legislation, the Planning Commission will first have to go through review and approval.

title: Election Judge Imbalance Stirs Concerns in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Election judge imbalance stirs concerns in Talbot County

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1009
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Concerns over election judge appointments made by the Talbot County Board of Elections are being raised by residents and local officials.Adding an unexpected agenda item to the Talbot County Council's Tuesday meeting, Council Member Dave Stepp voiced such concerns, which deal with the party makeup of Talbot County's election judges for the November election. He said the elections board is not following a state law that requires an equal number of election judges from the two political parties.
"I feel like there's certain aspects of election law that are trying to be skirted here, from both an elections director from Talbot County as well as the majority of members of our Talbot County elections board," Stepp said.
According to Election Director Tammy Stafford, current judges consist of 62 Democrats, 50 Republicans and 11 unaffiliated, though that makeup is "fluid" and will change up until Election Day. Currently, she says there are no vacancies.
The 123 election judges, people who are responsible for running polling places and verifying voters, will work at 10 different polling places in the county.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
Stafford told the Star Democrat that election judge selection is "based on recruitment numbers," which has been a challenge for the county and something the board is "committed" to fixing. "Even if we use everyone on our list, it would be hard pressed to be 50-50," Stafford said.
"Our recruitment levels are still low, and the interest of certain parties is low," Stafford added. She said the board's goal is to "be as party balanced as possible."
Richard Osborne, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, says he's heard from many Republicans over the past two years that they had applied to be an election judge but were never selected.
This year, the central committee began to document those who were not accepted, Osborne said.
"We have a backlog of almost 30 Republicans who have applied to be an election judge over the last three to four months," Osborne said. "They have not been able to do any of the training. They have been turned down."
Stafford said since canvassing of mail-in ballots begins on Oct. 15, the county's elections board "will not have space for training" or the resources to train individuals who have applied to be judges but have not been accepted yet.
"We have a window of time when we train individuals," Stafford said. Those that have applied will be "one of the first groups of people that we contact for 2026," she said.
Other factors, such as prior experience, play a role. Stafford said the board is also "looking to diversify the age of the election judges throughout the county."
The five members of the Board of Elections are appointed by the governor to four-year terms, with approval from the House of Delegates. The election director is appointed by the county board.
Osborne said the issue boils down to the state code not being followed.
"It's just incredible to me that you have state employees and people that have been appointed to the state board knowingly agree to break the law," Osborne said. "Our committee is not done with fighting this battle."
COUNCIL DEBATETuesday's County Council meeting came after a special meeting held Tuesday morning by the Board of Elections to discuss election judges. Stepp and Council President Chuck Callahan attended that morning meeting and brought forth their worries to council members, leading to tense discussion.
In an agenda item added at the start of the council meeting, Stepp asked the council to send a letter reminding Stafford and the elections board to follow state law, garnering support from Callahan.
The council's three other members, who did not attend the elections board's special meeting that morning, were not immediately willing to send a letter to the election director.
"I understand your concern," Council Vice President Pete Lesher said to Stepp. "That's a serious allegation. But I'm not sure that I could substitute my lower level of expertise here for the judgment and command of the data that the Board of Elections has to take action."
Council Member Keasha Haythe said, "I cannot sign onto a letter that I haven't received any type of information regarding this going on or any constituent complaint," adding that council members typically have a draft of the letter to view prior to signing it.
Stepp said he's heard of citizen complaints and was aware of the Republican Central Committee's efforts to provide judge applications to ensure an even distribution between the two parties.
"I believe it's very timely that we do this because if we miss the opportunity today, I feel like it's going to be a totally missed opportunity," Stepp said of sending the letter.
"Witnessing what was going on this morning was concerning," Callahan said. "There's one thing us five don't want to do, is meddle into an election. That's not what we're here for."
"I think that's what you're doing," Mielke said to Callahan.
"With all due respect to the two councilmen, I think it's sort of based on hearsay and interpretation (of) what they saw," Mielke later stated, saying she didn't have enough information to sign the letter. "And you're tainting the public's view of this election."
"So we just don't bring it up at all then?" Callahan responded. Mielke followed, "No, we don't bring it up in the letter. We have other options."
Callahan and Stepp voted in favor of sending the letter, while Lesher, Haythe and Mielke all voted no.
After Stepp's motion to send a letter failed, he provided additional comment at the end of Tuesday's meeting, emphasizing that the Board of Elections is not in compliance with Maryland law.
"He's just tainted our elections," Mielke said. As Stepp continued, Mielke asked County Attorney Patrick Thomas, "is this appropriate to make accusations as a comment of council?"
Stepp finished his comment asking the Board of Elections to balance its selection of judges.
"Follow the law, do your job, be transparent and train more Republican election judges immediately, and have them ready to work our general election," Stepp said.

title: West End Sewer Project Showing Improvements, Completion Expected in January
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
West End sewer project showing improvements, completion expected in January

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With the West End sewer project more than halfway complete, the city and its residents are noticing improvements.The project aims to address sanitary sewage overflow in the lowest lying area of the city at Water Street and Hambrooks Boulevard.
Lou Hyman, a resident of Ward 1 — the ward in which the project is located — said that sewage overflows mean brown water flooding the streets and people's yards.
"It was just really nasty when you're trying to walk your dog," he said.
Cambridge City Engineer Carl "Bucky" Jackson said as the cracks and leaks in the sewer system along Hambrooks Boulevard from Choptank Avenue to Somerset Avenue are repaired, less ground water and tidal water is flowing into the sewers. This means that the sanitary sewer flow is lower, so there aren't as many overflows during rain and high tide events.
"The tidal influence we've had just recently in the last five days, we more than likely would have had a sanitary sewer overflow prior to this project," Jackson said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Sept. 24. "But we have not experienced it in the last week."
Hyman said while there is still flooding, the water is now clean.
As the project progresses, Jackson said the sewer lines between Glenburn and Somerset avenues still need to be completed, along with "some minor work along the way." Jackson said after repairs have been made to the sewers, the next step will be to pave the entire stretch of road from Somerset Avenue to Choptank Avenue.
Jackson said completion of the project is expected in January, as long as they are able to get asphalt before the asphalt plant closes for the winter.
Although the project is currently slightly ahead of schedule, Jackson said it's too early to say if the project will get completed earlier than planned. He said that some bad weather is typical for the months ahead and so the project might not remain ahead of schedule.
The $3.8 million West End sewer project is the first of four projects part of a five-year, $20 million capital program to address water and sewer infrastructure. Jackson said the $4.1 million Trenton Street pump station replacement, also part of the capital program, is currently awaiting permitting.
Cambridge Ward 1 Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said that along with sewage overflowing onto the street, some residents in her ward have had issues with their drains and with flushing their toilets in instances when the tide is high and the streets are flooded.
"That's definitely a problem," she said. "Everybody needs to be able to use their facilities."
She said she has heard from residents who live along the waterfront that they are feeling relief from the West End sewer project.
Hyman said there is still more work to do.
"But we're not getting the sewer line overflows that we were getting," he said.
Atkiss said that many of the city's current projects are to correct mistakes made in the past. She said some of the plumbing practices used 100 or 150 years ago aren't environmentally sound or don't have "effective, long-term results."
"When they get into some of these streets, they're unearthing a puzzle — almost at every intersection — of what was done over the years and how they have to untangle it and correct it," she said. "So they don't even know what they're getting into until they get to each block."

title: Oxford Commissioners Pass Meeting Policy, Residents Express Concerns
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Commissioners pass meeting policy, residents express concerns

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 651
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Gasps, sighs and exclamations could be heard throughout a Commissioners of Oxford discussion on Tuesday evening that ended in a 2-1 vote to pass a resolution establishing town meeting procedures.The resolution, introduced by Commission President Norm Bell at a town meeting on Sept. 10, establishes general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings. During the Sept. 10 meeting, Bell said the purpose of the policy "is to create an atmosphere where the elected officials, staff and members of the public can attend to business efficiently, fairly and with full participation."
Specifically, the policy limits when and for how long public commenters can speak and prohibits heckling, defamatory comments and profanity. The resolution also makes it so commissioners do not have to answer questions residents ask during public comment.
The different limitations, as well as the way in which the resolution was passed, drew concern from residents.
Both Bell and Commissioner Tom Costigan said during the discussion that the commissioners had been receiving responses from residents regarding Bell's proposed resolution since the previous town meeting when it was introduced.
Commissioner Katrina Greer — who voted against passing the resolution — brought up the town's charter, which says, "the rules of the commissioners shall provide that residents of the town shall have a reasonable opportunity to be heard at any meeting in regard to any municipal question."
Greer said she is proposing a different resolution, which hadn't yet been posted on the town website prior to Tuesday's meeting. Greer said she wanted to schedule a workshop, gather input and put together one merged resolution to vote on.
"There is a need, and most towns have it, for a little bit of rules," she said. "But this is something that the town needs to participate in and see the documents."
Greer said that unlike Bell's proposal that restricts public comment to the end of a meeting, hers would allow for public comment before actionable items, or items that are voted on.
"Letting people talk at the end of the meeting about something that has already been voted on is useless and does not satisfy the requirement for a reasonable opportunity to be heard at the meeting," she said. "It is also dismissive of the right of citizens to participate."
Tensions rose throughout the discussion, which public comment was not allowed during. At one point, one resident asked the commissioners, "Are you really not going to allow public comment on this?"
Bell responded that the commissioners had received feedback prior meeting. When another resident spoke up, Bell said, "Excuse me, there will not be back talk. Please."
At another point, when resident Susan Kordell started to make a comment, Bell banged his gavel and told her to "sit down, please."
At the end of the meeting, Bell said he acted "quickly" to try to stop commenters due to concerns about the commissioners' time to discuss the matter at hand.
Although Greer felt the commissioners should not vote on meeting procedures Tuesday evening, both Costigan and Bell said they were ready to vote.
"It's a resolution, and if there are any amendments to it, we can certainly address them in the two weeks, and we (can) vote on any amendments or changes or adoption of one over the other," Bell said.
Along with approving Bell's proposed resolution, Bell and Costigan agreed to schedule a workshop on the topic for next week so at the next town meeting, the commissioners can consider any amendments that might be suggested.
At the end of the meeting, resident Emilie Knud-Hansen said she though thought the procedure around the resolution at the meeting was unfair.
"We deserve to find out what you're voting on before you say, 'We'll vote on this resolution and then we'll deal with amendments,'" she said. "I think that's really backwards."
Resident Dave Donovan said at the end of the meeting that there was irony in the fact that a resolution on public comment "was itself enacted without public comment."

title: Second community meeting for Easton Crossing development
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Second community meeting for Easton Crossing development

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over a month after Chesapeake Community Development's initial community meeting for a planned mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue, dozens of people once again gathered to learn more about the plans.The Sept. 18 meeting provided the opportunity for developers to show initial designs for Easton Crossing, a six-acre development in Easton, based on feedback received at a community meeting in July. Leaders of Chesapeake Community Development, the developer for the project, have made a point to work with local community members on the overall outcome of the development.
According to Ross Benincasa, vice president of Chesapeake Community Development, Wednesday's meeting showed attendees the initial site plan. The plan broke down the five buildings on the property, as well as open spaces and plans for parking, general traffic and pedestrian flow, all of which were concerns raised in July.
"It was extremely important, just from the standpoint of making sure that our residents had a chance to not only see what we were thinking, but then to give feedback again on that, to tell us kind of what we got right and maybe what we missed," Benincasa said.
Chris Wheedleton, consultant at Rivers and Roads, was hired on the project to lead in gathering feedback from the community. Wheedleton said the meeting provided a chance to answer any questions residents might still still have regarding the new site.
After a presentation of the site plan, people were separated into groups and were encouraged to answer two questions: "Would you like what you saw?" and "What would you like to see differently moving forward?"
Wheedleton said he received general positive feedback from the site plan. Major point raised by residents included diversity of housing options offered and making sure the development would integrate properly with the existing community.
An additional concern addressed was the potential for a grocery store to be built on the development. Benincasa took time to make clear that a grocery store was considered by developers but it would not be included in the project moving forward.
It was felt by Chesapeake Community Development that nearby local and international grocery stores are close enough to the project to meet the need of future residents.
Bob Porter, owner of the Sharper Graphics, said his business is next door to the planned Easton Crossing development. He attended the meeting on Sept. 18.
Porter said the piece of territory is important to him due to his 44-year history living near it. For Porter, he was excited to hear the development would serve all incomes in the community.
"The project is going to be made available at lower rates to to family, people that are working in the in the neighborhood and living in the neighborhood and making sure that they can afford to participate in the project without being in some kind of a federal or state project program," Porter said. "And that was very meaningful to me."
Wheedleton said there are still opportunities for people to weigh in and give their feedback and input into the project. A third meeting will take place sometime in December, details have yet to be released, this meeting will show development and further renderings of the project before it goes before all necessary approvals.

title: Talbot County Looks into Restrictions on Food Processing Residuals
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County looks into restrictions on food processing residuals

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals are in the works for Talbot County.The county's Planning Commission and County Council held a preliminary work session Tuesday to discuss regulations for the residuals, which are animal waste from the food processing process.
Earlier this month, Caroline County passed a bill to restrict the storage of the residuals, which are often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in storage tanks.
Talbot County is looking to the neighboring county and hoping to be proactive.
"We think we need to get ahead of it," Planning Commission Vice Chairman Chip Councell said. He noted that Caroline and Wicomico counties were "behind the eight ball" in enacting legislation.
Councell said he met with the Talbot County Farm Bureau regarding potential restrictions.
"I think they would like to see some restrictions put on it, one being that any type of food residuals storage would have to be enclosed, so it couldn't be open-air," Councell said. "The storage of it would have to be used in that agricultural operation. A farmer couldn't store it for everybody in the neighborhood. He could store it for his operation only, so there wouldn't be commercial storage."
Councell clarified the county would focus on the storage of the residuals, not the land application. State legislation that went into effect July 1 created a formal permitting process for the usage of food processing residuals.
"There's a few bad actors out there that, frankly, I think see profit potential with handling the material," said Alan Girard, advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, during Tuesday's meeting.
While Wicomico County banned the storage of residuals, temporary storage for 45 days is allowed. In Caroline County, storage is allowed once a permit is acquired, as long as the storage tank has a closed top.
Councell said the 45-day allowance may be adjusted once the legislation begins to be drafted.
"I think 45 days might be a little bit tight," Councell said.
At the end of the work session, Planning and Zoning Director Brennan Tarleton said discussion of potential DAF legislation will be added to the Planning Commission's agenda in November.

title: Talbot County Establishes Bike and Pedestrian Committee
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County establishes bike and pedestrian committee

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 409
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A bicycle and pedestrian advisory committee will soon be up and running in Talbot County after the Talbot County Council unanimously approved an administrative resolution on last week.Council Vice President Pete Lesher made the request for the resolution, which will create a committee intended to gather community input regarding bike and pedestrian safety and accessibility in Talbot County.
Lesher said it came in response to a bike and pedestrian trails public workshop held in July.
"I was asked that we put this together to advise council, as we have with other advisory boards, to ensure that we're getting input from representative groups around the county," Lesher said.
He said the committee will be made up of representatives from varying disciplines, including the farming, business, school and police communities.
Heather Grant, executive director of Talbot Thrive, a nonprofit dedicated to outdoor safety and health, said in an interview that it's important for the county to push for a bike and pedestrian master plan. This committee can be a first step in that effort, similar to what she's seen in neighboring Queen Anne's County.
"We really thought that that's needed in Talbot County," Grant said of a master plan. "And the way that Queen Anne's County went about getting that done is they first established a bike and pedestrian advisory committee back in 2008. So we really thought Talbot County was kind of behind the eight-ball on that."
At the July workshop, county officials, employees and community members gathered to discuss plans for a 9.5-mile Frederick Douglass Rail Trail, stretching from the town of Queen Anne to just north of Easton.
Some farmers expressed concerns about safety if that trail is built, referencing potential dangers of farmers using large equipment in such proximity to bikers and walkers.
Grant said the committee will facilitate "perspectives from all different groups" in Talbot County.
"We want them to have a seat at the table, and this is the best way to do that," Grant said.
She is excited for the committee's establishment, not just for the benefit of bicyclists, but also those who walk or use wheelchairs.
"I really think that we can really change our community and make it more friendly and safer for those people," Grant said. "And I think that everyone should be excited about having a more friendly community where we don't totally depend on cars."
After council members granted approval for the committee's creation, Lesher said the next step is working with county staff to recruit committee members.

title: MACo and Talbot County Council Discuss Fiscal Pressures Facing State
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo and Talbot County Council discuss fiscal pressures facing state

 September 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 490
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — When entering last year's General Assembly, the fiscal situation Maryland faced needed serious attention. In some ways, that fiscal pressure has increased since.Michael Sanderson, the executive director of the Maryland Association of Counties, briefed the Talbot County Council on those financial troubles and more during a special meeting Tuesday.
He told council members a budget shortfall of potentially $600 to $800 million could be facing lawmakers in Annapolis. Fixing that is "not easy, but not impossible," he said.
"There are a couple of years of that in our forecast, and then it gets really serious," Sanderson said.
When fiscal year 2028 arrives, Sanderson warned that the state will run out of money in its trust fund that's been used for The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's expansive and optimistic education initiative.
Many counties have been under significant financial pressure due to state requirements stemming from Blueprint. Sanderson says the state will be feeling that level of pressure soon.
"The counties are feeling it now," he said. "The state doesn't really feel it for a couple years down the road, and that has been a meaningful disconnect."
Without significant timeline adjustments for Blueprint from the state, MACo feels there will continue to be that disconnect between the fiscal situation of the state versus the situation counties are facing. State funding for transportation, though, is already causing serious impacts, Sanderson said.
"The canary in the coal mine that's already chirping is in transportation," he told the council members. " … The conversation in the summer time is sometimes ambiguous and hazy and that sort of thing. But this year, not so much. They were just saying, 'If there aren't already shovels in the ground, we can't afford the next thing.'"
The Maryland Department of Transportation has been forced to delay many statewide projects amid a significant budget deficit. Earlier this month, the department released a draft plan that showed $1.3 billion in cuts from the state's six-year transportation plan.
Sanderson noted the "state's transportation challenge is not a function of the Key Bridge" rebuild, which is set to begin next year.
At the county level, council Vice President Pete Lesher said Talbot County is "finding itself in a slightly different place" than others.
"We are going through a number of capital construction projects, our health department, our sheriff's office, our 911 center," Lesher said, emphasizing some of those projects are receiving "pandemic-era related funds" from the federal government.
"The pinch that a lot of counties are feeling right now, the income tax, is not yet being felt in Talbot County," Lesher said. "We can look around at our neighbors and see what is coming, even though we are not yet in that position now."
Lesher thanked Sanderson and MACo President Johnny Olszewski Jr. for their work to represent the counties at the state level year-round.
"We know that we are stronger together in Annapolis," Lesher said. "And we see every year what a powerful voice MACo is for all of us jointly."

title: Dorchester County Voters Face Slew of Amendments
author: Stephen Rideout
content:
Dorchester County voters face slew of amendments

 September 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Stephen Rideout | Section: Columns 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This Nov. 5, voters in Dorchester County will have a number of things to vote on in addition to the candidates who are running for election.Some will be voting early and by mail. There is a proposed state constitutional amendment regarding reproductive rights and six proposed Dorchester County Charter Amendments that were placed on the ballot by the County Council from proposals that were made by the Charter Commission appointed by the County Council pursuant to the County Charter.
Prior to the county elections in 2022, the Dorchester Citizens For Better Government sought to collect enough signatures on referendum petitions to have votes on some of the issues that will be voted on this year. While we were successful in gathering over 1,300 signatures, that was not enough to meet the legal requirements to have our questions placed on the ballot in 2022.
This effort, however, prompted the Charter Commission to be appointed by the current County Council. The prior County Council had appointed a Charter Commission that made recommendations for changes to the County Charter, but those recommendations were turned down by the prior County Council. The current Charter Commission has done the hard work that resulted in the proposed amendments that the voters will address.
Some of the proposals are simple administrative changes to help the County Council and staff be more efficient in running the county government. Question A, if approved, changes when the existing review of the administrative structure of county is to be done. Currently, there was no direction on timing, and the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government found that it was not being done as required.
The proposed Charter Amendment requires that it be done "within the first fiscal year of each County Council term" so that the council can act at the beginning of their term to make what they determine are necessary changes.
Question B is another administrative matter. It changes the date by which the council shall prepare the annual budget from the current May 1 to May 15 and the date by which the council will adopt the budget from May 31 to June 15. This simply allows the council and staff to have more time in which to do their work in preparing and passing the annual county budget. This is a complicated process that has to consider many points of view, so having more time to accomplish this is certainly reasonable.
Question C proposes amending the charter to remove the requirement that the county manager be a resident of Dorchester County. This is something that the Dorchester Citizens For Better Government considered and felt was a good idea but decided not to address given the number of important but potentially less controversial issues we felt needed to be addressed.
Finding the right person to be the county manager is or can be a challenging task. There are certainly capable and talented people living in the county that can do the job, and the current county manager, Jerry Jones, is clearly one of them. However, restricting County Council to only hiring someone who must live in the county limits their ability to look for and find someone who could be the best person for the needs of the county.
Certainly, the County Council can consider that issue as part of their hiring process, but mandating it is not in the best interests of the county, its citizens or its employees. As an example, someone could apply who has the best credentials who lives in a nearby county and owns a home or family farm there. If he or she were the best candidate, the current charter would probably cause them to decline to apply for or be the County Manager, as moving would cost them money.
Other reasons might be a spouse that has a job in that other county or children who are in their senior year of high school and moving would impact them. Leaving the final decision as to the issue of residence is best left in the hands of the council members that we have elected to make the best decisions for all of us.
I will stop here and address the remaining three proposed Charter Amendments next time. Before closing, I want to commend and thank the members of the Charter Commission that put so much time and effort into these proposals. They are William Layton, Allen Nelson, Glen Bramble, Linda Henry, George "Phillip" Reed, Susan Dukes and Robert Murphy.

title: St. Michaels Approves Accommodation Tax Increase
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels approves accommodation tax increase

 October 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: General Assembly 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST MICHAELS — The accommodation tax has long been a topic of controversy in the town of St Michaels, and some residents expressed concerns about a proposed 2% increase in the tax during a Sep. 25 commissioners meeting.The tax increase endorsement was approved by a majority of the town's commissioners at the meeting following months of discussions.
Since August, Talbot County has made moves for a 2% increase in accommodation tax countywide. The county has the lowest hotel tax rate in the state at 4%, which has been in place since 2005.
According to council Vice President Pete Lesher, in order to enact the tax increase, the county would need to ask state delegates this month to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year.
Prior to legislative submittal, Oxford, Easton and St. Michaels would need to approve an endorsement for the increase. St. Michaels' approval was the last the county needed to move forward.
The county attempted to raise the accommodations tax in 2021, but St. Michaels' commission at the time was not on board.
In town, discussion of a potential increase of accommodation tax has been in the works since the commissioners' race in May, when the three newly elected commissioners, David Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, all showed support for the increase.
According to St. Michaels Commissioner Alfred Mercier, the tax would increase the cost of rooms by around $2 to $8.
Mercier said because the increase in tax is minimal, it "really doesn't have any impact" in terms of the number of people who stay over in a destination site.
Additionally, Mercier said the increase in tax would have a larger impact if the incremental rate, the total change in tax, is "fairly significant," meaning if the increase was above 10%.
"I just wanted to get rid of the misconceptions on this because this is not a tax on the hotel," Mercier said. "This is truly a way to tax, if you will, visitors that come into town, and there has been other discussions on how we can generate money, and I know they're out there."
Commissioner Alexis Roiter said she agreed with the points made by Mercier and made clear her support for the raise in tax, especially since it will be paid by tourists.
"2% is very small," Roiter said. "And this isn't passed down to the actual people coming to town who use our garbage cans, park their cars illegally, throw their trash out and increase the cost of our own services like water. The fact that we are the lowest in the state doesn't make any sense."
Commissioner Katrina Whittington reminded commissioners that if they voted against the endorsement, it would be taking away the opportunity for Easton and Oxford to get the additional money, since all three towns would have to agree to raise the accommodation tax.
Although there seemed to be unanimous support among commissioners, business owners and residents in town were concerned of the potential harm the increase would have on businesses.
George Wilson, owner of the Old Brick Inn, shared that occupancy is down for lodging in town, and an increase could have negative effects for businesses like his. Wilson said the tax increase should be met with more scrutiny due to lingering unanswered questions.
"Where is the accommodation tax going? Because I don't think we have done our due diligence," Wilson said. "We know what we need, I understand that, but what are we doing with what we have?"
Wilson said the town was ignoring other potential revenue sources, like entertainment taxes on restaurants and stores.
During the public hearing Sep. 25, former St. Michaels Commissioner Tad DuPont brought up concerns involving the loss of smaller inns in the area within the last two years. Along with those concerns, DuPont mentioned the negative affect that undocumented Airbnbs are having on inns.
Whittington said undocumented Airbnb rentals have been a longstanding issue among the town and encouraged residents to report addresses they may suspect of hosting Airbnbs so the town could investigate.
After the public comment, Mercier requested the commissioners move the vote for a later meeting to obtain more information.
Wojciechowski said delaying the vote would interfere with the county's deadline to bring the issue to state legislators.
A motion was passed for the endorsement of the tax increase with a 4-1 vote. Mercier, who previously supported the increase, voted against the motion, stating there were "a lot of unanswered items."

title: Oxford Commissioners Discuss Amending Meeting Procedures Resolution at Workshop
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners discuss amending meeting procedures resolution at workshop

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — During a Commissioners of Oxford workshop Wednesday morning, the three town commissioners presented their recommendations for amending a recently passed resolution establishing town meeting procedures.By the end of the workshop, the commissioners agreed to have an amended resolution drafted for the next town meeting on Oct. 8. The commissioners also agreed to continue the discussion at that meeting before taking a vote.
The current resolution in place, passed on Sept. 24, establishes general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings. Specifically, it limits when and for how long public commenters can speak and prohibits heckling, defamatory comments and profanity.
When Commission President Norm Bell introduced the resolution in early September, he said the resolution was developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at a previous town meeting in August.
At the meeting on Sept. 24, some residents expressed concerns with the limitations on public comment in the resolution, as well as the way in which the resolution was passed.
During the workshop, each commissioner brought their own approach to allaying those concerns.
Bell proposed an amendment to make it more explicit that residents can speak before a vote on an agenda item — not including ordinances, as ordinances require public hearings — at the discretion of the commissioners.
"From time to time, the Commissioners of Oxford may expressly invite public testimony, questions, comments or other forms of public participation during specifically-designated agenda items," Bell read from his draft of the amended resolution.
Bell said his draft amendment would also change the language so commissioners "may" respond to comments and questions from residents during public comment periods, and will answer all questions after the meeting "as quickly" as they can. The resolution passed last week states comments and questions will receive written responses after the meeting is over.
Working off Bell's new draft, Commissioner Katrina Greer said when it comes to public participation during agenda item discussions, the word "may" in Bell's draft should be changed to the word "shall." This change would make it so that public comment must be offered for each agenda item.
Greer said the commissioners don't always know what issues residents will want to speak on.
"Sometimes we're surprised by what's important to the public," she said. "We can't know that until we take the temperature of the room."
Commissioner Tom Costigan proposed having a public comment section at the beginning and end of every meeting like St. Michaels does. He said residents would be able to address any agenda items before they are voted on at the opening of the meeting and ask questions or give comments on any issue before the end of the meeting.
"This structure allows the commission to conduct the town's business without constant interruptions," he said. "It also affords the opportunity for more citizen comment in a constructive and respectful manner."
Greer said she thinks it would be better to limit public comment to each agenda item before a vote is taken because it would better inform the commissioners' vote.
The commissioners agreed to use "shall" instead of "may" in a new draft resolution based on Bell's draft, which they can vote on following discussion at the next town meeting.
At the end of the workshop, residents shared their views. Some said they favored Greer's suggestion of using "shall" and a few said they favored Bell's use of the word "may."
Resident Jim Wilcox suggested that instead of the commissioners choosing between "shall" and "may," they amend the resolution to say that at least one commissioner needs to request public comment on a specific agenda item for it to be added.

title: Talbot County Proposes Hotel Tax Increase to Local Delegation
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County proposes hotel tax increase to local delegation

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County leaders met with the local delegation Tuesday afternoon to discuss creating legislation during the upcoming General Assembly to raise the county's hotel taxes.Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels or short-term rentals in the county, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or one of three towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties not within those boundaries.
A potential increase to 6%, which would increase total revenue collected by around $1 million in fiscal year 2024, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of tourism and economic development, along with Talbot County Council members briefed Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) on the proposed increase.
"I'm anticipating that this is going to be our principal legislation request for the delegation this year," council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Adams and Mautz explained that state lawmakers will be tasked with addressing significant budget problems in the upcoming session. Adams said it's likely lawmakers will try to pass the budget by voting for state tax increases that were not passed last year.
He said it's probably the first year he will vote against the budget. Any tax bill will require his careful consideration, Adams noted, saying he'd like to hear the council's opinions on potential hotel tax legislation.
Council Member Keasha Haythe said the spike would help "level the playing field" for the county, as well as increase funding for the tourism and economic development department. Revenue the county collects from the accommodations tax goes to that department.
"This particular tax I do believe is necessary for Talbot County and tourism and (the) hospitality industry," Haythe said.
Mautz agreed with Haythe's points but brought up the benefits of Talbot County's low accommodations tax rate.
"I also agree with the perspective that would say, if your accommodation tax is lower than the neighboring county, then you have an advantage as far as attracting (people)," Mautz said. He added that the council should take into consideration that it may make the area more attractive for investors.
Jessica Bellis, CFO at the Avalon Foundation and a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed her support for the increase. She said the taxes benefit her organization since they are cycled back into Talbot County's and Easton's respective economic development and tourism departments.
"We can't market in the big world, as tiny little Avalon Foundation or as a small Airbnb in Talbot County," Bellis said. "We really rely on that tourism office for its marketing power."
Hutchinson said the county should ensure business owners are on board and lay out to the delegation how the taxes collected cycle back into the local economy.
Council President Chuck Callahan said it's important for the county to do its "due diligence" and gather feedback from businesses before voting on the topic as a council. While the bill could be pre-filed by the local delegates in November, January was agreed upon as a deadline for the county to have a draft bill ready for the legislators.
"This is a really important issue," Mautz said. "We definitely don't want to be in a situation where we go up to Annapolis and are not prepared."
"It's a different discussion when you go across the bridge," he said.

title: Dorchester Finance Director Gives Update on County Audits, ARPA Money
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester finance director gives update on county audits, ARPA money

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 355

 CAMBRIDGE — At a Dorchester County Council meeting Tuesday, county Finance Director Karen Tolley gave an update on the status of the county's audits and the remainder of the county's American Rescue Plan Act funds.Tolley said the Finance Department has wrapped up its work on the fiscal year 2022 audit. She said the audit is currently under external review.
As soon as the audit is released — which Tolley anticipates will be in the coming days — it can be published and will be put on the county website.
In September 2023, a WHCP reported the county's failure to submit financial reports and audits since 2020. That month, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said county staff had been working "tirelessly" with independent auditing firm UHY to complete the missing audits.
At the meeting this week, Tolley said the county finance department had done a lot of work internally to help move the process along.
"I couldn't be more proud of our finance team that we're building out here in the county," she said.
Tolley said she expects to see repeat recommendations in the fiscal year 2022 audit because it is from years go, but she expects "the gray clouds" will "start clearing" for the fiscal years 2023 and 2024.
Council member Ricky Travers said it is important the auditors release the fiscal year 2022 audit as soon as possible because it is holding up county projects.
"We need to keep pushing (the auditors) every single day to make this happen so that we can get these projects moving that are on hold because of this," he said.
Tolley said that with the audit in the hands of the auditors, all the county can do is wait for the release.
Tolley also talked about the county's remaining $1.4 million in ARPA funds at the meeting. She said the county received a total of $6.2 million in ARPA funds.
The remaining $1.4 million will need to be obligated by the end of the year. To consider the funds obligated, there will need to be a contract or memorandum of understanding with a vendor, Tolley said.
The deadline to spend the ARPA money is Dec. 31, 2026.

title: Trappe Council Discusses Procurement Policy Changes
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe council discusses procurement policy changes

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 284
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Wednesday evening, the Trappe Town Council discussed making revisions and updating current procurement policy in an effort to save money and more swiftly receive needed services.The current procurement policy requires the town to make a request for proposal for any services or item. Requests for proposals are a form of reverse auction that solicits a business proposal by an organization interested in the procurement of a service or product from potential suppliers.
According to Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's attorney, towns on the Eastern Shore, including Queenstown, have recently made similar changes.
Ryan said last year leaders of Queenstown we're finding it difficult to go through the formal advertising and drafting process every time they wanted to make a purchase.
Queenstown developed a tiered system so any purchase under $10,000 wouldn't require requests for proposals to be sent out. Purchases between $10,000 to $25,000 would require staff to reach out to firms and seek quotes for purchases.
Any purchase over $25,000 would have the advertised proposal process, where a formal request for proposal would be required.
Ryan said these revisions would help cut costs. When going through the procurement policy, costs are driven up by having to pay attorneys, engineering firms or other experts to draft the full requests for proposals and then have to pay $400 to advertise it in the newspaper.
"As time progresses, things get more expensive," Ryan said. "You just to keep increasing that number, because it becomes too burdensome. When you get to the $25,000 (mark), that's a substantial amount of money. So you want that public competitive procurement process."
Trappe Commissioners unanimously decided to have a draft of the revised policy ready for consideration for the next council meeting on Nov. 6.

title: State Board of Elections Weighs in on Election Judges Amid Concerns in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
State Board of Elections weighs in on election judges amid concerns in Talbot County

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After some Talbot County officials and residents raised concerns about the partisan breakdown of election judges, the Maryland State Board of Elections is telling voters that election judge affiliations will not bring about disenfranchisement at the polls in November.Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced last week after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 3-2 vote.
One week later, Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble sent a letter to the Talbot County Board of Elections, "strongly" urging the board to follow state law.
The following day, Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, released a statement regarding the assignment of election judges. In it, he emphasized that Maryland voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," DeMarinis wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections. The party affiliation of an election judge does not stop them from casting their ballots or disenfranchise a voter. And to say otherwise is disingenuous."
DeMarinis noted in his statement the strict rules election judges must follow, bounding them "to conduct the election in a nonpartisan manner and fashion."
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Following a closed session meeting on Friday for legal advice, the Talbot Board of Elections is set to meet Monday at 1 p.m. to discuss of a statement to send to the public, according to Talbot County Election Director Tammy Stafford. She said election judge assignments are on the agenda for a second special meeting Tuesday at 9:30 a.m.
Stafford did not respond to questions from the Star Democrat rabout the election judges and whether legal counsel has advised if the board is in compliance with law or not.
Election judges are appointed 13 weeks prior to the primary elections, DeMarinis said, and recruiting judges is an ongoing process local boards of elections undertake.
"There are never enough election judges on call to serve," the statement read. "Individuals get sick, have emergencies, have transportation issues, and a whole list of other things that might prevent them from serving on an assigned day. Having election judges assigned to being on call is the only way to mitigate this problem and ensure smooth election operations."
LETTER FROM SHERIFFIn Gamble's letter sent to the board and Election Director Tammy Stafford, the sheriff stated he's received more than 25 complaints regarding the election and "feelings of disenfranchisement."
"Complaints received highlight a clear disparity among one party over another and in this current instance, registered Republican voters are not being equally represented," Gamble wrote.
In an interview, Gamble, a Republican, explained the reasoning for his concerns and why he sent the letter.
"We provide security at the polling places," Gamble said. "We also escort ballots back. The election judges, we follow them back and make sure that the election's not tampered with by outsiders, however they might do that. I think to have free and fair elections, you need to be transparent, and you need to follow the law."
DeMarinis' statement addressed the role of local sheriff's offices in elections.
"The Sheriff's office does not have any legal authority to conduct security checks or a role in securing the ballots in a polling place," DeMarinis wrote. "Nor does the Sheriff enforce the requirements of the Election Law Article. The legal authority to keep the peace, to preserve the integrity of the voting process and maintain order in the polling place is entrusted to the election judge. In fact, a police officer must obey the order of the election judge at the polling place."
Gamble said he's not heard back from the county or state elections boards. In an interview, he expressed worry that the election judge controversy may affect safety during the election process.
"It causes me security concerns, too, because people are going to get frustrated," Gamble said. "We've already seen violence associated with this election cycle with two assassination attempts of the former president.
"And we don't want any issues here in Talbot County with people getting frustrated and then taking their frustrations out in some criminal manner," he said.

title: Make Your Plan to Vote
author: Staff Writer
content:
Make your plan to vote

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 According to state Board of Elections, Instructions and Information for Challengers, Watchers, and Other Election Observers, reissued Oct. 14, 2022, Part III, Item 19 answers the question: "Can a polling place open if the election judges represent only one political party?" "Yes." Under advice from the attorney general, the election judges present must open the polling place by the required time, even if there are election judges of only one political party present.As an election judge who has served in the past, I am honored to execute this civic service with my fellow judges, regardless of their affiliation.
First-time judges are often humbled and impressed by the security, objectivity, support and training mandated and effected by both the state and county Boards of Elections.
Talbot County's director of elections has repeatedly made it known that there is an imbalance of affiliation and has encouraged recruitment of Republican applicants.
For staffing purposes, the board must have a commitment from anyone wishing to serve well in advance of the election. I think the board contacted judges who had participated in 2022 as early as October 2023 to inquire about interest in serving for the 2024 cycle.
It is a long game. Not quite as long as the campaigns, thankfully.
Judges report to their assigned polling places by 5:45 a.m. and must stay until all eligible voters have voted, the equipment is secured and the chief judge is ready to take the results to the board office. Everyone leaves as a group. It is a long day. The board must also staff and support early voting (Oct. 24-31).
Please make your plan to vote and do so with faith and trust that election staff and judges want to provide an objective environment to cast your ballot.
ROBIN K. PAGE
Easton

title: Attorney General: Sheriff Has Limited Role in Electoral Process
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Attorney general: Sheriff has limited role in electoral process

 October 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown wrote a letter to Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gable detailing the "limited role of local law enforcement, including our sheriff's office in the electoral process."The letter from Brown was read aloud by Tammy Stafford, election director for Talbot County, during an Oct. 7 Board of Elections special meeting.
Although the letter is not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said he hopes the letter is helpful in setting forth the roles of law enforcement officers during elections.
The letter is the latest salvo on the topic of sometimes tense back-and-forth between the Talbot County Board of Elections, the Talbot County Sheriff and local elected officials in recent weeks.
Brown's letter responds to a letter sent by Gamble to the Board of Elections on issues concerning the upcoming election, in which Gamble "strongly" urged the board to follow state law.
In Brown's letter, he addresses the role of law enforcement, security, authority on election law violations and concerns involving election judges.
"State law does, specifies and carefully circumscribes the authority of local law enforcement and polling places while conferring primary responsibility for election law enforcement on other agencies," Brown said. "I understand that local law enforcement agencies do provide assistance to local boards of elections in some jurisdictions, including deploying personnel to provide security and transporting election materials. But importantly, this is done at the request and under the direction of the local Board of Elections itself."
Gamble's letter came in the midst of intense discussions centering concerns over the partisan breakdown of election judges ahead of the Nov. 5 General Election.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 3-2 vote.
In his letter, Brown emphasized state law "does not require equality in the total number of judges" recruited and trained by the local Board of Elections.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown said.
Toward the end of Brown's letter, he advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to "closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there."
After the reading of the letter, the county Board of Elections weighed whether to release its own letter or statement to the public addressing the election judge concerns.
Denise Lovelady, a member of the board of elections, said the issue with Brown's letter is it is still subject to "clarification." She said the letter speaks more to security issues than election judge equality.
After a bit of discussion, board members voted 3-1 to sent out Brown's letter instead of drafting their own. Lovelady voted against sending Brown's letter.
"I don't feel that it services the public, that it's giving them the full information that they need," Lovelady said. "The board is kind of skirting the issue that it needs to be defined better than what it has been in these meetings."

title: Queen Anne's Looking to Connect County Trails
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Queen Anne's looking to connect county trails

 October 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 494
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Centreville — Cross county trail connectivity is on the right path as Steve Chandlee, Queen Anne's Parks and Recreation director and Steve Cohoon, public works public facilities planner, presented updates on the ongoing multi-phase county trails project Sept. 24.From Matapeake to Route 50, the six-phase project seeks to establish pedestrian and biking routes and safely connect existing South Island and the Cross Island trails, according to Chandlee.
Phase 1 of the Queen Anne's County Trail Project includes Ellendale Connector near Waterman Joe and is currently under construction, Cohoon said.
Phase 2 entails the Matapeake School Complex to Mowbray Park is permitted and construction is expected from Oct. 1 through Feb. 28, 2025, and will include tree clearing, stone base and stormwater installation and extensive grading.
Phase 3 involves the wooded area through the back of Mowbray Park to Waterman Joe and is currently in design and engineering and waiting on final construction plans and permits with estimated construction expected March 5 through May 30.
Phase 4 involves the Route 8 crossing to Christ Church to the Matapeake Trailhead and is seeking design and funding. This portion is expected to be the most expensive due to the marshy area and many trees to be removed.
Phase 5 entails the Thompson Creek and is seeking design and funding with funding needed for the construction of the road.
Phase 6 involves U.S. Route 50/301 overpass crossing.
There are three potential locations for crossing that take into account county-owned property or easements, Cohoon said.
A key aspect of the project moving forward will be a required feasibility study by the State Highway Administration to determine where the best crossing location would be and where connections to existing trails systems can be made, he said.
This study will take into account future plans including bay crossing and the widening of Route 50.
The department is currently seeking grant funds for the approximately $120,000 to $150,000 feasibility study, Cohoon said.
A timeframe for completion is undetermined at this point as the different potential locations may have different impacts, he said.
Many of the construction aspects are weather dependent, he said.
Progress also is developing on the Cross County Connector Trail Extension, according to Cohoon. Queen Anne's County received $80,000 from the Baltimore Regional Transportation Board through the adoption of the 2024 Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan earlier this year. This grant is to conduct a feasibility study to extend the Cross County Connector Trail from Long Point Park to the Nesbit Road overpass by 2.8 miles.
This study includes feasibility of pedestrian and bike facilities on existing overpasses crossing U.S. 50/301 at Chester River Beach Road and Nesbit Road, Cohoon said. Work is underway with RK and K Civil Engineering as the consultant for this portion and is expected to be completed by the end of the year, he said.
"The ultimate goal with any of these crossings is to connect the South Island Trail with the Cross Island Trail. That's been a long-standing goal for many, many years for the county," Cohoon said.
