title: Central Committees on the Shore Encourage Voting Early, Mail-In Ballots
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Central committees on the Shore encourage voting early, mail-in ballots

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 With Election Day less than a month away, Democrat and Republican officials across the Mid-Shore are encouraging voters to participate in early voting.Sarah Gavian, chair of the Dorchester County Democratic Central Committee, encourages voters to make a plan, whether that plan includes mail-in voting, early voting or voting on Nov. 5.
"(If) you want your people to vote, you start encouraging them to do so at the first opportunity," Gavian said. "Because if they miss the first one, they can catch the second one. If they miss the second one, they can catch the third one."
Richard Osborne, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, said it's important for everyone to vote and encourage those that they know to do so as well. He said a benefit of early voting is avoiding a situation on Election Day where results begin to trickle in while polls are still open.
"The reason why you want to do that is because if you wait until the last day and you see maybe elections lost, it might discourage you from voting," Osborne said.
Across Maryland, more than 150,000 people participated in early voting during the presidential primary election in May.
In Talbot County, 7.08% of eligible active voters voted early, tied for the highest percentage of any county with Kent. In Caroline and Dorchester, 4.43% and 4.1% of voters participated in early voting, respectively.
At a Sept. 14 rally in Denton, local Republican politicians gathered to campaign in front of Caroline County voters. During the event, many calls for early voting surfaced.
First District Congressman Andy Harris (R-Md.), the featured speaker at the event, asked attendees to vote early for Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said the same.
"You need your vote in the bank," Harris said. "You must bank your vote."
"It's incredibly important," he continued. "We have to beat the Democrats at their game, and their game is voting before Election Day."
Chairs of local central committees, such as Talbot's Democratic Committee Chair Patrick Firth are noting that the unexpected can happen on Election Day, such as long lines, car troubles or work emergencies.
Firth said all voters should make a plan, emphasizing the security and efficiency of not just early voting days, but mail-in ballots.
"Sometimes the easiest way to make sure that your voice is heard is get it done along the way," Firth said. "And that's what's so efficient and common sense about participating in the election via the mail-in ballots."
Julie Quick, chair of the Caroline County Republican Central Committee, said her team is emphasizing to voters the multitude of voting options in the first post-COVID general election cycle.
"I think a lot of people here are so used to voting in person, and we just really want to raise awareness that there are so many options," Quick said.
General election early voting in Maryland begins Oct. 24 and runs through Oct. 31.

title: Cambridge Candidates Dispute Peace Order Request, Residency Requirements
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge candidates dispute peace order request, residency requirements

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With questions swirling about the residency of candidates in Cambridge's Oct. 19 election, three candidates headed to Dorchester County District Court Wednesday morning for a peace order hearing between one candidate and another's wife.Ward 4 Cambridge Commissioner Sputty Cephas, who is running for reelection, was denied a final peace order Wednesday against Natalee Bradshaw, the wife of former Cambridge Mayor and current mayoral candidate Andrew Bradshaw.
Andrew Bradshaw called the peace order request "a malicious use" of the court system "performed specifically for political purposes."
Cephas told the Star Democrat he had no intent behind filing the peace order other than not wanting to be bothered.
On Oct. 2, Cephas was granted a temporary peace order against Natalee Bradshaw. The peace order entailed that Natalee Bradshaw neither abuse Cephas, nor contact Cephas, nor enter his residence.
During the hearing Wednesday, Cephas asked Judge Abigail Marsh to grant a final peace order, which would extend the length of the temporary peace order.
Cephas testified that on Oct. 1, after leaving a Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, he noticed a white Lincoln follow him to his home. Cephas said when he backed into his driveway, he saw the white Lincoln slow down and the driver of the vehicle snap photos before driving away quickly.
Cephas said he got back into his vehicle and drove behind the white Lincoln to get identification. He was able to identify the driver as Natalee Bradshaw. Cephas said he then spoke with Andrew Bradshaw for a minute or so.
Cephas then brought the issue to his sister, Commission President Lajan Cephas — who is running against Andrew Bradshaw and La-Shon Banks-Foster in the mayoral election — before going to the police department.
During the hearing, he told the judge that he felt harassed and stalked.
"I just want to be left alone," he said.
Natalee Bradshaw's attorney Philip Cronan argued Sputty Cephas' petition should be dismissed because none of his allegations was sufficient. Cronan said Natalee Bradshaw never made contact with or approached Sputty Cephas the night of Oct. 1.
Before denying the final peace order, Judge Abigail Marsh said Natalee Bradshaw is on notice that Sputty Cephas does not want any contact.
Marsh said harassment and stalking allegations require a pattern of behavior for a final peace order to be granted, and this was a single incident.
RESIDENCY REQUIREMENTSDuring the hearing, Cronan brought up statements that have been made questioning whether Sputty Cephas and/or Lajan Cephas are following the city's residency requirements for candidates.
Questions regarding the residency of candidates have circulated through Cambridge in the last month.
At a City Council meeting Sept. 9, one resident brought up the importance of verifying candidate applications. In response, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said city staff has heard rumors regarding applicants and their residency, but no formal complaints had been filed. He encouraged residents to submit formal complaints so that they can be looked into.
In an interview Wednesday, Andrew Bradshaw alleged that Lajan Cephas has not been residing at the Cambridge address on her application. He said that his wife "may well have been" seeing about residency the night of Oct. 1. He said if that is the case, her actions were based on "real and genuine" concerns.
Lajan Cephas said in an interview Wednesday that she is not sure of Natalee Bradshaw's intent. Cephas said she has met every requirement to be a candidate in the city's election.
Sputty Cephas said during the hearing that the city has a process to do its due diligence for candidate applications.
Andrew Bradshaw said his wife has never expressed to him why she was outside Sputty Cephas's home Oct. 1. He said that in the privacy of their home, she has sworn she did not take any photos.

title: Caroline County Towns Forge Connections at Chamber Event
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline County towns forge connections at Chamber event

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Around 70 members of the Caroline Chamber of Commerce met at the Greater Impact Church to have a dialogue of connection between six towns in the county.On Oct. 9 representatives from Preston, Denton, Greensboro, Goldsboro, Federalsburg and Ridgely were given 10 minutes to talk about their municipality. There were six tables, one for each municipality, and attendees rotated between them.
Everybody in the room was a stakeholder for Caroline County. A lot of business cards and handshakes were exchanged.
Tracey Snyder, executive director of the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce, coached the town leaders to "Share what is happening in your fabulous, wonderful town. Share who you are and let them share who they are."
She said, "The power is the municipalities. If they don't communicate with each other, how are we going to grow? We need each other. We are a small but mighty county. Not competing, supporting."
Although this was Snyder's idea, she had a think tank to help her.
The audience contained economic development departments, commissioners, CASA, Caroline GOP, Chesapeake College, Channel Marker, Compass Regional Hospice, Choptank Community Health and more.
Not only the town representatives showed up. There were also county, state liaisons in attendance.
Carl Anderton Jr., director of rural economic strategy from the Maryland Department of Commerce and Gov. Wes Moore's office, said, "The whole point is there is strength in numbers.
"There may be something that Federalsburg is doing well that Denton is trying to do. Then Denton uses it from Federalsburg ,and there is no need to recreate the wheel," Anderton said.
He said there are 16 rural counties in Maryland, and his goal was to be available to help counties and municipalities, especially if they are have trouble with agencies.
Amber Korell, town manager of Preston, went from table to table.
"I met so many folks that I need to invite to our Preston Connects Program. I have gotten over twenty business cards. Preston Connects is a program we offer to partners and other organizations to come out to our town and utilize our office space," she said.
Another town representative, Stephanie Berkey, clerk treasurer for the town of Ridgely, shared information about the town's upcoming events.
"We have a website www.christmasinridgely.com It is all things we do throughout the holiday season. Starting at Thanksgiving through New Year's Day. We have a lights display. They are already putting the lights up," she said.
She was very animated in her presentations.
"As a townsperson this was fun. I made some good contacts. I gave a lot of ideas about our holiday Christmas in Ridgely to people," Berkey said.
After attendees rotated to all six tables, Snyder called time and everyone clapped. All the town representatives were called up to the stage for a group photo.
Blue tote bags were given out to everyone so they could carry out all the swag and business cards. People kept talking all the way out to the parking lot.

title: Talbot County Council Discusses Election Judges, Route 50 Housing Project
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County Council discusses election judges, Route 50 housing project

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Tuesday's public meeting, members of the Talbot County Council revisited the ongoing dialogue surrounding the partisan breakdown of election judges in Talbot County for the upcoming election.Council Member Dave Stepp originally raised concerns at a Sept. 24 council meeting regarding an imbalance of election judges selected by the Talbot County Board of Elections to work polling places this November. At the time, the board's breakdown of judges was 62 Democratic, 50 Republican and 11 unaffiliated.
At Tuesday's meeting, Stepp said the difference between Democratic and Republican judges had lowered to seven. "I ask that we keep up that work," Stepp said.
He also thanked Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble for sending a letter to the Board of Elections and Election Director Tammy Stafford last week. In that letter, Gamble "strongly" urged the board to follow state election law.
Council Member Lynn Mielke, as she did on Sept. 24, disagreed with Stepp. She brought up a letter written by Attorney General Anthony Brown that was sent to Gamble on Monday.
In that letter, Brown addressed the "limited role of local law enforcement … in the electoral process." While not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said achieving "exact party balance" isn't always possible for local election boards due to volunteer rates, training and no-shows on Election Day.
"My Office has consistently advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there," Brown wrote in his letter.
Mielke said Tuesday, "We have rulings from the attorney general that the procedure that was started by (Council Member) Stepp and others, were overruled … And that there was nothing found … that the local board of elections have done wrong."
ZONING WAIVERCouncil members unanimously approved a zoning change waiver for around 17 acres of land off of U.S. Route 50 that developers aim to use for an affordable multifamily housing project in Easton.
The development on the east side of Ocean Gateway is planned by developers Corrigan & Trippe Ventures. Easton Town Council approved the annexation of the land in July.
The resolution passed Tuesday approves a waiver that will allow a proposed zoning change to take immediate effect without a five-year hold. The area will be rezoned from the county's town conservation zoning to the town's residential zoning, providing developers with a higher approved density.
"They would essentially be locked into the uses that are permitted under the county's TC zoning now for a period of five years," County Attorney Patrick Thomas said if the waiver was not passed.
Zach Smith, an attorney representing the developers, said the maximum density under the town's residential zoning is 3.5 units per acre, along with a 5-unit-per-acre mark permitted by the town's multifamily housing special exception.
If developers plan to exceed those marks, they will have to come before the Easton Town Council for a planned unit development approval. Smith noted developers would then need to revisit the County Council for a supplemental waiver.
Smith emphasized to council members that while developers are obligated within the annexation agreement to reach a 50% mark of affordable units, the goal is for 100% of the units to be affordable.
"This housing is not necessarily housing designed to attract new folks to our community, it's really to serve folks that are already in our community," Smith said.

title: Cambridge Candidates Talk Local Issues at Candidate Forum
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge candidates talk local issues at candidate forum

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 936
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge City Council candidates and the city's residents flowed in and out of the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center Saturday afternoon for a nearly five-hour candidate forum conducted by the League of Women Voters.Ten of the 14 commissioner and mayoral candidates running in the Oct. 19 election were at the forum.
The forum was split into three sessions for the different races. Ryan Anthony of the Cambridge Spy, Sharon Smith of the Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods, Jim Johnson of the Dorchester Star and Jim Brady of WHCP moderated the forum.
Ward 2 candidate Jenna LeCompte, Ward 4 candidate Dave Cannon, Ward 3 candidate Frank Stout and Ward 5 candidate Brian Roche — who is running uncontested — were not at the event.
In an email to WHCP on Friday, LeCompte said she is "taking a step back" from her campaign and would not be at the event. She did not respond to requests for clarification from the Star Democrat on what that means.
MAYORAL FORUM
Sandwiched between two commissioner candidate sessions, the mayoral forum gave candidates Lajan Cephas, Andrew Bradshaw and La-Shon Banks-Foster the opportunity to share their perspectives on an array of Cambridge issues, from the waterfront, to revitalizing the city's downtown, to race relations.
During the session, candidates were asked whether the city should get more involved in Dorchester County Public Schools, which is one of Maryland's lowest ranked school systems.
Bradshaw said he would like to implement a mentorship program, which would reach across racial and socioeconomic lines, and encourage the Board of Education to implement a charter school program. He said charter schools across the state tend to perform at the state average, which is "significantly better" than Dorchester schools.
"And they are only located in counties and jurisdictions with poor performance," he said, "so there's corollaries where they can succeed in places like Cambridge."
Foster, who attended the forum virtually, said every graduate from Dorchester County high schools is a county resident and could be a Cambridge resident.
"We cannot ignore the fact that whoever graduates from either of the schools that I mentioned can and will impact the City of Cambridge, and we must have an active role," she said.
Cephas said it is important for the city to be "extremely supportive" of the county, but there is no need to "reinvent the wheel." She said there are nonprofits already in place to address education concerns.
"So it's extremely important that we understand what's already in place, support those nonprofits that are already in place, and each of us just pick up a book and read to someone," she said.
COMMISSIONER FORUMS
The seven commissioner candidates at the forum were split into two groups. All commissioner candidates were asked the same questions from the moderators.
Kicking off the event were Ward 1 candidates Brett Summers and Laurel Atkiss, as well as Ward 3 candidate Gary Gordy. Ward 2 candidates Jermaine Anderson, Shay Lewis-Sisco and Nancy Jackson, as well as Ward 4 candidate Sputty Cephas, closed out the event.
When asked about code enforcement and overall housing quality in the city, Summers said hiring tenant advocates to promote a tenants bill of rights would be beneficial.
"Because if the tenants feel like they can contact the city inspector and have them come out without fear of getting evicted or some other kind of retribution, then the tenants are empowered to improve our housing stock," he said.
Atkiss said the city has implemented a software system to make it easier to enforce things like building code violations. She said Cambridge is doing city-wide building inspections and recently hired a new code enforcement officer.
"We've invested money, we've invested time," she said, "and now we're going to invest the manpower, and we're going to start to see some results that I hope everybody's going to be really happy with."
Lewis-Sisco said code enforcement should strategically target houses where renters are living in deplorable conditions. She said community engagement should also be a focus.
"So that when code enforcement officers go out to a homeowner or a property, they are able to offer those additional supports or let them know what additional resources exist," she said.
The issue of addressing crime in Cambridge was also brought up during the forum.
Gordy said improved lighting, more cameras and more monitoring of those cameras are needed in the city's "hot spots" in order to lower crime rates. When talking about monitoring cameras, he brought up a shooting that occurred over the weekend.
"Because last night police got there so fast, but they couldn't see who it was," he said about the need for 24-hour camera monitoring.
Jackson said addressing the issue of crime in Cambridge might start with more than detaining people. She said she would work to help resolve those problems if elected.
"There is something deep where this person is committing these acts," she said. "It could be the home life or it could be the environment."
Cephas said strengthening the police department's community policing division is important. He talked about programming for youth to attract "local and diverse talent" as another solution.
"Let's do a cadet program to get some of these young people before they get out into the community and do wrong things or bad things," he said.
Anderson said these problems have existed for a long time and won't be a quick fix. He stressed the importance of being proactive and communicating.
When asked about the greatest threat to the city, both Atkiss and Anderson talked about the city standing in its own way.
"But the biggest opportunity is imagine if we get out of our own way," Anderson said. "Think about the opportunity that would pose for this city ... how much of a difference that would make."

title: Local Leaders Share Their Journeys in New Book
author: Tom McCall
content:
Local leaders share their journeys in new book

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — "Leadership: Our Journey and Culture" is a new 300-page anthology edited by Savannah Winston.This Preston resident and third year doctoral student has taken her own entrepreneurial journey, and she invited 19 other leaders to talk about their values and strategies for the book.
The book is already an Amazon best seller, with electronic sales for ebooks doing well. The printed version will be available for purchase this week.
There are several Eastern Shore locals among the 20 leaders in the book, including Kathleen Brenton, Angel Perez, Cheryl Beulah, Stefanie Johnson, Cathy Cassell, Victoria Weaver and Michelle Boulden Hammond. The forward author is Bishop Dane A. Coleman.
Winston, the book's visionary and president of Preston Town Commission, said, "Part of my research is cross cultural competency. With this book, my vision was to bring together leaders of various backgrounds and cultures and have them share their stories. As a visionary, my chapter is entitled 'Embrace Your Journey.'"
Some of the local leaders sat down at the Culinary Center in Denton to talk about their paths to make an impact.
"My momma used to call me headstrong all the time. If I can have an impact on someone, that is what it is all about. I want to help them bridge the gap," said Beulah, executive director and owner of Aaron's Place and a licensed mortician.
She listens to people as part of her leadership style.
"People come into the food pantry and want to tell their stories. They automatically assume, 'You don't know what you are talking about.' I say. 'You don't know me. You don't know my journey. So let's not assume. Let's see if we can help each other and build each other up,'" Beulah said.
Strength is a part of being able to keep going.
"I want to focus on how to be a strong leader. What gives you your strength. If it doesn't break you, it is going to make you. Take those battles turn them upside down and draw strength from them," Beulah said.
Another contributor showed that her leadership was based in her spirituality and a message passed down through generations.
Boulden Hammond, representing community and behavioral health, said, "You have to have a servant's heart. As leaders we have to understand that we are dealing with community. If you are a leader, show forth with your servitude. I love serving."
Perez, Caroline Pride CEO, also finds his strength in helping others. His chapter is titled "Purpose in Life."
"The satisfaction of the work we do and seeing how you can change people's lives in the positive way. It is worth more than money," Perez said.
He uses his challenges to connect with people.
"I was homeless, and how I get out of that moment in life and how to use that moment to help others. The work you do out there, you do it because you want to make a difference out there. Not the recognition. The satisfaction of helping someone do better and know you did your part for that to happen is better than a paycheck," Perez said. "It is not about power. It is not about influence. It is about service."
Brenton, owner and broker of Brenton Realty Group, said "I wanted to be a back up dancer for Tina Turner. I didn't want to be the lead, I wanted to be in the back. But seriously I lived through the crash, when the whole country crashed. I went from steaks to hotdogs in one year. I had to reinvent myself from six digits down to two. My chapter is called 'Resilience,'" Brenton said.
Winston said she was very happy the way it all came together and that she was honored to be a part of telling the empowering stories.
The book can be purchased online at amazon.com/Leadership-Journey-Culture-Savannah-Winston-ebook/dp/B0DJH39M24.

title: Criminal Records on Cambridge City Council: Mayoral Candidates Give Their Takes
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Criminal records on Cambridge City Council: mayoral candidates give their takes

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a Cambridge candidate forum conducted by the League of Women Voters on Oct. 5, the city's three mayoral candidates gave their takes on whether a criminal record should disqualify someone from being a mayor or commissioner in Cambridge.The question is one of relevance to the city's mayoral election, specifically.
Mayoral candidate Andrew Bradshaw, who served as Cambridge's mayor in 2021, resigned from the position in January 2022 after being charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. He later pleaded guilty to five of those counts.
Now that the mayoral term — which he started but did not finish — is ending, Bradshaw is running for mayor again in the city's Oct. 19 election.
Mayoral candidate and Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas has also faced legal issues. In 2022, she was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
During the forum, mayoral candidate La-Shon Banks-Foster, who is running against Bradshaw and Cephas, said the answer to whether a criminal record should disqualify someone from being on the City Council is not a yes or no question. She said it depends on the crime, whether that person has been rehabilitated and what steps they've taken since.
Cephas said the question should be up to the voters. She added that one of a mayor's responsibilities is to meet with different people.
"Are they going to feel comfortable being in a photograph with someone that's known for a nation-wide headline that was, not only embarrassing to that person, but the victim and also that community that person represented?" she said.
Bradshaw said he felt the question was directed toward him. He said that in a city where many people have made mistakes, a large portion of the population shouldn't be disqualified from serving on the City Council because of the "errors of their past."
"And likewise, when people have overcome the failures that they've made, when they can move forward in their lives, we shouldn't turn away from the people that have talent and ability to contribute to a community," he said.
In response to Cephas' comments, Bradshaw said his convictions were withdrawn and removed by the state and his probation has been abated.
According to court documents, in November 2023, Judge Thomas G. Ross ordered that the judgements of guilt for Bradshaw's five counts of distributing revenge porn be stricken and Bradshaw be granted probation before judgement.
In an interview with the Star Democrat on Oct. 8, Bradshaw said he didn't want to go into detail on how this came about, but it was a decision made by his attorneys, the Office of the state Prosecutor and Ross.
A court document filed in June said Bradshaw's probation abatement date — the end to active supervision of the defendant — was May 13.

title: Oxford Commissioners Repeal and Replace Meeting Procedures Resolution
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners repeal and replace meeting procedures resolution

 October 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 360
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — After a workshop last week and additional discussion at a town meeting Tuesday, the Commissioners of Oxford have come to an agreement on how to amend the wording of a recently passed resolution establishing town meeting procedures.The original resolution, passed Sept. 24, establishes general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings, including when and for how long public commenters can speak. When Commission President Norm Bell introduced the resolution in early September, he said it was developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at a previous town meeting in August.
At the town meeting on Sept. 24, some residents expressed concerns with the resolution's limitations on public comment, as well as the way in which the resolution was passed.
On Tuesday, the commissioners unanimously voted to repeal and replace the current resolution with one that adjusts the wording regarding public comment. Specifically, it states that commissioners shall invite public questions and comments before a vote is taken on a resolution or an ordinance.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the commissioners also would have the discretion to open up other agenda items for public comment. She said that because ordinances already require public hearings, this resolution would essentially add the requirement of holding public comment before voting on resolutions.
One of the main discussions during a workshop Oct. 2 was whether the resolution should say that commissioners "may" invite public comment on agenda items or "shall" invite public comment on agenda items. The former would give commissioners discretion on which items should be opened up for public comment.
Toward the end of the workshop, the commissioners agreed to use "shall" instead of "may" in a new draft resolution, which they could vote on following discussion at the town meeting Tuesday.
The vote to repeal and replace the resolution on Tuesday garnered applause from residents in the audience.
Before the commissioners came to a decision, they heard from residents. The majority of residents who spoke shared that they think "shall" should be used.
Resident Jane McCarthy said she didn't think the commissioners had the right to use the word "may" in the resolution.
"We are the people," she said. "We are the taxpayers in this town."

Cambridge City Council approves tax abatement for Ocean Gateway property

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council unanimously voted to approve a property tax abatement for a property tucked between Peking House Restaurant and Advance Auto Parts on Ocean Gateway at a meeting on Oct. 7.During the council meeting, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said this property, located at 2721 Ocean Gateway, is the site of an old gas station that hasn't been operational for more than a decade. Currently on the site, there is a concrete block building, which was once the gas station storefront.
According to an Oct. 4 memo from Hesson to City Council, the vacant and underutilized property tax abatement program was created in Cambridge in 2016 to incentivize development of vacant and underutilized properties in the city.
The abatement will only apply to the improved value of the property, not the original assessed value of the property.
In the memo, Hesson said the Ocean Gateway property, owned by Delmarva Real Estate Management Group LLC, qualifies for the vacant and underutilized property tax abatement. The owner wants to remove the building to take away liability.
"If he removes the building now, without approval, the property will not be eligible for the program," Hesson said in the memo.
At the meeting, Hesson asked for approval of the property tax abatement. According to the memo, the abatement would be applied once a new commercial building has been built. There would be a "sunset" of June 2026 on the abatement in the case that no improvement has been made at the property.
"We do want to incentivize it, but we also want to incentivize it now," Hesson said.
After Hesson spoke, multiple commissioners said they were happy to see the abatement program used.
"That is prime real estate because it is right there on 50," Commission President Lajan Cephas said. "So thank you for using this resource."

title: Talbot County Nonprofit Says Heating Cost 'Crisis' Looms Amid Gaps in Funding
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County nonprofit says heating cost 'crisis' looms amid gaps in funding

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Representatives from the Neighborhood Service Center spoke during an Easton Town Council meeting Monday evening, requesting funding from the town for what's been deemed a potential heating cost "crisis" this winter.The nonprofit assists families in Talbot County with heating costs during cooler weather. Marilyn Neal, executive director of the Neighborhood Service Center, told council members that a "drastic change" in funding will limit the assistance provided by the organization to residents in the form of kerosene, heating oil, propane and electric.
"I fear we are going to have a crisis," Neal said. " … I'm worried that our seniors and some low-income individuals in Talbot County, as well as the town of Easton, may not be able to keep warm this winter, and it keeps me up at night."
Neal said the nonprofit provides financial assistance to local residents and is then reimbursed by the Maryland Energy Assistance Program, a state program under the Department of Housing and Community Development that is federally funded.
Cardeaner Robinson, the Maryland Energy Assistance Program director, said the number of customers for the energy assistance program statewide has doubled. She said Gov. Wes Moore "wanted to see more people use the program," which led to changes in eligibility requirements.
Increased eligibility and funding cuts for the Maryland Energy Assistance Program will impact how much financial assistance the Neighborhood Service Center can provide to county residents, Neal and Robinson said.
"It sounds like really, really bad policy making and planning on the part of the state," Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said.
Neal said it happens "with every administration," but that she's "not seen a crisis as large" as what may come this winter.
Neal asked for "at least $50,000" from the town to aid the center's energy assistance efforts. Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis and Montgomery each asked for Neal to bring a breakdown of how many Easton residents are served by those efforts.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello asked that the council and town employees take a look at where the money may come from if the town contributes to the Neighborhood Service Center's program.
Following the presentation and questions from councilmembers, Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council will put follow-up questions together requesting further information and details from the Neighborhood Service Center.
"I don't see how our seniors living on a fixed income will be able to sustain," Neal said. "Normally, the subsidy would take them through the winter. Well this year, it won't fill their propane tanks up, it won't give them a full tank of kerosene.
"And the Neighborhood Service Center has expended 85% of our funding. … By December, all the funding will be gone."

title: Changes Made to St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Changes made to St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 534
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The Commissioners of St. Michaels have made changes to the controversial Tourism Advisory Board, including additional members and updated language.According to Commissioner David Wojciechowski at a Wednesday meeting, the ordinance establishing the board was "re-drafted" to take into consideration comments from the commissioners and the public.
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during the town election last May. Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were all later elected as commissioners, said during their campaigns that they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
During an August commission meeting, the proposed tourism board was met with pushback from residents, who raised an array of concerns about potential conflicts of interest and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
A major change to the ordinance Wojciechowski pointed out was a change in language. For the purpose of the board, language was changed to "manage, promote and stabilize the economic health of the town's tourism economy."
"One of the objectives here is to stabilize tourism, to make it to the right size, if you will. Not too large for the town, not too small, but to manage tourism doesn't get out of hand," Wojciechowski said.
Additionally, there were changes to the amount of members on the board. Originally, the board would comprise seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership would include a resident not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
There was outcry by residents over the low number of residents on the board. Now membership has been changed to include two town residents.
Public CommentDuring public comment, resident Daniel Spiegel, who in the past has shared concerns over the establishment of the tourism board, said he and other residents have marked issues with what he describes as a "seriously flawed ordinance."
Spiegel's main concerns involved potential conflicts of interest and the town's level of involvement in private business operations and gathering data. He stressed there are already small business associations, such as the lodging association, which could gather the necessary information that the tourism board would gather.
According to Spiegel, by creating a government board rather than an advisory board outside of the town's legal boundaries, it will create conflict of interests where the business owners on the board could propose budgetary expenditures that could directly benefit them.
"There's nothing wrong with promoting tourism," Spiegel said. "The question is whether the town wants to be deeply engaged in the way that this ordinance is. Which for a town of (this) size, is really surprising. We're not a county, we're not a big city, we're a small town, and I think you will regret that you've set it up this way."
After public comment, the board unanimously approved moving the ordinance toward a public hearing. The hearing will be held on Nov. 13.

title: Idlewild Park's Cherished Tile Wall to Remain Up Until the Spring
author: Konner Metz
content:
Idlewild Park's cherished tile wall to remain up until the spring

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 572
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Easton's plans to tear down an Idlewild Park walkway adorned with hand-painted tiles has brought back cherished memories for many Easton residents.Like many others, Easton resident Michael McCormack remembers painting his tile around 17 years ago. He was eight years old, and it included trees and grass, which fit with his then-involvement in Boy Scouts and camping outdoors.
His tile is one of hundreds that make up a winding path next to the playground at Idlewild Park — some include handprints, names or school classes. While the tiles remain, they are weathered and damaged from the time that's passed.
After the town initially announced on Sept. 25 that the tile walkway would be taken down in October, many town residents asked to retrieve their tiles, with others suggesting a new community art project go in its place.
The town has said the tiles have too much wear and tear to be retrieved without damaging the wall entirely. But the outpouring of community input led town officials to delay the removal of the tiles to the spring of 2025.
"It has been truly heartwarming to see all of the community response regarding the tile wall at Idlewild Park," the town wrote in a Facebook post on Sept. 27. " … Hopefully this way everyone who wishes to visit will have a little more time to make the trip and take photos before the tiles are gone."
McCormack said he's reconnected with old friends in recent weeks after going to Idlewild Park to look at the tiles.
"You bring back these memories that aren't necessarily attached to the tile, but they're attached to the person," McCormack said. "Just seeing their name and seeing what they did makes you laugh."
Mayor Megan Cook was a driving force behind Idlewild Park's construction in 2006. As co-chairman of Project Idlewild at the time, Cook helped spearhead a community-led effort to fund and build the park that opened in the summer of 2007.
"The whole thing from start to finish was a massive undertaking with so many volunteers," Cook said, "and then so many people came to build it over a two-week period."
Cook said hundreds of people showed up to help construct the park. There was even a dedicated team in charge of watching over the kids so parents could come chip in.
The hand-painted tiles cemented the park as a community-driven project, the mayor said.
"The hope had always been that, as a community project, … there would always be that link back in community," Cook said.
She said the town is considering ideas to incorporate the tiles into a new design once the tile wall is taken down. The town's Parks & Recreation department is "all ears" on ideas from residents, it said in a Facebook post.
McCormack hopes to see the piece of Easton history commemorated, even if all of the tiles cannot be saved.
"It would be cool to save the ones they can," McCormack said. "People my age are starting to have kids, so it'd almost be cool to have their kids paint it. And then you could connect two generations together out there."
"You can see the weather, you can see the time has taken its toll on those things for sure," he said. "So you can see why they need to be taken down. It's just one of those things that I don't think people in the town really appreciated until they realized it was going to be gone."

title: Let's Let County Election Officials Do Their Job
author: Staff Writer
content:
Let's let county election officials do their job

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 730
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Board of Elections received some high-level backing — and vindication — this week. The Maryland attorney general and the state administrator of elections both backed the work and processes used to ensure fair elections in the county.Recently local election officials must have felt they were under siege. First a county council member called for the County Council to send a letter to the elections board reminding Election Director Tammy Stafford and the elections board to follow state law.
Days later county Sheriff Joe Gamble sent the board a letter strongly urging them to follow state law.
This comes against a continuing drumbeat of challenges by Talbot County residents that has been ongoing for most of this year.
The word from on high: Back off, there is nothing being done that violates state law.
Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown wrote a letter to Gamble detailing the "limited role of local law enforcement, including our sheriff's office in the electoral process."
The letter from Brown was read aloud by Stafford during an Oct. 7 Board of Elections special meeting.
Although the letter is not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said he hopes the letter is helpful in setting forth the roles of law enforcement officers during elections.
The letter is the latest salvo on the topic of sometimes tense back-and-forth between the Talbot County Board of Elections, the Talbot County sheriff and local elected officials in recent weeks.
In Brown's letter, he addresses the role of law enforcement, security, authority on election law violations and concerns involving election judges.
"State law does, specifies and carefully circumscribes the authority of local law enforcement and polling places while conferring primary responsibility for election law enforcement on other agencies," Brown said. "I understand that local law enforcement agencies do provide assistance to local boards of elections in some jurisdictions, including deploying personnel to provide security and transporting election materials. But importantly, this is done at the request and under the direction of the local Board of Elections itself."
Gamble's letter came in the midst of intense discussions centering concerns over the partisan breakdown of election judges ahead of the Nov. 5 General Election.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 2-3 vote.
In his letter, Brown emphasized state law "does not require equality in the total number of judges" recruited and trained by the local Board of Elections.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown said.
Toward the end of Brown's letter, he advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to "closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there."
The week prior, Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, released a statement regarding the assignment of election judges. In it, he emphasized that Maryland voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," DeMarinis wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections. The party affiliation of an election judge does not stop them from casting their ballots or disenfranchise a voter. And to say otherwise is disingenuous."
DeMarinis noted in his statement the strict rules election judges must follow, binding them "to conduct the election in a nonpartisan manner and fashion."
With these statements of support by top level state officials, we hope that the seemingly partisan attacks on the integrity of Talbot County elections can end. County election officials have a big job ahead of them — ensuring the smooth and secure election ahead on Nov. 5. Let's let them do their job.

title: More Information on Dorchester Charter Amendments
author: Stephen Rideout
content:
More information on Dorchester charter amendments

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Stephen Rideout | Section: Columns 
 
 618
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last time I wrote about the first three proposed Charter Amendments that are on the ballot in Dorchester County this November. Two of the next three are similar and one has more background information required to help you understand the reason for it.Question D seeks to clarify certain of the responsibilities of the county manager including the day-to-day operation of county government and establishing procedures for certain vacancies. This requires some explanation.
When the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government began to look at the day-to-day management of county government, we found a couple of things. Every employee was an "at will" employee, and anyone could be terminated upon a vote of three members of the council for whatever reasons they might have, no matter how long the person had worked for the county.
We also found that at times some of the council members were telling the staff what to do and how to do it. The county manager position went for months without any effort by the council to find a replacement.
The Charter Commission did significant work on this proposed amendment to help ensure that there was a more timely transition when a county manager left or was terminated, allowed for the appointment of an assistant county manager subject to funding, allowed for studies to be done when appropriate, established a time limitation for searches for a replacement of the county manager, and most importantly established that the county manager is responsible for the day-to-day operations of county government and that the council is to deal with the administrative and departmental services through the county manager and not through direct orders to staff members.
Adding the above language to the existing language that "all departments, agencies, and offices of the Government shall be subject to the direction, supervision, and control of the County Manager under the authority of the Council…" ensures that the employees work with and under the authority of the county manager and that he or she is subject to the direction and authority of the County Council.
Of all of the proposed amendments, the passage of this one will help to ensure a more efficient and effective working environment that will benefit the entire county and its residents.
With Question E, the proposed change removes the requirement that the director of finance be a resident of Dorchester County. As this is a particularly important job in county government and finding the best person can be a challenge and restricting the council in where the finance director can live simply limits their ability to find the most qualified person. What is true about where the county manager lives is also true for the finance director.
The current County Council has informally addressed the final Question F. When the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government saw what challenges people faced with attending the council meetings in person, we urged that the meetings go on the internet so that people could watch government at work and be able to communicate about the meetings without having to be there in person. The prior council rejected these requests at first and finally agreed to them. Having the meetings on Town Hall Streams benefited everyone.
The language of this Charter Amendment simply puts it in the law that the current and all future councils shall ensure the transparency of the county government by having the ability of the public to attend meetings in person or virtually and have a clear understanding of their right to access to public records.
The vote in November for all of these questions should all be "yes" so that the running of county government is more transparent and more efficient and effective for the benefit of all of the citizens of Dorchester County.

title: Easton Airport Day a Roaring Success
author: Tom McCall
content:
Easton Airport Day a roaring success

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News

 EASTON — The 14th annual Easton Airport Day drew hundreds on a blue-skied fall day, Oct. 12, to see the roaring spectacle of WW II planes, Naval Academy parachute jumpers and tidily kept up biplanes.The keynote speaker was Gustavus McLeod, the executive director of the Glenn L. Martin Maryland Aviation Museum.
"Look up into this cloudless sky. It is like you can see forever," McLeod said.
Event attendees were allowed to explore some of the aircraft on the tarmac, like the Maryland State medevac helicopter Trooper 6. Kids put on flight helmets, and aviation enthusiasts took the opportunity to come aboard.
Trooper 6 does more than carry the sick and injured. The team also does search and rescue missions and can work with their camera to assist with police chases. The camera is so strong that it can identify what kind of beer you are drinking from a mile and a half away said Cpl. Jeff Kelly.
"It is a lot of fun just to talk to people. We get to surprise people because a lot of people don't know what we do. If you put in a call for help, there is no charge for that. The citizens of Maryland have decided that we collectively have to pay for this," Kelly said.
For $7, attendees could climb into the Spirit of Freedom, which flew in the 1949 Berlin Airlift and gave Franklin D. Roosevelt a ride.
When planes got into formation and buzzed overhead, everybody looked up and shaded their eyes from the sun.
The food tents were bustling with the smell of bacon and funnel cakes.
Congressman Andy Harris addressed the crowd.
"The airport is such an important part of the economy and this runway extension project is going to keep us the premier general aviation airport in the whole region," Harris said.
Micah Risher, the Easton Airport manager, seemed to be enjoying the festivities, though pulling this show together is logistical feat.
"We have been planning this for about a year," he said. "Every event is a little different. We have so many elements to make it special, like the paratroopers and seeing Placid Lassy taking off and lead the mass formation. When engines start and for the next 90 minutes, it is going to be an amazing display. This is a celebration of our history. Our airport has been here since 1942."
There is a connection between these warbirds and the airport, which was built to support the war, he said.
The climax of the event was the rubber chicken drop contest. Flying planes tried to hit the target of a truck on the airfield with rubber chickens.
There were loudspeakers throughout the event that broadcasted both PSAs and hitmakers like Eric Clapton.
This perfect fall day brought out families. There were lots of kids, some with noise-canceling headphones, pretending to be airplanes while their parents watched.
"There are lot of beautiful airplanes out and a lot great things to look at," said Sarah Andrew. She was with her husband and 4-year-old daughter.

title: Property Owners Learn About Potential Compensation for Rails to Trails
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Property owners learn about potential compensation for Rails to Trails

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLock — Landowners with property adjacent to future Rails to Trails projects may be entitled to compensation, according to attorneys from Missouri-based law firm Lewis Rice.The law firm is representing about a dozen Mid-Shore residents who have signed onto a lawsuit seeking compensation from the federal government for potential trail projects.
A handful of people sat in the Unity-Washington United Methodist Church on the evening of Oct. 14 to learn about what this effort looks like in Dorchester County.
The county is in the process of obtaining the rights of way for rail lines from Preston to Hurlock and Linkwood to Cambridge. When the state grants them these rights of way, the county will be able to implement Rails to Trails on those pathways.
In an interview Tuesday, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the county has no immediate plans to implement Rails to Trails in those places. He said the county hasn't even started to discuss implementation and would need to seek public input first.
"It would be a community process," he said. "And again, we don't have any money to do anything like that. So it's nothing that's going to happen in the near future."
But during the event at Unity-Washington United Methodist Church, attorneys gave a presentation to inform landowners with property adjacent to the rail lines about potential compensation from the federal government.
Attorney Meghan Largent led the presentation, which detailed the process of making a claim. She said neither the government, nor the railroads, nor the trail groups involved are required to notify landowners when a certificate of interim trail use is issued by the Surface Transportation Board.
"We have challenged that," Largent said. "What the courts have found is that publishing it in the federal register is effective notice."
Largent said landowners usually don't know what's happening or what their legal rights are until lawyers show up.
Pfeffer said in an interview that in this particular situation, the state had made notice of the easements, but he was unsure of the exact status. He said his understanding is that the state published a press release and then law firms directly contacted property owners of land adjoining the rail lines.
Largent said that once the certificate of interim trail use was issued on Aug. 30 for this potential project, it triggered a six-year statute of limitations. This means property owners have six years to file a claim for compensation. She said that although six years seems like a long time, it can sneak up quickly.
Largent said that within a week of the issuance of the certificate, Lewis Rice filed a lawsuit seeking this compensation for residents. The U.S. Department of Justice has 60 days from the filing of the lawsuit to answer.
Lewis Rice is currently representing about a dozen local property owners, but there are more than 50 property owners who they believe have a good claim. Largent said they have sent mail to property owners who they believe will be successful in receiving a claim.
"We do have to follow the solicitation rules in the state, which require us to market as an advertisement," she said in an interview. "So, whether everybody got that information, I can't confirm, but we certainly sent it."
Currently, Lewis Rice can still add landowners to the lawsuit. Largent said she doesn't have an exact date that this period of adding landowners will end. She said that if property owners don't file a claim, they won't be compensated.
"It's not a class action," she said. "Government's not going to reach out to them and offer them money."
After the presentation, one resident said he appreciated the attorneys reaching out because neither the federal government nor county government notified him of the turning over of rights of way.
Largent said she wanted to make it clear that Lewis Rice wasn't there to advocate for or against the trail. She said compensation to property owners doesn't mean less funding for the trail.
"We might have clients that love the trail," she said. "We might have clients that really dislike the idea of a trail. Some that are ambivalent. But that's not what we're here to do. They'll be hosting the trail through their property, and they should be compensated."

title: Republicans Continue to Push Talbot Board of Elections on Election Judge Breakdown
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Republicans continue to push Talbot Board of Elections on election judge breakdown

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 775
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — County Republicans continued to push the Talbot County Board of Elections to equal its selection of election judges during the board's monthly meeting on Wednesday morning.The breakdown by party was 62 Democratic judges, 50 Republican judges and 11 unaffiliated judges in September, according to Election Director Tammy Stafford. Local officials have indicated at meetings that the number of judges for each party may now be closer to equal, but this has not been confirmed by the Board of Elections.
Election officials have said the makeup is "fluid" and will change up until Election Day. During Wednesday's meeting, Stafford said "judges are always needed" and that her office "continuously" accepts interest forms.
According to Sept. 18 meeting minutes read aloud Wednesday, staffing for the election began in June of 2023. Training for those who filled out interest forms began in early 2024.
In the last month, concerns have circulated regarding a party imbalance of election judges, or those who staff polling places on Election Day.
Local officials, including Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp, have cited that the board is not in compliance with state law.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
These concerns led to a flurry of responses from state agencies emphasizing the security of the electoral process. In an Oct. 2 statement responding to a letter sent by Gamble to the Talbot Board of Elections, State Board of Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis said voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
Attorney General Anthony Brown weighed in as well, writing a letter to Gamble on Oct. 7.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown wrote.
Stafford stated at the Sept. 18 meeting that the training for election judges can no longer be done after Oct. 8 since the room used for training is also used for canvassing.
During Wednesday's public comment, Gary Judy, a member of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, said he's heard from Republicans who applied to be an election judge but were not told there are no vacancies for this year's general election. He said the fact that the board did not achieve exact party balance is "extremely alarming to Talbot County voters."
"We decided to keep close track on it this year," Judy said, "and can confirm that there were more than enough Republicans who signed up to be election judges to fill the available Republican positions of the equal representation required by Maryland election law."
On Wednesday, Judy provided board members with copies of a letter written by the Maryland Republican Party addressing election judge concerns in Talbot County. Adam Wood, executive director of the Maryland Republican Party, later told the Star Democrat that the letter was a "draft" letter and had not been sent to the state board.
Shari Wilcoxon, also a member of the Republican central committee, spoke during public comment, asking the board to ensure "parity" of election judges.
"I think that it is an actual embarrassment that this board is allowing the executive director free rein to break the law," Wilcoxon said. "It is your duty to hold her feet to the fire, and that she does what is Maryland law."
Wilcoxon questioned why election judge applications were denied in February and March.
"February and March had to do with the primary," Stafford responded. "Let's be specific here. That was the primary. Those were the first people who were contacted for the general (election)."
This led to tense back-and-forth between Wilcoxon and Stafford.
Board President Susan MacKinnon stepped in, asking Wilcoxon to stop speaking.
"You have had the opportunity to speak, you are now being disruptive," MacKinnon said to Wilcoxon. "You are being disruptive, and if you continue being disruptive, I will call a recess and have you removed."
Wednesday's meeting was the board's last regularly scheduled meeting before the election Nov. 5. During Stafford's report to the board, she said "logic and accuracy testing on the electronic equipment was completed" on Sept. 16. The Board of Elections will have its logic and accuracy testing documentation available for public inspection Friday at 10 a.m. at 215 Bay Street in Easton.

title: Three National Races Top the Ballot in Maryland
author: Tom McCall
content:
Three national races top the ballot in Maryland

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot, Caroline and Dorchester voters are gearing up to elect their next president, senator and congressman on Nov. 5.Republican Donald Trump and Democrat Kamala Harris are on the top of the ticket as they run for president. There are several others on the presidential ballot including Jill Stein and Robert Kennedy, Jr. (although he dropped out of the race, he is still on the ballot).
For U.S. senator there is Democrat Angela Alsobrooks and Republican Larry Hogan. Running for Congress in District 1 are Republican Andy Harris, Democrat Blane Miller III and Libertarian Joshua W. O'Brien.
For the Appellate Court of Maryland Stephen H. Kehoe is on the ballot.
There are different ways to vote.
Registered voters can vote by mail-in ballot if they do not want to go to an early voting center. You can request an early voter mail-in ballot if you have a Maryland driver's license or a MVA issued ID card. There is a mail-in ballot request form on the Maryland Board of Elections website.
Anyone who is registered to vote can vote during early voting.
The polling station for Talbot is Easton Fire Hall at 315 Aurora Park Drive in Easton. If you are in Dorchester, go to the Dorchester Election Office at 1000 Goodwill Avenue, Cambridge. Caroline County's station is at the Health and Public Services Building 403 S. Seventh St. Room 112, Denton.
You can register to vote if you are a U.S. citizen, a Maryland resident and at least 16 years old. You can register to vote Election Day at your local polling place.
These voters can satisfy the identification requirement by providing one of the following:
The voter's driver's license number, MVA ID card number or the last four digits of the voter's Social Security number, and election officials will attempt to verify this information with MVA or the Social Security Administration.A copy of a current and valid photo identification (Maryland driver's license, MVA ID card, student or employee photo ID card, military ID card, passport or any other state or federal government issued ID card).A copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or other government document that shows the voter's name and address.
Voting is a civic duty and a relatively easy one to participate in. Most voters are on the voter list in their county. After voting you can show off your "I Voted" sticker.

title: Hogan Visits Port Street
author: Tom McCall
content:
Hogan Visits Port Street

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 358
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Port Street got a distinguished visitor at the Neighborhood Service Center. Former Gov. Larry Hogan is running for the open U.S. Senate seat and stopped in Easton Friday to talk with people at the service center.He visited the facility on 126 Port Street and asked questions.
The Responsible Father Initiative, founded by Corey Pack and co-facilitated by Lou Dorsey, is an outreach program to help men become better fathers. It is a nonprofit and is all confidential. It provides food, clothing and first month's rent to people in need. These men gave Hogan the tour of the center.
Pack spoke to the governor about what they teach.
"We go over what is called the three E's. Emotion, energy and expression. And we talk about effective listening skills," Pack said. "We run through the 7/38/55 rule. 7% of the way we communicate is verbally. 38% is with our tone and 55% is with our body language."
The governor listened closely.
"I did not realize that," Hogan said. "That is an important lesson for me to learn."
He listened to more about the program.
"We try to develop more nurturing and caring fathers in this program. Most of the guys grew up in a home without a father. Some have been incarcerated with no contact with their children. It is great for them to see their children and establish a relationship with their children," Dorsey said.
Hogan recognized that a lot of men needed these services and saluted their dedication to helping these men flourish.
"It sounds like you guys are doing really important work here," Hogan said.
One of the Neighborhood Service Center workers asked Hogan to run for president. He smiled.
Hogan toured spaces intended for children. Then he went into the kitchen and in another room saw where they store clothes to give away.
At the end of tour, he was give two T-shirts and a coffee mug that touted the Neighborhood Service Center.
After his visit he stopped to do an interview in the parking lot. Hogan said his campaign is focused on the economy and crime.
"We are meeting voters every day," he said. "The people of Maryland know me after eight years of being governor."

title: Talbot not alone facing criticism on elections
author: CALEY FOX SHANNON and MORGAN LEASON Capital News Service
content:
Talbot not alone facing criticism on elections

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CALEY FOX SHANNON and MORGAN LEASON Capital News Service | Section: Local News 
 
 1225
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — As local election boards work around the clock to recruit and train workers before early voting starts next week, some Maryland counties are facing pressure to hire more Republican election judges.Elections officials across the state told Capital News Service they are still working through the challenge of hiring an equal number of Republican and Democratic election judges, who administer the vote and then count ballots.
"Parity is something we always aspire to," David Garreis, Anne Arundel County election director, told CNS. "But frequently what you're gonna find is that the participation rates between the parties are very different."
By Maryland law, local boards of elections must make every effort to staff polling places with an equal number of judges who are registered Democrats and Republicans. That's what Garreis and other local election officials tell CNS they are working on now.
But officials in some counties aren't offering their recruitment numbers or providing updates to the public — even in the face of concerns from local Republicans who say they'd like to volunteer but can't seem to get a foot in the door.
"I think they're not being fair with me, and they're not being transparent about the situation," said Shawn Poulson, a Kent County Republican and former local party official who says his application to serve as a judge was sidelined by his local board.
CNS spoke with non-partisan election officials, party leaders and would-be Republican judges in multiple counties to understand this issue, which has elevated the conversation about election integrity in Maryland.
TALBOT COUNTYIn an Oct. 1 letter to the local board of elections, Talbot County Sheriff Joseph Gamble said he had received 25 complaints from residents over the uneven party distribution of election judges.
Among those complaints, Gamble said, were several Republicans who wanted to serve but were instead placed on standby and told that there were no vacancies at the time. Elections aren't under Gamble's purview as sheriff, but he told CNS he was weighing in due to the high volume of complaints he had received.
Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, quickly tried to reassure the public in a press release following Gamble's letter.
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," he wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections."
The head of the local board said the numbers are getting pretty close to even.
Tammy Stafford — Election Director, Talbot County Board of Elections, Julie Ervin — Chair, Talbot County Board of Elections, and other members are working on it.
Tammy Stafford, Talbot County's election director, told CNS this week that she has hired 124 election judges, including 61 Democrats, 53 Republicans and 10 unaffiliated judges. She emphasized that these numbers are subject to change.
Stafford said that 106 of the election judges in her county are returning after having worked in the primary. She said her office continues to take applications from interested voters, but as of now, the 10 polling places across Talbot County are fully staffed.
KENT COUNTYPoulson, 47, of Worton, told CNS that he applied to be a Republican election judge in Kent County and was placed on a standby list instead of being assigned to a polling place.
Poulson previously served as an election judge and was chair of the Kent County Republican Central Committee. After stepping down from the committee this spring, Poulson said he immediately applied to be an election judge. He said he wanted to be a chief judge — one of the two judges who run a polling place and manage other judges.
Instead, Poulson was disappointed to receive a letter last month stating he was assigned as a standby judge. Poulson said he is not aware of an update from Kent County Election Director Cheemoandia Blake.
Blake declined to speak with CNS or provide an update on the number of election judges hired in Kent County by party.
ANNE ARUNDEL COUNTYGarreis said his team is working tirelessly to recruit judges through events at churches and schools as well as by direct mail and social media. These efforts include partnership with both the Democratic and Republican Central Committees in Anne Arundel County.
"With our election judges, usually the first qualification is, do you have a pulse?" Garreis said. "Because it's usually very hard to find election judges. The only reason that we would really turn someone away is if they are at a precinct, and we've already filled all the spots at the precinct."
Garreis said he has hired more than 2,100 judges so far and needs to hire roughly 400 more. Of those judges, more than half are Democrats, just over a quarter are Republicans, and the rest are unaffiliated.
Registered voters need to attend a three-hour training session in person before they can serve as an election judge.
CALVERT COUNTYKristen Scott, deputy elections administrator in Calvert County, told CNS she has recruited 368 election judges: 181 Democrats, 140 Republicans and 47 unaffiliated. She said the uneven party split should not be of concern to voters.
"The one thing that we really do stress to our election judges is that this is a nonpartisan position," Scott said. "When you're in that polling place, there's no political talk. It's very nonpartisan, and you're there to serve the voter, whatever party it is."
Like Garreis, Scott said she doesn't immediately turn away judges but places them on a standby list. In the the event that someone cannot serve, she can replace those individuals with Republicans on standby. She said she prioritizes parity on a precinct level.
Scott said that voters can also be poll watchers. Watchers, sometimes called "challengers," register with their party and are approved to be onsite at precincts to watch election judges. Watchers are unpaid and do not interact with voters or make decisions regarding the vote, but they can report misconduct or other concerns.
CECIL COUNTYGary Holmes, Cecil County's election director, told CNS he has fully staffed his precincts, hiring approximately 150 Republicans, 140 Democrats and 46 judges who are unaffiliated or third-party.
Although President Joe Biden won Maryland in the 2020 general election, voters in Cecil County overwhelmingly favored Donald Trump.
Holmes said that when he attends training sessions, he tells prospective election judges, "You're not here to be political. You're not here to express an opinion."
Holmes said that his team is proactively fighting misinformation about the election, sharing proper links through social media and directing voters to the state's election rumor-tracking page.
Holmes said that the state's rigorous system of checks and balances ensures that the vote is secure.
"We don't care who you vote for as long as you get the chance to vote, and we can assure you that we're very particular about how these records are being kept," he said.
MONTGOMERY COUNTYGilberto Zelaya, public relations officer at the Montgomery County Board of Elections, told CNS that he couldn't say how parity is shaping up between Democrats and Republicans because his team is still in the thick of recruiting.
To hire between 3,500 and 4,000 election judges, Zelaya said, his team holds an average of 500 events annually. Zelaya said he works closely with both parties and has held at least four meet-and-greet events this year at the local GOP office in Rockville.
Stacey Sauter, vice chair of the Montgomery County GOP, also plays a role in voter education and election judge recruitment.
"It's an overwhelming task for the Board of Elections," Sauter told CNS. "And what I have witnessed so far is what they do is very fair and balanced, but they are the apparatus. You cannot control what happens with the people when they go to work at the polls."
