title: After Months of Debate, St. Michaels Tourism Board Is Approved
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
After months of debate, St. Michaels Tourism Board is approved

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of heated discussions, revisions and compromises, the St. Michaels Tourism Board was unanimously approved by commissioners on Wednesday evening.According to Commissioner David Wojciechowski, the board will help provide additional resources in case funds from different avenues, including federal funds, are reduced after the election.
"It's a proactive measure to get ahead of the curve," Wojciechowski said. "A lot of things have happened in the past two weeks, we're counting on a lot of grant money coming into this town. There might be an administration in place right now that jeopardizes that grant money. We need to preserve and protect the revenue that's coming into the town."
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
According to the ordinance, the board will be composed of seven members including a mix of business types from the community and residents. The now approved board will recommend to commissions an annual promotional plan and budget that will manage tourism for the upcoming year.
The board would include representatives of several businesses including lodging, food and beverage, retail or service, marinas and nonprofits. The commissioners will appoint the members of the board and appoint one commissioner to participate as a non-voting member of the board.
The idea of a tourism board was suggested during the town election last May. Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were elected as commissioners, said during their campaigns that they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The tourism board faced pushback soon after its suggestion. During an August commission meeting, residents raised an array of concerns over potential conflicts of interest and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment on Wednesday evening, Daniel Spiegel, a member of Residents Association of St. Michaels, said he and other residents have four issues with the proposed ordinance.
Spiegel said the issues include a lack of adequate data and evidence, an underrepresentation of residents on the tourism board, a "dangerous and unwelcome built-in conflict of interest," and the potential for "managed tourism."
According to Spiegel, managed tourism is a "code word" for moving tourism "upscale," which he has based on previous discussions among commissioners with business representatives.
"I think it's inappropriate for a town, which basically says, 'Bring in the Porsches and keep out the buses and day trips,'" Spiegel said. "I don't think a government policy should be advocating this type of upscale tourism. I think it's not appropriate."
Following comments included a sentiment from residents that St. Michaels is more than a tourism town and a request to focus on already existing institutions.
Debbie Jackson said she is a longtime resident and the town has "always been businesses." Jackson addressed what she described as anti-business sentiment from the residents who said the town was more than just businesses.
According to Jackson, business owners have seen a decline in sales the past two years and support the establishment of a tourism board. Additionally, Jackson said there has been a "wedge" she had seen in town between residents and business owners.
"What prompted all the citizens of St. Michael's to feel this way? Or is this just one little group that's gotten together to hype this up?" Jackson said.
After comments from residents and business owners, Commissioner Alfred Mercier brought the matter up for a vote. The commissioners unanimously voted to approve the tourism board.

title: Delaware college town could lift longtime ban on tattoo, piercing shops
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware college town could lift longtime ban on tattoo, piercing shops

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Newark, Delaware's decades-long prohibition on tattoo and piercing shops may be coming to an end.A majority of city council members indicated earlier this month they would be in favor of allowing such businesses to open. A formal vote will be taken later.
The discussion was initiated by a request from Brittnie Lopez, the owner of B13 Tattoos, currently located on Miller Road in Wilmington.
After operating the shop for three years, Lopez wants to move it to Newark's Main Street, noting that many of her customers are down here. B13 Tattoos operates on an appointment-only basis, and Lopez is the only employee.
"As the City of Newark has continued to thrive and add new additions and create different opportunities, I think that this would be perfect for the center of Newark," Lopez told council members.
She is in negotiations to lease a vacant storefront at 170 E. Main St, the building that also houses Frolic, Oishii Sushi & Ramen and Occupy Studio.
"I recently found out you guys have no tattoo parlors in the City of Newark, and I would love to be first," Lopez said.
In order for her to do so, however, city council must add body art establishments — a term that encompasses both tattoo and piercing shops — to the zoning code. Currently, body art establishments are not listed as an allowable use in any of the zoning districts, meaning they are essentially banned from opening anywhere in city limits.
This is not the first time Newark has discussed legalizing body art establishments.
In 2016, a business owner wanted to open a piercing shop on Main Street, but he ultimately dropped his request before it came to city council for a vote.
The topic came up again in 2022 when councilmen Travis McDermott and Jason Lawhorn said they had heard from people who wanted to open tattoo shops in the city. Council directed staffers to research the issue, but it fell by the wayside amidst other priorities and was never formally considered.
Lawhorn said tattoos and the people who have them were once stereotyped, but he argued that times have changed.
"Maybe in the '50s or '60s, it seems like it was associated with biker clubs and prostitution and things like that," he said. "It has evolved well past that."
Lawhorn, who said he has four tattoos himself, cited statistics that show that more than 40 percent of adults under 50 have a tattoo.
Allowing tattoo shops will bring something new to downtown Newark, he said.
"I think it adds some flavor and some culture to the city," Lawhorn said. "We love our restaurants, but there's not a lot of grit to Main Street."
Councilwoman Dwendolyn Creecy noted that tattooing goes back centuries and is important in many cultures.
"I don't have a problem with this. Not one," Creecy said.
The only council members opposed were Corinth Ford and John Suchanec.
"I really don't think that this is a business that would be compatible or required on Main Street," Suchanec said. "I probably have to come up with 1,000 reasons why I'm taking this position, other than my personal preference not to have tattoo parlors on Main Street."
He also worried that University of Delaware students would upset their parents by getting tattoos.
"One big, big concern is students going home and showing off their tattoos," Suchanec said, speculating their parents would respond by saying, "you didn't ask my permission."
Ford said her concerns are about safety and sanitation.
"I really do not want this kind of business on Main Street," she said.
The planning department will now work on language to add body art establishments to the zoning code.
It's expected that the law will require a special-use permit, meaning that each business owner will need permission from city council to open a tattoo or piercing shop. The permit can be denied or revoked if council determines that the business would be a detriment to the community. The city is also considering requiring body art establishments to operate on an appointment-only basis to eliminate spur-of-the-moment tattoo decisions.
The planning commission will vote on the law Dec. 3, with a final vote by city council in February.

title: Never Forgotten: Veterans Point at Wells Grove Holds Ribbon Cutting
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Never forgotten: Veterans Point at Wells Grove holds ribbon cutting

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 KENT NARROWS — In Queen Anne's County, the National Anthem comes accompanied by the sound of bay waves lapping the pier and the cries of gulls overhead.With a clear sky, a light bay breeze wafted Old Glory at the Wells Grove pier where veterans and their community honored all who served with the dedication of Veterans Point at Wells Grove Nov. 11.
The project was spearheaded by the Queen Anne's County and Center for the Military and Veteran Family, operated by the Veteran and Military Support Alliance (VAMSA).
Through collaboration with community organizations and county departments and representatives, Veterans Points at Wells Grove serves as a physical manifestation of Queen Anne's County's dedication to the sacrifices made by the military and their families, Eric Johnson, VAMSA executive director, said.
The memorial stands not just a tribute to those who fought and fell, but all who have served and the sacrifices made by waiting families and supporting communities, said Master of Ceremonies Wes Guckert, United States Air Force and Vietnam veteran and VAMSA board of director member.
"This place now marked in the heart of Kent Narrows serves as a sanctuary where memories will be honored and history will be remembered," he said, noting the dedication ceremony as a "momentous occasion."
Guckert teared up as he shared the impetus behind the memorial sought to ensure the loneliness experienced by returning Vietnam veterans never happened again.
VAMSA believes in operationalizing "thank you for your service" and works to address needs along with their families, according to Johnson.
"For every veteran that comes in with a need, there is a member of that family that is also in crisis," he said.
For All Seasons serves as a strategic partner with VAMSA for mental health services and healing and Beth Anne Dorman, Executive Director, noted services are available to families as well as the community
Open access telehealth provides help for those who need it regardless of ability to pay and a new no wait list system provides services quickly, she said.
"We're able to say to veteran families, your service means something, you are valuable as a community member and we are here," she said.
Remembering that freedom and liberty are not free, keynote speaker USMC Lieutenant General (Retired) John Sattler urged honor, education and encouragement: honor those who have served, educate others on the sacrifices made, and encourage instilling core military values and carrying on an 'If not me then who?' mentality just as generations of veterans before have shown.
Bagpiper Randy Welch said it was always an esteemed honor to bring memories back into the lives of veterans as they listen to him play, whether they spring to their feet as their branch of the armed forces medley plays or when their eyes shine with pride with America the Beautiful.
Singing of the National Anthem was performed by United States Air Force TSgt. Megan May.
Having a local spot commemorating veterans is incredibly meaningful, according to veteran and VAMSA volunteer Sarah Stallings, "It shows the community cares."
VAMSA serves as an extended family to all veterans and their families and connects them with the resources they need. "We're all in this to help each other," she said.
The monument was built by Chester River Landscaping.
Funding was made possible by the W. Earl and Barbara Griffin Foundation and Chair Micheal Foster hoped for Veterans Point at Wells Cove to be the first of many projects together with VAMSA.
Invocation services were performed by Mark Hamilton, chaplain of Kent Island American Legion Post 278 and benediction services were provided by Rabbi Jason Goldstein of Beth Tfiloh Congregation of Baltimore.
At a lunch reception at the neighboring Bridges Restaurant, veterans reminisced and shared stories of service.
With community as the heart and soul, officials seek Veterans Point as a place of reflection and welcome families to use the space as a way to honor legacies and carry the spirit of endurance as it continues to inspire.
More information about VAMSA can be found at qacveteransupport.org.

title: Oxford Planning Commission Makes Decision That Could Affect Inn's Plans
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Planning Commission makes decision that could affect inn's plans

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 583
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Oxford Planning Commission has voted to not proceed with a draft ordinance that would allow apartments, townhomes and condos in the town's C-2 general commercial district by special exception.The Tuesday afternoon vote was of particular importance to David Snyder, owner of the Robert Morris Inn.
During a Planning Commission meeting on Oct. 1, Snyder requested a text amendment that would allow him to create luxury villas on the inn's property, which he believes will help make the business profitable. He said the inn has faced economic challenges since he took ownership this past year and he is losing over $30,000 every month.
At the outset of the Planning Commission meeting Tuesday, Commission Chair Lucy Garliauskas clarified the commission did not have any plans to take action on the draft ordinance. She said she asked for language to be drafted because the town's planning and zoning coordinator was leaving the position and the commission is currently working on a comprehensive long-range plan.
"But we are not dealing with anything related to any development or plans on Robert Morris Inn," she said.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the draft ordinance — if pushed through and approved by the Commissioners of Oxford — would make apartments, townhomes and condos "presumptively permitted" in the C-2 general commercial district unless the particular location of the special exception request "would have an adverse effect above and beyond what it would have at a C-2-zoned property anywhere else in town."
Garliauskas said drafting the legislation might be considered "putting the cart before the horse," but offered a good opportunity for clarification. "And I think at this point, I think we're all in agreement that we're not going to pursue this ordinance," she said.
Commission member Steve Mroczek made the motion to not pursue the ordinance, which passed unanimously.
"The sense that we've gotten over the last month is that this is not something the community is very interested in," he said. "And like it or not, we try to reflect what the community's interested in doing."
During the meeting, Snyder interjected a few times to ask if he could speak. He was told it was not a public hearing and he cannot call out in the middle of a meeting. However, at one point, he did express his concerns.
"I spoke with the town attorney at the outset, and I was told I would have an opportunity to speak on the record," he said. "And I also need to make a motion to recuse, and I need clarity on this because I was blindsided by this. This is not what I expected out of this process."
Ryan said Snyder had not submitted a formal application or petition to the Planning Commission. Snyder said he had reached out to Ryan and hadn't gotten calls back for "weeks now."
"It is not my job to represent you as a property owner," Ryan replied. "I represent the town."
Snyder said he would have submitted the appropriate paperwork if he had known about it.
"I'm in a real bind," he said.
Ryan said she had told him in a past conversation that he could submit a petition to the town for a text amendment or the Planning Commission could make a change on its own volition. Ryan said she also told him the Planning Commission process would be faster.
"And so you said you were going to pursue that," she said to Snyder. "But you were made aware of the petition. If you would like to submit one, you have the right to do so."

title: Cambridge City Council Approves Obligation of Remaining ARPA Funds
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge City Council approves obligation of remaining ARPA funds

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge is reallocating $1.39 million in non-obligated American Rescue Plan Act funds in order to meet an end-of-the-year deadline.The decision to reallocate the city's remaining ARPA funds was made during a Cambridge City Council meeting on Nov. 12. With this decision, those funds can be obligated, and the city will be protected from having to return that money to the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
According to a Nov. 6 memo to the City Council from Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman and Finance Director Perry Peregoy, the city received $12.08 million in COVID-19 relief funding through the American Rescue Plan Act. The memo states $10.68 million of those funds have been spent or obligated.
The remaining $1.39 million in funds has to be obligated — meaning there is an executed contract or issued purchase holder — by Dec. 31 to ensure no money has to be returned to the federal government.
At the meeting Nov. 12, Steckman talked about what the city recommends obligating those remaining funds to. He talked about three potential Department of Public Works purposes: a bucket truck, a Vac-Con trailer and a sweeper to clean sidewalks.
He said the sweeper would be beneficial when it comes to the areas where people take out their trash.
"It will help especially with the fall now coming and leaves are blowing into areas where our storefronts, the doors are set back," he said. "We'll be able to get in there and clean it up. So it should be able to make the downtown area, especially, look nicer while we have tourists coming into town."
According to the Nov. 6 memo, the remaining funds would also go to Rescue Fire Company for fire apparatuses, the Economic Development Division for the Hyatt Bridge, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. for the Cambridge Harbor project, Cannery Park for lighting and the Engineering Division for GIS equipment.
The commissioners voted to approve the obligation of the remaining ARPA funds to these recommended projects and purchases with a unanimous vote. Commissioner Jameson Harrington was absent from the meeting.
At the end of the meeting, Commissioner Brian Roche thanked city staff for making sure the money will be spent and not sent back to the federal government. He said COVID-19 has had a significant negative impact on the youth in Cambridge.
"And one of the things (the city) did, which is not obvious, is they've actually saved the money that we wanted to allocate for a new park, Leonards Lane, and a brand new (one) which is slowly developing by the Packing House, Cannery Park," he said.
Roche said this ensures the city will be able to move forward with the creation of these two brand new parks.
"I just want to applaud staff for making that happen, making sure that could happen," he said. "Because I think the development of those two parks, connecting them in safe ways, is going to be just tremendous for the youth of this community to continue to have green space and enjoy outdoor recreation for their health and well-being."

title: Oxford Election Board Makes Recommendations for Future Town Elections
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Election Board makes recommendations for future town elections

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 399
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Oxford Election Board discussed ways it believes the town's election process could be improved during a Commissioners of Oxford workshop Tuesday.At the meeting, Election Board members and town's commissioners went through a list of different recommendations from the Election Board. Some of those recommendations would need to be addressed by the commissioners.
The board is recommending some changes to the charter. Pam Baker, who is on the board, asked that the voter registration process be clarified in the town charter. She said the board uses a list of registered voters from the county when it comes to verifying voter registrations.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said the town charter does not say anything about registering to vote with the county. Baker said that is why they are recommending the process be clarified in the charter.
Baker said the charter also needs to be cleaned up and corrected when it comes to the election process.
"It's probably worth going through it carefully and picking up all those changes at one time," she said. "A lot of things have been done piecemeal in the past. It's a little bit hard to follow."
Along with charter changes, Baker talked about the board's interest in requiring candidates in town elections to disclose campaign finances.
"We felt that transparency was talked about an awful lot in the last several campaigns, but one area that remains totally opaque is finances," she said. "And I think it's worthwhile for voters in Oxford to understand where the financial support is coming from for candidates."
When it comes to transparency in the voting process, Baker said the board prefers livestreaming the election rather than allowing poll watchers. She said having board members as well as poll watchers in the room could be intimidating for voters.
Before the last town election in June, resident Josh Coder requested poll watchers be present. At a town meeting that month, the commissioners voted to recommend livestreaming, which was implemented.
Other recommendations the board made at the workshop Tuesday include setting up a locked mailbox in the town office for absentee ballots and limiting political signage.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said limiting signage could raise an issue with the First Amendment.
Baker also talked about procedural changes the Election Board can implement itself, including getting better signage and rearranging the voting room.
Moving forward, Baker said she would like to sit down with Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan to look through the charter for errors.

title: Visitors Shower Cambridge with Compliments
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
Visitors shower Cambridge with compliments

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 490
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Maryland Municipal League (MML) was in Cambridge for three days during the first week of November for its annual fall conference. It was the largest fall conference that the MML has ever had with over 400 attendees from 90 municipalities across the state.I do not know what others heard from those attending, but all I heard were compliments about the Hyatt, the city, the training programs, the beauty of our community and the warm welcome that our visitors received.
The first day of the conference brought people downtown for tours provided by city staff about our housing initiative and Linda Harris from the Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center. In addition the welcoming reception was held at the Dorchester Center for the Arts after which people had the opportunity to dine at our local restaurants.
The MML is almost 100 years old, and I learned at our meeting that our new city manager was previously the president of the MML some years ago. The conference provided training for newly elected officials and staff as well as those with years of experience on topics that will help them to return to their communities and provide improved and up-to-date services and ways for their towns and cities to work more effectively and efficiently. They also learned the importance of greater community engagement in finding solutions for the unique challenges in each of our cities.
We received presentations on ways to address infrastructure issues — water, sewer, streets and city property — as well as the challenges that Maryland and its communities face regarding the cost of electricity, solar farms, transmission towers and lines, and how to help citizens address some of the challenges that they face with utility costs.
Large and small cities and towns met in groups to learn from one another about issues that they are facing with regard to a variety of issues such as juvenile justice, the challenges in hiring and retaining staff including police officers, housing and the like.
It was exciting and rewarding to participate in this event and to see how much Cambridge has accomplished over the years since the establishment of its city council-city manager form of government in 2015. It has been because of the leadership of the city managers that we have had, the hard work of our excellent staff and the vision of our elected leadership that we were able to shine for those who came to the conference.
In January, a new council will be sworn in for the next term. It is important that the residents of Cambridge be engaged, observant and supportive of the good work that will be done while also reaching out to the new mayor, commissioners and city manager to let them know what concerns you have that they may not see. Having what is called "new eyes" on new challenges and old ones that have not been addressed are critical in ensuring that improvements continue here in Cambridge.

title: Approved Silo Square housing project generates resident opposition
author: Konner Metz
content:
Approved Silo Square housing project generates resident opposition

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 815
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Maury Schlesinger knows the town needs more housing, but when he takes the short walk from his home to 410 Needwood Ave, he can't quite envision the development that's being planned for the lot.A recently approved 28-unit townhouse development has garnered mixed opinions from the Easton community, particularly East End residents like Schlesinger.
The property is currently home to 10 unused grain bins from a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation. The Arc bought the 2.36-acre lot from Perdue and received approval from the Easton Planning Commission in October to move forward with developing the site into mixed-income housing.
While not immediately surrounded by residences, the lot is close to a number of single-family homes. Schlesinger, who's been outspoken at town meetings against the design of the project, says the project is "inappropriate" and "out of context" with the surrounding residential areas.
"You're putting a tear through the fabric of our town," Schlesinger said.
Schlesinger, along with other neighbors, say they support bringing more affordable and workforce housing to Easton, and even to the lot in question. Many of their concerns stem from the design of the townhomes and the process by which Silo Square was designed and approved.
"Most all folks ... are on record supporting housing at the site, simply not as proposed, and not in the manner that this has been done," said Matt Carberry, who lives within viewing distance of the grain bins.
DESIGN CONCERNS
Planning Commission members voiced split opinions on Silo Square designs during two hearings in September and October.
Commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint, Vice Chairperson Michael Ports and Chair Pro Tem William Ryall each complimented developers for how the townhomes looked in renderings. Commission members Victoria McAndrews and Thomas Klein were less receptive to the design, though both joined the other three in approving the project at the Oct. 17 meeting.
Residents who spoke during public comment were more unified in their opposition.
Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said in an interview that developers want to use high-quality materials and avoid creating something that's a "faux representation of a different time period."
"We're not in downtown Easton," Benincasa said. "We didn't really like the idea of replicating just another kind of brick facade, or another kind of 1990s-looking townhome community. We want to make sure when people look back on it, they know that this was built in 2024."
Resident Loretta Hatzel-Geraci says her largest gripe with the design is that the townhomes face inwards on the lot.
"Inward-facing doesn't really promote community interaction," she said.
"I can appreciate the community's concerns around inward-facing," Benincasa said. "The reality with the site is that because we have no other homes around us, if we made it outward-facing, those homes are just going to face the back of industrial properties."
Benincasa said that of the 28 units, around 21 will start off at market-rate rent prices, with the other seven priced at workforce rates achievable for those making around $55,000 to $70,000 annually.
APPROVAL PROCESS
Since the project falls within the town's planned redevelopment overlay district, it did not require approval from the Easton Town Council. The Planning Commission could have approved it at a September meeting, though it asked developers to procure a traffic study and return one month later.
Between the two commission hearings, developers held a meeting with Silo District residents. Benincasa said two main topics were discussed: the design and entrances to the development, the latter of which was adjusted to move the main entrance onto Maryland Avenue.
Still, East End residents wish that public input played more of a role and that the process wasn't so quick.
"The public gets to see the project too late in the process," Schlesinger said. " … There's no opportunity for dialogue. There's only the opportunity to shout yay or nay."
Both Hatzel-Geraci and Carberry say they felt the approval was a done deal, whether the residents spoke out or not.
"Whatever observations or comments made by the community, if considered, were essentially dismissed by the Planning Commission," Carberry said. "The appearance was that the project's approval was basically pre-approved absent any community input."
Schlesinger says he wishes developers were required to reach out to the community before an application is sent to the town. He added that the process for Easton Crossing, The Arc's mixed-use project on Brookletts Avenue, included the level of community outreach he wishes Silo Square was afforded.
Benincasa said he's heard from community members that The Arc is held to a "higher standard," a challenge the organization welcomes.
"I would agree that I think moving forward, for our projects, we're going to try and make sure there's more community outreach well ahead of time," Benincasa said.
"The normal developer kind of builds, fills, and sells, that's how they make their money. We don't," he continued. "And so we go into a project with the attitude that we're going to be neighbors. We need to make sure that we have a good relationship."

title: Talbot's 1-Cent Amendment Passes by Slim Margin
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot's 1-cent amendment passes by slim margin

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 By a razor thin margin, Talbot County voters approved a charter amendment extending the county's ability to raise residents' taxes for public safety funding.According to Maryland Board of Elections data, 10.968 Talbot County ballots approved the measure, 400 more than voted against the measure. Ballot canvassing was completed by the local Board of Elections on Friday.
The 1-cent amendment authorizes the Talbot County Council to raise property taxes one cent per $100 of assessed value each fiscal year. The council already had the authorization to do so through fiscal year 2026 thanks to a previous charter amendment.
This year's charter amendment passing means the county, if it deems necessary, can raise revenue derived from those taxes through fiscal year 2033.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, a vocal proponent of the amendment, said he hopes the council does not have to enforce the additional tax hike, acknowledging that "nobody wants to pay higher taxes."
"We don't want to do that anymore than the public wants it," Lesher said in an interview on Monday. "And I think my hope is that we will not have to do that, that inflation will be under control (and) will be under 2%."
However, if inflation does not decrease, Lesher says, then the county may elect to collect additional tax revenue to fund public safety measures. While it hasn't always been collected, it has contributed to areas such as sheriff's deputy salaries and retirement for correctional officers when the county did choose to collect it, Lesher said.
"If inflation does not come down as we're expecting, (then) we may need this tool, just to keep up, just to be able to fill those positions," Lesher said.
Martha Sparks, the county's finance director, said at a July county meeting that the 1-cent measure has helped the county in adding 26 public safety positions, including paramedics, EMTs, school resource officers and 911 operators.
In 2020, voters approved the original 1-cent amendment by a wider margin. Just over 10,000 voters approved it, with around 7,200 voting against it at the time.
Lesher said he understands why Talbot County voters may have voted against the measure in 2024. He emphasized that the county has followed through on using any of the additional tax revenue to improve public safety.
"All of the funds that we've raised through that extra penny and more have gone toward public safety," Lesher said. " … We've kept our word."

title: Caroline Commissioners Hear from County Workers, Discuss School Budget
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline Commissioners hear from county workers, discuss school budget

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners convened on Tuesday and several topics were discussed, including the Employee Advisory Board's desire to attract and retain workers, approving changes to the fiscal year 2024 Caroline Board of Education budget and a restructuring of the Department of Public Works.BOARD OF EDUCATION BUDGETDerek Simmons, superintendent of Caroline County Public Schools, and Jill Hignutt, CFO of The Caroline Board of Education, requested amendments to the Board of Education's 2024 budget.
"We are here to share where the budget adjustments needed to take place in the operating budget and align those with the actuals at the end of the fiscal year," Simmons said.
Hignett gave the commissioners a copy of her short presentation, then began detailing the request.
"Starting with prescriptive revenues, there is a change of $6,389,071 related to our grant funding. Many of our grants cross fiscal years, so we must adjust the revenues to match the expenditures that were actually seen at year end," Hignutt said.
Then she shifted the attention to expenditures like driver salaries for transportation. Between fuel costs and bus driver salaries, the school system overspent about $39,000. She also mentioned parking lot repavement projects and classroom renovations.
There was a $5,782,498 surplus noted in the total budgeted revenues. According to Daniel Fox, deputy county administrator, the excess of revenue over expenditures is retained by the Board of Education to go to its fund balance.
The commissioners approved the amended budget.
EMPLOYEE ADVISORY BOARDNext up was the Employee Advisory Board, an authority that overlooks the corrections, emergency services, planning and codes, public works, recreation and parks, and administration departments. There is also a non-voting member department, the Department of Human Resources.
Todd Lord, chairman of the Advisory Board for Caroline County, thanked the commissioners for improving pensions for retirees and achieving competitive pay increases to help with recruitment and retention.
The board also wants cost of living adjustments due to the inflation following the pandemic.
Lord proposed an initiative to go forward as he hears from staff about pay and salaries.
"We recommend merit pay increases annually for step based off of employee evaluations. We want to get away from the bunching of salaries. Health care plans for retirees, that is another one of our initiatives being discussed heavily in departments," Lord said.
He said the goal was to increase retention and have attraction for the employees under the board's care.
"Right now we want to provide a health care plan that employees can take into retirement," Lord said. "Having their pension in retirement would be a huge benefit in retention for our staff."
Commissioner Frank Bartz responded, "Health care for retirees, that is a hard undertaking for the county."
Another commissioner said the same.
Porter said, "I don't foresee that we are going to be able to do health care benefits for people who are retiring at 55. The same inflation figures that you are using, we are facing as well."
President Travis Breeding said, "We have to find that balance — taking care of our employees and taking care of our tax payers and the constituents of the county."
PUBLIC WORKS REORGANIZATIONRobin Eaton, director of the Department of Public Works, asked the commissioners for the authority to reorganize the department to create a project manager position. He spoke of maintaining the 80 miles of dirt roads in the county.
"Our original structure had three crew leaders, so doing away with one of those crew leader positions and creating a project inspector slash utility locator," Eaton said.
"It is actually three crews. Two under crew leaders and one dirt road crew with four employees under the road superintendent," Kathleen Freeman, county administrator, said.
The commissioners approved the reorganization.

title: Dayspring Residents Face Potential Eviction Amid Safety, Health Concerns
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Dayspring residents face potential eviction amid safety, health concerns

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 724
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — For months, residents of the Dayspring Townhomes have raised concerns regarding the safety and conditions of an apartment complex just outside of Ridgely. Now, around half of them are potentially facing eviction.On Nov. 13, the Dayspring Townhomes filed 23 complaints against tenants for failure to pay rent. The complex, located just outside town limits on School Street Lane, is owned by the county and managed by a Delaware-based company.
Failure to pay rent notices were posted to front doors at Daysprings on Friday. A joint trial date for all of the tenants facing eviction is set for this coming Friday afternoon in the Caroline County District Court.
A number of tenants have raised concerns this year about living conditions at the 46-unit complex, including broken appliances, mold, unresponsive property management and an ineffective work order process.
"I've been here 10 years, I ain't never been through this mess," resident Andrea Conaway said on Friday, echoing some of those same concerns.
Those worries only intensified after a non-fatal shooting outside of the complex in August. The incident lead to the county purchasing security cameras, which are now placed at the front of the complex.
Bridge Maryland Inc., a nonprofit organization based in Baltimore County, has held meetings for residents to air their concerns and is assisting the tenants of Dayspring Townhomes with the court process. Bridge Maryland President the Rev. Angelique Mason says residents have experienced the same problems with living conditions for multiple years with no fixes.
"We do know that some of them are not being vocal because they might be behind in their rent," Mason said in an October interview. "They had this idea that they might be evicted if they speak up. And that's really why Bridge is being the voice for the people, because some of them do have fear of eviction. … Nobody should have to live (like that)."
Amid the worries about living conditions, Caroline County paid $2,530 for an independent inspection of the complex on Oct. 23, completed by First State Inspection Agency.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said of the 46 units, one was found to have potential mold or mildew. "Outside of that, generally speaking, the most significant issues (were the) smoke detectors," she said in an interview.
The county administrator said East Coast Property Management, the Delaware-based management company that runs the complex, agreed to install the smoke detectors for all units, among other fixes. Attempts by The Star Democrat to reach the company by phone, by email and at their Milford office were unsuccessful.
On Tuesday, Freeman noted that property management informed the county it has addressed electrical issues, fixed broken door frames and ordered window replacements. She said she's expecting other items to be "addressed by the site manager," along with an update next week from East Coast.
The property, which was built in 1994, has been discussed at numerous Caroline County Commissioners meetings since complaints about the apartments surfaced early this year.
On Nov. 12, Commission Vice President Larry Porter expressed his hope that the county sells the property.
"Our position at this point that we're going to express is the possibility of selling that property to a qualified nonprofit organization," Porter said.
In an interview, Porter said the mortgage on the property is deferred because of state involvement, with that deferral conditioned upon the county's ownership and the prerequisite that the property remain a low-income complex.
The complex was previously developed by a nonprofit entity. At last week's commission meeting, Porter said a management agreement between East Coast and the nonprofit — which is no longer in operation — was completed in 2000, and that the language in the agreement needs to be updated.
On Friday evening, some residents in the Dayspring Townhomes had pulled down the notices off of their doors, beginning to process what the future may hold.
Conaway said it was the first time she's received the notice in nearly a decade of living at the complex. Conaway and her daughter, Tiana Corsey, say the living conditions of the 30-year-old townhomes have significantly declined, particularly under the current property manager.
While talking to tenants who had received the notice last week, Bridge Maryland organizer Hannah Freeman said it's time the tenants stand up for themselves, beginning in court this Friday.
"This is why it's important for us to stick together," Hannah Freeman said.

title: Lawsuit Compels Chestertown Council Member to Resign
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Lawsuit compels Chestertown Council member to resign

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 420
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Since mid-October, the Ward 1 spot in the Chestertown Council has been vacant.The reason being that earlier this month, former council member of that ward Tim O'Brien submitted his letter of resignation after serving over three years.
O'Brien wrote, "It has been a great honor to serve on the Town Council, and I am proud of the work we have done during my term period today, November 4th, 2024, I am writing to announce that after careful deliberation regarding the best interest of the Town, I made the difficult decision to voluntarily resign from my seat on the council, effective immediately. I hope to remain active in the community, and I look forward to what's to come in the future of Chestertown."
The formal letter came on the heels of a Writ of Summons issued Oct. 18, from a Robert Miller and John and/or Jane Doe against O'Brien, according to court documents. The plaintiff's claim is that the Chestertown Charter forbids O'Brien to continue serving since he moved from Ward 1 to Ward 4, October of last year.
According to the Town Charter, Resolution 06-2023, "Councilmembers shall dwell for not less than 30 days in the ward which he is elected to represent, and in case he moves during his term of office from the ward from which he was elected, his term shall at once terminate and there shall exist a vacancy".
There was an amendment to this however, making an exception for council members moving after serving two years, but the plaintiffs claimed the amendment pertains only to new members, not those currently in office.
It would not apply to O'Brien, elected in November, 2, 2021, they state.
The plaintiffs requested not only O'Brien be removed, but all his council actions taken after the date of his move, October 23, 2023, be nullified. Attorney for the plaintiffs are Stephen Meehan, Lauren Castelli and Victoria Devore and defending O'Brien, are attorneys Lyndsey Ryan and Carly Landolfi.
O'Brien's attorneys filed for a motion to dismiss, for which a hearing will take place at the Kent County Circuit Court on Dec. 18, at 1 p.m. with Judge Harris Murphy presiding.
Chestertown Mayor David Foster and Town Administrator Larry DiRe both urged residents to help select the next Ward 1 Council member by special election on Tuesday, Jan. 21.
Residents of Ward 1 must be registered with the Kent County Board of Election Supervisors on or before Friday, Dec. 20. All Town of Chestertown residents currently registered with the County are automatically registered to vote in Town elections.

title: Trappe to Make Changes to Playground and Get a Speed Trailer
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe to make changes to playground and get a speed trailer

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 342

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Town Council held a special meeting to discuss the use of over $277,000 in remaining funds from the American Rescue Plan Act. Council members voted to approve using funds for the Lakeview Playground and a speed trailer.During the meeting, Erin Braband, Trappe's clerk, gave a run down of the ARPA funds, pandemic relief money from the federal government. The town has already obligated the majority of the funding it received through the program.
Braband said in the past the council had discussed usages for the remaining funds and needed a final decision before the Dec. 31 deadline, by which time all ARPA funds must be obligated or returned to the federal government.
The first purchase decision was made for the Lakeview Playground. During past meetings, council members discussed contracting a company to install softer ground materials for children if they were to fall during play.
Several businesses made bids with different alternative playground flooring, including pea gravel, small stones with rounded edges and gavel bases.
After some debate, two bids were awarded by the council.
The first was to Peak Contracting for the removal of the mulch currently at the playground. Additionally, the company will add two layers of fabric to the playground floor and a sandbase for a total of $5,550. The second bid was for Playground Outfitters for four inches of rubber mulch for a total of $10,021.40.
"I don't know my thought of a kid falling off of a swing or something like that, falling on the pea gravel just doesn't sound as appealing as falling on the rubber," Council Member Brian Schmidt said.
The bids were approved 4-1 with Council President Jeremy Newnam voting against.
Council members also approved the purchase of a speed trailer from 95 Traffic Safety Supply for $12,289.80. This trailer will have red and blue flashers and have the ability to collect traffic data. Possible locations for this trailer will be Main Street, Maple Street or Greenfield.
This was unanimously approved.
Further discussion on usage of funds will be held during a Dec. 4 council meeting.

title: Department of Community Services Highlights Caregivers and Resources
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Department of Community Services highlights caregivers and resources

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 462

 CENTREVILLE — Proclaiming National Caregivers Month and celebrating all family caregivers in the nation, the Department of Community Services also presented annual updates to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners Nov. 12.Families are often the primary source of support and care for older adults and people with disabilities and according to the National Caregivers Month proclamation, over 53 million Americans are currently family caregivers for loved ones and a large number provide care 24 hours a day.
"Ironically we depend more so on family caregivers than on paid caregivers to manage needs with family, elders, young adults, anyone who is requiring caregiving," said Cathy Willis, director of the county's Community Services.
Caregivers are encouraged to take moments for themselves to re-vitalize and attend caregiver meetings and reach out to the Queen Anne's County Area Aging Agency for support resources.
The Queen Anne's County Department of Community Services includes the Area Agency on Aging, County Ride public transit, Housing Authority and the Local Management Board.
The Housing Authority division is newly a part of the Community Services Department, and putting a face to the names of the essential work, Executive Director Mike Clark of the Housing and Family Services introduced staff to the commissioners during the Nov. 12 meeting.
The Division of Housing and Community Services aims to help residents with affordable housing with the ultimate goal of creating opportunities for brighter futures by offering "a hand up, not a handout," according to Clark.
The county's transit service, County Ride, takes around 100 riders to and from work weekly and goes to all four senior centers on a daily basis, according to Chief of Aging and Transportation Anne Sparks.
County Ride also partners with high schools to teach graduating seniors with special needs how to ride public transportation.
For 2024, County Ride is shaping up to finish with over 5,000 rides more than 2023 and 20,000 rides more than 2022, she said.
"It's very successful," Sparks said.
Currently the Queen Anne's County Local Management Board is focusing on Community Reinvestment Repair Funds, which were established by the Queen Anne's County Local Management Board under Maryland's 2023 Cannabis Reform Act in support of initiatives to uplift communities impacted by historical inequities, fostering economic empowerment, youth development, and housing stability, according to Clark.
Through the Local Management Board and the Queen Anne's County Economic and Tourism Development, priorities include homelessness prevention, after-school programs, community resource needs and minority business programs, Clark said.
The Active Aging Center at the Queen Anne's County YMCA in Centreville is also celebrating its one year anniversary, according to Sparks. With an overall attendance of more than 4,000 participants, the new location has seen over 500 new memberships, as well as a large number of congregant meals served, she said.
More information about community services, including County Ride schedules can be found at qac.org/1291/Community-Services.

title: Easton Town Council Hears Update on Seafood Odor Mitigation
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council hears update on seafood odor mitigation

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council heard an update Monday evening from Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a business on Maryland Avenue that's drawn complaints from residents for its odor in recent months.At a Nov. 4 town meeting, councilmembers discussed a draft ordinance to limit seafood processing uses in business commercial zoning through special exception only.
That exception would require that seafood by-products are "stored within a closed or refrigerated vehicle," with operators required to install "odor control technology" so "no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner/operator Mitchell Hughes, spoke Monday regarding the town's Nov. 4 discussion and how the potential legislation may impact Hughes' business. Smith said finding a new site for Chesapeake Brand Seafood, as was previously suggested by Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry, is not his client's preferred course of action.
"I did speak to Mitchell about that, and that is not preferable," Smith said. " … He located there lawfully. He followed the town's rules. The town zoning still allows that use in that location. So he doesn't necessarily feel like he should have to relocate."
Smith said Hughes has invested around $200,000 in "fitting the space" for his operation. Additionally, many employees live within walking distance of the current site, the attorney said.
"While things are pretty good at the moment, you never know when fisheries are going to decline, when regulations are going to cause restrictions, and so he just doesn't know," Smith said. "The prospect of investing a large amount of money to relocate just doesn't seem reasonable to him at this time."
Hughes' attorney said the business owner is "committed" to addressing the odor and has looked into an odor mitigation solution that may be viable. "I think he would hope there could be some cost-sharing in that," Smith said.
The proposed ordinance, which would require existing businesses to comply by Jan. 1, 2026, was not voted on Monday, and the public hearing was left open.
Carla Howell, a resident on South Aurora Street, asked the council to consider a compliance deadline earlier than 2026.
"I was hoping we'd get some relief when the crab season was over, but we haven't," Howell said. " … I'm hoping you all will at least change the date, and we can go along with (Smith's) idea. I think it would be marvelous if they just put in some kind of a filter system."
Carolyn Johnson, an employee at Chesapeake Brand Seafood and Hughes' aunt, vouched for her nephew and his work as a local business owner.
"He has always wanted to be a good neighbor, and whenever we've had a situation, a complaint from the mayor's office or the town, we have addressed it," Johnson said. "He's taken care of it. And I feel that that shows what he is. He wants to be in business here in Easton. And he was allowed to be in business here in Easton. You guys, the town, gave him that permission."
Councilmembers offered limited perspective on the seafood legislation Monday, as it will likely be revisited at Town Council's Dec. 2 meeting. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he's "pleased" that a solution for all parties is in the works.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who represents the area in which the business is located, spoke to his constituents and told them "their concerns have not been brushed aside."
In previous meetings, Davis pushed for a deadline sooner than Jan. 1, 2026. He also contended that seafood processing should not be allowed in business commercial zoning at all.
"If I have to stand by myself, I will," Davis said regarding a potential council vote on the matter. "I will represent the voices and the members of that community in such a fashion that they are heard and represented at the table whether they're there or not. So I want all of my colleagues to know that's where I stand."

title: CWDI Votes to Amend Articles of Incorporation
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI votes to amend Articles of Incorporation

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors has voted in favor of amending the organization's Articles of Incorporation.With this vote, made during a closed session meeting on Nov. 20, the amendments will be sent for approval to Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, who is CWDI's sole member.
CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said if Rideout approves the amendments, they will be sent to the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation.
"Once they have accepted and filed it, then it becomes our actual articles," she said.
During a Cambridge City Council work session on Nov. 4, City Attorney Patrick Thomas said that in September, a group — which included Thomas, Rideout, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman, Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) — met to discuss proposed revisions to the Articles of Incorporation.
At the council meeting, Thomas outlined proposed changes to the document and said that if the City Council, state and Dorchester County Council all favorably recommend the changes to the document, those changes could then be adopted by the CWDI board.
In an interview with the Star Democrat Thursday, Hengst said she was happy CWDI was able to work with the city, county and state.
"We're just happy that we were able to all work together and come up with something that everyone is happy with and can move forward," she said.
PROPOSED CHANGESIf approved by Rideout and filed by the state, the Articles of Incorporation amendments would address membership, board membership and the process of amending CWDI's Articles of Incorporation and bylaws.
Specifically, one amendment would expand the board of directors from seven to nine members. The two additional seats would be for the city and county managers, who would not be able to vote but would be entitled to attend all meetings, including closed session meetings.
Another amendment would increase the number of CWDI members from one to three. Members — which are different from board members — are comparable to shareholders of a company. Having three members would make it so that the city, county and state can be represented.
The city and county members would be made up of their respective councils. The state member would be made up of Dorchester County's state delegation and the state's secretary of housing and community development. This means that for the CWDI members to vote on a particular item, a majority of its commissioners, council members or state representatives would have to vote a certain way first.
The amendments also state that if the board of directors declines the removal of a director, then the appointing authority, such as the county or city, has the ability to remove them after 45 days of the request for removal.
Lastly, the amendments clarify that the CWDI Board of Directors has the authority to amend the Articles of Incorporation as long as it provides the amendments to CWDI members for approval first. It also clarifies that the board of directors can amend its bylaws as long as advance notice is provided to CWDI members.

title: Town of Oxford to Lose Another Employee in Town Office

Town of Oxford to lose another employee in town office

 November 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 OXFORD — Oxford Clerk-Treasurer Vickie Sharp, the last full-time employee standing in Oxford's town office, is leaving her position at the end of the year.In an interview with the Star Democrat Friday, Sharp — who was sworn into the role in April — said she preferred not to say why she was leaving, but she said she has found other employment. Her last day will be Dec. 31.
Staffing changes have become somewhat normal in Oxford over the last year.
Former town manager Cheryl Lewis, who had been employed by the town for 12 years, retired at the end of June. In October, the town lost it's planning and zoning coordinator, Marilyn Williams. Williams had started the role at the end of February. Assistant Clerk Lisa Willoughby retired at the end of October after 37 years with the Oxford Town Office.
Commission President Norm Bell said the town commissioners are taking "an orderly approach" to town staffing issues.
"We're looking at all of the options available to us and coming up with a plan going forward," he said, "modifying the plan that we have and moving forward."
The town currently has a consultant doing town planning work on a contract basis as it searches for a permanent planning and zoning coordinator. Bell said a temp from a staffing agency will be coming in Dec. 10 to fill the assistant clerk position.
The commissioners are also moving forward with their town manager search, Bell said, adding that they hope to make a decision before the end of the year. During a town meeting on Nov. 12, Commissioner Katrina Greer said they have narrowed their list down to five town manager candidates.
Bell said the town office has already cut back on its hours and he can't yet say how exactly Sharp's departure will affect the office.
"I can't say right now how it's going to impact our work going forward until we get everybody in here and see how we can operate and see how much training we can get done before Vickie leaves," he said.
Bell said the frequency of staff departures in the town office is concerning to the commissioners. He said that right now, they are focused on filling the open positions and "keeping the town office moving."

title: ‘A Force in Washington’: Sen. Cardin Stops in Easton for Farewell Tour
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
‘A force in Washington’: Sen. Cardin stops in Easton for farewell tour

 November 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 569
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Local leaders and officials thanked Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.) for his service to the Eastern Shore on Friday morning as the 81-year-old nears his final days of his 18th year in the U.S. Senate.In his farewell tour to the Eastern Shore, the longtime congressman made a stop at the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy to speak with local representatives, including Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan.
These officials and state legislators, including Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), thanked Cardin for his professionalism, ability to work across the political aisle and commitments to the Eastern Shore.
In September, Cardin and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced $10.6 million in federal funding for Chesapeake Bay restoration, $2.8 million of which went to the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy. On Friday, Mautz emphasized Cardin's success in providing money to maintain the shoreline.
"At a critical juncture where we are in the world and all the things that are happening, Sen. Cardin is a force in Washington," Mautz said.
"I'm going to miss you," Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "The one thing I respect (about) you most is that you're going out on top. I see a lot of politicians who don't know when to step down."
Revisiting his top initiatives throughout his three terms in the Senate, Cardin noted the work done at Capitol Hill to improve Maryland colleges and universities, expand healthcare on the Shore and upgrade water infrastructure.
"There's so much competition for clean water and wastewater facilities that sometimes rural areas don't get their fair share," Cardin said. "We're able to work together to make sure you get your fair share under the revolving funds, but also then use our earmarks for where gaps have taken place."
Cardin said local leadership on the Shore is as impressive as it gets across the state, and he thanked local councils for ensuring rural areas achieve a balance of having an economic future and maintaining a sense of uniqueness.
Cardin spoke highly of Easton — a town he says is attracting much attention in the nation's capital. The senator added that officials in Talbot County are adequately serving all people.
"You also have challenges, hunger and low-income families," Cardin told members of the Talbot County Council. "And you're taking steps to deal with those issues as well, so we appreciate that. … There is diversity here. And you have helped deal with preserving dignity for all of the people in the county."
PASSING THE TORCHCardin opted not to run for reelection, leaving an open seat in the Senate that will be filled by Democrat Angela Alsobrooks, who defeated Republican opponent and former Gov. Larry Hogan in November's election.
Having worked with Alsobrooks, the Prince George's County executive, Cardin said he's confident in Maryland's newest senator.
"We've had several conversations," Cardin said in an interview. "I think she understands the responsibilities, so she has the whole package. I think she'll do a great job."
Cardin emphasized that former Sen. Barbara Mikulski (D-Md.), a mentor of his who he served alongside in the Senate from 2007 to 2017, taught him the tradition of Maryland's delegation working together instead of separately. He hopes Van Hollen and Alsobrooks carry that torch beginning in January.
"I think that tradition will continue, no doubt about it," Cardin said. "Sen. Alsobrooks will continue to be not only an incredible leader, but also part of a great team."

Iota Alpha Alpha provides turkeys, meals to hundreds of Easton families

 EASTON — Hundreds of turkeys and packaged meals were handed out to Easton residents Saturday afternoon on Glenwood Avenue.Iota Alpha Alpha, an Easton chapter of the national Omega Psi Phi fraternity, organized the distribution, which was held at the American Legion Blake-Blackston Post 77. Residents lined up around noon Saturday to pick up turkeys and meals.
Doug Rogers, a member of Iota Alpha Alpha, and Mayor Megan Cook each spoke at the start of the distribution.
"This is a great opportunity to give back to your community," Cook said.
She thanked the local organizations for their contributions that will help Easton residents not just the week of Thanksgiving, but throughout the entire holiday season.
Rogers said organizations such as the Dock Street Foundation, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, Neighborhood Service Center and Building African American Minds Center were important partners with Iota Alpha Alpha for the event.
"This truck, it was filled to the brim," Rogers said of the truck that held the meals and turkeys. "… We passed out over 200 turkeys and 200 certificates for meals. And if people don't come and pick up those turkeys, it's great, because we're going to give the overflow to the Neighborhood Service Center. If they don't eat today, they'll eat next week."
The men of Iota Alpha Alpha joined with sister organizations and community members to not just pass out food, but to give away winter clothing to those in need as well.
It was the chapter's first Thanksgiving distribution at Blake-Blackston Post 77. Rogers said he hopes it continues and grows in future years.
Founded in 1911 at Howard University, Omega Psi Phi is predicated upon public service, Rogers said. A motto of the fraternity is "friendship is essential to the soul," something Rogers says the Easton chapter strives to do in the local community.
"When we start talking about giving, we start talking about (what) the Lord calls us to do, (He) calls us to serve people," Rogers said. "We're a service organization first and foremost. We're called to serve people. The little bit that we can do, the little bit that we can gather, is about serving God as people. So that's at our core."
Rogers said Saturday's cheerful and upbeat turkey and meal distribution was an example of the Iota Alpha Alpha chapter carrying out its mission and helping local residents in need during what can be trying times.

title: Campaigning Practices Questioned at Cambridge City Council Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Campaigning practices questioned at Cambridge City Council meeting

 November 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 644
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In the final week before Cambridge's heated run-off election for its next mayor, residents are bringing up concerns with candidate campaigning practices.During a Cambridge City Council meeting on Nov. 25, two residents detailed their concerns with candidates door knocking at apartment complexes where elderly people and people with disabilities live.
Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas and former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw are both running to fill the open mayoral seat. Their campaigns have been gearing up as the city draws nearer to the Dec. 3 run-off election.
At the council meeting, resident Mya Woods read a letter from another resident, GeriLeigh Farrow, that called out Cephas and her campaign.
In the letter, Farrow said she was working at Conifer Village at Cambridge, an apartment complex for seniors, when she noticed a man standing outside.
"I noticed the man outside, which now I know as Lajan's boyfriend or husband, while she was inside," the letter read.
Before Woods could finish reading the letter, Mayor Stephen Rideout told her public comments must be made to or about the entire council, not a single commissioner.
Woods went on to ask that the city's elected officials make sure they make decisions with the residents best interests, not just their own.
"... Just remember, the town is broken and they need people who can lead them and not take advantage of them," she said.
Michael Jones, a resident of New Horizons Apartments, told the City Council he has seen people come in and out of his apartment for campaign reasons. He recounted an experience where he received a knock at his door and later found a campaign flier at his door.
Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said Conifer Village residents have been reaching out to her about "problems with their building being infiltrated."
"The measures that people go to these days to take advantage of our vulnerable and elderly and differently-abled is really heart wrenching," she said. "They do everything from selling fake extended car warranties or service contracts to stealing home equity lines of credit."
Atkiss — who has endorsed Bradshaw in the upcoming election — said she has also heard that a campaign gained access to New Horizons and the Bradford House Apartments. Atkiss later told the Star Democrat she was talking about Cephas' campaign.
Atkiss said that when she wanted to go door knocking inside Conifer during her campaign, she was told she couldn't as a security measure for residents.
"It's not up to me to decide that my cause is greater than their privacy and their right to not be disturbed," she said.
Atkiss continued on to say that no one voted for the commissioners "so they could see what we could get away with."
"But I know, if this is how elected officials act, I don't blame people for not coming out and voting," she said.
Cephas responded to the comments, acknowledging the issue has nothing to do with city business.
"But since people want to spin a narrative, I'm going to be transparent," she said.
Cephas said she was invited by a resident to do a meet and greet at Conifer on Nov. 26 and said she was invited by management to do a meet and greet at Bradford House on Dec. 2.
"I think we need to understand that canvassing is not illegal," she said. "Canvassing is an intentional way of interacting with the residents. Everyone doesn't have social media. Everyone doesn't have email. So we all knock on everyone's door that we're allowed to knock on."
She said her concern is not with "sensationalized behaviors," but with making sure everyone is able to vote.
"And I just really find it a shame that we have other people who are trying to say that (canvassing is) being used to take advantage when we're trying to engage," she said.
The Cambridge run-off election will be held on Dec. 3 at 447 Race St. The polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

title: Cambridge Mayor Thanked at His Last Council Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge mayor thanked at his last council meeting

 November 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Bundled in bubble wrap and layers of tissue paper, and tucked inside a neatly wrapped box, lay Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout's parting gift from Cambridge and its City Council: A key to the city.With all its wrappings, it took Rideout more than a minute to unveil it during his final City Council meeting on Nov. 25.
After serving as a city commissioner and then as mayor, Rideout is retiring. In October, Rideout told the Star Democrat that he and his wife plan to move to a continuing care retirement community in Frederick.
As a result, he is cutting his term as mayor a few weeks short. His last day in office is Dec. 3.
Rideout was elected to the position in a special election in 2022 following the resignation of former Mayor Andrew Bradshaw, who resigned after being charged with distributing revenge porn on Reddit.
At the final Cambridge City Council meeting before Rideout leaves office, residents, commissioners and city staff thanked Rideout for his service to the city.
"Thank you for leading the city through a very difficult, tough, challenging time," Commission President Lajan Cephas said. "You helped stabilize the city. And we got in a position where we were able to get department heads in place (and) fully staff our police department."
Commissioner Brian Roche said that although he didn't always agree with Rideout, he will always respect Rideout for his persistence. Roche talked about Rideout's contributions in getting Cambridge to have a weak mayor form of government.
"So you left it better than you found it," Roche said about Rideout's impact on Cambridge. "And you did that by fundamentally changing the way that the city and now the county do business for the next generation. So thank you."
Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said he has enjoyed working with Rideout over the last couple of years, particularly on issues concerning youth.
"The conversations, the guidance and the experience that you brought here, we have made a lot of progress, and I'm looking forward to seeing that continue," Todd said.
Residents Carlos Estin and Goldie Cooper thanked Rideout during the meeting. Cooper, who is the executive director of Dr. Theresa Stafford's New Beginnings Learning Academy, said she and the center wish him the best of luck.
"I just wanted to come and thank the mayor for all that he's done for the children of Cambridge," Cooper said.
Along with the key to the city, Rideout was given a citation that acknowledges his service as a Ward 1 commissioner and as mayor. After Cephas read the citation, people in the meeting room applauded.
Rideout thanked the voters and residents of Cambridge, as well as city staff, for the opportunity to be mayor.
"It has really been a privilege," he said. "I've enjoyed it most of the time. There have been some times that have been real challenges. But I know that whoever was involved in whatever I became involved in had the city's best interests at heart, worked hard for the city and has really made the city an even better place than it was when we first moved here."
