title: Rideout’s Parting Advice: Listen and Listen Again
author: Staff Writer
content:
Rideout’s parting advice: Listen and listen again

 November 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 639
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Mayor Stephen Rideout will be missed when he leaves Cambridge on Tuesday.Rideout was everything a small town would want in a mayor. He had a vision for what Cambridge could become, and he had a strategic plan for achieving that vision.
Most important, Rideout listened. He listened to city residents. He listened to the City Council, and he listened to the city manager.
He took what he heard and turned it into action for the betterment of Cambridge.
In an interview with Star Democrat reporter Maggie Trovato, Rideout said one of the things he is most proud of are the recent changes in management and ownership at the Bradford House Apartments, which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs.
Over the past year and a half, residents have expressed concerns about the safety of the building, from bed bug infestations to call-for-aid systems not working to a lack of security.
Rideout said the city was able to get the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.), Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and the local state delegation involved. He added that city staff put in "so much work" to get the issues at Bradford House addressed.
"The changes now are happening," Rideout said. "And that to me is how government can work, should work."
Rideout ran for mayor when then Mayor Andrew Bradshaw resigned in January 2022 after being charged for distributing revenge porn on Reddit.
"I felt it was important to have a calming voice during what I anticipated and expected would be a transition until this election," Rideout said. "Because I was only going to do it for the two years."
Lajan Cephas, who served as interim mayor until Rideout was elected, said Rideout "brought stability back to Cambridge" following Bradshaw's resignation. She said he also brought "steady decision-making."
"He was extremely thoughtful of everyone on both sides," Cephas said. "It's something that I learned from him being the commission president while he was the mayor."
Last week, Rideout was lauded with compliments from the City Council, which presented him with a key to the city in thanks for the work he has done.
"Thank you for leading the city through a very difficult, tough, challenging time," Cephas said. "You helped stabilize the city. And we got in a position where we were able to get department heads in place (and) fully staff our police department."
Commissioner Brian Roche said that although he didn't always agree with Rideout, he will always respect Rideout for his persistence. Roche talked about Rideout's contributions in getting Cambridge to have a professional city manager as the main decision-maker for day-to-day operations rather than the mayor.
"So you left it better than you found it," Roche said about Rideout's impact on Cambridge. "And you did that by fundamentally changing the way that the city and now the county do business for the next generation. So thank you."
The list of Rideout's accomplishments is extensive.
He worked with Dorchester County on proposed changes to the county charter, most of which were approved by voters in the recent election.
He challenged the way decisions were made by Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., calling for a process that was transparent to city residents.
He fought for improvements in services for youths and families in Cambridge.
A decade from now, Rideout hopes Cambridge will be a place where students excel in schools, early childhood education programs are teaching kids how to read and write, and new businesses are moving in. He said focusing on the future generations is an important element of making progress in Cambridge.
"Because we aren't going to get businesses who come here who have employees who have children until our school system is improving," he said.
Rideout's main piece of advice to the next mayor of Cambridge is to listen.
"And listen again," he said.
That is good advice for anyone in a governing position.

title: Changes to City, County Charters Highlight Career
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
Changes to city, county charters highlight career

 November 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 734
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The other day I was asked what I thought was the most significant and important thing to happen in Cambridge in which I was involved. While there are a number of things that could be the answer to that question, the one that popped into my mind first was the community effort to change the charter for Cambridge to create a city manager form of government.It was not easy and took the work of many people in the community and on City Council to make it happen.
We took over 2½ years to research, develop a plan, implement it and convince the city commissioners that our idea had merit. Since our success in 2015, the city has had four city managers, all of whom helped to improve Cambridge, its staffing, its funding, and how well it works. While we are not yet at a place where we can claim total success, our community is at a place where we can be assured that the commissioners in 2015 made the right decision.
During these last two years as mayor of Cambridge, I have been able to see the effectiveness of good governance, quality staff and staff leadership, and a committed group of elected commissioners. Successes include creating a summer jobs program for our youth, the arrival and development of new programming in the community as well as expansion and strengthening of old programs, all to the benefit of the children and families in the city.
Over the past few years, I have seen an improving school system that will benefit from the leadership and vision of our superintendent, Jymil Thompson, a committed school staff and available funds to address the multiple challenges that have existed here but were not being addressed.
We have seen improved policing within the city and a reduction in crime. We have also seen efforts to improve the condition of housing for our poor and elderly here in the city.
One might think that positive change should be easy to obtain, but it is not. One first must convince many people that it is positive change and not some crazy idea that has not been tested. It takes time to try to convince both the people who are eager for the change who are called early adopters, those that won't immediately think that the change is good and finally those that resist the change and may never accept it. Obtaining a majority to implement the change is the goal.
An example of that is the recent charter changes that were approved by the voters for Dorchester County. The one major change was something that the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government worked on for several years seeking signatures to a petition for a referendum. While we were unsuccessful in our efforts, it moved the county government to establish a charter commission that proposed that change and others to the County Charter that went on the ballot in November where it was approved.
The charter change will allow the county manager to manage the day-to-day operations of the county and to be the person to whom the county council members need to direct all of their requests. In the past, the county council members were able to direct staff on things that they wanted done and could hire and fire staff for any reason, good or bad. Now those decisions must go through and depend on the good judgment of the county manager.
No longer will county employees be subject to being fired simply because a council member was able to get two other council members to decide to fire them, even if there was no basis for doing that. The hiring and firing will be up to the county manager, Jerry Jones, who has been an excellent choice.
Change happens either because it is imposed on us without our approval and because we did not prepare for it or because there are those in the community who are leaders who have a vision and work collaboratively with others to develop a plan for change that will benefit the community. Finding those people is one of the primary challenges and keeping them involved has to be one of the long-term goals.
My wife and I will soon be leaving for a retirement home. I hope to continue to send articles from the western shore to help provide you with thoughts about how you might be able to improve the lives of others.

title: Lajan Cephas Elected Cambridge's Next Mayor
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Lajan Cephas elected Cambridge's next mayor

 December 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1027
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After months of campaigning in a close election that stirred up controversies and got voters talking, Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas has been elected the city's mayor.Tuesday night, Cephas secured 53% of the vote, or 787 votes, in a run-off election against former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw, who received 47% of the vote with 697 votes. There were 1,484 ballots counted in the election. Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson told the Star Democrat Tuesday that there are 9,183 active, registered voters in Cambridge.
Cephas said she knew it would be a tight race.
"But I'm truly excited that the majority of the voters, that they've decided that they're happy with the direction the city is going and they want to see four more years of this," she said. "So it's my commitment to make sure these projects (get done) and to also make sure our neighborhoods are improved at the highest level."
A HEATED ELECTIONFrom past criminal charges to residency requirements to campaigning practices, the race gave voters a lot to talk about.
Bradshaw's bid for mayor came a little over two and a half years after he resigned from the position. He resigned after he was charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. He later pleaded guilty to five of those counts.
In August, Bradshaw told the Star Democrat he wanted to keep the focus of his 2024 campaign on where Cambridge is currently and where it is going, rather than on his past legal issues. He said he thought voters felt the same way.
During a Cambridge candidate forum conducted by the League of Women Voters in early October, Cephas questioned whether people would feel comfortable associating with a mayor known for an "embarrassing" national headline.
At the forum, Bradshaw said that in a city where many people have made mistakes, a large portion of the population shouldn't be disqualified from serving the city because of the "errors of their past." He said his convictions were withdrawn and removed by the state and his probation has been abated.
According to court documents, a judge ordered in November 2023 that the judgements of guilt for Bradshaw's five counts of distributing revenge porn be stricken and Bradshaw be granted probation before judgement.
Bradshaw wasn't the only candidate who has received criminal charges. In 2022, Cephas was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
Along with past legal controversies, questions regarding candidate residency were also brought up as the two candidates vied for the open seat.
At a City Council meeting Sept. 9, one resident brought up the importance of verifying candidate applications. In response, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said city staff has heard rumors regarding applicants and their residency, but no formal complaints had been filed. He encouraged residents to submit formal complaints so they could be looked into.
The issue was also mentioned during a peace order hearing in early October between family members of the mayoral candidates.
At the hearing, Lejan Cephas' brother Cambridge Commissioner Sputty Cephas, who was running for reelection at the time, was denied a final peace order against Bradshaw's wife, Natalee Bradshaw. Sputty Cephas said he filed the peace order after he noticed Natalee Bradshaw following him around the city one evening.
During the hearing, Natalee Bradshaw's attorney Philip Cronan brought up statements that have been made questioning whether Sputty and/or Lajan Cephas are following the city's residency requirements for candidates. In an interview, Andrew Bradshaw alleged Lajan Cephas has not been residing at the Cambridge address on her application. Lajan Cephas told the Star Democrat she has met every requirement to be a candidate in the city's election.
Cambridge residents also raised concerns regarding campaigning practices in the mayoral election. Last week at a Cambridge City Council meeting, residents brought up concerns with candidates door knocking in apartment complexes where elderly people and people with disabilities live. In a letter partially read at the meeting, resident GeriLeigh Farrow called out Cephas and her campaign for door knocking at Conifer Village at Cambridge, an apartment complex for seniors.
Cephas responded to the comments made at the meeting, noting that she had invites to two apartment buildings for meet and greets. She said canvassing is not illegal.
"And I just really find it a shame that we have other people who are trying to say that (canvassing is) being used to take advantage when we're trying to engage," she said during the meeting.
THE NEXT FOUR YEARSCephas said she is excited and "ready to work."
"What I'm most looking forward to are the residents," she said, adding that on the campaign trail, she was made aware of many concerns from residents.
Cephas said she is excited to follow up with those residents and help get their concerns addressed.
Bradshaw said he reached out to Cephas Tuesday night to congratulate her. He said he hopes Cephas will find a way to move the city forward.
"If that's not the case, then in four years, the voters will get the opportunity to make different choices," he said.
Bradshaw said he is "not giving any thought" to whether he will run in four years. He said he wants his supporters to know that although the campaign was a rough one, he tried to run it as clean as he could.
"And in spite of the loss, I feel a lot of pride that we tried to avoid going into the gutter," he said. "And that I think that though we didn't get the result that we expected or wanted to see, that we can have pride in trying to have been the best that we could as competitors, and as a candidate and as a movement or a campaign."
Cephas said this win means that the networks that have been built in the city can be made "even stronger." She brought up the idea of forming partnerships with the school system in an effort to support the city's youth.
"And economic development falls under that," she said. "So the better schools we have, the better opportunities that we'll have, not only for our youth, but also our young adults trying to get into the workforce."

title: Easton Passes Ordinance to Mitigate Seafood Processing Odors
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton passes ordinance to mitigate seafood processing odors

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council approved an ordinance Monday that aims to crack down on odors from seafood processors by requiring the installment of odor control technology.In a 4-0 vote, the town passed Ordinance 835, which was drafted following resident concerns about the odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis was outspoken Monday evening about bringing his constituents relief from the odors they smell during crab season.
"Constituents in the neighborhood should not have to go through another season of having to endure that kind of odor," Davis said. "And if the business is friendly and working with the community, something of this nature should have been worked out prior to now."
The ordinance, which will go into effect later this month, requires that seafood processing operations install odor control technology "in such a manner that no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing Chesapeake Brand Seafood, said the business' concerns center the spray application system it plans to install — which will cost around $20,000 and may not fulfill the town's new requirements of "no odor" being detectable.
"We're confident it will address the issue, at least to some extent," Smith said. "But we're not confident, not necessarily confident, it'll meet that standard."
Smith requested a compromise, stating he thinks the ordinance should not retroactively apply to "existing, lawful seafood processing uses" such as his client. He submitted proposed revisions to the ordinance that were read aloud Monday evening.
Following a lengthy council discussion, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said he was ready to pass the ordinance as written, without Smith's proposed changes. Council President Frank Gunsallus agreed those changes were "overly specific."
Abatiello made a motion to approve the ordinance, which was seconded by Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry. Gunsallus and Davis joined in voting yes. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery was absent from Monday's meeting.
TIMELINE DEBATEIn the approved ordinance, businesses must comply with odor control and storage requirements by July 1, 2025. Prior to Monday, the compliance date on the draft ordinance was Jan. 1, 2026. The change stirred discussion Monday evening.
Davis pushed for that date to be even sooner — Jan. 1, 2025 — though he was outnumbered by Gunsallus, Abatiello, and Curry, who all voted in favor of amending the ordinance to the July date.
Curry maintained that it's important the town be fair to the business since it's planning to pay up for the new odor control system to address the problem.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said she had legal concerns about shortening the period, saying that "even January (2026)" is pushing it.
"They've had time to comply," Davis said.
"But they didn't have this ordinance," VanEmburgh responded. "The ordinance is what would be challenged."
"I mean the worst case scenario is that we go to court, and is that the end result? Then so be it," said Davis. " … If you say comply by 2026, just think about this for a moment. The same people who live in Ward 4 have to suffer through this this year again until January 2026."
"I have to stand on what I believe in, and I believe that they've already had enough time to do it," Davis later stated. "It seems to me that we're more worried about going to court than listening to the people. And I think we should listen to the people."

title: Caroline County Looking to Make Security Upgrades at Courthouse
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County looking to make security upgrades at courthouse

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Upgraded security measures may soon be installed at the Caroline County Courthouse in Denton.On Nov. 26, the Caroline County Commissioners approved sending out an application letter for state funding to install 16 new bulletproof windows.
Circuit Court Administrative Judge Heather Price brought the proposed security upgrades to the commissioners at the county's most recent public meeting. She indicated a review from the state noted window and front door security as weak points for the courthouse.
As originally presented, if awarded, the county would receive $118,724 from the state to make the improvements to the windows and door. Price's ask was that the commissioners approve a memorandum of understanding between the county court and the county commission.
"This is a reimbursably-based grant," Price said. "So the commissioners would hopefully agree to front the money and then be reimbursed for that by the state. We're not guaranteed that we'll be picked for this."
During the meeting, Price said she has received death threats due to her job, including multiple that resulted in the person making threats serving jail time.
While the commissioners were on board to apply for funding for the new windows, they did not motion for the Circuit Court to apply for funding for a new door.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter raised concerns about removing the current door. He emphasized the historical nature of it and said he could foresee the Caroline County Historical Society having similar worries.
Price said she had "anticipated that concern" and already talked to Kathy Mackel of the Historical Society. Price said Mackel was agreeable to the request for new door funding "on the basis that we would save the old, historic door that could be reinstalled if the secure door was no longer necessary."
Commissioner Frank Bartz, however, felt if the door was removed and stored, it could become lost or forgotten.
"If you take the door out (and) say 'Hey, we're going to save it, we're going to put it back,' it gets stuck in a corner somewhere," Bartz said. "Twenty years from now, 'Where'd this door come from?'"
Porter said the photos he's seen of the potential door replacement aren't up to historical standards, likening one photo from a door quote to a Dollar General entrance. Commissioners asked that Price and the county go back and search for door replacements that fit within the courthouse's nature, even if they are more expensive than anticipated.
"I'm not saying that I won't support improving the safety of the door, but not with what the design that I've seen so far," Porter said. "It's got to comply more with the historic character of the building."
Commission President Travis Breeding agreed with his fellow commissioners, saying it's best to go "back to the drawing board" with the potential door replacement. Commissioners unanimously voted to approve funding 16 new windows with the potential of receiving money from the state's courthouse security application, which closed Dec. 3.

title: Liquor License Discussion Draws Large Crowd
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Liquor license discussion draws large crowd

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Rock Hall residents showed up to offer support for their local liquor store, Rock Hall Liquors & Deli, an establishment serving the area for several years with a good reputation among many. Following two hours deliberation, the Kent County Commissioners decided unanimously to grant the requested Class A liquor license for beer and wine, but not liquor — to the Rock Hall One Stop Shop — a compromise between both establishments.At the Kent County Commissioner's regularly scheduled meeting on Nov. 19, County Attorney Tom Yeager led the open session discussion of a Class A liquor license request from M&M Rock Hall, LLC, Rock Hall One Stop Shop, (formerly Shore Stop) owned by Bilal Mustafa, president and Hassan Mahmood, vice president.
Rock Hall Liquors, represented at the meeting by owner Shweta Sethi, expressed to the commissioners concerns over the gas station across the road, Rock Hall One Stop Shop, seeking a liquor license.
She was supported by a room full of Rock Hall residents along with a written petition of support from 300 town residents.
Mustafa was represented by MacLeod Law Group LLC, attorney Lance Young who stated if the application was not approved, it would set a precedent for any liquor establishment to do the same in the future.
"When somebody is dealing with government, they need to know the policies will be applied to them equally," he said of his concern that due process be ensured.
Young vouched for his clients. They are good clients, he stated, and unlike many liquor store owners, have been in the county for almost 25 years. And to meet the town's needs, they fixed the outside lights, expanded items on the menu, and agreed to stay open 24 hours, even though it would not benefit them financially.
"They are making a better establishment, which is better for Rock Hall, and so better for the county," Young said.
Representing Rock Hall Liquors, attorney from Booth, Cropper and Mariner, Lyndsey Jones Ryan, countered some of Young's points.
She claimed that between Bayside Market and Rock Hall Liquors the public need is more than met already — citing a diminishing population sinking to about 1,188, according to a 2020 census.
Ryan vouched for her client's character and dedication to their business, pointing out the family has been in the community for 19 years, working on improvements the last three years to make it nicer.
Responding to Young's claim that it would set a precedent, Ryan said these applications are considered on a "case-by-case basis," especially in a little town like Rock Hall.
And it could be a public danger as well, she claimed. If the store next door gets a liquor license, and stays open later, it could force Rock Hall Liquors & Deli to stay open longer also. With limited staff, and female employees, that could endanger them.
Adding up all these factors, Ryan was looking for Commissioners to reject the application.
Open to public comment, residents provided their input, an overwhelming majority siding with Rock Hall Liquors & Deli.
One man, living in Rock Hall for three years, appreciated the community feel of Rock Hall Liquors & Deli. He said on the contrary, he did not feel that at the other store. Under new ownership he lamented, some familiar faces were no longer there.
Many held reasons along this line. Family friendly, comfortable, they know everyone's names. The owners love the community.
Some residents noted the danger or at least public nuisance that granting a Class A Liquor license would prove. People hanging around the store at 1 a.m., stated Mark Einstein, is when alcohol becomes a problem.
Those close to the Rock Hall Liquors family, said unlike Mustafa who has other businesses in Chestertown, this is their only store, their "bread and butter," a term that was used a lot throughout the hearing.
Some giving testimony were in support of healthy competition, however they did not support a beloved Rock Hall business closing their doors, something they believed would become a reality with the granting of this license.
Yeager asked Young if his client would accept a license for beer and wine, excluding liquor. Subsequently after a brief recess, Young agreed on behalf of his One Stop Shop clients, on the condition they could return in six months to reapply for liquor to be added to the use.
Commissioner John Price acknowledged they are in full support of businesses, but supported the compromise, while warning attendees this issue will not go away in the future.
Commissioner Albert Nickerson commended the level of decorum between both parties and residents.
"In my two years, this has been the best-attended meeting," he said, "I appreciate the emotion going into this. We want to support the community, and the people that make up the community."

title: Easton Town Council OKs Delmarva Pride Festival Permit
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council OKs Delmarva Pride Festival permit

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 362
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A permit for the 2025 Delmarva Pride Festival was unanimously approved by the Easton Town Council on Monday evening, a stark change from the council's split decision concerning the 2024 festival permit.Next year's festival, the town's fourth annual, is slated for June 14, 2025. Its expected attendance is around 4,000, according to the permit application. The Easton Police Department recommended approval.
The festival is organized by the Delmarva Pride Center and features vendors, businesses and food, with attendees lining South Harrison Street for the celebration of the LGBTQ+ community.
Council President Frank Gunsallus and Councilmembers Maureen Curry, Don Abatiello and the Rev. Elmer Davis all voted for the permit's approval. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery was absent from Monday's meeting.
In January, Gunsallus and Montgomery voted against approving the public assembly permit for 2024's event. At the time, Montgomery brought up concerns of "overtly sexualized performances and behavior" from dancers at the festival.
At the January meeting, festival organizers maintained that the dancers were professionals and not "scantily clothed." The 2024 permit was narrowly approved 3-2, with Curry, Abbatiello and Davis in favor.
Montgomery told the Star Democrat on Tuesday that if he was present at the most recent council meeting, he would have once again voted against approving the permit.
Earlier this year, Gunsallus was heavily scrutinized by town residents for questioning whether the town should use funds to hang Pride banners and for stating the Pride flag is "antithetical to America."
But on Monday, Gunsallus initiated the motion to approve the festival permit for 2025, which this time was passed with no back-and-forth council discussion.
Tina Jones, co-founder of the Delmarva Pride Center, thanked the council for its unanimous vote during public comment Monday evening.
"I know in the past we've had some difficult conversations in this room," Jones said. "I'm glad to see that we have moved beyond those. And we look very much in favor of continuing to work very closely with this town.
"Personally for me, it's a great sign for all of our community that this has happened tonight. As Rev. Davis said at the beginning, this is a community that's made better by everybody that's here, and your vote tonight showed that."

Cost for pedestrian trail bridge connector estimated at 8 million

 CENTREVILLE — An overview of the pedestrian bridge plans to connect the Cross Island and South Island trails were presented to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners Nov. 26.In conjunction with the Parks and Recreation Department, Southern Kent Island Trail Extension Project staff obtained preliminary construction cost information for a pedestrian bridge crossing over MD Route 50, Chief Roads Engineer Shane Moore said.
Engineering consultant Kimley-Horn was contracted to complete a preliminary evaluation of several Route 50 pedestrian crossing locations east and west of the Route 8 overpass.
Utilizing the MDOT cost estimator to estimate a pedestrian crossing construction costs, As part of this evaluation Kimley-Horn estimated a pedestrian crossing construction cost at the Cracker Barrel location at $8.1 million, Moore said.
Construction only cost estimates were taken from similar type projects including Virginia's Tysons Old Meadow Pedestrian Bridge over Route 495 at $8 million and the Lane Place Pedestrian Bridge over Route 295 at between $10.8 and $12.4 million, according to Moore.
Several locations have been selected for a preliminary study through Kimley-Horn but there has been no final decision yet, according to Moore.
For safety, pedestrian bridges have to be built at a higher elevation than a typical vehicle overpass, Moore said.
With the commissioners' approval, Public Works staff will work with the BMC and RK&K Civil Engineering to develop a scope of services and costs for a final location study of the County's proposed MD Route 50 pedestrian bridge crossing.
Next steps include meeting with Maryland Transportation Authority and the State Highway Administration to begin discussions to nail down a final location for the construction of a pedestrian crossing, Moore said.
Queen Anne's County currently has about $120,000 in Baltimore Metropolitan Council (BMC) monies to be used for this study. In addition, BMC has also federally approved pre-established consulting contracts with RK&K, Moore said.
Federal and state partners have been supportive of this project to serve as alternative transportation connecting the county, County Administrator Todd Mohn said.

title: QAC Hears 5-Year Capital Project Preview
author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QAC Hears 5-Year Capital Project Preview

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 675
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Centreville — With a number of large projects on the horizon, the Queen Anne's County finance department provided a head-start to the budget process with an overview to the County Commissioners Nov. 26.Jeff Rank, director of budget and finance, presented data from a Capital Budget Work Session including a preview of major capital projects currently in the planning stages for the upcoming five years.
Due to the fact that the county has more costly projects than usual, the finance department sought to present an early start to the review process, he said.
The total capital project expenditures programmed for the current year and planned for the next five years is about $285 million, according to Rank.
Going back 20 years, the average capital plan was about $31 million per year, which adjusted for inflation is about $35 million per year, he said.
"If we stick to this average which has been our current comfort zone this puts us at about $96 million above that threshold over the next five years, " Rank said.
Upcoming major projects include a new regional detention center in Church Hill at about $24.2 million, a potential Centerville Middle School replacement at $20.5 million, a $20 million recreation center, new sheriff facilities at $16 million, and historic courthouse renovations at $10 million, he said.
Proposed projects not yet programmed into the capital plan include Queen Anne's County Library expansion, new Board of Elections facility, and potential uses for the old Board of Education building.
Also presenting an overview of debt measures and debt management policy, Queen Anne's County has a cap of 10% for debt as a percentage of general fund expenditures, Rank said, noting over the next five to six years, the county is not expected to hit that cap.
Another county debt measure is debt as a percentage of real property assessable base, with a cap set at 2.5%. The county is only expected to hit a high of about 1.5% by the end of 2030, Rank said.
The other debt measure is per capital debt as related to per capita income. With a policy stating a maximum of 8%, the county is in compliance with 5% come 2030, he said.
Over the past two years Queen Anne's County hasn't had any debt, but there is potential in the next three years, Rank said.
Current debt measures are recommended by the Government finance Officers Association for counties nationwide, according to Rank, noting Maryland counties have burdens that most other counties in the country do not.
Maryland counties are required to provide funding for local boards of education, pay for County Road systems to a higher proportion than most other counties in the country and Maryland also has high levels of service for public safety efforts in the county, he said.
Excluding funding for the Board of Education, the county typically keeps annual cost increases very close to the annual inflation increases of three to four percent, Rank said.
For each year debt service increases at rates above inflation, cuts must be made to other county services including public safety, education, roads, and park maintenance, he said.
"It's when that happens we find it difficult to maintain our current levels of service with all the other things we have to pay for in the county," Rank said.
The Finance Department meets with the Board of Education quarterly to keep in better sync with their programming and projects, according to Rank.
Moving forward the finance department recommends a smoother flatter debt burden from year to year rather than wild increases, he said.
For the upcoming capital budget schedule, departments have begun preparing budgets for next year's capital plan due Jan. 10.
Early to mid March will see finance meetings with County Administrator Todd Mohn who will submit the proposed budget to the commissioners March 25.
Budget work sessions will be held at the end of March or early April and ideally the final budget will be adopted June 10.
Many projects are dependent on state shared revenues and grants that the county can leverage additional dollars for, which will also be part of the decision making process going forward, Mohn said.

title: Legislators Talk State Budget Before Heading Back to Annapolis in January
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators talk state budget before heading back to Annapolis in January

 December 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The state of the state's budget took up a large part of the conversation at a Dorchester Chamber of Commerce luncheon with state legislators on Dec. 4.The Lower Shore delegation answered questions from chamber members regarding concerns about Maryland's fiscal health, with a looming $2.7 billion state budget deficit predicted in fiscal year 2026.
"The reality is that if you continue to do the things that have gotten us into this deficit, it's only going to take us back there again," Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said. "There needs to be a structural, fundamental change."
Mautz and Dels. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all spoke at the chamber lunch. They, along with the rest of the state's legislators, will head back to Annapolis in January for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.
In talking about the state's budget, Mautz also said there should be incentives in place to try to drive state agencies to save money.
Sample-Hughes said the state should do its fiscal homework and find out what it "really (has) to work with."
"But I do believe that we can still address and attack some of these goals that we have, whether it's education, whether it's climate, whether it's criminal justice," she said. "We can do it in a pragmatic way."
Adams said to solve the budget problem, the state has to leverage and grow its private sector.
"You do not do what we've done for the past two years," he said. He said the state and its leadership need to stop spending so much, own up to the problem and stop blaming it on COVID-19.
Hutchinson expressed his concerns with the transportation budget and the lack of funding for many infrastructure projects across the state.
"We've got to pay attention to our transportation budget," he said.
BLUEPRINTThe legislators also talked about the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion over a 10-year period.
Sample-Hughes said although Blueprint's goals are important, the General Assembly's decision to pass the plan has contributed to the state's budget deficit. She later advocated for giving more resources to the nonprofits that already serve 3 and 4 year olds, rather than putting money toward expanding early childhood education in the state's public school systems.
Mautz said he thinks the project needs to be paused so that the plan's strengths and weaknesses can be better evaluated.
JUVENILE CRIMEThe legislators also talked about the state of juvenile crime in Maryland, with Sample-Hughes calling for the removal of Department of Juvenile Services Secretary Vincent Schiraldi.
Hutchinson said that with recent juvenile justice reforms going into effect Nov. 1, he doesn't think a lot of legislators are going to want to discuss juvenile crime this upcoming session.
"Because they'll say, 'We just put that in place. We haven't even been able to see the results,'" he said.
Adams said law enforcement is needed now more than ever and officers need to be able to do their jobs.
"If you want a society, if you want a City of Cambridge, if you want an Eastern Shore (or) State of Maryland, if you want a United States that is civil, there have to be consequences," he said.

title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Lack of State Guidance on Cannabis Reinvestment Funds
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss lack of state guidance on cannabis reinvestment funds

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — As Caroline County works to comply with a section of Maryland's Cannabis Reform Act of 2023, concerns are being raised about a lack of direction from the state in spending money collected from cannabis sales tax.The Cannabis Reform Act created a Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund, designed to allocate 35% of the collected taxes from cannabis sales back into communities most affected by the disproportionate enforcement of previous cannabis laws.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced an emergency bill during Tuesday's meeting that if passed, would establish a Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund at the county level, which is required by the 2023 state legislation.
However, four counties — Caroline, Garrett, Kent and Queen Anne's — do not have any communities identified by the state's Office of Social Equity as "disproportionately impacted areas."
The Reform Act defines those areas as ones that "had above 150% of the state's 10-year average for cannabis possession charges."
"So as we sit here today and we're talking about introducing this legislation, we don't know where the money can be spent in the county?" Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked during Tuesday morning's weekly meeting.
Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said his correspondence to the Office of Social Equity seeking guidance on where the county is permitted to spend the money has gone unanswered for more than a month.
"I cannot, with an honest heart, sit here and tell you that we have any guidance," Fox said.
"In a phone call, the guidance was, 'you guys can certainly interpret it how you want and self-identity disproportionately impacted areas,'" Fox later said. "And I think my question was, 'OK, so we get to this reporting period, what's to say you're (not) going to pull the rug out from under us?'"
County Attorney Stewart Barroll said the 2024 portion sent to Caroline County was just over $367,000. The county's bill introduced Tuesday would give the county the ability to spend that money.
Porter said while he supports introducing the bill to work toward the creation of a county reinvestment fund, he's "not going to be big on self-interpreting anything when it comes to this money."
"My recommendation would be if we don't have an answer on where we can spend this money," Porter said, "we don't spend a dime until we get a specific answer."
Commission President Travis Breeding said even if the county were to spend the money on low-income communities that fall within the legislation's other guidelines, it could be breaking the state law since it technically doesn't have any "disproportionately impacted areas" as defined by the state.
"To me, the Legislature needs to go back and amend it," Breeding said.
Breeding, Porter and Commissioner Frank Bartz all voted to introduce the emergency bill. A second reading and public hearing will be held Dec. 17, with a third reading and potential vote on the bill set for Jan. 7.
"We need guidance," Porter stated earlier in the meeting. "The money is coming. It's a substantial amount of money. If there are going to be regulations or requirements on this … we need to know that."

Similar to child abuse registry, the animal abuse registry will provide accountability to those found guilty of animal abuse in the past, Commissioner Phil Dumenil said, and considered the registry a "huge step in the right direction" in protecting animals from getting in the wrong hands.

title: Trappe Approves Accommodation Tax Increase
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe approves accommodation tax increase

 December 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — Talbot County is moving forward in support of a countywide accommodation tax increase. On Dec. 4, the Trappe Town Council approved a 2% increase for all short-term rentals in the area.The accommodation tax has been a hot topic issue among residents of the county over the last year. Though an accommodation tax raise would immediately benefit towns with large tourism traffic such as St. Michaels and Easton, Trappe does not have an influx of tourism.
However, Trappe voted in favor of the increase with hopes of establishing a strong foundation for tourism growth. The motion was passed with four votes in favor. Commissioner Jeremy Newnam abstained.
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels or short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
According to Trappe Commissioner Brian Schmidt, there are currently no short-term rentals in Trappe. The town had recently suspended the only short-term rental in town due to the operators not giving accommodation tax funds to the town.
Although there is a lack of rentals, over the past few months Trappe has prepared for potential growth by updating regulations for short-term rentals.
Cassandra Vanhooser, director of economic development and tourism, said even though, at the moment, Trappe does not have short-term rentals to collect funds from, there is growing potential especially with the increase in population due to the Lakeside residential property.
"It's not outside the question that you could someday have a Route 50 hotel or even an inn or an Airbnb," Vanhooser said. "You have some beautiful homes here. Someone might come along someday and buy one of these beautiful homes and make it an inn, and then you have 10 rooms generating some significant income. And that would be income and revenue to your bottom line."
During the meeting, Commissioner Jeremy Newnam raised questions concerning use of marketing from the county. Newnam said Trappe currently does not have the clientele base to benefit from tourism but in the future when the town has grown, he asked how Trappe could be represented in the county when it is up against towns such as St. Michaels and Easton.
Vanhooser said she seeks to represent all towns in the county fairly "because all the county paid my salary."
Later in the meeting, Vanhooser brought up the public meeting at the Talbot County Free Library on Dec. 5 where a number of business owners and managers pushed back on the proposed increase to the county's accommodation tax rate.
According to Vanhooser, the approval of the increase would provide additional revenue for the towns. Furthermore, the towns can spend their money anyway they want to offset the cost of tourism.
Vanhooser mentioned that tourists who stay in the towns use local services such as roads, police and garbage collection. She said during the previous public meeting participants had issues with fund usage going toward offsetting the cost of tourism.
"Some people don't see it that way. … Some people want all the money for themselves and none of the money for the people providing the services, which I find disingenuous."

title: New Cambridge Solar Ordinance Will Have 'Immediate Effect'
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
New Cambridge solar ordinance will have 'immediate effect'

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Along with passing an ordinance regarding solar energy systems on wooded lots, the Cambridge City Council has directed city staff to look into removing community solar from a 350-acre maximum on solar permitted in the city.During a City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council unanimously approved an ordinance amending the city's Unified Development Code for solar energy systems on wooded lots. Specifically, the amendment allows small-scale solar and community solar on wooded lots as long as the solar project complies with the city's Forest Conservation Ordinance or the state's Model Forest Conservation Ordinance.
Before the ordinance was passed, Cambridge Planning and Zoning Director Brian Herrmann said it was consistent with the city's comprehensive plan and the Planning and Zoning Commission had approved it in early November.
Herrmann said the ordinance would apply to sites that are at least 40,000 square feet. He said requirements of the ordinance include that the area cleared on the wooded lot cannot exceed 10 acres and impacted trees must be replanted at a 2-to-1 ratio or a fee be paid in lieu.
Small-scale solar energy systems are typically located on a homeowner's property, Herrmann said.
"It's essentially generating electricity where it is used," he said.
Community solar energy systems provide power to the residents of a community. Herrmann said that in Maryland, 40% of the output of a community solar system must serve low- to moderate-income residents.
During the meeting, Tony Kupersmith, a lawyer representing a renewable energy company, said the company he represents has a community solar project on Leonards Lane and this ordinance is "critical" for that project.
"So I get to let you know that what you do tonight would have an immediate effect for an actual project that is ready to go forward, that wants to go forward, and the only issue right now holding us up is the wooded lot issue," Kupersmith said before requesting the council adopt the ordinance.
Herrmann told the council that the city's 350-acre solar maximum — which it is close to reaching — limits the impact of this ordinance.
"We have two projects in the final stages of the development review process," he said. "If those two are to go through, we're going to be at 325 acres. So there's only about 25 acres left before we actually hit this amount. So I guess you can see we're not talking about a lot of solar systems that are going to be built even if this does pass."
Commissioner Brian Roche asked why community solar is included in that 350-acre maximum that also includes medium- and large-scale solar energy systems. He said it should be excluded.
"We don't want to see our entire land base covered with solar panel projects, but the way I understand community solar is really it is to the benefit of people that cannot either put it on their roof (and) they want to collaborate ... or they otherwise may not be able to have it," he said. "To me, I would strike that out from that maximum."
Roche asked that only medium- and large-scale solar energy systems be included in the 350-acre maximum and not community solar energy systems.
City Attorney Patrick Thomas said that because Roche's request goes "beyond the scope" of the ordinance on the table, it would need to go through a separate text amendment process. He said a separate ordinance to address the maximum could be prepared.

title: Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 879
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A controversial proposal to raise the accommodation tax was voted down by the the Talbot County Council Tuesday.During an impromptu public comment period, lodge owners and community members expressed concerns over the increase in the accommodation tax saying it would hurt profits and tourism in the county. Additional comments concerning a lack of information were shared resulting in the proposal not passing.
The rise of the accommodation tax was presented by Cassandra Vanhooser, director of the department of Economic Development and Tourism, on Tuesday who gave an overview of the steps taken by her department to get a proposal in front of the council including approval for the Tourism Board of Talbot County and receiving support from Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels and Trappe.
"(Talbot County Council is) being called on to balance the effects on tourism businesses with the benefits to the towns and the county," Vanhooser said. "The Tourism Board has weighed the evidence, and they believe that the benefits outweigh the disadvantages."
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels and short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Despite voting down an increase, the council voted to strengthen the existing accommodation tax.
Martha Sparks, financial director for Talbot County, suggested removing the 120-day grace period for owners of short-term rentals to provide accommodation tax collected to the county before the county can impose a 10% penalty. Sparks proposed that the council approve a request to the legislature to reduce that period of time.
The council unanimously approved the proposal.
Prior to voting on a letter of support for the accommodation tax increase, several people began to raise their hands in order to get their opinions on record. Commission President Chuck Callahan opened the floor for public comment.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment, business owner Scott Wagner expressed concern on raising taxes saying that though the accommodation tax has not been raised in 20 years, prices of rooms for rentals have, which in turn provides more funds from accommodation tax.
Wagner said room rates have "ridden the wave of inflation" and described raising the accommodation tax to "feeding the monster."
"This is feeding the monster, and the monster is asking for a million dollars more next year, so when the monster is going to get fatter. I've never seen the tax go down, quite frankly."
In contrast, Jessica Bellis, a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed concern over the negative connotation with the accommodation tax.
"We can use words like the monster that you're feeding, but the monster is making sure that we do have the roads and the infrastructure and the police department and the marketing to be able to promote and sustain tourism, which is a major industry in Talbot County," Bellis said.
Included in public comment were concerns over information. Kevin Hartmann, Easton resident, said lodging providers were not asked for comment at the time of the town's vote. He said the towns were "significantly under-educated as to the ramifications."
According to Hartmann, two surveys were conducted to gather the opinions of lodging operators. One was done by the Talbot County Tourism Board and the other was conducted by Hartmann. The board's survey, he said, showed 75% of operators did not support the increase in tax. For the survey done by Hartmann it was over 84%.
The survey by the tourism board was released on Dec. 5 and the last town to vote on supporting the raise was on Dec. 4.
"You have in your package, letters from your five towns of Talbot County, each one of those voted for the increase," Hartmann said. "But the significant difference is this: None of those towns heard what you're hearing tonight, none of those towns have the results of the survey at the time of their vote. None of those towns held a public hearing on the matter."
After hearing the comment given by Hartmann, Easton Council President Frank Gunsallus, spoke and shared his thoughts on the information provided.
"Our vote already occurred, but after hearing all the testimonies tonight, and especially Mr. Hartmann's … perhaps we could have been better educated before we voted," Gunsallus said. "I believe that people reserve the right to change their mind, and I know our votes were cast, but I am, on your record, withdrawing my support for this accommodation tax."
After much deliberation from the council, the motion was denied in a 3-2 vote with Councilmembers Pete Lesher and Keasha Haythe voting in support of the proposal.
Vanhooser, director of Economic Development and Tourism, said Wednesday that the proposal failed and will not move forward this state legislature period.
"The Tourism Board obviously supports this, because they see it as a way to fund my department and tourism marketing and promotion, and the towns, you know, were in favor, despite what was said last night, because it raises their revenue, which they need for the various things they spend the money on."

title: Dorchester County Council Stresses Need for Conservative Budget in FY2026
author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council stresses need for conservative budget in FY2026

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County begins preparing for budget season, "conservative" is the name of the game.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on Dec. 3, council members stressed the importance of the county being conservative and efficient with how it spends its money in the upcoming fiscal year.
In response to County Manager Jerry Jones' question of whether the council has any priorities for the fiscal year 2026 budget, Council Member Ricky Travers said he wants to "hold the status quo" without raising taxes.
"My goal would be to be very conservative because we don't know where we're going to be at, what money we're going to have to spend," he said.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer brought up the budget deficit facing the state.
"With the state facing a $2.7 billion deficit, we're not sure exactly what the governor's going to cut," Pfeffer said. "So I think we're going to have to be very dynamic and make changes on the go as we go through this next budget cycle."
According to Dorchester County's budget adoption schedule, the County Council will begin holding budget work sessions in late February. Following public hearings, the adoption of the budget is scheduled for June 10.
The county's fiscal year 2025 budget, which included a 5% raise across the board for county employees, totaled $86.52 million. The operating budget increased by about $2.5 million, or roughly 3%, compared to fiscal year 2024, and the capital budget decreased by about $6.3 million, which is roughly 58%.
During the meeting on Dec. 3, Council Member William Nichols and Council Vice President Mike Detmer both agreed that not raising taxes — particularly for seniors — is important.
"It would be the last thing I would do," Nichols said about taxing seniors.
Detmer said he values the county manager and county staff for being consistent and increasing efficiency in county government. He said that along with being conservative and consistent, the county should also make sure it remains creative when it comes to the budget.
"We can't just be in shutdown mode, you know?" he said. "There's low-hanging fruit out there that we've got to be able to convert little things and enrich the life here."
Pfeffer said that the county's budget goals will be discussed more during the upcoming budget workshops.
"We're going to hear from all our department heads and see what the real needs versus wants are going to be from the county," he said.

title: Shore Residents Share Mixed Views on New Chesapeake Bay Bridge
author: Andrea Grabenstein
content:
Shore residents share mixed views on new Chesapeake Bay Bridge

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1059
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Informational displays lined the walls of Kent Island High School's cafeteria Wednesday, laying out narrowed-down options for a new Bay Bridge.The self-paced open house welcomed the community to gather information and submit feedback as the Maryland Transportation Authority conducts Tier 2 of the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study. The study, launched in 2017, seeks to examine the state's options when it comes to the aging bridge.
Melissa Williams, Maryland Transportation Authority director of the division of planning and program development, said the team that developed the various plans for the new bridge went through in-depth analysis on the traffic data gathered throughout the year. It has developed seven proposed alternatives to the current Bay Bridge, with one alternative being a no-build option.
"We are proposing to remove both existing Bay Bridge spans due to the substantial cost of future maintenance and repair the impact to the traveling public associated with those repairs," Williams said.
Bridge spans, full tunnels, bridge tunnels and double decker bridge options were evaluated during the study. Bridge spans were recommended as construction would have fewer environmental impacts and a lower cost compared to other options. Additionally, the bridge spans would allow for greater flexibility in maintaining traffic during maintenance and emergency response situations.
The proposed alternatives include either a new eight-lane or 10-lane bridge consisting of two spans constructed north or south of the existing bridge.
The proposed alternatives consider bus service improvements, part-time shoulder use, interchange consolidation, park and ride facilities, congestion pricing, and pedestrian and bicycle shared use.
The Kent Island open house marks the third total, and second in-person, open house held by the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Tier 2 Study. On the Dec. 11, 129 attended the meeting. An in-person open house was also hosted at Broadneck High School in Annapolis Dec. 9, with 192 in attendance. In-person open houses followed a virtual open house on Dec. 4, in which 435 individuals logged on.
According to Williams, the open houses provided a transparent view of the project to the community.
"It's great to show lines on paper, " she said.
Patty Baker, of Kent Island, remembers the construction of the westbound span of the Bay Bridge. "It was impressive to watch," she said.
Baker attended several of the study's open houses last year and was interested to see how progress and updates have developed. "I couldn't have dreamed what would happen," she said, noting now the once rural area has become more and more part of a freeway and for so long summer beach traffic has detected weekend activities for locals. With the potential for roadway widening, Baker voiced concerns about areas so close to Route 50 including the Stevensville Cemetery, where her own family plots are. She said she appreciated the open house's layout and staff clarification to questions, particularly as to why the new bridges cannot be placed in different corridors.
"They are doing the best they can with what they are working with," she said.
Attending the project's last open house a year ago, Martin Gleason, of Grasonville, was interested in continual aspects of the project and found it to be very informative in regards to the "when, where, and how."
An area resident of 47 years, Brian H. of Kent Island, considered the potential new bridge "long overdue" and found the study thoroughly researched. He was enthusiastic about how the potential lane widening change would improve traffic flow.
Tom Helfenbein, of Kent Island, found the open house informative and offered suggestions of widening certain merging areas and moving chokepoints down to Route 404. "All consideration seems to stop at the (Queenstown) Outlets," he said.
Despite opportunities for public comment, Jennifer Laird, of Chester, claimed she didn't feel like the opinion of locals was being considered and did not approve of any aspect of the project, stating, "It's going to change everything," including bringing in more people from the western shore. Laird claimed the infrastructure was unequipped to handle the traffic and strongly preferred the new bridge be placed elsewhere.
Cheryl Gover, of Queenstown, voiced concerns of bottlenecking, traffic congestion impacts, and was worried how the proposed bridge shared use path would affect jumpers. Gover also recommended finding ways to create alternative routes off the bridge for locals.
Working in Glen Burnie, Jay Diepenbrock, of Centreville, takes a round trip over the Bay Bridge at least twice a week and knows personally how bad traffic can be. Noting it gets worse before it gets better, Diepenbrock was a little disappointed by the the projected timeline, with scheduled construction completion no sooner than about 2035.
"It will probably happen when I'm too old to be driving," he said. Nonetheless, Diepenbrock was optimistic it would be a much needed improvement for future generations.
Heather Lowe, project manager for the Bay Crossing Tier 2 Study, said a multi-use path for bicycles and pedestrians would be separated from travel lanes by a physical barrier across the more than four-mile bridge.
December open houses serve as formal scoping meetings to hear comments on the issues that will be evaluated in an environmental impact statement, according to Andrew Bing, virtual open house facilitator. Included in the areas of environmental considerations are impacts to natural resources, impacts to parks and recreation areas and impacts on historic properties and archaeological sites.
The Environmental Impact Study will focus on socioeconomic resources and land use, and minority and low income population. After time to consider and evaluate public feedback, a draft impact study is anticipated to be published in November 2025, followed by additional public hearings.
A final environmental impact study and record of decisions are anticipated for fall 2026, along with identified selected alternatives.
The Transportation Authority is anticipating finishing the current phase of the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study in 2026. Five years of design and permitting would follow with construction anticipated for 2032, Bing said.
Anyone unable to attend the open houses still has time to submit comments through the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study website. Comments received by Jan. 13 will be part of the study's summarization, Williams said, and comments will continue to be received after this date. "We want to hear what you have to say," she said.
Following the data collection, the study is expected to return with additional open houses next year.
Viewing of the virtual open house is available online. More information, as well as feedback submissions and public comments with personal information redacted are available for viewing at baycrossingstudy.com.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this story.

title: St. Michaels Raises Penalties for 6 Town Code Violations
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels raises penalties for 6 town code violations

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Significant increases in fines for various violations of town codes were approved by the St. Michaels commissions on Wednesday evening.The increases were made on six different town codes and included including raises in fines for short-term rental, transient vendors and leash animal control violations. The fines for some infractions increased by more than 10 times.
Violation fines for short-term rentals operating without permission from the town doubled from $250 to $500.
Condemnation, otherwise known as "housing standards," increased from a steady $100 to $250 for a first violation, $300 for a second violation and $500 for a third violation.
Addressing non-compliance currently has a violation fine of $25. It has been increased to $150. This means that any owner of a building or premises that is not posted with the official street number within 30 days after said owner receives notice of the official street number shall be punishable by a fine of $150. Each day that the owner fails to display the official street number will constitute a separate offense.
Fines for violations relating to transient vendors, or vendors who sell produce or seafood at a roadside or a temporary location, were increased from $25 to $250.
Public urination fines were increased from $25 to $250, and public defecation fines went from $50 to $500.
Finally, leash animal control violation fines doubled from $50 to $100.
Commissioner David Wojciechowski asked if code enforcement officers would issue a warning first prior to issuing fines on the violations. Officer Jeffrey Oswald said on most of the violations there will be warnings prior to the penalties. This would not be the case for public urination and defecation.
After Commissioner Alfred Mercier opened a quiet public hearing on the increases, the commission unanimously approved the fine raises.

title: Legislators Hear Cambridge's Priorities Before General Assembly Session Begins
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators hear Cambridge's priorities before General Assembly session begins

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Before the regularly scheduled Cambridge City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council and city staff shared their priorities with state legislators, who are preparing to go back to Annapolis for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.During the legislative delegation work session, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman acknowledged getting state funding this year will be difficult and asked that the Lower Shore delegation notify the city if they come across anything during session that could benefit Cambridge.
Steckman said the city doesn't have a list of laws or law changes that it wants enacted by the General Assembly.
"We're not here to try to make laws and recommend the law changes, but to show you what the issues that the elected leadership here is dealing with and the appointed staff is dealing with," he said. "We're looking for your help and guidance on the legislative level."
The six priorities — which Steckman detailed during the meeting and said are in no particular order — are to:
Preserve and renovate Cambridge's historic City Hall on Gay Street.Continue to move the Cambridge Harbor project forward.Improve housing and revitalize the Pine Street neighborhood.Make enhancements and improvements to city youth services.Update and improve the city's water and sewer infrastructure.Provide local workforce development programs and opportunities.
Steckman said when it comes to workforce development, it can be difficult for residents without transportation who are seeking employment or training opportunities in other counties.
"Obviously, if we want to grow the industrial part of the economy or (the) commercial (part), we need more job training to prepare, not only our existing workforce, but our workforce coming up through the school system," he said.
After Steckman discussed the city's priorities, Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all chimed in.
Hutchinson said he sees improving youth services as a very important priority, referencing a local teen who had been detained by the Department of Juvenile Services for stealing a car.
"This is a really serious issue," Hutchinson said. "If we have children who are saying, 'I'm bored and it's fine,' then we really need to work on that and correct that."
Sample-Hughes said that some of the bills on rentals and housing that didn't get passed during last year's session could come back to the General Assembly this year. She said it would be useful for the city to keep in touch as the legislators hear these bills brought back.
"I think your on the ground insight is very beneficial to what we have to do when it comes to the policy work and not only just the financial side of things," she said.
Adams told the council this year will be a "budget year." The state faces a predicted $2.7 billion budget deficit in fiscal year 2026.
"We know that this is going to be a tough year," Adams said. "So legislative requests that revolve around funding capital projects are going to be tough. There is always bond money, and we as a delegation will surely do our part ... in submitting those requests."
Mautz asked that the council stay in touch with the Lower Shore delegation throughout the upcoming legislative session. He said that when the governor's budget comes out, the city should make sure there aren't cuts that will negatively affect the city.
"If there's an actual cut that's going to affect something in the City of Cambridge, somebody needs to call (us)," he said.

title: Developers Host 3Rd Community Meeting For Easton Crossing Project
author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Developers host 3rd community meeting for Easton Crossing project

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Developers and residents gathered Wednesday evening for a third community meeting concerning a planned mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue.Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, hosted the meeting to update neighbors on its draft site plans and facilitate community feedback.
The Easton Crossing infill project is expected to add around 120 units where a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation used to sit. Additionally, there are significant plans for commercial use and open areas.
Renderings show six buildings planned for the 6.5-acre site. Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said the first building, which will have 15 residential units, is projected to open in December 2027.
Benincasa emphasized the mixed-income aspect of the project on Wednesday. Some units will be at market rate, and others down to where people "will be paying $500 to $600 a month for a new apartment."
"Unlike most developers, we don't build affordable units and market-rate units," Benincasa said. "We build the same unit across the site, and we just have specific ratio goals that we hit for that site. If I'm living in an affordable unit and Joe is in a market-rate unit, and I go over to … Joe's apartment one night, I will have no idea who pays what."
Based on previous feedback, developers and architects are looking into using bricks that are darker in color to match surrounding buildings. They also touched on other topics that were raised at previous community meetings this year, such as lighting, open space and plantings.
"You're going to be seeing a mix of pedestrian (lights) and some larger lights in the areas of the parking lot," Benincasa said. "But those larger lights, from a sizing perspective, are going to feel more like downtown Easton."
There will be a focus on maintaining open space at the property, as well as around 70% native plantings. Benincasa added that once finished, there will be "around four to 10 shrubs or trees per 50 feet."
All parking spots will be screened, some by shrubs and trees and others by buildings. While Benincasa said South Street will be a "secondary" exit and entrance for residents, developers "fully anticipate" most drivers to use Brookletts Avenue.
"But we don't want them on Brookletts. That's the point," resident Harriett Page said.
Benincasa said a traffic study was completed by Lenart Traffic Consulting last week, which did not signify worries about the traffic increase around the site. An increase of around 20 cars during peak hour on Brookletts Avenue is projected.
Resident Joe Minarick said "with Brookletts being the main thoroughclear and the main import" for the site, those projections "(seemed) a little funny."
"Brookletts might be the front of the project, but it is not the only way that people are going to go in and out," Benincasa said. Those heading east toward Caroline County may use Kemp Lane to access Dover Road, he said.
As for the commercial aspect of the site, Benincasa said developers aren't expecting national businesses. In fact, Chesapeake Community Development is looking for local businesses "emotionally invested in their success."
Developers may also encourage businesses to hire people with disabilities, a segment of the population that The Arc strives to serve.
"We have had discussions about if a business wants to hire people with disabilities, then there would be, sort of, credits for that," said Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc. "Or for hiring local as well."
"That will be coming in 2026, 2027," he continued, "as we think about what those incentives are as we begin to market the commercial spaces."

MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the Commissioners of St. Michaels voted to give police authority to cite docking infractions and approve bids for trash and recycling services.Amendments were made to town Boats and Boating code regarding town-owned slips. St. Michaels' staff reached out to other trash and recycle businesses for new bids but only Republic Services sent in a bid. Ultimately, the commissioners approved the three year contract with Republic Services.
TOWN MANAGER RECRUITMENTFinally, a bid was approved for the Mercer Group Associates as the firm to lead recruitment of the next Town Administrator. The firm's bid was for $24,000 to provide services including position analysis, recruitment process, resume review, candidate screening and interview process.
Mercer Group will also assist in the negotiation of an employment contract after completing the roughly 100-day recruitment process.
